TL;DR: FSB-Net is a frequency-spatial boundary network for brain stroke lesion segmentation in NCCT scans, using wavelet-based boundary detection, cross-attention between frequency and spatial features, and a spectral boundary loss to improve boundary sharpness. It outperforms U-Net, UNet++, MANet, and DeepLabV3+ on a public Brain Stroke CT dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning methods optimize region-level overlap but lack explicit boundary modeling, leading to imprecise delineation due to low contrast, heterogeneous lesion morphology, and ambiguous boundaries in NCCT scans, which affects volumetric assessment and treatment planning.

Method: FSB-Net introduces three components: (1) Wavelet Boundary Detection Head (WBDH) using discrete wavelet transform on multi-scale encoder features to extract high-frequency sub-bands as boundary representations; (2) Frequency-Spatial Cross-Attention Module (FSCAM) for bidirectional attention between wavelet boundary features and spatial decoder features; (3) Spectral Boundary Loss penalizing high-frequency discrepancies in the Fourier domain. Built on a PVTv2-B2 encoder.

Result: FSB-Net outperforms U-Net, UNet++, MANet, and DeepLabV3+ across all metrics, achieving state-of-the-art performance in mean Dice, mean IoU, and HD95 on a public Brain Stroke CT dataset containing both ischemic and hemorrhagic cases.

Conclusion: Frequency-domain boundary modeling via wavelet transforms and spectral loss effectively improves stroke lesion segmentation accuracy, particularly for boundary delineation, over conventional spatial-only deep learning methods.

Abstract: Accurate segmentation of brain stroke lesions in non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) scans is critical for rapid clinical decision-making, yet remains difficult due to the low contrast between lesion and normal brain tissue, heterogeneous lesion morphology across ischemic and hemorrhagic subtypes, and ambiguous boundaries caused by partial volume effects. Current deep learning approaches primarily optimize region-level overlap but lack explicit boundary modeling, leading to imprecise delineation that can affect volumetric assessment and treatment planning. We propose FSB-Net, a frequency-spatial boundary network that leverages frequency-domain analysis for boundary-aware stroke lesion segmentation. FSB-Net introduces three components: (i) a Wavelet Boundary Detection Head (WBDH) that applies the discrete wavelet transform to multi-scale encoder features, extracting high-frequency sub-bands as boundary representations; (ii) a Frequency-Spatial Cross-Attention Module (FSCAM) that performs bidirectional attention between wavelet boundary features and spatial decoder features for selective boundary enhancement; and (iii) a Spectral Boundary Loss that penalizes high-frequency discrepancies in the Fourier domain to optimize boundary sharpness. Built on a PVTv2-B2 encoder, FSB-Net is evaluated on a public Brain Stroke CT dataset containing both ischemic and hemorrhagic cases. Experimental results show that FSB-Net outperforms U-Net, UNet++, MANet, and DeepLabV3+ across all metrics, achieving state-of-the-art performance in mean Dice, mean IoU, and HD95.

</details>


### [29] [Unsupervised Metal Artifact Reduction in Dental CBCT using Fine-tuned Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20977)
*G. L. T. Chamika,S. N. A. Dhanapala,P. H. S. V. Nimalaweera,Maheshi B. Dissanayake,Ruwan D. Jayasinghe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: An unsupervised CycleGAN-based framework is proposed for metal artifact reduction in CBCT dental imaging, using unpaired ~4,000 image datasets, achieving significant improvements in BRISQUE (34.6%), FID (207.03→157.04), and SSIM (0.9105) with 3.03 ms inference per slice, recommended as a decision-support tool under human oversight.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Metal artifacts from dental implants degrade CBCT volumes, obscuring anatomical structures and reducing diagnostic accuracy; supervised MAR methods are impractical due to the unattainability of voxel-aligned paired datasets.

Method: An unsupervised CycleGAN integrating U-Net-based generators and PatchGAN discriminators, trained on ~4,000 unpaired images from the public ToothFairy dataset, tuned to reduce generative hallucinations and preserve morphology.

Result: 34.6% BRISQUE improvement, FID reduced from 207.03 to 157.04, SSIM of 0.9105, and 3.03 ms inference time per slice; expert validation confirms high fidelity.

Conclusion: The framework effectively suppresses artifacts and preserves anatomical detail with real-time efficiency; recommended as a clinical decision-support tool under human-in-the-loop oversight for reliability in extreme cases.

Abstract: Metal artifacts generated by dental implants significantly degrade cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) volumes, obscuring critical anatomical structures and compromising diagnostic precision. To address this, an unsupervised deep learning framework has been proposed for Metal Artifact Reduction (MAR) utilizing a Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Network (CycleGAN) optimized for high-fidelity restoration. Unlike supervised methods that rely on unattainable voxel-aligned paired datasets, the proposed approach leverages an unpaired dataset of approximately 4,000 images, curated from the public ToothFairy dataset. The architecture integrates U-Net-based generators and PatchGAN discriminators, specifically tuned to mitigate generative hallucinations and preserve morphological integrity. Quantitative benchmarking on a held-out test set demonstrates a 34.6\% improvement in the Blind/Referenceless Image Spatial Quality Evaluator (BRISQUE) score, a substantial reduction in Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) from 207.03 to 157.04, and a superior Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) of 0.9105. The framework achieves real-time efficiency with a 3.03 ms inference time per slice, effectively suppressing artifacts while preserving anatomical detail. Expert validation confirms high fidelity; however, to ensure reliability in extreme cases, the architecture is recommended as a clinical decision-support tool under human-in-the-loop oversight. By enhancing diagnostic clarity via a scalable software pipeline, this study provides a robust solution for high-fidelity dental implant imaging.

</details>


### [30] [Distribution-Alignment Bridge for Uncertainty-Aware Text-to-Video Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20984)
*Kyeongmo Chae,Jihoon Lee,Sangtae Ahn*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The Distribution-Alignment Bridge (DAB) reformulates text-to-video retrieval as distribution alignment, using Gaussian embeddings and a diffusion-inspired bridge to iteratively refine text distributions toward video distributions, with a KL-divergence-based contrastive loss, outperforming baselines on MSR-VTT, MSVD, and VATEX.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional text-to-video retrieval relies on deterministic point matching, which fails to capture modality-specific uncertainty. The paper aims to address this by reconceptualizing retrieval as a distribution alignment task.

Method: DAB models text and video embeddings as Gaussian distributions (mean + variance), uses a deterministic diffusion-inspired bridge to iteratively refine text distributions toward video distributions via truncated refinement, and optimizes with a distribution-aware contrastive loss based on KL divergence.

Result: Significantly outperforms existing probabilistic and diffusion-based baselines on MSR-VTT, MSVD, and VATEX benchmarks; provides calibrated uncertainty-aware ranking via bridge-induced distributional margins.

Conclusion: Probabilistic modeling and distributional transformation can be unified into an end-to-end trainable system for text-to-video retrieval, with demonstrated gains in both accuracy and uncertainty calibration.

Abstract: This paper proposes the Distribution-Alignment Bridge (DAB), a framework that reconceptualizes text-to-video retrieval as a distribution alignment task rather than traditional deterministic point matching. By modeling both text and video embeddings as Gaussian distributions defined by mean and variance, DAB explicitly accounts for modality-specific uncertainty. We employ a deterministic, diffusion-inspired bridge to iteratively refine text distributions toward their target video distributions through a truncated refinement process. This approach unifies probabilistic embedding and distributional transformation into a cohesive, end-to-end trainable system. To optimize cross-modal similarity, we introduce a distribution-aware contrastive loss based on Kullback-Leibler divergence. Extensive evaluations on MSR-VTT, MSVD, and VATEX benchmarks confirm that DAB significantly outperforms existing probabilistic and diffusion-based baselines, while providing calibrated uncertainty-aware ranking through bridge-induced distributional margins.

</details>


### [31] [HyWorldVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Hybrid World Modeling for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20988)
*Quanfu Yu,Xian Wu,Hao Xu,Liulong Ma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HyWorldVLA is a hybrid world-VLA framework for autonomous driving that combines pixel-level supervision with latent representation learning, achieving state-of-the-art results on NAVSIM benchmarks by unifying both approaches' strengths while mitigating their weaknesses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLA models face a trade-off: pixel-level future prediction is robust for spatiotemporal reasoning but fragile in noisy driving scenarios, while latent-based world models are more noise-robust but suffer from limited interpretability and representational degradation due to lack of pixel-level grounding.

Method: HyWorldVLA uses a two-stage pipeline: (1) pre-training with hybrid supervision — predicting video latents from a pre-trained video VAE while simultaneously reconstructing video frames for pixel-level grounding; (2) co-fine-tuning where the model predicts only latent features, which are fed into an action expert for trajectory generation.

Result: HyWorldVLA significantly outperforms both pixel-based and latent-based world model baselines on NAVSIM v1 and v2 benchmarks. It also provides the first comprehensive qualitative and quantitative analysis of world model noise robustness in autonomous driving.

Conclusion: The hybrid approach effectively reconciles the trade-off between pixel-level grounding and latent-level robustness, setting a new benchmark for evaluating future world model architectures in autonomous driving.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models augmented with world modeling represent a promising paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving. While pixel-level future prediction enables fine-grained spatiotemporal reasoning, it compromises robustness in noisy driving scenarios. Conversely, latent-based world models alleviate this sensitivity but often incur limited interpretability and representational degradation due to absent pixel-level grounding. To reconcile this trade-off, we propose HyWorldVLA, a hybrid world-VLA framework that unifies pixel-level supervision and latent representation learning. In the pre-training stage, HyWorldVLA predicts video latents encoded by a pre-trained video VAE, while simultaneously reconstructing video frames to provide precise pixel-level grounding. During the subsequent co-fine-tuning phase, the model exclusively predicts latent features, which are fed into an action expert to generate trajectories. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 benchmarks demonstrate that HyWorldVLA significantly outperforms both pixel-based and latent-based world model baselines. Notably, we present the first comprehensive qualitative and quantitative analysis of world model noise robustness in autonomous driving, establishing a new benchmark for evaluating future architectures.

</details>


### [32] [Latent Variable-Mediated Cross-Learning for Few-Shot Acoustic Impedance Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20989)
*Junheng Peng,Yong Li,Mingwei Wang,Yi Bao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RD-SCL integrates regularized deconvolution with semi-supervised cross-learning for acoustic impedance imaging, using a differentiable closed-form Tikhonov deconvolution operator to dynamically estimate wavelets without prior assumptions or auxiliary networks, achieving SOTA results on SEAM and Marmousi 2 with only 56.5k parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Acoustic impedance imaging is severely ill-posed due to unknown seismic wavelet, band-limited observations, and extremely scarce well-log labels (<1% of traces). Existing semi-supervised methods rely on inaccurate prior wavelet assumptions or introduce auxiliary networks, causing unstable optimization and degraded performance.

Method: Proposes RD-SCL with a differentiable, closed-form first-order Tikhonov deconvolution operator that dynamically estimates the latent wavelet in the frequency domain during training, providing stable physics-guided feedback without explicit auxiliary networks or fixed wavelet priors. A symmetric cross-learning enforces consistency between predictions on labeled and unlabeled data.

Result: Outperforms SOTA supervised and semi-supervised methods on SEAM and Marmousi 2 benchmarks with substantial gains and lower computational cost, using only 56.5k learnable parameters.

Conclusion: RD-SCL offers a practical, physically consistent, and efficient solution for acoustic impedance imaging under extreme label scarcity and ill-posed conditions.

Abstract: Acoustic impedance imaging is a fundamental yet severely ill-posed problem in subsurface analysis: the seismic wavelet is unknown, observations are band-limited, and labeled well-log samples are extremely scarce (typically <1% of all traces). Existing semi-supervised deep learning methods mitigate few-shot problem by incorporating forward modeling, yet they either rely on inaccurate prior wavelet assumptions or introduce auxiliary networks, leading to unstable optimization and degraded performance. We propose RD-SCL, a novel framework that integrates regularized deconvolution with semi-supervised cross-learning. At its core lies a differentiable, closed-form first-order Tikhonov deconvolution operator that dynamically estimates the latent wavelet in the frequency domain during training, providing stable physics-guided feedback without explicit auxiliary networks and fixed wavelet priors. Building on this operator, we design a symmetric cross-learning that enforces consistency between predictions on labeled and unlabeled data, thereby effectively exploiting abundant unlabeled traces. Extensive experiments on the SEAM and Marmousi 2 benchmarks demonstrate that RD-SCL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and semi-supervised methods, achieving substantial gains with lower computational cost. With only 56.5k learnable parameters and competitive runtime, RD-SCL offers a practical, physically consistent, and efficient solution for acoustic impedance imaging.

</details>


### [33] [Sparse Concept Channels in Frozen 3D CT Vision Encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20993)
*Farhad Nooralahzadeh,Lea Bogensperger,Christian Bluethgen,Michael Krauthammer*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Concept Channel Probe (CCP), a training-free method that identifies sparse (~10) vision-encoder channels responsible for encoding individual radiological findings in frozen 3D medical VLMs. CCP matches full-feature classification, generalizes across architecturally unrelated models (Pillar-0 and Merlin), and outperforms CT-CHAT on clinical efficacy (F1 0.549 vs 0.184) and NLG metrics (BLEU 0.483 vs 0.373) at 22x lower latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand which internal units of large vision-language models encode specific clinical findings and where that information resides in the representation, addressing the lack of interpretability in 3D medical image interpretation models.

Method: The authors propose Concept Channel Probe (CCP), a training-free method that probes frozen vision embeddings from 3D VLMs. They identify sparse sets of ~10 vision-encoder channels corresponding to each radiological finding, validate by ablating these channels (finding-specific score collapse with unrelated labels stable), and replicate findings across two architecturally unrelated models (Pillar-0 for chest, Merlin for abdominal). A corpus-derived report template is paired with CCP for report generation.

Result: CCP matches full-feature classification performance and far exceeds zero-shot text prompting. Turning off finding-specific channels collapses that finding's score while preserving unrelated labels. The sparse probe pattern replicates across architecturally unrelated 3D VLMs. CCP outperforms CT-CHAT on clinical efficacy (F1 0.549 vs 0.184) and NLG metrics (BLEU 0.483 vs 0.373) at 22x lower latency.

Conclusion: Frozen medical encoders represent clinical findings via sparse channel-specific encodings, a general property across different 3D medical VLMs. CCP provides a clear, reproducible, training-free method for interpretable finding localization and report generation with superior efficiency and performance.

Abstract: Large vision-language models are becoming increasingly dominant in 3D medical image interpretation, but we rarely know <i>which</i> internal units encode clinical findings or <i>where</i> that information lives in the representation. We first study this on a 3D chest vision-language model (Pillar-0) by probing its frozen vision embeddings. We show that (i) each radiological finding is encoded by a <i>sparse</i> set of ~10 vision-encoder channels that match full-feature classification performance and far exceed a zero-shot text prompting; (ii) turning off the channels tied to one finding, that finding's score collapses while unrelated labels stay stable; and (iii) the same sparse probe <i>replicates</i> on an architecturally unrelated 3D abdominal VLM (Merlin) suggesting a general property of frozen medical encoders. Our training-free concept channel probe (CCP) method, paired with a corpus-derived report template, outperforms published CT-CHAT on clinical efficacy and NLG metrics (F1 0.549 vs. 0.184; BLEU 0.483 vs. 0.373) at 22x lower latency. Our results provide a clear, reproducible characterization of how frozen medical encoders represent findings, demonstrating direct applicability across models.

</details>


### [34] [AUCH-Net: Action Unit-Based Consistency-Aware Hypergraph Network for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Facial Expression Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21004)
*Xinhan Qiu,Yan Yan,Rui Zhu,Si Chen,Hanzi Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AUCH-Net leverages Action Units and consistency-aware hypergraphs to improve cross-domain few-shot facial expression recognition by learning transferable AU and visual features, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on both lab and wild datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CF-FER methods suffer from poor transferable feature learning due to large domain discrepancies and limited target samples, and the potential of Action Units (AUs) for bridging domain gaps has not been fully exploited.

Method: Proposes AUCH-Net with two modules: (1) an AU feature learning (AFL) module guided by relation consistency loss and AU regularization loss, and (2) a visual feature learning (VFL) module supervised by relation consistency loss and classification loss. Consistency-aware hypergraphs are constructed on AUs to model connections between AUs and expression categories.

Result: Consistently outperforms several state-of-the-art methods on both in-the-lab and in-the-wild datasets, demonstrating that modeling AU relationships significantly boosts CF-FER performance.

Conclusion: Modeling relationships among Action Units holds significant potential for facial expression recognition under cross-domain few-shot scenarios, effectively bridging fine-grained facial variations and high-level expression categories.

Abstract: Recently, cross-domain few-shot facial expression recognition (CF-FER) has received considerable attention. However, the performance of existing CF-FER methods is still unsatisfactory due to inferior transferable feature learning under large domain discrepancy and limited target samples. Fortunately, the action units (AUs), which indicate the movements of different facial muscles, provide consistent conceptual semantics for describing expressions within and across domains. Inspired by this, we propose a novel Action Unit-based Consistency-aware Hypergraph Network (AUCH-Net), which constructs consistency-aware hypergraphs on AUs, for CF-FER. Specifically, AUCH-Net presents a new AU feature learning (AFL) module and a new visual feature learning (VFL) module. The AFL module learns AU features under the guidance of a novel relation consistency loss and an AU regularization loss, while the VFL module learns visual features supervised by a relation consistency loss and a classification loss. By learning consistent AU features, AUCH-Net effectively models the connections between AUs and expression categories. As a result, we can bridge the gap between fine-grained facial variations and high-level expression categories, greatly facilitating the learning of transferable feature representations.Extensive experiments on both in-the-lab and in-the-wild datasets show that our method consistently outperforms several state-of-the-art methods. Our results clearly show that modeling the relationships among AUs holds significant potential for FER under cross-domain few-shot scenarios.

</details>


### [35] [Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21007)
*Abhijeet Narang,Kartik Kuckreja,Shreya Ghosh,Muhammad Haris Khan,Usman Tariq,Jianfei Cai,Abhinav Dhall*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026, built on the XPlainVerse benchmark, tasks participants with both classifying images as real/fake and generating dual-level natural-language explanations (complex for technical users, simple for general users), evaluated on classification accuracy, semantic similarity, simplicity, and intent-aware grounding metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deepfake detection needs to move beyond binary classification to also provide interpretable visual evidence, enabling diverse users to understand why an image is considered manipulated, which is critical for real-world verification.

Method: The challenge requires participants to output a real/fake label along with two explanations per image: a detailed complex explanation for technical users and a concise simple explanation for general users. Evaluation combines classification metrics with semantic similarity, simplicity, and intent-aware grounding metrics that verify whether explanations correctly identify manipulated entities and supporting visual evidence. The benchmark uses XPlainVerse, a million-scale dataset for explainable deepfake detection.

Result: The challenge benchmarks joint classification and explanation generation capabilities; the resulting methodologies aim to advance next-generation explainable deepfake detectors. Evaluation scripts, baseline models, and code are publicly available.

Conclusion: The challenge promotes developing deepfake detectors that not only detect manipulations but also explain them in a human-understandable manner, catering to different user expertise levels, thus bridging the gap between detection accuracy and interpretability.

Abstract: Deepfake detection is moving beyond binary classification decisions toward systems that can also explain the visual evidence supporting those decisions. This transition is important for real-world verification settings, where diverse users need to understand not only whether an image is manipulated, but also why it is considered suspicious. The Explainable Deepfake Detection Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 is designed to benchmark this joint capability. Built on XPlainVerse, a million-scale benchmark for explainable deepfake detection, the challenge evaluates methods on image classification and grounded natural-language explanation generation. Participants submit a real/fake label together with two explanations for each image: a detailed complex explanation for technical users and a concise simple explanation for general users. The evaluation combines classification metrics with semantic similarity, simplicity, and intent-aware grounding metrics that assess whether explanations identify the relevant manipulated entities and supporting visual evidence. The methodologies developed through the challenge will contribute to the development of next-generation explainable deepfake detectors. Evaluation script, baseline models, and accompanying code are available on https://github.com/Abhijeet8901/XPlainVerse-ACMChallenge.

</details>


### [36] [ProCap: Prominence-guided Object Rectification for Faithful and Comprehensive Video Captioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21022)
*Debjyoti Das Adhikary,Aritra Hazra,Partha Pratim Chakrabarti*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes a training-free, iterative post-hoc rectification framework for video captioning that uses a prominence-aware scoring mechanism (based on spatial saliency, temporal persistence, and relational dynamics) to progressively inject missing but contextually relevant objects into captions, achieving up to 48% improvement in completeness and 45% reduction in hallucination without retraining or reference captions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video captioning models either require expensive retraining of large vision-language models, or use training-free approaches that apply only a single fixed correction pass without prioritizing which objects are most important, leading to omission of semantically significant content.

Method: A prominence-aware, iterative post-hoc rectification framework: (1) a lightweight scoring mechanism ranks detected objects by spatial saliency, temporal persistence, and relational dynamics; (2) an iterative, prompt-driven refinement loop uses this ranking to progressively inject missing yet contextually relevant objects over multiple rounds, without modifying the underlying captioning model's parameters.

Result: Validated on MSVD and MSR-VTT using object-grounded metrics, a 110-participant human study, and qualitative comparison against ChatGPT and Gemini. Human evaluation shows up to 48% improvement in perceived completeness and up to 45% reduction in hallucination relative to a strong pretrained captioning baseline.

Conclusion: The prominence-guided iterative rectification is a lightweight, scalable, and model-agnostic approach to more complete and trustworthy video captioning, with relevance to accessibility, retrieval, and multimedia understanding applications.

Abstract: Improving video captioning quality typically demands retraining large vision-language models, an expensive and often impractical requirement. Existing training-free alternatives instead ground captions in detected objects to curb hallucination, but apply only a single, fixed correction pass without prioritizing which objects matter most, leaving semantically significant content omitted. We propose a prominence-aware, iterative post-hoc rectification framework that overcomes both limitations without modifying the underlying captioning model's parameters: a lightweight scoring mechanism ranks detected objects by spatial saliency, temporal persistence, and relational dynamics, and an iterative, prompt-driven refinement loop uses this ranking to progressively inject missing yet contextually relevant objects into the caption over multiple rounds. We validate the framework on MSVD and MSR-VTT using object-grounded automatic metrics, a 110-participant human study, and qualitative comparison against ChatGPT and Gemini; in human evaluation, the framework raises perceived completeness by up to 48% and reduces hallucination by up to 45% relative to a strong pretrained captioning baseline, all without retraining or reference captions. These results position prominence-guided iterative rectification as a lightweight, scalable, and model-agnostic route to more complete and trustworthy video captioning, with direct relevance to accessibility, retrieval, and other multimedia understanding applications.

</details>


### [37] [WAT3R: Feedforward Underwater 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21023)
*Jiayi Xu,Jiahao Lu,Ziqiang Zheng,Yihao Tan,Yaolong Zhu,Yuan Liu,Sai-Kit Yeung*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WAT3R is a feed-forward framework that directly reconstructs 3D underwater scenes from images/videos by using a lightweight neural module to adapt to underwater degradation effects (light attenuation and backscattering), outputting pixel-aligned 3D point maps and camera poses in a single pass, and outperforming SOTA on FLSea, SQUID, and USOD10K datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Underwater 3D reconstruction is challenging due to light attenuation and backscattering that degrade visual quality and disrupt feature consistency across views, leading to inaccurate multi-view geometry. Existing methods struggle to handle these degradation effects in a feed-forward manner.

Method: WAT3R integrates a lightweight neural adaptation module that treats degradation adaptation as a geometry-constrained process, flexibly accounting for underwater imaging effects. The framework operates in a single forward pass, directly outputting pixel-aligned 3D point maps and camera poses from underwater videos.

Result: Experiments on FLSea, SQUID, and USOD10K datasets demonstrate consistent outperformance over state-of-the-art methods on multi-view/monocular depth estimation and camera pose estimation tasks.

Conclusion: WAT3R effectively addresses underwater visual degradation for 3D reconstruction by using a lightweight degradation adaptation module, achieving efficient and high-quality feed-forward reconstruction directly from underwater images/videos.

Abstract: Reliable feedforward underwater 3D reconstruction remains challenging due to severe light attenuation and backscattering, which degrade visual quality and disrupt feature consistency across views, leading to inaccurate multi-view geometry. To address this issue, we propose WAT3R, a feed-forward framework for reconstructing 3D scenes directly from underwater images. By leveraging degradation adaptation as a geometry-constrained process, WAT3R integrates a lightweight neural adaptation module to flexibly account for these underwater imaging effects, thereby improving multi-view reconstruction quality. Implemented in a single forward pass, WAT3R directly and efficiently outputs pixel-aligned 3D point maps and camera poses from underwater videos, allowing a high-quality underwater 3D reconstruction. Experiments conducted on the FLSea, SQUID, and USOD10K datasets show that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on 3D reconstruction tasks, including multi-view/monocular depth estimation and camera pose estimation.

</details>


### [38] [GroupVideo: Multi-Identity Customized Text-to-Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21027)
*Xinyang Song,Libin Wang,Jianxin Sun,Qi Li,Dandan Zheng,JingDong Chen,Zhenan Sun*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GroupVideo is a novel framework for multi-identity customized video generation that uses multimodal identity alignment (visual and semantic), an ID localization module with spatial guidance, and a new 20,000-video dataset to overcome identity confusion and unnatural motions seen in prior single-identity or naive multi-identity approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing identity-customized video generation methods are limited to single-identity scenarios; extending them to multi-identity settings causes identity confusion and unnatural "copy-paste" facial expressions/motions due to the lack of explicit identity separation mechanisms.

Method: GroupVideo is built upon Video Diffusion Transformers with multimodal identity alignment: (1) visual alignment jointly encodes multiple face images for robust identity references; (2) semantic alignment via a semantic perceiver enhances motion naturalness; (3) an ID localization module with spatial guidance, bounding box constraints, and mask regularization loss mitigates identity blending and improves training efficiency. A curated 20,000-video multi-ID dataset supports training.

Result: Extensive experiments show GroupVideo outperforms existing methods in generating multi-character videos with consistent identities and natural motions.

Conclusion: GroupVideo effectively addresses identity confusion and unnatural motion in multi-identity video generation through multimodal alignment and spatial guidance, and the new dataset provides a foundation for future research.

Abstract: Current identity customized video generation methodologies are predominantly limited to single-identity scenarios, as the lack of explicit identity separation mechanisms often leads to identity confusion in multi-identity settings. Existing multi-identity approaches, which directly extend single-identity frameworks by concatenating face images as input conditions, frequently result in unnatural facial expressions and motions, manifesting as the "copy-paste" phenomenon. To overcome these limitations, we introduce GroupVideo, a novel framework that leverages multiple individual photographs to generate identitycustomized video. Built upon Video Diffusion Transformers, GroupVideo incorporates multimodal identity alignment: visual alignment jointly encodes multiple face images to provide robust identity references, while semantic alignment introduces a semantic perceiver to enhance the naturalness of motions. An ID localization module with spatial guidance is introduced to address identity blending and enhance identity fidelity, along with bounding box constraints and mask regularization loss, to focus on facial regions and improve training efficiency. In response to the shortage of multi-ID video datasets, we have curated a comprehensive high-quality dataset of 20,000 videos, thereby establishing a crucial resource to advance future research in multi-ID video generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GroupVideo outperforms existing methods in generating multi-character videos with consistent identities and natural motions.

</details>


### [39] [Spectral-Spatial Synergistic Guided Network for Hyperspectral Salient Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21032)
*Yanyan Peng,Tingfa Xu,Yao Xiao,Peifu Liu,Shuyan Bai,Fengxiang Xu,Jianan Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: S3GNet is a lightweight hyperspectral salient object detection network that uses spectral derivatives, hierarchical modeling, cross-stream attention, and multi-scale refinement to robustly distinguish intrinsic material properties from illumination-induced spectral variations, achieving superior accuracy and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hyperspectral salient object detection methods confuse incidental spectral variations (e.g., illumination changes) with intrinsic material spectral differences, leading to fragile representations and noisy predictions.

Method: S3GNet introduces three key components: (1) a parameter-free Spectral Structure-Aware Module using spectral derivatives and regional hierarchical modeling for illumination-robust features; (2) a Stream-Aware Attention Module for inter-stream global interaction and intra-stream spatial guidance; and (3) a Progressive Gated Refinement Decoder for multi-scale feature integration and precise boundary recovery.

Result: S3GNet achieves superior performance in both computational efficiency and detection accuracy compared to existing methods on hyperspectral salient object detection.

Conclusion: The spectral-spatial synergistic guided approach with structure perception as core effectively addresses illumination sensitivity issues, delivering robust and efficient hyperspectral salient object detection.

Abstract: Hyperspectral salient object detection aims to identify visually salient regions from hyperspectral images. Existing methods often fail because they fundamentally misunderstand the data, confusing incidental spectral variations caused by external factors such as illumination with essential spectral differences caused by the intrinsic material properties of the object. This leads to fragile representations and noisy predictions. To this end, we propose a lightweight and efficient Spectral-Spatial Synergistic Guided Network (S3GNet), with structure perception as the core, to build a closed-loop information flow around spectrum robust modeling, cross-stream co-perception and multi-scale refinement decoding. S3GNet introduces a parameter-free Spectral Structure-Aware Module that leverages spectral derivatives and regional hierarchical modeling to extract intrinsic features of robustness against illumination variations. Our Stream-Aware Attention Module achieves effective spectral-spatial collaboration through inter-stream global interaction and intra-stream spatial guidance. Furthermore, a Progressive Gated Refinement Decoder ensures precise object boundaries and detail recovery by optimally integrating multi-scale features. Experimental results show that S3GNet achieves superior performance in both computational efficiency and detection accuracy compared to existing methods.

</details>


### [40] [GeoThreat: Transferable Targeted Adversarial Attacks on Large Vision-Language Models for Remote Sensing Image Interpretation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21036)
*Yimin Fu,Yuefeng Bai,Baicheng Pan,Zhunga Liu,Michael K. Ng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GeoThreat is a transferable targeted adversarial attack method against large vision-language models (LVLMs) for remote sensing image interpretation, which manipulates adversarial representations at both conceptual and perceptual levels to achieve cross-modal semantic manipulation under black-box settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adversarial attacks mainly focus on corrupting visual inputs in general vision-language tasks, while remote sensing fields remain largely underexplored. Remote sensing image interpretation requires joint reasoning over local discriminative cues and global scene context, posing additional challenges for transferable semantic manipulation under black-box settings.

Method: GeoThreat modulates adversarial representations at conceptual and perceptual levels: (1) uses class tokens from surrogate image encoders as conceptual representations; (2) distills perceptual representations from patch tokens via collaborative importance estimation; (3) incorporates adversarial-target similarity gradients to characterize relevance of local visual cues; (4) dynamically aligns perceptual representations with target patch tokens via cross-attention; (5) iteratively updates adversarial perturbations through ensemble-based joint optimization of conceptual calibration and perceptual adaptation.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse LVLMs demonstrate the superiority of GeoThreat in both transferability and controllability.

Conclusion: GeoThreat effectively addresses the underexplored challenge of targeted adversarial attacks in remote sensing for LVLMs, achieving improved transferability and controllability across diverse models under black-box settings.

Abstract: Adversarial attacks against large vision-language models (LVLMs) serve as an effective means of assessing their robustness in cross-modal semantic understanding. Existing studies mainly focus on corrupting visual inputs to induce predefined erroneous responses in general vision-language tasks, whereas corresponding investigations in remote sensing fields remain largely underexplored. Compared with natural image understanding, remote sensing image interpretation requires joint reasoning over local discriminative cues and global scene context. This poses additional challenges to achieving transferable semantic manipulation toward specified responses under black-box settings. To tackle these challenges, we propose GeoThreat, a transferable targeted adversarial attack method against LVLMs for remote sensing image interpretation. Specifically, GeoThreat modulates adversarial representations in accordance with the target content at both conceptual and perceptual levels. The class tokens from surrogate image encoders are employed as conceptual representations, while perceptual representations are distilled from patch tokens of the adversarial example through collaborative importance estimation. Beyond merely rolling out attention scores across layers, we incorporate adversarial-target similarity gradients to more faithfully characterize the relevance of local visual cues to the intended semantic manipulation. The perceptual representations are then dynamically aligned with target patch tokens in a cross-attentive manner, facilitating the adaptation of local cues toward designated semantic details. Finally, adversarial perturbations are iteratively updated via ensemble-based joint optimization of conceptual calibration and perceptual adaptation. Extensive experiments across diverse LVLMs demonstrate the superiority of GeoThreat in both transferability and controllability.

</details>


### [41] [HyperImageNet: A Large-Scale High-Spatial Resolution Hyperspectral Imagery Classification Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21050)
*Chuguang Zeng,Jingtao Li,Yinhe Liu,Yanfei Zhong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HyperImageNet is a large-scale benchmark dataset of 26,084 airborne hyperspectral image patches (224 spectral bands, 138 land-cover categories) with pixel-level labels and instance masks, supporting semantic/instance segmentation and open-environment evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of large-scale, fine-grained, and open-environment benchmarks for hyperspectral land-cover understanding that support both semantic and instance segmentation tasks.

Method: Constructed a dataset of 26,084 hyperspectral patches (224 bands, 138 categories) with raw imagery, pixel-level semantic labels, and object-level instance masks; established an open-environment benchmark with strict spatial separation to evaluate methods including the HyperFree foundation model.

Result: Experimental results validated the effectiveness of HyperImageNet for fine-grained hyperspectral understanding and open-environment remote sensing research.

Conclusion: HyperImageNet serves as a valuable large-scale benchmark for advancing fine-grained hyperspectral land-cover understanding, particularly in open-environment settings.

Abstract: We present HyperImageNet, a large-scale benchmark for fine-grained hyperspectral land-cover understanding. The dataset contains 26,084 airborne hyperspectral image patches with 224 spectral bands and 138 fine-grained land-cover categories. Unlike existing datasets, HyperImageNet provides raw imagery, pixel-level semantic labels, and object-level instance masks, supporting both semantic and instance segmentation. Furthermore, we establish an open-environment benchmark with strict spatial separation to evaluate representative methods and the HyperFree foundation model. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of HyperImageNet for fine-grained hyperspectral understanding and open-environment remote sensing research.

</details>


### [42] [Achieving Text-based Person Retrieval with Any Granularity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21057)
*Jialong Zuo,Hanyu Zhou,Dongyue Wu,Yongtai Deng,Mengdan Tan,Nong Sang,Changxin Gao,Xiang Bai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Text-based Person Retrieval with Any Granularity, addressing the challenge of query granularity uncertainty. It provides: (1) a five-level granularity spectrum and the UFine6926-MG multi-grained dataset; (2) MG-Eval evaluation benchmark with cross-identity labels; and (3) the CMAM framework using orthogonal-expert perception, probabilistic alignment, and granularity-consistent reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art results across all granularities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-based person retrieval faces an under-explored challenge: the inherent uncertainty of query granularity in real-world scenarios, where queries can range from coarse (e.g., "a person in red") to fine-grained (e.g., "a man wearing a red Nike t-shirt and blue jeans"). Existing methods assume a fixed granularity, which is unrealistic for practical applications.

Method: The authors propose CMAM (Cross-modal Multi-grained Aligning and Matching) with three key components: (1) orthogonal-expert perception to disentangle granularity-specific features; (2) probabilistic alignment to model many-to-many matches under query uncertainty; (3) granularity-consistent reasoning to steer feature learning via joint cross-modal granularity verification. They also construct a multi-grained dataset (UFine6926-MG) and evaluation benchmark (MG-Eval).

Result: CMAM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across all five granularity levels on the proposed benchmarks.

Conclusion: This work establishes a foundational benchmark and a robust baseline for text-based person retrieval under any query granularity, paving the way for more practical person retrieval systems.

Abstract: Text-based person retrieval faces a critical but under-explored challenge: the inherent uncertainty of query granularity in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a new paradigm, Text-based Person Retrieval with Any Granularity, and provides a systematic solution. First, we formalize a five-level granularity spectrum and construct UFine6926-MG, a high-quality multi-grained dataset annotated comprehensively at all granularities via a novel Multi-grained Text Annotation Engine. Second, acknowledging that coarse queries naturally correspond to multiple valid candidates, we propose MG-Eval, a holistic evaluation benchmark with progressively detailed texts and cross-identity labels that reflect real-world semantics, alongside tailored evaluation metrics and protocols. Third, after a comprehensive diagnosis reveals the systemic limitations of existing research, we propose the Cross-modal Multi-grained Aligning and Matching (CMAM) framework. CMAM achieves granularity-aware retrieval through: 1) orthogonal-expert perception to disentangle granularity-specific features; 2) probabilistic alignment to model many-to-many matches under query uncertainty; and 3) granularity-consistent reasoning to steer feature learning via joint cross-modal granularity verification. Experiments demonstrate that CMAM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across all granularity levels. This work establishes a foundational benchmark and a robust baseline, paving the way for more practical person retrieval systems.

</details>


### [43] [MVEI & EmObserver: Empowering MLLM-Oriented Visual Emotional Intelligence via Emotion Statement Judgement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21061)
*Daiqing Wu,Dongbao Yang,Jiashu Yao,Hongrui Zhang,Can Ma,Yu Zhou,Sicheng Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces Emotion Statement Judgement (ESJ), a statement-verification formulation for evaluating visual emotional intelligence in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). It presents INSETS-462k dataset, MVEI benchmark, and EmObserver model, addressing structural mismatches between traditional AICA and MLLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLMs lack systematic evaluation of visual emotional intelligence due to a structural mismatch between traditional AICA paradigms (classification-based) and MLLMs' open-ended, instruction-driven nature. Four key limitations are identified: omission of plausible responses, limited emotion taxonomies, neglect of contextual factors, and labor-intensive annotation.

Method: Proposes Emotion Statement Judgement (ESJ) — a statement-verification formulation that preserves expressive input space while constraining outputs to discriminative judgments. Develops INSETS-462k dataset via a labor-efficient pipeline, creates MVEI benchmark (covering sentiment polarity, emotion interpretation, scene context, perception subjectivity), and builds EmObserver model optimized on ESJ via multi-stage recipe.

Result: Extensive evaluation of broad-spectrum MLLMs on MVEI reveals fine-grained insights into current visual emotional intelligence. Experiments on multiple AICA benchmarks demonstrate EmObserver's accuracy, generalization, and reasoning faithfulness.

Conclusion: ESJ is established as a practical formulation, MVEI as a comprehensive benchmark, and EmObserver as an advanced baseline for advancing MLLM-oriented visual emotional intelligence.

Abstract: Affective Image Content Analysis (AICA) aims to recognize and understand emotions elicited by visual content, representing an indispensable step toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). However, despite the rapid progress of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), systematic evaluation of their visual emotional intelligence remains largely absent from recent model releases. We attribute this gap to a structural mismatch between conventional AICA paradigms and the open-ended, instruction-driven nature of MLLMs, where further analysis reveals four major limitations: omission of plausible responses, limited emotion taxonomies, neglect of contextual factors, and labor-intensive annotation. To overcome these barriers, we introduce Emotion Statement Judgement (ESJ), a statement-verification formulation that preserves the expressiveness of the input space while constraining outputs to discriminative judgements. We further develop INSETS, a labor-efficient pipeline that instantiates ESJ at scale by constructing INSETS-462k and supporting MVEI, a rigorously refined benchmark spanning sentiment polarity, emotion interpretation, scene context, and perception subjectivity. Beyond evaluation, we build EmObserver, an emotion-oriented MLLM optimized on ESJ through an elaborate multi-stage recipe. Extensive evaluation of broad-spectrum MLLMs on MVEI reveals fine-grained insights into current artificial visual emotional intelligence, while experiments on multiple AICA benchmarks demonstrate the accuracy, generalization, and reasoning faithfulness of EmObserver. Collectively, these results establish ESJ as a practical formulation, MVEI as a comprehensive benchmark, and EmObserver as an advanced baseline for advancing MLLM-oriented visual emotional intelligence. Code will be released at: https://github.com/wdqqdw/EmObserver.

</details>


### [44] [Do Pathology Vision-Language Models Truly See Pathology?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21065)
*Chengyang Zhang,Wenchuan Zhang,Bo Li,Xinyu Liu,Jiaming Yang,Mengran Li,Chenxun Deng,Jie Chen,Yang Zhang,Wei Ju,Yuhao Yi,Hong Bu,Jiancheng Lv*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PathBind benchmark reveals that current pathology VLMs exhibit a significant gap between their answer accuracy and actual visual-semantic binding, as existing evaluations overlook issues like text-only shortcuts, inflated gains from domain training without true visual grounding, and diffuse entity-level attention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing pathology VLM evaluations overestimate multimodal capabilities by overlooking three issues: (1) models achieve high accuracy without visual input, (2) domain training boosts accuracy without proportional visual binding improvements, and (3) attention maps are diffuse and not query-specific, leading to misjudgments of actual multimodal understanding.

Method: The authors introduce PathBind, a benchmark with 2,600 samples across three components: PathBind-VQA (1,500 questions, six dimensions), PathBind-PTA (600 questions from private teaching atlas), and PathBind-Grounding (500 expert-curated region-level samples). Each component uses task-specific automated filtering and expert review to reduce textual shortcuts. They evaluate 18 VLMs on VQA tasks and 10 VLMs on grounding tasks.

Result: Evaluation of 18 VLMs on PathBind and 5 existing pathology VQA benchmarks, plus 10 VLMs on grounding tasks, shows current pathology VLMs still have a substantial gap between answer-side performance and true visual-semantic binding.

Conclusion: Current pathology VLMs are overestimated in their multimodal capabilities; PathBind provides a more rigorous benchmark to reveal deficits in visual grounding that accuracy-based metrics alone miss.

Abstract: Pathology vision-language models (VLMs) have recently progressed rapidly and are commonly evaluated by answer accuracy on pathology VQA benchmarks. However, we dig into current evaluations and identify three overlooked issues: 1) Visual evidence is not always necessary. For instance, Gemini-3-Pro achieves 53.5% average accuracy across 5 VQA benchmarks without any visual input. 2) Domain training can improve accuracy without proportional gains in visual binding. Compared with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Patho-R1-7B exhibits a 5.8-point lower multimodal gain and a 3.7-point lower attention IoU. 3) Entity-level attention is diffuse and weakly query-specific. On PathVG, attention maps remain highly correlated across different entity queries. These issues can lead to substantial misjudgments of pathology VLMs' actual multimodal capabilities. To this end, we present PathBind, a benchmark comprising 2,600 samples: PathBind-VQA with 1,500 questions across six dimensions, PathBind-PTA with 600 questions from a private pathology teaching atlas, and PathBind-Grounding with 500 expert-curated region-level samples. Each component undergoes task-specific automated filtering and expert review to reduce textual shortcuts and improve entity-region correspondence. We evaluate 18 representative VLMs on VQA samples of PathBind and five existing pathology VQA benchmarks, and further evaluate 10 VLMs on PathBind-Grounding and PathVG. Results show that current pathology VLMs still exhibit a substantial gap between answer-side performance and visual-semantic binding.

</details>


### [45] [Show, Don't Tell: Evaluating Spatial Cognition in Generative Pixels Rather Than LLM Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21072)
*Xu Wang,Kaixiang Yao,Miao Pan,Xiaohe Zhou,Xuanyu Liu,Wenqi Zhang,Xuhong Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ProVisE is a benchmark-agnostic framework that evaluates image-generation models on spatial reasoning tasks by having them produce protocol-constrained visual answers (e.g., pointing, marking, drawing) instead of text/coordinates, and parsing these into structured predictions. Alongside SpatialGen-Bench (470 samples, 14 subtasks), experiments show image-generation models excel at pixel-space spatial expression while text-output VLMs outperform in compositional spatial reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing spatial reasoning benchmarks use coordinates, options, or text as answer formats, which creates a mismatch for image-generation models that naturally express spatial judgments (locations, regions, paths) via pointing, marking, or drawing in pixel space. This makes it difficult to fairly evaluate image-generation models under the same task semantics as text-output VLMs.

Method: ProVisE (Protocolized Visual Evaluation) is a benchmark-agnostic framework comprising: (1) eliciting protocol-constrained visual answers from image-generation models, and (2) parsing those visual outputs into structured predictions compatible with original benchmark metrics. It includes an Agentic builder that constructs and validates task-specific protocols for new benchmarks. A curated diagnostic benchmark, SpatialGen-Bench (470 samples, 14 spatial subtasks, 4 capability levels, diverse answer forms), is introduced for evaluation.

Result: Image-generation models are competitive when spatial answers can be externalized directly in pixel space, while text-output VLMs maintain a clear advantage in compositional spatial reasoning. The Agentic protocol construction is validated on six external spatial benchmarks.

Conclusion: There are complementary strengths between pixel-space expression (image-generation models) and text-based reasoning (text-output VLMs). ProVisE establishes a metric-compatible testbed for studying spatial cognition in image-generation models.

Abstract: Spatial intelligence is essential for agents to move from static semantic understanding toward interacting with the physical world. Many spatial tasks are grounded in continuous visual scenes, where locations, regions, and paths are more naturally expressed by pointing, marking, or drawing than by reporting precise coordinates or discrete textual symbols. Yet existing spatial reasoning benchmarks usually require coordinates, options, or text, creating an answer-interface mismatch for image-generation models. This makes it difficult to evaluate image-generation models under the same task semantics as text-output VLMs, despite their ability to externalize spatial judgments directly in pixel space. We propose ProVisE (Protocolized Visual Evaluation), a benchmark-agnostic framework that elicits protocol-constrained visual answers from image-generation models and parses them into structured predictions compatible with original metrics. ProVisE also includes an Agentic builder that constructs and validates task-specific protocols for new benchmarks. We further introduce SpatialGen-Bench, a curated diagnostic benchmark of 470 samples across 14 spatial subtasks, four capability levels, and diverse answer forms. We evaluate representative text-output VLMs and image-generation models in a unified setting and validate Agentic protocol construction on six external spatial benchmarks. Results show that image-generation models are competitive when spatial answers can be externalized directly in pixel space, while text-output VLMs retain a clear advantage in compositional spatial reasoning. These findings reveal complementary strengths of pixel-space expression and text-based reasoning and establish a metric-compatible testbed for studying spatial cognition in image-generation models.

</details>


### [46] [C-PTQ: Fisher-weighted Channel-wise Sensitivity for Post-training Quantization of MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21076)
*Jiameng Li,Han Zhou,Matthew B. Blaschko*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: C-PTQ proposes a Fisher-weighted channel-wise scaling method for post-training quantization of MLLMs, using second-order derivative-based Hessian approximation to align task sensitivity with quantization error, achieving SOTA without auxiliary modules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PTQ methods for MLLMs use modality- or token-level metrics for channel-wise scaling that fail to capture channel-wise impacts on task-specific loss, leading to misalignment between importance and scaling factors, causing suboptimal performance and quantization degradation due to outlier channels.

Method: C-PTQ introduces a Fisher-weighted objective as a tractable Hessian approximation (motivated by second-order derivatives) to inject task sensitivity into the scaling process, harmonizing task-specific loss perturbation and quantization error for unified channel-wise post-training quantization.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on Qwen2.5VL, InternVL2, and LLaVA-OV across 8 benchmarks in both weight-only and weight-activation quantization settings, without auxiliary modules like LoRA.

Conclusion: The proposed approach effectively addresses outlier channel degradation in quantized MLLMs by aligning importance measurement with task loss via second-order information, maintaining high efficiency while improving quantization fidelity and accuracy.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require huge memory and computational costs, which limits their practical deployment. Post-training quantization (PTQ) techniques offer an efficient solution for model compression and inference acceleration. Yet, the quantized model faces performance degradation due to outlier channels, which are highly sensitive to quantization and substantially impair activation fidelity and task accuracy. To protect these salient channels during quantization, existing PTQ methods leverage modality- or token-level metrics to guide channel-wise scaling (CWS) of LLM decoders. However, these orthogonal measurements fail to capture channel-wise impacts on task-specific loss, and the misalignment between importance and scaling factors ultimately leads to suboptimal performance. To address this issue, we propose C-PTQ, a unified channel-wise PTQ method that harmonizes task-specific loss perturbation and quantization error. Motivated by second-order derivatives, we design a Fisher-weighted objective as a tractable Hessian approximation, seamlessly injecting task sensitivity into the scaling process. Notably, we achieve state-of-the-art performance without auxiliary modules like LoRA, thereby maintaining high efficiency. Experiments on Qwen2.5VL, InternVL2 and LLaVA-OV across 8 benchmarks demonstrate our effectiveness in both weight-only and weight-activation settings.

</details>


### [47] [The RealDefocus Benchmark for Defocus Deblurring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21078)
*Tim Seizinger,Zhuyun Zhou,Radu Timofte*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents RealDefocus, a benchmark for Single-Image Defocus Deblurring derived from the RealBokeh dataset, providing paired defocused/sharp images, standardized splits, and a unified evaluation framework with cross-dataset validation protocols.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rigorous and reproducible evaluation of Single-Image Defocus Deblurring (SIDD) is challenging due to the scarcity of realistic, high-resolution datasets with well-aligned defocused/sharp pairs and standardized evaluation protocols.

Method: The authors build RealDefocus from the real-world RealBokeh dataset (originally for Bokeh Rendering), creating paired defocused inputs and sharp ground truth, with predefined splits and a unified evaluation framework. They propose a benchmarking protocol with cross-dataset validation.

Result: A new benchmark dataset with standardized evaluation protocols for comparing image restoration and neural rendering approaches in defocus deblurring.

Conclusion: RealDefocus provides a reproducible and rigorous evaluation framework for SIDD, addressing the lack of standardized benchmarks in the field.

Abstract: Single-Image Defocus Deblurring (SIDD) aims to recover an all-in-focus image from a single defocused observation, but rigorous and reproducible evaluation remains challenging due to the scarcity of realistic, high-resolution datasets with well-aligned defocused/sharp pairs and standardized protocols. We build on RealDefocus, a benchmark derived from the real-world RealBokeh dataset originally proposed for Bokeh Rendering. RealDefocus provides paired defocused inputs and sharp ground truth images, predefined training/validation/test splits, and a unified evaluation framework for comparing image restoration and neural rendering approaches. We further outline a benchmarking protocol with cross-dataset validation to assess reconstruction quality and generalization. The project page is publicly available at: www.github.com/TimSeizinger/RealDefocus-Benchmark.

</details>


### [48] [Geo3R: Mitigating Spatial Reasoning Hallucination in Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21085)
*Mingyu Wang,Weilin Jin,Wenbo Li,Haoyang Huang,Tong Jia,Ying Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MLLMs hallucinate on spatial reasoning due to 2D-3D gap; Geo3R is a training-free, plug-and-play framework using geometric evidence and structured 3D reasoning to mitigate this, outperforming existing methods on 18 tasks across 3 benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hallucination mitigation methods fail to address spatial reasoning hallucinations in MLLMs because they cannot bridge the gap between 2D visual representations and 3D spatial reality.

Method: Geo3R: a training-free, plug-and-play framework that incorporates geometric evidence and structured 3D reasoning to mitigate spatial reasoning hallucinations.

Result: Geo3R substantially reduces spatial reasoning hallucination across diverse MLLMs without additional training, outperforming existing models and methods on 18 tasks across 3 benchmarks covering perspective effects, object orientation, and viewpoint changes.

Conclusion: Spatial reasoning hallucination is a distinct subcategory of relation hallucination caused by insufficient spatial structure modeling; Geo3R effectively addresses it via geometric evidence and structured 3D reasoning.

Abstract: Despite remarkable progress in visual understanding, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) remain prone to hallucinations when reasoning about spatial relationships, often producing judgments that contradict the true 3D structure of the scene. Though several existing works have proposed to mitigate hallucinations, our analysis indicates that they show limited effectiveness in spatial reasoning, as they fail to bridge the fundamental gap between 2D visual representations and 3D spatial reality. Based on this finding, we define hallucinations arising from insufficient spatial structure modeling as spatial reasoning hallucination, a subcategory of relation hallucination that existing mitigation methods fail to address. We further identify three typical scenarios where such hallucinations frequently occur: perspective effects, object orientation, and viewpoint changes. To this end, we propose Geo3R, a training-free, plug-and-play framework that incorporates geometric evidence and structured 3D reasoning to mitigate spatial reasoning hallucination. Experiments on three benchmarks, covering 18 tasks across all three scenarios, show that Geo3R substantially reduces spatial reasoning hallucination across diverse MLLMs without additional training, outperforming existing models and methods.

</details>


### [49] [Loss Landscape Topology Reveals Why Simple Baselines are Competitive at 3D Point Cloud Segmentation Under Class Imbalance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21089)
*Antonis Savva,Christos Kyrkou,Theocharis Theocharides*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates 11 class imbalance mitigation methods for 3D point cloud semantic segmentation and finds that standard cross-entropy loss performs competitively (within 0.8-3.3% mIoU of specialized methods) across extreme (641:1) and moderate (56:1) imbalance ratios. The authors provide mechanistic analysis showing that imbalance severity shapes the optimization landscape (narrow basins under extreme imbalance, flat plateaus under moderate imbalance), which constrains the effectiveness of loss-level modifications. This offers the first mechanistic explanation for why 2D imbalance methods do not readily transfer to 3D point cloud segmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While class imbalance is severe in 3D point cloud segmentation, it is unclear whether specialized imbalance-aware methods from 2D computer vision are effective in 3D contexts. The paper aims to systematically evaluate these methods and provide mechanistic explanations for their (limited) effectiveness.

Method: The paper evaluates 11 imbalance mitigation approaches (including loss-level modifications) across two datasets with extreme (641:1) and moderate (56:1) imbalance ratios, using two representative architectures. It conducts multifaceted mechanistic analysis of error patterns, decision boundaries, and the geometry of the optimization landscape.

Result: Standard cross-entropy with uniform weighting achieves competitive performance, typically within 0.8-3.3% mIoU of specialized methods across architectures and datasets. Specialized methods offer modest improvements but risk substantial degradation if poorly tuned.

Conclusion: Imbalance severity shapes the optimization topology (narrow solution basins under extreme imbalance, flat plateaus under moderate imbalance), constraining the effectiveness of loss-level modifications. Standard cross-entropy provides a robust baseline, and this work offers the first mechanistic explanation for why 2D imbalance techniques do not readily transfer to point-based 3D segmentation.

Abstract: Semantic segmentation of 3D point clouds faces severe class imbalance, yet the effectiveness of specialized imbalance-aware methods from 2D computer vision remains unclear in 3D contexts. We systematically evaluate 11 imbalance mitigation approaches across datasets with extreme (641:1) and moderate (56:1) imbalance ratios, revealing a surprising finding: standard cross-entropy with uniform weighting achieves competitive performance, typically within 0.8-3.3% mIoU of specialized methods across architectures and datasets. Through multifaceted mechanistic analysis of error patterns, decision boundaries, and the geometry of the optimization landscape, our analyses suggest that imbalance severity shapes the topology, creating narrow solution basins under extreme imbalance and flat plateaus under moderate imbalance. This appears to constrain the effectiveness of loss-level modifications, as all methods must navigate these geometric constraints. Our findings offer practical guidance; standard cross-entropy provides a robust baseline, with specialized methods offering modest improvements (0.8-3.3% mIoU) that vary by architecture and dataset but risk substantial degradation if poorly tuned. This work provides the first mechanistic explanation for why techniques proven effective in 2D do not readily transfer to point-based 3D point cloud segmentation, validated across two representative architectures.

</details>


### [50] [HalluScope: Fine-grained Hallucination Diagnosis for Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21105)
*Weilin Jin,Mingyu Wang,Wenbo Li,Haoyang Huang,Yifan Wu,Ying Li,Gang Huang,Zhonghai Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces HalluScope, a fine-grained hallucination diagnosis framework for MLLMs that jointly performs detection, classification, and interpretable explanation generation. It presents HalluScope-30K dataset and two diagnosis models (4B/8B) achieving SOTA, with diagnostic feedback successfully correcting hallucinations in target models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hallucination detection methods for MLLMs are coarse-grained and lack fine-grained diagnostic information (e.g., hallucination types, explanations) needed for understanding and mitigating hallucinations effectively.

Method: (1) Proposes a unified fine-grained hallucination diagnosis task (detection + classification + interpretable explanation). (2) Builds an automated data generation pipeline and HalluScope-30K dataset (8 sources, 5 task categories). (3) Designs a multi-granular joint reward function. (4) Trains HalluScope-4B and HalluScope-8B diagnosis models.

Result: HalluScope models achieve SOTA on MHALO benchmark and a fine-grained hallucination classification benchmark. Detection and classification mutually benefit under joint optimization. Diagnosis-driven feedback substantially outperforms baselines in correcting hallucinations in Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and LLaVA-1.5-7B.

Conclusion: Fine-grained hallucination diagnosis with joint optimization improves both detection/classification accuracy and downstream hallucination mitigation, demonstrating that diagnostic explanations effectively guide target models to self-correct.

Abstract: Although Multimodal Large Language Models have achieved strong performance across a wide range of vision-language tasks, they still suffer from hallucinations, where model outputs become inconsistent with the visual content, textual context, or commonsense knowledge. Existing studies primarily address this problem through coarse-grained detection. However, these approaches often provide insufficient diagnostic information for understanding hallucination types and supporting downstream hallucination mitigation. To bridge this gap, we propose fine-grained hallucination diagnosis for MLLMs, a new unified task that jointly performs hallucination detection, classification, and interpretable explanation generation. We develop an automated data generation pipeline and construct HalluScope-30K, a large-scale diagnostic dataset covering eight sources and five task categories. Based on this dataset, we design a multi-granular joint reward function and train two diagnosis models, HalluScope-4B and HalluScope-8B, which achieve state-of-the-art performance on both the MHALO benchmark and our fine-grained hallucination classification benchmark. Notably, detection and classification are mutually beneficial under joint optimization. Furthermore, diagnosis-driven feedback experiments show that the fine-grained diagnostic explanations produced by our model effectively guide target models to correct their hallucinations, with full diagnosis substantially outperforming all baselines on both Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and LLaVA-1.5-7B.

</details>


### [51] [The Second LoViF 2026 Challenge on Real-World All-in-One Image Restoration: Methods and Results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21118)
*Xiang Chen,Hao Li,Jiangxin Dong,Jinshan Pan,Xin Li,Hongbo Ding,Junpeng Jiang,Xingyu Qiu,Yilian Zhong,Yuxiang Chen,Shibo Yin,Zixuan Huang,Yushun Fang,Xilei Zhu,Yahui Wang,Chen Lu,Xiaodong Zhou,Qingyue Cao,Changwei Gong,Jingyun Liu,Xingchen Yi,Hansen Shi,Ruiyi Liu,Jirui Xie,Tao Liu,Wenzhuo Ma,Hongzhen Li,Yongyong Chen,Zheng Zhou,Jingyong Su,Jie Liu,Haijin Zeng,Cheng Li,Peishuai Zha,Ziyi Wang,Jian Tang,Yan Chen,Long Bao,Heng Sun,Jiyuan Zhang,Shuai Liu,Wei Ding,Chengjun Guo,Yibin Huang,Xiaotao Wang,Dongqing Zou,Lei Lei,Xiaofeng Wang,Xiao Liu,Yulin Wu,Yuhan Zhao,Shurui Peng,Chao Ren,Yu-Kai Wang,Kosuke Shigematsu,Asuka Shin,Rong-Lin Jian,Cheng-Jun Kang,Jin-Hui Jiang,Jialin Zhou,Kuo Yuan,Songyu Zhang,E B Benson,Ashfaq Hussain,Pruthvikanth AC,Qirui Chen,Jinyuan Chen,Jun Zhang,Xu Zhang,Xuhui Cao,Jiaqi Ma,Laibin Chang,Yuchun Miao,Yichu Xu,Yuanzhi Yao,Shi Chen,Yuning Cui,Huan Zhang,Lefei Zhang,Saeed Ahmad,Ik Hyun Lee,Jun Young Park,Ji Hwan Yoon,Shangquan Sun,Behrooz Nobahar-Moghanlou,Majid Edalatjou,Karim Shahi-Niyar,Ruibo Zhang,Dexiang Hong,Xinyan Liu,Shengeng Tang,Weidong Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper reviews the second LoViF Challenge on real-world all-in-one image restoration, providing a benchmark for unified models handling blur, low-light, haze, rain, and snow. With 158 participants and 20 final teams, it analyzes solutions and results to establish updated benchmarks and effective design strategies for future research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To advance unified image restoration under diverse real-world degradation conditions and provide a common benchmark for evaluating restoration accuracy, robustness, and generalization capability of models across multiple degradation categories within a unified framework.

Method: A competition-based approach where 158 registered participants submitted solutions for all-in-one image restoration. The top 20 teams' results were reproduced and verified, followed by comprehensive analysis of submitted solutions and corresponding results.

Result: 20 teams were included in the final ranking after successful reproduction and verification of their results, with effective design strategies identified through analysis of submitted methods.

Conclusion: The summarized methods and empirical findings reveal effective design strategies and establish an updated benchmark for future research in real-world low-level vision.

Abstract: This paper presents a review of the second LoViF Challenge on Real-World All-in-One Image Restoration. The challenge aims to advance unified image restoration under diverse real-world degradation conditions, including blur, low-light, haze, rain, and snow. It provides a common benchmark for evaluating the restoration accuracy, robustness, and generalization capability of models across multiple degradation categories within a unified framework. The competition attracted 158 registered participants, and 20 teams were included in the final ranking after their submitted results were successfully reproduced and verified. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the submitted solutions and corresponding results, highlighting recent advances in real-world all-in-one image restoration. The summarized methods and empirical findings reveal effective design strategies and establish an updated benchmark for future research in real-world low-level vision.

</details>


### [52] [Causal-AgentIR: Self-Evolving Causal Memory for Adaptive Image Restoration Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21125)
*Hu Gao,Yulong Chen,Lizhuang Ma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Causal-AgentIR is a hierarchical multi-agent framework with self-evolving causal memory that organizes restoration knowledge as structured causal memory graphs instead of static textual descriptions, enabling dynamic accumulation, verification, and forgetting of experience for collective image restoration intelligence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing image restoration agents store knowledge as static tool descriptions, manually defined priors, or unstructured textual summaries, limiting the accumulation, verification, revision, and forgetting of restoration knowledge over long-term experience.

Method: Causal-AgentIR organizes degradation patterns, image regions, restoration tools, actions, quality changes, and user preferences into a structured causal memory graph, supporting graph-based retrieval and multi-hop causal reasoning. It uses a multi-agent collaborative system including planning, degradation analysis, tool expertise, causal memory reasoning, outcome critique, and memory curation agents.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Conclusion: Causal-AgentIR provides a structured, evolving memory mechanism for image restoration agents, allowing restoration experience to be dynamically added, updated, merged, reinforced, ignored, or discarded based on observed quality changes and feedback, maintaining reliable and transferable restoration knowledge.

Abstract: Image restoration agents have recently emerged as a flexible paradigm for handling diverse and unpredictable degradations in real-world scenarios. Existing agents typically formulate restoration as a tool-using process, where the agent perceives degradations, searches candidate tools, executes restoration operations, and revises the plan through reflection or rollback. However, their knowledge is often stored as static tool descriptions, manually defined degradation priors, or unstructured textual summaries, which limits the accumulation, verification, revision, and forgetting of restoration knowledge over long-term experience. In this paper, we propose Causal-AgentIR, a hierarchical multi-agent framework with self-evolving causal memory for collective image restoration intelligence.
