### [103] [InferenceBench: A Benchmark for Open-Ended LLM Inference Optimization by AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468)
*Jehyeok Yeon,Ben Rank,Maksym Andriushchenko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InferenceBench evaluates AI agents on optimizing LLM inference speed using an H100 GPU and two-hour budget, finding agents outperform naive baselines but fall short of simple hyperparameter search, suggesting the bottleneck is not domain knowledge but the ability to systematically explore diverse configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate agents on prescribed workflows or narrow action spaces, and even nominally open-ended tasks can be solved by retrieving known recipes, making it unclear whether strong results reflect genuine optimization or memorized solutions. The authors wanted to create a benchmark that requires genuine optimization in an open-ended AI engineering setting.

Method: InferenceBench requires each agent to deploy an OpenAI-compatible inference server and optimize LLM inference speed on one H100 GPU within a two-hour wall-clock budget. It includes three scenarios isolating distinct bottlenecks (prefill latency, decode latency, concurrent request throughput) and a fourth balancing all three. 15 frontier agent configurations were evaluated.

Result: Agents reliably improve over a naive PyTorch baseline (up to 8.08×), often match or exceed vLLM default settings (4.05×), but fall below a simple hyperparameter search under the same time budget (up to 11.53×). Qualitative analysis shows agents enumerate relevant techniques but converge on a single inference framework, test few configurations, and spend remaining budget on re-measuring, repairing, or optimizing hyperparameters rather than exploring different strategies.

Conclusion: The bottleneck in agent performance is not domain knowledge but the ability to propose diverse configurations, evaluate them systematically, and submit the best solution. InferenceBench reflects the ability of agents to operate in open-ended AI engineering settings where memorized solutions lead to limited improvements.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly used to automate research and development tasks, yet existing benchmarks typically evaluate them on prescribed workflows or narrow action spaces. Even nominally open-ended tasks can often be solved by retrieving a well-known recipe and tuning a few hyperparameters, making it unclear whether strong results reflect genuine optimization or memorized solutions. We introduce InferenceBench, where an agent must deploy an OpenAI-compatible inference server and optimize the speed of LLM inference. Each agent receives a target LLM, one H100 GPU, an optimization scenario, and a wall-clock time budget of two hours. Three optimization scenarios isolate distinct bottlenecks of inference (prefill latency, decode latency, and concurrent request throughput) and a fourth balances all three at the same time. Across 15 frontier agent configurations, agents reliably improve over a naive PyTorch baseline (up to $8.08\times$) and often match or exceed serving engines with default settings ($4.05\times$ for vLLM), but still fall below a simple hyperparameter search under the same time budget (up to $11.53\times$). Qualitative analysis of agent trajectories shows that although agents enumerate many relevant optimization techniques, they overwhelmingly converge on a single inference framework. They test only a few distinct configurations and spend the remaining budget re-measuring, repairing, or optimizing hyperparameters rather than exploring substantially different strategies. This suggests the bottleneck is not domain knowledge, but the ability to propose diverse configurations, evaluate them systematically, and submit the best identified solution. Overall, InferenceBench reflects the ability of agents to operate in an open-ended AI engineering setting, where memorized solutions lead to limited improvements.

</details>


### [104] [ExecuGraph: A Multi-Agent, Execution-Grounded Framework for Reliable Backend Code Synthesis with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20499)
*Sai Deekshith Lekkala,Jothi Prabha Appadurai,Rohith Reddy Bellibatlu,Manpreet Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ExecuGraph is a multi-agent framework for backend code synthesis that uses execution-based validation with six specialized agents coordinated by a typed directed workflow. It shows that multi-agent decomposition provides marginal gains over single-agent baselines, with strongest improvements when using more capable base models (e.g., +22.5 pp on DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs generate plausible backend code but lack correctness and runtime reliability guarantees in single-pass generation. The authors aim to address this gap by placing execution-based validation at the center of code synthesis through a multi-agent decomposition approach.

Method: Proposes ExecuGraph, a multi-agent framework with six agents (Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, Explainer) coordinated by a typed directed workflow with bounded retry budget, implemented on LangGraph with locally hosted models (Ollama), optional retrieval layer, and subprocess-isolated sandbox with wall-clock timeout.

Result: On internal-30 (n=30), conditions are statistically indistinguishable. On HumanEval, multi-agent gains +3.1 pp. Strongest result: with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite, multi-agent improves from 57.5% to 80.0% (+22.5 pp). The framework enables controlled ablation across one-shot, execution-retry, and multi-agent configurations.

Conclusion: The primary contribution is methodological: a configurable codebase enabling controlled measurement of each lever's marginal contribution. Multi-agent decomposition value scales with base-model capability. Detailed per-agent ablation, retry-budget sweep, error-class taxonomy, and test-source audit are reported.

Abstract: Large Language Models generate plausible backend code, but a single-pass paradigm provides no guarantee of correctness or runtime reliability. We present ExecuGraph, a multi-agent framework that places execution-based validation at the center of backend code synthesis. Six specialized agents (Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, and Explainer) are coordinated by a typed directed workflow with a bounded retry budget, implemented on LangGraph with locally hosted models (Ollama) and an optional retrieval layer for algorithmic technique recall. A subprocess-isolated sandbox with a wall-clock timeout guards every evaluation. We evaluate on a curated 30-problem DSA suite (internal-30), HumanEval (n=64), and an APPS-introductory subset, contrasting ExecuGraph against a single-agent one-shot baseline and a single-agent execution-retry baseline (a Reflexion-style ablation that isolates the contribution of multi-agent decomposition). On internal-30, the three conditions are statistically indistinguishable (n=30; paired Wilcoxon p=0.59 MF vs. SO, p=0.08 SR vs. SO); 95% bootstrap confidence intervals on all pairwise mean differences include zero. On HumanEval, multi-full edges ahead by +3.1 pp. The strongest signal is cross-model: with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite, graph-category accuracy improves from 57.5% (oneshot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp jump that supports a scaling hypothesis: the value of multi-agent decomposition grows with base-model capability. The framework's primary contribution is methodological: a single codebase that collapses by configuration into one-shot, execution-retry, and per-agent ablation conditions, enabling controlled measurement of each lever's marginal contribution. A per-agent ablation, retry-budget sweep, error-class taxonomy, and test-source audit are reported.

</details>


### [105] [DecodeShare: Tracing the Shared Subspace of LLM Decode-Time Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20469)
*Zishan Shao,Lixun Zhang,Kangning Cui,Yixiao Wang,Ting Jiang,Hancheng Ye,Qinsi Wang,Zhixu Du,Yuzhe Fu,Fan Yang,Danyang Zhuo,Yiran Chen,Hai Helen Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DecodeShare identifies a low-dimensional subspace shared across tasks in LLM decode-time hidden states. Disturbing this subspace degrades performance more than prefill-derived or random subspaces. This shared subspace has implications for activation steering, where projecting it out separates functional roles, and decode-time steering yields more reliable signals than prefill-based proxies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether there exists a task-general structure in LLM decode-time hidden states (under KV-cached inference) that plays a causal role in decoding, distinct from prefill-time representations.

Method: Proposes DecodeShare, a protocol that identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states, then tests its causal role by ablating that subspace only during decoding and comparing against prefill-derived or random subspace interventions.

Result: Disturbing the discovered decode-shared subspace degrades decision performance significantly more than disturbing prefill-derived or random subspaces under the same intervention budget. The decode-shared subspace overlaps with common activation steering directions.

Conclusion: The decode-shared subspace serves as a compact but high-leverage causal channel at decode time. Projecting it out separates functional roles of steering components, and decode-time steering evaluation yields more reliable signal for downstream deployment than prefill-based proxies.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) handle many tasks with one set of parameters, but under KV-cached inference it is unclear what task-general structure, if any, is used at decode time rather than during prefill. We propose DecodeShare, a protocol that identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states, and then tests its causal role by removing that subspace only during decoding. In our experiments, disturbing the discovered shared subspace degrades decision performance far more than disturbing either a prefill-derived or random subspace under the same intervention budget. We further show this decode-shared subspace has practical consequences for activation steering: common steering directions can overlap the task-general decode channel. Projecting out this shared subspace directly separates the functional roles of the two components, while evaluating steering vectors at decode-time yields more reliable signal for downstream deployment than prefill-based proxies. Despite its compactness, the shared subspace can serve as a high-leverage causal channel at decode time. Code is available at: https://github.com/Zishan-Shao/decodeshare.git.

</details>


### [106] [StrideDiffusion: Accelerating Diffusion Models for Time-series Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20545)
*Du Yin,Estrid He,Julián Jerónimo Bañuelos,Yang Yang,Feng Hu,Yuchen Luo,Hao Xue,Stephan Sigg,Flora Salim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StrideDiffusion is a training-free, spectral-aware sampler for time-series diffusion models that adaptively selects denoising strides based on band-level spectral activity (relative band energy, log-power drift, phase velocity), achieving up to 18.9x speedup with 14-66 function evaluations instead of 500/1000 steps while preserving or improving generation quality across unconditional generation, imputation, and forecasting tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models for time series require many sequential denoising steps at inference, limiting practical use. Existing fast samplers use fixed or generic timestep schedules, ignoring the fact that different spectral bands evolve at different rates during the reverse diffusion process.

Method: StrideDiffusion monitors three spectral indicators (relative band energy, log-power drift, phase velocity) at each step to determine whether high-frequency dynamics are still active. It takes fine steps when rapidly varying bands are active and larger jumps when only stable low-frequency structure remains. A bandwise stability analysis shows inactive bands change linearly with jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates, justifying spectral activity as a step-size indicator.

Result: On six unconditional benchmarks, StrideDiffusion uses only 14-66 function evaluations vs. 500/1000 steps (up to 18.9x wall-clock speedup) with preserved or improved quality. For conditional imputation and forecasting, it achieves 5-14x average acceleration with comparable predictive accuracy.

Conclusion: Spectral evolution provides a practical and principled signal for fast time-series diffusion sampling, enabling significant speedups without sacrificing generation quality.

Abstract: Diffusion models have become competitive generators for time series, but their practical use is limited by the large number of sequential denoising steps required at inference time. Existing fast samplers typically use fixed or generic timestep schedules, overlooking a distinctive property of time-series diffusion: different spectral bands evolve at different rates during the reverse process. We introduce StrideDiffusion, a training-free spectral-aware sampler that adaptively selects the denoising stride from band-level activity. At each step, StrideDiffusion monitors relative band energy, log-power drift, and phase velocity to identify whether high- frequency dynamics remain active or whether the trajectory is dominated by stable low-frequency structure. It then takes fine steps when rapidly varying bands are active and larger jumps once only coarse components remain. A bandwise stability analysis shows that inactive frequency bands change only linearly with the jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates, providing a local justification for spectral activity as a step-size indicator. Across six unconditional time-series generation benchmarks, StrideDiffusion uses only 14-66 function evaluations instead of 500/1000 denoising steps, achieving up to 18.9x wall-clock speedup while preserving or improving generation quality. On conditional imputation and forecasting, it further delivers 5-14x average acceleration with comparable predictive accuracy. These results show that spectral evolution provides a practical and principled signal for fast time-series diffusion sampling. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/stridediff-ts.

</details>


### [107] [PlanE: Meta Planning of Data, Tuning, and Inference for Extractive-based LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20470)
*Jiacheng Wang,Weiyan Zhang,Guangya Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PlanE is a planning framework for constructing extractive-based LLMs that includes data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference, along with a DTI planner to select optimal base-LLM and its combinations for specific datasets, achieving effectiveness across different datasets and base-LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large instruction-tuning datasets impose high annotation costs and lack optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific tasks.

Method: Proposes PlanE, a planning framework with data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference; introduces a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner to select optimal base-LLM and DTI combinations for specific datasets.

Result: Effectiveness demonstrated across different datasets using the same base-LLM, and on the same dataset using different base-LLMs; generalizability of DTI planner validated under different optimization objectives.

Conclusion: PlanE effectively enhances task-specific LLM construction efficiency and the DTI planner generalizes well across different optimization objectives.

Abstract: Enhancing the task-specific capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) primarily requires substantial instruction-tuning datasets. However, the sheer volume of such data imposes a considerable annotation cost, and a lack of optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific tasks. To address the above issues, we propose a \textbf{Plan}ning framework for constructing \textbf{E}xtractive-based LLMs called \textbf{PlanE}, which includes data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference. Additionally, we introduce a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner, aimed at selecting the optimal base-LLM and its DTI combinations for specific datasets to improve construction efficiency. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our PlanE from two views: (1) across different datasets using the same base-LLM, and (2) on the same dataset using different base-LLMs. Furthermore, we validate the generalizability of the proposed DTI planner under different optimization objectives. The codes are publicly available at https://github.com/gugugu-469/PlanE.

</details>


### [108] [Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20972)
*Swapnanil Saha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Coding agents rely on deliberate memory (documents), but human expertise relies on involuntary, situationally-cued memory. The paper argues agents need a second-tier, harness-owned memory system for reliable long-running operation, and demonstrates that voluntary memory use is near-zero in practice while deterministic cue-based injection works reliably.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current coding agents only have deliberate memory (documents, plans, memory directories), but humans rely on involuntary, situationally-cued "second tier" memory (gotchas, locations, conventions). This gap severely limits long-running agent reliability.

Method: (1) Two-tier design theory grounded in cognitive science (memory offloading, incidental encoding, event-based prospective memory); (2) cue-anchored memory model with deterministic trigger conditions over path/symbol/semantic/event/temporal vocabularies; (3) controlled evaluation on real coding tasks measuring voluntary vs. injected memory use.

Result: Voluntary memory use was near zero (0 memory operations in 114 turns). Deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms. 39% of intra-session re-reads re-bought content across compaction boundaries. Conversation-only facts vanished at first summary (absent in 106/108 compactions). Harness-injected facts survived all 138 compact-resumes.

Conclusion: Delivery, not storage, is the product. The reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about — memory must be a harness property, not an agent choice.

Abstract: Coding agents ship with one kind of memory: documents. Instruction files, plan artifacts, and auto-written memory directories are deliberately authored and deliberately retrieved: the agent must choose to write them and choose to read them back. Human expertise runs on a second tier that never gets written down: situationally-bound operational facts (gotchas, locations, local conventions) encoded as a side effect of the work and retrieved involuntarily when the situation cues them. We argue this second tier is the load-bearing one for long-running agents and must be a harness property, not an agent choice. We contribute: (1) a two-tier design theory grounded in the cognitive literature on memory offloading, incidental encoding, and event-based prospective memory, each mapped to an architectural requirement; (2) a cue-anchored memory model where memories carry first-class trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal), evaluated deterministically by the harness, a composition no surveyed academic or shipped system provides; (3) a controlled evaluation on a real coding task showing that voluntary memory use is near zero even with a pre-seeded store (0 memory operations in 114 turns), that deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms, and that 39% of intra-session re-reads re-buy content paid for before a compaction boundary; (4) a repeated-compaction decay probe: ten facts held only in conversation vanish at the first summary and stay absent from 106 of 108 compactions, and the deprived agent greps the harness's own session files to rebuild them, while the same facts injected from a harness-owned store arrive intact through all 138 compact-resumes as the final summary carries none. Delivery, not storage, is the product: the reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about.

</details>


### [109] [Benchmarking the Personalization Capabilities of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20471)
*Ashutosh Srivastava,Siddharth Yedlapati,Vinay Aggarwal,Yaman Kumar Singla,Shashwat Dixit,Jitendra Ajmera,Balaji Krishnamurthy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SDR-Bench is a new benchmark (6,279 customer stories, 22 industries) for evaluating how well LLMs perform two-party personalization (Bayesian Persuasion framework). Tests show all models plateau; none statistically separates successful from failed outreach. Field validation with 12 sales reps shows 48% usefulness and high expert agreement (Pearson 0.82).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM personalization benchmarks evaluate sender-side adaptation (same user the model serves), but the two-party question—whether a generated message induces intended action from a third party—has only been studied via A/B tests and small-scale human studies that are not reproducible on demand against new models.

Method: Adapts the Bayesian Persuasion framework (Kamenica & Gentzkow, 2011) to generative agents; instantiates it in sales with temporally constrained simulation to prevent data leakage. Releases SDR-Bench (6,279 customer success stories) and SDR-Arena for reproducible evaluation.

Result: All frontier LLMs and deep-research agents show a consistent personalization plateau; on a Fortune 100 tech cohort, no model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach. Field deployment with 12 sales reps: 48% of model-generated content rated immediately useful, senior-expert agreement at Pearson 0.82.

Conclusion: Current LLMs exhibit a fundamental personalization plateau in two-party settings; the public release of SDR-Bench and SDR-Arena enables reproducible study of generative personalization at scale.

Abstract: Personalization, the act of varying a message to induce action from a specific receiver while keeping sender, channel, and time fixed, has a long tradition in psychology and marketing as a two-party problem in which sender and receiver have independent objectives. Large language models remove the bounded-inventory constraint of classical retrieval-and-ranking approaches by generating a continuum of message variants conditioned on inferred receiver state, raising the question of how well current models perform personalization in the classical sense. Existing LLM personalization benchmarks measure sender-side adaptation, in which the receiver is the same user the model is serving. The two-party question, whether a generated message induces its intended action in a third party, has been investigated only through A/B tests and small-scale human studies that cannot be re-run against a new model on demand. We adapt the Bayesian Persuasion framework of Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) to generative agents and instantiate the formulation in sales, where receiver actions are routinely logged against the outreach that induced them. We release SDR-Bench, a public corpus of 6,279 customer success stories spanning 22 industries and approximately 200 enterprises, served through a temporally constrained simulation that prevents future-data leakage. Across frontier LLMs and deep-research agents, we observe a consistent personalization plateau and on a Fortune 100 tech cohort no model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach. A field deployment with 12 professional sales representatives validates the framework, with 48 percent of model-generated content rated immediately useful and senior-expert agreement at Pearson 0.82. We release SDR-Arena and SDR-Bench publicly to support reproducible study of generative personalization at scale.

</details>


### [110] [HiMe: Real-Time Self-Hosted Personal Agent Platform for Health Insights with Wearable Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21019)
*Wei Liu,Siya Qi,Linhai Zhang,Lorainne Tudor Car,Yulan He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HiMe is a locally deployable, privacy-first agent platform that enables real-time, personalised health signal analysis from wearable devices by treating the database as a first-class component, jointly optimising effectiveness and efficiency, and modelling users over the long term.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional wearable health analysis suffers from rigid frameworks and limited personalisation. Existing LLM agent solutions are not open-source, locally deployable, or capable of real-time privacy-preserving health data processing.

Method: HiMe is built on three design principles: (1) treating the database as a first-class component, (2) jointly optimising effectiveness and efficiency for a Pareto-optimal balance, and (3) real-time data processing with long-term user modelling.

Result: The platform achieves a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance between effectiveness and efficiency, enabling continuous, personalised health monitoring compatible with various wearable devices.

Conclusion: HiMe makes Personal Health Agents practical for individuals by providing a privacy-first, locally deployable solution for adaptive and contextual health insights in real time.

Abstract: Traditional approaches to wearable health signal analysis, such as smartwatches, are constrained by rigid analytical frameworks and limited personalisation. The emergence of LLM agents creates a new opportunity for Personal Health Agentic Analysis, where health insights can be generated adaptively and in context. However, currently there is no open-source locally deployable platform capable of processing personal health data in real time while preserving privacy. We present HiMe, a locally deployable, privacy-first agent platform that is fully compatible with real-time health data ecosystems across a wide range of wearable devices. HiMe is guided by three design principles. The database is treated as a first-class component. Effectiveness and efficiency are jointly optimised to achieve a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance. Data are processed in real time while the user is modelled over the long term. Together, these principles make it practical for individuals to harness Personal Health Agents for continuous, personalised health monitoring for better wellbeing.

</details>


### [111] [Robust Critics: Defending LLMs Against Multi-Turn Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20472)
*Roman Belaire,Arunesh Sinha,Pradeep Varakantham*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DCGS infers user intent across multi-turn dialogue to improve LLM safety against adversarial attacks, modeling conversation as a Markov Decision Process and using value/regret critics to reweight responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety frameworks use context-free, bandit-style rules that ignore conversational trajectory, making them unable to distinguish genuine attacks from well-meaning questions, especially in multi-turn settings where harmful intent emerges gradually.

Method: DCGS models adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process, learns value and regret-based critics at token and utterance levels, and performs inference-time reweighting via action-value critics. This reweighting approximates exponential tilting of the base policy, guaranteeing expected return improvement for any finite candidate pool.

Result: Outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, and Harmbench. Transfers to frontier models, improving robustness without fine-tuning.

Conclusion: DCGS provides a principled, theoretically-grounded safety framework for multi-turn adversarial dialogue that dynamically infers user intent from conversation history, guaranteeing improved expected return.

Abstract: When a user asks a language model something harmful, is it a genuine attack or a misunderstood but well-meaning question? This ambiguity is one of the central challenges of LLM safety. A model that assumes the worst harms legitimate users; one that assumes the best is easily exploited. The problem is compounded in multi-turn dialogue, where an attacker's true intent may only reveal itself gradually across many exchanges, yet existing safety frameworks apply a contextual bandit treatment, ignoring the trajectory of the conversation.
  To that end, we propose Dialogue Critic Guided Sampling (DCGS), a framework that addresses this by inferring user intent at every turn of dialogue. Instead of applying a fixed rule about what is or is not safe, DCGS learns what the user's intent is likely to be based on the full conversational history and generates responses accordingly. Formally, we model adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process and learn value and regret-based critics at both the individual token and utterance (full response) levels, scoring candidate responses via an action-value critic. We prove that this inference-time reweighting approximates exponential tilting of the base policy, guaranteeing improvement in expected return for any finite candidate pool, a property that group-relative objectives do not exhibit. Evaluated on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, and Harmbench, DCGS outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on adversarial dialogue tasks. DCGS also transfers to frontier models, improving their robustness without fine-tuning.

</details>


### [112] [Euclid-MCP: A Model Context Protocol Server for Deterministic Logical Reasoning via Prolog](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21412)
*Bartolomeo Bogliolo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Euclid-MCP is an open-source MCP server that provides deterministic logical reasoning via SWI-Prolog, using a novel intermediate representation (Euclid-IR) for Horn-clause logic. It enables LLM clients to delegate inference through a translate-run-inspect-repair loop, outperforming pure LLMs on multi-step logical reasoning tasks in security and compliance domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs excel at language tasks but are unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning in safety-critical domains. Existing neuro-symbolic approaches lack standardized interfaces for tool-augmented agents, and semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for rule enforcement.

Method: Euclid-MCP implements an MCP server with SWI-Prolog backend, introduces Euclid-IR as an engine-agnostic intermediate representation for Horn-clause logic, and provides a translate-run-inspect-repair loop tool interface for LLM clients to delegate reasoning while accessing proof traces and derivation logs.

Result: LLMs alone suffice on small knowledge bases but hallucinate systematically on larger problems. Euclid-MCP delivers exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs. Semantic RAG is shown to be unsuited for rule enforcement.

Conclusion: Euclid-MCP can serve as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems, addressing the reliability gap in neuro-symbolic integration for logical reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at natural language understanding and generation but remain unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning, especially in safety-critical or compliance-sensitive domains. Recent neuro-symbolic approaches address this gap by coupling neural models with external symbolic engines, yet most integrations are bespoke and lack a standardized interface for tool-augmented agents. This paper presents Euclid-MCP, an open-source MCP server that provides deterministic logical reasoning via SWI-Prolog. Euclid-MCP introduces Euclid-IR, an engine-agnostic intermediate representation for Horn-clause logic that is human-readable, easy for LLMs to generate, and straightforward to compile into Prolog or alternative backends. The server exposes a compact tool interface that supports a translate-run-inspect-repair loop, enabling LLM clients to delegate inference while retaining full access to proof traces and derivation logs. We evaluate Euclid-MCP on a realistic IT security and compliance use case. Results show that while LLMs alone are sufficient on small knowledge bases, they hallucinate systematically on larger problems, whereas Euclid-MCP delivers exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs. We argue that semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for rule enforcement, and that Euclid-MCP can serve as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems.

</details>


### [113] [Incomplete Prompt Jailbreaks in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20473)
*Yeonjea Kim,Bumjin Park,Jaesik Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs' sentence completion feature remains vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts (IPJ). The paper characterizes this vulnerability, shows that refusal is systematically delayed, and that standard safety tuning fails to generalize. It identifies two functional neuron types—termination and continuation neurons—and proposes neuron-level interventions for more robust defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To formalize and systematically characterize the vulnerability of LLMs to incomplete prompt jailbreaks (IPJ), where open-weight models with safety safeguards still produce harmful continuations when given incomplete harmful prompts.

Method: Empirical characterization of IPJ by analyzing diverse attractor types associated with incomplete sentence continuation; parameter tuning experiments to test refusal generalization across content domains and attractor types; identification of two functional neuron types (termination and continuation neurons) via neuron-level analysis.

Result: LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination; parameter tuning fails to generalize refusal to incomplete harmful prompts across different content domains and attractor types; two functional neuron types (termination and continuation neurons) are identified as targets for fine-grained control.

Conclusion: Neuron-level interventions targeting termination and continuation neurons offer more precise and robust defenses against IPJ compared to standard parameter tuning approaches.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly released as open-weight models with safeguards against harmful requests. Nevertheless, sentence completion remains vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts. In this work, we formalize this phenomenon as incomplete prompt jailbreaks (IPJ) and provide a systematic empirical characterization of when and how incomplete prompts elicit harmful continuations. We analyze diverse attractor types associated with incomplete sentence continuation and show that LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination. We further demonstrate that training models to refuse incomplete harmful prompts via parameter tuning is insufficient, failing to generalize across both content domains and attractor types. To enable fine-grained control, we identify two functional neurons: termination and continuation neurons. By clarifying their roles in sentence completion, we highlight the potential of neuron-level interventions for more precise and robust IPJ defenses.

</details>


### [114] [VeriSimpl: Robust Optimization Modeling from Natural Language using Simplification-based Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20474)
*Sumaya Abdul Rahman,Seckhen Ariel Andrade Cuellar,Ghani Raissov,Mohammad Raza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriSimpl is a solver LLM framework that uses simplification-based verification—generating simplified diagnostic queries via the optimization solver—to enable LLMs to robustly translate natural language problem descriptions into correct optimization formulations, achieving improved accuracy and a novel self-verification signal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To ensure automatically inferred optimization formulations from natural language correctly implement the intended task, addressing the key challenge that existing LLM-based approaches may produce formulations that execute without errors but are semantically incorrect.

Method: Simplification-based verification: the optimization solver generates simplified diagnostic queries (along dimensions of constraints and decision variables) that allow the LLM to reason locally under fixed global contexts about the correctness of a candidate formulation relative to the task description.

Result: Consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods across optimization benchmarks, plus a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

Conclusion: Simplification-based verification is an effective strategy for robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization, providing both higher accuracy and a reliable self-verification capability.

Abstract: Natural language interfaces can greatly benefit the accessibility and usability of optimization modeling, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs) show promise in automatically translating textual problem descriptions into executable solver formulations. However, a key challenge for existing approaches is to ensure that the inferred formulation correctly implements the intended task, even if it may execute without errors. We introduce VeriSimpl, a solver LLM framework for robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization. Our approach is based on the idea of simplification-based verification, where the optimization solver is leveraged to generate simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation to allow the LLM to tractably reason about the correctness of the formulation with respect to the task description. We present such simplification strategies along different dimensions with respect to problem constraints and decision variables, which allow the LLM to reason locally under fixed global contexts. Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks show how our approach provides consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods, while also providing a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

</details>


### [115] [SonicSampler: Unified Tile-Aware Kernels for LLM Sampling and Speculative Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20475)
*Pragaash Ponnusamy,Shivam Sahni,Jue Wang,Tri Dao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SonicSampler is a unified Triton kernel suite that vertically fuses the complete LLM sampling pipeline (logit processing, token selection, speculative verification) into a single, CUDA Graph-compatible kernel, achieving up to 16x speedup over baselines via a novel hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM sampling implementations are fragmented: they accelerate only subsets of the pipeline, rely on multiple kernel launches, or assume homogeneous sampling across a batch. This limits support for dynamic serving workloads (e.g., per-request grammar constraints, penalties) and prevents efficient CUDA Graph execution.

Method: SonicSampler employs tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuse the entire sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. It introduces a hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm that exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs for efficient large-vocabulary selection, and supports dynamic per-request sampling features (grammar decoding, penalties, logit bias, top-k/top-p/min-p filtering, speculative verification) within a single batched kernel.

Result: The hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm achieves up to 10x speedup over competitive baselines. On heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to 16x speedup over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving flexible batched execution.

Conclusion: SonicSampler demonstrates that vertical fusion of the entire sampling pipeline into CUDA Graph-compatible, tile-aware kernels delivers substantial speedups and flexibility for modern LLM serving, overcoming the fragmentation of prior approaches.

Abstract: Sampling in LLM inference comprises a combinatorial set of logit processing, token selection, and verification operations for speculative decoding. However, existing implementations either accelerate only subsets of this pipeline, rely on multiple kernel launches, or assume homogeneous sampling behavior across a batch, limiting support for dynamic serving workloads and preventing efficient CUDA Graph execution. We present $\textbf{SonicSampler}$, a unified suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuses the complete sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. Our kernels support dynamic per-request sampling behaviors, including grammar-constrained decoding, repetition, frequency and presence penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-$k$ / top-$p$ / min-$p$ filtering, and speculative verification - within a single batched kernel while remaining fully CUDA Graph-compatible. Central to our approach is a novel hierarchical two-stage top-$k$ algorithm that achieves up to $\textbf{10x speedup}$ over competitive baselines and exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs to enable efficient selection over large vocabularies. Across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to $\textbf{16x speedup}$ over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving flexible batched execution.

</details>


### [116] [Benchmarking Large Language Models on Multi-Sensor Physical Hazard Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20476)
*Faizan Iqbal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Five large language models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) fail to generate precautionary warnings when multiple physical hazard sensors are simultaneously elevated below individual safety thresholds, despite near-perfect accuracy on single-sensor threshold violations. Tested on 60 scenarios (1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0), models scored near zero on multi-sensor joint assessment (Category A Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) vs. strong single-sensor performance (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether large language models can reliably assess multisensor physical hazard data for safety monitoring applications, particularly in scenarios where multiple sensors are elevated but individually remain below their safety thresholds.

Method: Empirical benchmark testing five LLMs across 60 scenarios in three categories (multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, pattern disambiguation) using 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0; also tested structured tabular formatting vs. plain prose.

Result: All models scored near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) vs. near-perfect on single-sensor threshold violations (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). Structured tabular formatting showed no consistent advantage; ChatGPT-4o performed significantly better under prose (p = 0.001).

Conclusion: Current LLMs exhibit a critical blind spot in multi-sensor joint assessment, failing to generate precautionary warnings when multiple sensors are elevated below individual thresholds, which has direct implications for deploying these models in physical safety monitoring systems.

Abstract: We present an empirical benchmark evaluating how five large language models assess multisensor physical hazard data. Testing 60 scenarios across three categories - multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, and pattern disambiguation - with 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0, we find that all tested models consistently produced no precautionary warning signal across the tested scenarios where multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated below their individual safety limits, while achieving near-perfect accuracy on single-sensor threshold violations. All five models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) score near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) compared to strong performance on single-sensor scenarios (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). Structured tabular formatting shows no consistent advantage over plain prose; ChatGPT-4o performs significantly better under prose (p = 0.001). These findings have direct implications for practitioners deploying the tested models in physical safety monitoring systems.

</details>


### [117] [Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20477)
*Yurui Lai,Samir Moustafa,Renchi Yang,Tsz Nam Chan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a unified semi-supervised framework called \algo{} for distilling Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) that integrates graph topology with textual semantics. It uses Wasserstein Distance-guided collaborative encoding, graph sketching, and LLM-based text synthesis to achieve state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-offs for both GNN and LLM downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing representation learning methods on Text-Attributed Graphs suffer from scalability bottlenecks when combined with LLMs, and current data distillation approaches fail to capture graph-text interplay, struggle with label scarcity, and cannot produce human-readable textual attributes required for LLM-based tasks.

Method: \algo{} introduces: (1) a graph-text collaborative encoding module with dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and graph-free) in a collaborative self-training scheme for pseudo-labeling and feature fusion; (2) a Wasserstein Distance-based graph sketching algorithm for condensation; (3) a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module using cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent summaries for condensed nodes.

Result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that \algo{} achieves state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-offs on both GNN- and LLM-based downstream tasks.

Conclusion: \algo{} enables effective and efficient TAG learning and analytics by addressing scalability, label scarcity, and text readability challenges in a unified semi-supervised framework.

Abstract: {\em Text-Attributed Graphs} (TAGs) have emerged as an expressive data model for integrating graph topology with rich textual semantics. Existing representation learning methods over TAGs suffer from severe scalability bottlenecks, particularly together with {\em Large Language Models} (LLMs). While data distillation offers a promising data-centric solution, existing methods fail to capture the complex interplay between graph and text modalities, struggle with the label scarcity inherent in semi-supervised settings, and lack the ability to produce the human-readable textual attributes required for downstream LLM-based tasks.
  To address these challenges, we propose \algo{}, a unified semi-supervised framework guided by the {\em Wasserstein Distance} (WSD). Grounded in our empirical findings on real TAGs, \algo{} introduces a graph-text collaborative encoding module that utilizes dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and -free) within a collaborative self-training scheme to harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse complementary graph-text features. Furthermore, we develop a theoretically grounded WSD-based graph sketching algorithm and a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module, which leverages cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that \algo{} achieves a state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-off in terms of both GNN- and LLM-based downstream tasks, enabling effective and efficient TAG learning or analytics.

</details>


### [118] [Beyond Liars' Bench: The Impact of Lie Typology, Depth, and Sparsity on Deception Detection in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20479)
*Amr Moustafa,Max Feser,Florian Mai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper systematically studies factors affecting deception detection probes in LLMs, finding that representation depth is dataset-dependent, expressive probes offer only selective gains, sparse features match dense states, and lie typology in training data significantly impacts detectability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training probes to detect deceptive outputs from LLMs remains an open problem, as detection probes fail especially in out-of-domain scenarios where training on one type of lie does not transfer well to other deception scenarios.

Method: The authors augment standard benchmark training data with a supplementary dataset containing diverse types of deception (fabrication, omission, exaggeration) and analyze factors across seven probe types, examining representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse feature representations, and lie typology.

Result: Optimal representation depth is highly dataset-dependent; more expressive probes provide only selective gains over linear baselines; sparse autoencoder features perform similarly to dense hidden states; and the choice of training data and lie typology substantially changes detectability.

Conclusion: Deception detection is a highly representation-dependent problem, with lie typology and training data composition being critical factors for probe performance.

Abstract: Training probes to detect deceptive outputs from large language models is still an open problem. Recent work has demonstrated that detection probes fail especially in out-of-domain scenarios -- training on one type of lie does not transfer well to deception scenarios involving other types of lies. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on how various factors impact detection performance: representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse feature representations, and the lie typology of the training data. To this end, we augment standard benchmark training data with a supplementary dataset containing diverse types of deception, including fabrication, omission, and exaggeration examples. Analyzing these factors across seven probe types, our experimental results show that the optimal representation depth is highly dataset-dependent, more expressive probes provide only selective gains over linear baselines, and sparse autoencoder features perform similarly to dense hidden states. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the choice of training data and lie typology substantially changes detectability, highlighting that deception detection is a highly representation-dependent problem.

</details>


### [119] [Enabling Scalable Topology Inference in Distribution Systems via Constrained Multi-Source Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20480)
*Haoran Li,Lihao Mai,Muhao Guo,Jiaqi Wu,Yang Weng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a constrained inference framework for distribution topology identification that refines utility-provided base topologies using heterogeneous evidence (electrical, spatial, operational constraints), achieving >95% reconstruction accuracy on 8,000+ AMI meters across three feeders while significantly reducing computational effort compared to global inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate distribution system topology is critical for outage localization, voltage analytics, and grid operations, but maintaining reliable connectivity records is challenging due to heterogeneous and imperfect utility data. Existing methods relying on electrical similarity or spatial records alone become unreliable in dense feeders and under inconsistent metadata conditions.

Method: The framework formulates topology identification as a constrained inference problem: it detects inconsistent assignments in a utility-provided base topology, performs localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods to ensure scalability, and iteratively enforces physical feasibility. A falsification-driven reliability metric evaluates the strength of each inferred connection relative to alternatives.

Result: Validated on three feeders with >8,000 AMI meters in collaboration with a U.S. utility. Achieves >95% topology reconstruction accuracy with significantly reduced computational effort compared to global inference. Correlation-based methods alone produce ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders, while the proposed method combining electrical, spatial, and operational constraints enables robust recovery.

Conclusion: Combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints enables robust and scalable topology recovery under realistic deployment conditions. The reliability metric helps utilities prioritize verification efforts while preserving system-wide observability.

Abstract: Accurate distribution system topology is essential for outage localization, voltage analytics, and operation of distribution grids, yet maintaining reliable connectivity records remains challenging in practice due to heterogeneous and imperfect utility data. Existing topology identification methods often rely primarily on electrical similarity or spatial records alone, which become unreliable in dense feeders and under inconsistent metadata conditions. This paper formulates distribution topology identification as a constrained inference problem that refines a utility-provided base topology using heterogeneous evidence while enforcing spatial feasibility and physical operational constraints. Instead of reconstructing connectivity from scratch, the proposed framework detects inconsistent assignments, performs localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods to ensure scalability, and iteratively enforces physical feasibility to produce operationally consistent topology estimates. In addition, a falsification-driven reliability metric evaluates how strongly each inferred connection is supported relative to alternative feasible assignments, enabling utilities to prioritize verification efforts while preserving system-wide observability. The framework is validated using operational data from three feeders comprising more than $8{,}000$ AMI meters in collaboration with a large U.S. utility. Results demonstrate over $95\%$ topology reconstruction accuracy while significantly reducing computational effort compared with global inference approaches. The study further shows that correlation-based methods alone produce ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders, whereas combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints enables robust and scalable topology recovery under realistic deployment conditions.

</details>


### [120] [Routing Without Training: Controllable-Ratio LLM Offloading via Reliability Gating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20481)
*Evan Chen,Shiqiang Wang,Kevin S Chan,Su Wang,Christopher Brinton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CARGO is a training-free routing framework for local-cloud LLM collaboration that uses the local model's own inference-time agreement across sampled responses to decide when to offload to a stronger cloud model, outperforming both training-free baselines and supervised routers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing local-cloud collaboration methods rely on trained routers or collaboration-aware finetuning, which tie routing behavior to a particular operating regime and require additional training overhead. The authors aim to show that training may be unnecessary by leveraging the local model's intrinsic response behavior.

Method: CARGO estimates agreement through prompt-varied sampling, applies Bayesian early stopping for sample-efficient uncertainty control, and supports arbitrary target collaboration ratios through lightweight deployment-time calibration.

Result: Across diverse reasoning and QA tasks, multiple local LLM families and scales, and both pretrained and finetuned local models, CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines and in several settings surpasses supervised learned routers.

Conclusion: Effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can emerge directly from the local model's intrinsic response behavior without requiring an additional trained router.

Abstract: Local-cloud collaboration is a practical way to deploy large language models under resource constraints, but existing methods often rely on trained routers or collaboration-aware finetuning that tie routing behavior to a particular operating regime. In this work, we show that such training may be unnecessary: the local model's own inference-time agreement across sampled responses already provides a strong signal for deciding when to trust local execution and when to offload to a stronger cloud model. We propose CARGO, a training-free routing framework that estimates this agreement through prompt-varied sampling, applies Bayesian early stopping for sample-efficient uncertainty control, and supports arbitrary target collaboration ratios through lightweight deployment-time calibration. Across diverse reasoning and question-answering tasks, multiple local LLM families and scales, and both pretrained and finetuned local models, CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines and in several settings surpasses supervised learned routers. These results suggest that effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can emerge directly from the local model's intrinsic response behavior, without requiring an additional trained router.

</details>


### [121] [PersonaTrail: Benchmarking Personalized Web Agents through Browsing Trails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20482)
*Seungbin Yang,Chaewoon Ki,Dohyun Lee,Jaegul Choo,ChaeHun Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PersonaTrail is a new benchmark for evaluating personalized web agents that must infer user preferences from raw browsing histories. The authors also propose PACMem, a memory framework that decomposes histories into factual and preference memories, consistently outperforming existing baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks fail to capture personalization in web agents because they either use fully explicit prompts or simplify web interaction history, whereas in practice users often give underspecified instructions requiring agents to infer context from raw browsing histories.

Method: The authors introduce PersonaTrail (a benchmark using realistic browsing trajectories) and propose Preference-Aware Contextual Memory (PACMem), a framework that decomposes raw browsing histories into factual memories (summarizing individual sessions) and preference memories (distilling recurring behavioral patterns), with relevant retrieval at inference time.

Result: PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both tasks in the PersonaTrail benchmark.

Conclusion: Personalized web agents can effectively leverage structured memory decomposition (factual + preference memories) to infer user preferences and recall past session information, and PersonaTrail provides a more realistic evaluation setting for such capabilities.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models have enabled web agents to autonomously execute complex tasks. In practice, users frequently provide underspecified instructions, requiring agents to infer the missing context from their raw browsing histories. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this form of personalization, as they either restrict tasks to fully explicit prompts or abstract web interaction history into simplified forms. To bridge this gap, we introduce PersonaTrail, a benchmark for personalized web agents operating in a managed open web environment. By leveraging realistic browsing trajectories as user history, PersonaTrail evaluates an agent's ability to infer user preferences and recall information from past browsing sessions. We further propose Preference-Aware Contextual Memory (PACMem), a framework that decomposes raw browsing histories into two types of structured memory: factual memories that summarize individual sessions and preference memories that distill recurring behavioral patterns. At inference time, the agent retrieves the most relevant entries from these memories to guide personalized navigation. Extensive experiments show that PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both tasks.

</details>


### [122] [Tractable Hierarchical Control of Autoregressive Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20483)
*Max Scribner,Antonio Vergari,Vaishak Belle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper shows that constraining LLM generation to satisfy LR(k) grammars can be done in polynomial time (improving from exponential), enabling efficient steering of LLMs toward syntactically valid output for languages like SQL and JSON.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Constraining autoregressive LLMs to produce syntactically valid output is critical for integrating them into formal systems like program synthesis, where languages (SQL, JSON) are often LR(k) context-free grammars.

Method: The authors distill the LLM to a tractable probabilistic model and use steering/masking to incorporate probabilities of satisfying logical constraints. They prove that satisfaction of any LR(k) grammar of finite duration can be computed in polynomial time.

Result: The satisfaction of any LR(k) grammar of finite duration can be calculated in polynomial time, a significant improvement over the previous exponential time methods.

Conclusion: This polynomial-time result enables efficient constraint and steering of LLM generation toward outputs that better satisfy formal syntactic constraints.

Abstract: Constraining the generation of autoregressive large language models (LLMs) is an important component of integrating language models into formal systems. In the generation of code and data for tasks like program synthesis, ensuring that language models produce syntactically valid output is a prerequisite for processing such output. These languages (such as SQL or JSON) are often designed as $LR(k)$ context-free grammars. By distilling the LLM to a tractable probabilistic model, its autoregressive generation can be steered and masked to incorporate the probability of satisfying logical constraints, ensuring high quality output that is guaranteed to be valid. This paper demonstrates that the satisfaction of any $LR(k)$ grammar of finite duration can be calculated in polynomial time, an improvement over the exponential time of applying previous methods to such grammars. This result enables efficient constraint and steering of LLM generation towards output that better satisfies formal syntactic constraints.

</details>


### [123] [The Devil is in the Spectrum: Mitigating Representation Collapse in LLMs via Topologically Regularized Side-Path](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20484)
*Yiheng Tao,Kaiwen Cheng,Yao Lu,Chang Liu,Jie Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRSP introduces a Topologically Regularized Side-Path with a Triangular Box mechanism and length-aware gating to resolve the trade-off between homogenization and isolation collapse in LLMs, achieving spectral balance in attention dynamics and significantly improving long-context performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs suffer from representation collapse in long-context scenarios, drifting into either homogenization collapse (e.g., attention sinks causing rank deficiency) or isolation collapse (e.g., local attention causing context disconnection). Existing standard attention mechanisms struggle to balance mixing efficiency (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank).

Method: TRSP is a non-invasive architectural intervention that achieves spectral balance via: (1) a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism to regularize token interaction topology, (2) a lightweight, length-aware gate for scaling, (3) proximal coupling to preserve effective rank, and (4) distal propagation to support non-degenerate mixing, all without altering core attention.

Result: TRSP shows significant improvements on general capabilities and long-context benchmarks. On NoLiMa at 8× the training length, it retains 83% accuracy, outperforming Differential Transformer by ~30 percentage points and Gated Attention by ~50 percentage points.

Conclusion: TRSP effectively resolves the spectral dilemma in LLM attention by promoting a geometrically healthier transition operator, enabling robust long-context generalization without modifying the core attention mechanism.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are fundamentally limited by representation collapse, a bottleneck that severely degrades long-context performance. We identify that existing approaches risk drifting into one of two pathological extremes: homogenization collapse (e.g., attention sinks causing rank deficiency) and isolation collapse (e.g., local attention causing context disconnection). Through spectral analysis of attention dynamics, we derive an intrinsic trade-off between mixing efficiency (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank) that standard mechanisms struggle to balance. To resolve this dilemma, we propose the Topologically Regularized Side-Path (TRSP), a non-invasive architectural intervention that achieves spectral balance. TRSP employs a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism, scaled by a lightweight, length-aware gate, to regularize the token interaction topology. By integrating proximal coupling to preserve effective rank and distal propagation to support non-degenerate mixing, TRSP promotes a geometrically healthier transition operator without altering core attention. Experiments show significant improvements across general capabilities and long-context benchmarks. Notably, on NoLiMa at $8\times$ the training length, TRSP retains $83\%$ accuracy and surpasses the Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by approximately 30 and 50 percentage points, respectively. Code available at: https://github.com/Eziotao-tyd/TRSP.

</details>


### [124] [Expectation Alignment of Language Models for Real-World User Expectations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20485)
*Miaomiao Li,Yang Wang,Bin Liang,Shudong Liu,Zhiwei Zhang,Kam-Fai Wong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs appear competent on standard benchmarks but fail to meet real user expectations. This paper introduces ExpectBench, a benchmark grounded in real user expectations, and proposes LENS, a framework that improves alignment by explicitly modeling latent user expectations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation methods (heuristics, expert rubrics, user simulation) fail to capture the diversity and subtlety of real human expectations, causing a fundamental misalignment between LLM performance on benchmarks and what users actually seek.

Method: (1) A principled procedure to extract semantically rich user expectations from real-world LLM interactions; (2) ExpectBench, a benchmark grounded in these real user expectations; (3) LENS (Latent Expectation-aware reSponse generation), a lightweight framework that internalizes user expectations to generate better-aligned responses.

Result: Current LLMs struggle to satisfy and anticipate user expectations. LENS consistently improves expectation satisfaction over baseline models, demonstrating the value of explicit expectation modeling.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling user expectations is crucial for realistic human-AI alignment; the proposed LENS framework offers a promising direction for bridging the gap between benchmark performance and actual user needs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance on standard benchmarks, yet it remains largely unexplored whether they truly meet user expectations. Existing evaluation approaches, relying on model heuristics, expert rubrics, or user simulation, fail to capture the diversity and subtlety of real human expectations, causing models to appear competent while misaligning with what users actually seek. We present the first systematic study of user expectations in real-world LLM interactions, proposing a principled procedure to extract semantically rich expectations and introducing ExpectBench, a benchmark grounded in real user expectations. Analyses reveal that current LLMs struggle to satisfy and anticipate what users hope to obtain, highlighting a fundamental source of misalignment. Building on these observations, we propose LENS, a lightweight latent expectation-aware response generation framework. LENS enables models to internalize user expectations and generate better-aligned responses, consistently improving expectation satisfaction and underscoring the importance of explicitly modeling user expectations for realistic human-AI alignment.

</details>


### [125] [OPTScientist: Multi-Agent Discovery of Typed Optimizer Programs for Transformer Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20486)
*Zhongzheng Li,Tiancan Feng,Wenhao Li,Qingsong Ran,Shikun Feng,Xiaoyuan Zhang,Yue Wang,Xiaoguang Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPTScientist is a theory-guided multi-agent framework for automated optimizer discovery using a typed DSL, combining evolutionary search with DSL extension mechanisms, leading to the discovery of RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing optimizers for modern deep learning is challenging due to the need to balance optimization geometry, state dynamics, numerical stability, implementation constraints, and generalization. Existing automated methods are either too flexible (producing invalid programs) or too constrained (limiting novelty).

Method: OPTScientist uses a typed domain-specific language (DSL) with six modules (direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, grouping) and four role agents (Theorist, Designer, Engineer, Reviewer) in a closed-loop orchestration. It combines evolutionary search over optimizer programs with a second-stage DSL extension mechanism that triggers when repeated failures indicate representational bottlenecks.

Result: Discovery of RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines under the authors' native evaluation protocol.

Conclusion: The results suggest a viable path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation.

Abstract: Designing optimizers for modern deep learning remains a challenging scientific problem, requiring the joint consideration of optimization geometry, state dynamics, numerical stability, implementation constraints, and empirical generalization. Existing automated optimizer discovery methods typically search either over unconstrained code spaces or within narrowly parameterized optimizer families. The former is flexible but often produces invalid or uninterpretable programs, while the latter is stable but limits novelty. We introduce OPTScientist, a theory-guided multi-agent framework for optimizer discovery in a typed domain-specific language (DSL). OPTScientist formulates optimizer design as a constrained scientific search process, where candidate updates are expressed through direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, and grouping modules. Four role agents, Theorist, Designer, Engineer, and Reviewer, collaborate within a single orchestration loop to propose hypotheses, synthesize DSL candidates, compile and evaluate optimizers, and critique results. To overcome the limitations of a fixed search space, OPTScientist combines evolutionary search over optimizer programs with a second-stage mechanism that proposes small DSL extensions when repeated failures reveal representational bottlenecks. Using this framework, we discover RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines under our native evaluation protocol. Our results suggest a path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation.

</details>


### [126] [Directional Hallucinations: Ideological Drift in News-Grounded LLM Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20487)
*Chendi Wang,Liam Cunningham,Tom Yishay,Jieying Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates ideological drift in LLM-generated political information by measuring hallucinations in document-grounded QA. Using 21,727 labeled U.S. political news articles, the authors find that while hallucination rates differ across models and topics, the content of hallucinations exhibits a systematic leftward ideological bias, with left-leaning hallucinations more common even when answering questions about right-leaning sources. Logit analysis links this drift to high-entropy generation contexts, suggesting an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for political information and election-adjacent tasks, where factual errors and ideological distortions carry high stakes. The authors aim to develop a reproducible framework to detect and measure ideological drift in LLM outputs by treating hallucinations (unsupported statements) as diagnostic signals.

Method: The authors use the QBias dataset (21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles from left, center, and right sources). Their framework: (i) generate article-specific questions, (ii) elicit document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, (iii) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison, (iv) classify the ideological valence of hallucinated sentences using a fine-tuned stance classifier, and (v) probe output logits to relate token-level uncertainty to hallucination and drift.

Result: Hallucination rates vary substantially across models and concentrate in contentious topics. Source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest. However, hallucination content exhibits robust leftward drift—a majority of hallucinated sentences are classified as left-leaning, including those generated from right-leaning sources. Logit analysis shows hallucinations arise in high-entropy contexts, and for some models, uncertainty predicts leftward drift, consistent with an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism.

Conclusion: The findings have implications for auditing AI-mediated political information and designing safeguards in election-relevant deployments, highlighting that ideological distortion in LLMs is not symmetric and may require targeted mitigation strategies beyond reducing overall hallucination rates.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about political information, including in election-adjacent information settings where factual errors and ideological distortions are high-stakes. We present a reproducible measurement framework that treats hallucinations, unsupported statements in document-grounded QA, as diagnostic signals of ideological drift. Using 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles from QBias spanning left, center, and right sources, we (i) generate an article-specific question, (ii) elicit document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, (iii) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison, (iv) classify the ideological valence of hallucinated sentences with a fine-tuned stance classifier, and (v) probe output logits to relate token-level uncertainty to hallucination and drift. Hallucination rates vary substantially across models and concentrate in contentious topics, while source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest. In contrast, hallucination content exhibits robust leftward drift: a majority of hallucinated sentences are classified as left-leaning, including among hallucinations generated from right-leaning sources. Logit-level analysis shows hallucinations arise in high-entropy generation contexts, and in some models uncertainty also predicts leftward drift, consistent with an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism. We discuss implications for auditing AI-mediated political information and for designing safeguards in election-relevant deployments.

</details>


### [127] [Autonomous Topology Mutation: Safe Runtime Restructuring for Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Capability, State, and Shadow Invariants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20488)
*Bronislav Sidik,Chaya Levi,Nizzan Kimhi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ATM is a runtime team-mutation mechanism for multi-agent LLM frameworks that detects overloaded agents via telemetry and safely factorizes them into specialized sub-agents, improving code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7% while preserving privacy and adding minimal latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM frameworks fix team topology at boot time and cannot restructure when agents become overloaded due to mixing action categories, tool error accumulation, or call queueing.

Method: ATM combines telemetry-driven overload detection (via a six-signal Bottleneck Index) with three safety invariants (capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, shadow-before-live validation) to factorize overloaded agents into specialized sub-agents with privacy-level-aware state routing.

Result: Code-task success improved from 3.3% to 61.7%; high-privacy memory exposure reduced from 2.0 to 0.0 events per task; p99 latency overhead <500μs on agent hot path.

Conclusion: Runtime topology mutation is viable and effective for multi-agent LLM systems, enabling dynamic restructuring without compromising safety or privacy.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM frameworks typically fix their team topology at boot time. When an individual agent becomes overloaded at runtime, for example by mixing too many action categories, accumulating tool errors, or queueing behind too many calls, the system has no mechanism to restructure itself. We introduce Autonomous Topology Mutation (ATM), a runtime team-mutation mechanism for multi-agent LLM frameworks. ATM combines telemetry-driven overload detection with three safety invariants that gate each structural change: capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, and shadow-before-live validation.
  ATM monitors a six-signal Bottleneck Index that includes queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, and cross-agent wait time. When a warmup-calibrated threshold is breached for multiple consecutive ticks, ATM factorises the overloaded agent into specialised sub-agents and hot-swaps the parent into a coordinator role while preserving its external identity. State transfer is controlled by privacy-level-aware routing: each memory atom is routed only to a permitted child set, or explicitly dropped with a logged reason. No candidate topology receives live traffic until it has passed a shadow validation window.
  On 720 DeepSeek-V3-driven task runs with deterministic tool stubs across four ablation conditions and three workloads, the ATM factoriser split lifts code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7%. The full rail-and-distillation system reduces detected high-privacy memory exposure under a regex classifier from 2.0 to 0.0 events per task while preserving task quality.
