Building upon the AppWorld framework with 9 popular simulated apps like Amazon and Spotify, we systematically modify original tasks to introduce ambiguities and constraints that necessitate various types of agent-user interaction. User behavior is simulated by an LLM prompted to respond with carefully designed knowledge boundaries, offering more reliable simulation than the unconstrained or overly rigid alternatives used in prior work. Our evaluation reveals that a state-of-the-art LLM, Claude Opus 4.7, achieves only 48.6% success on AppWorld-UL, and only 35.7% on the harder, compositional subset. On the stricter, scenario-level metric, compositional task performance drops to only 21.3%. Our analysis reveals that correct user-interaction is crucial for success. This demonstrates the benchmark's difficulty and its potential to advance research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents.

</details>


### [154] [CMI-Mem: Toward Generalizable Long-Term Memory Management via CMI-Augmented Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20553)
*Yubo Wang,Qiuyu Zhao,Zenghui Sun,Shichao Dong,Jinsong Lan,Xiaoyong Zhu,Haoyang Li,Bo Zheng,Lei Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CMI-Mem is a lightweight RL-based memory manager for agent systems that uses a hybrid reward combining downstream QA correctness and Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) to evaluate memory value without relying solely on LLM-judged synthetic QA pairs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory manager models rely on LLM-judged synthetic QA pairs, making memory valuation dependent on sampled queries and downstream readers, which limits generality and robustness.

Method: Proposes CMI-Mem, an RL-based lightweight memory manager with a hybrid reward: (1) downstream QA correctness for task grounding, and (2) Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) to intrinsically evaluate information contributed by new conversational inputs relative to current memory state without requiring sampled QA queries.

Result: The CMI-Mem-4B model checkpoint is released; CMI complements QA grounding to improve memory valuation.

Conclusion: CMI-Mem addresses the query-dependency limitation of prior memory managers by introducing CMI as an intrinsic reward signal, offering a more robust and generalizable approach to memory management in agent systems.

Abstract: Memory Manager models are pivotal in agent systems. Existing methods rely predominantly on LLM-judged synthetic question-answer (QA) pairs, making memory valuation dependent on sampled queries and the downstream reader. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{CMI-Mem}, a reinforcement learning(RL)-based lightweight memory manager model with a hybrid reward that combines downstream QA correctness and intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI). CMI evaluates the information contributed by new conversational inputs relative to the current memory state without conditioning on a sampled QA query, thereby complementing rather than replacing QA grounding. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/Wyb0627/CMIMem , and the CMI-Mem-4B model checkpoint is available at: https://www.modelscope.cn/models/wyb0627/CMIMem-4B

</details>


### [155] [AI-Driven Multi-Hop Relay Selection for Smart Urban NR-V2X Networks via Learning-to-Optimize Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20554)
*Giambattista Amati,Federica Mangiatordi,Simone Angelini,Emiliano Pallotti,Pierpaolo Salvo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a GNN-based Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework to approximate optimal MILP multi-hop relay selection for NR-V2X in dense urban environments, achieving comparable connectivity with orders-of-magnitude faster inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Limited RSU density, frequent NLOS conditions, and dynamic vehicular topologies prevent CAVs from maintaining stable single-hop connectivity; multi-hop relay selection under real-time constraints is computationally challenging.

Method: Formulates relay selection as MILP for optimality; models vehicular communication states as attributed graphs; uses an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) trained with offline MILP oracle supervision to approximate optimal decisions in real time.

Result: Achieves connectivity comparable to the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude on large-scale urban datasets from SUMO-GEMV2 simulation.

Conclusion: The L2O framework enables scalable, real-time NR-V2X relay selection using existing vehicular assets, cost-effectively enhancing urban V2X connectivity for smart city environments.

Abstract: Reliable and low-latency NR-V2X communications are essential for smart mobility in dense urban environments. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) density, frequent non-line-of-sight conditions, and highly dynamic vehicular topologies often prevent many Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable single-hop connectivity. Although multi-hop relay-assisted communication can extend infrastructure coverage, selecting relay links in real time under practical flow, capacity, and connectivity constraints remains challenging.
  Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) yields optimal multi-hop relay decisions, but its computational complexity scales sharply with network density, limiting real-time applicability. To address this, we propose a Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time NR-V2X relay selection. Vehicular communication states are modeled as attributed graphs, where CAVs and RSUs are nodes and candidate radio links are enriched with propagation-aware features. An offline MILP oracle provides optimal supervision, while an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) approximates oracle decisions with near-constant inference latency. Experiments on large-scale urban datasets generated by an integrated SUMO--GEMV2 simulation pipeline show that the proposed approach achieves connectivity comparable to that of the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude. The framework enables cost-effective enhancement of urban V2X connectivity by leveraging existing vehicular assets and supporting scalable, real-time NR-V2X operation in smart city environments.

</details>


### [156] [KeySI: An Interaction Framework for Tuning Text Embeddings Based on Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20556)
*Yan Zhu,Y. Chen,Rebecca Faust*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KeySI is an interaction framework that uses keyword-based concept specification to adapt pre-trained language models for domain-specific text analysis, reducing the need for manual document labeling and technical expertise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained language models struggle to capture domain-specific semantics when embedding text corpora, and adapting them typically requires large amounts of labeled data and technical expertise.

Method: KeySI enables feature-level feedback through keyword-based concept specification. Users organize extracted keywords into groups representing concepts, which are translated into document-level supervision for model tuning. The framework curates keywords, visualizes them via dimensionality reduction, allows interactive keyword grouping, and supports iterative refinement.

Result: Evaluated through a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments demonstrating effectiveness in capturing user intent and improving embedding alignment.

Conclusion: KeySI reduces the need for manual document inspection and labeling, lowering the barrier to adapting embedding models for domain-specific tasks.

Abstract: In large-scale text analysis tasks, pre-trained language models are often used to embed text corpora for downstream analysis. However, such models may struggle to capture domain-specific semantics and adapting them typically requires large amounts of labeled data and technical expertise to implement training pipelines. Recent approaches have demonstrated how visual interactions in document projections can capture human feedback as training signals for model tuning. However, these methods operate on document-level feedback, which requires users to open and assess individual documents in order to provide effective feedback. In this paper, we propose KeySI, an interaction framework that enables feature-level feedback through keyword-based concept specification. Users specify feedback by organizing extracted keywords into groups representing concepts, which KeySI translates into document-level supervision for subsequent tuning. By operating on keywords as the primary interaction medium, KeySI reduces the need for manual document inspection and labeling and lowers the barrier to adapting embedding models. We present a prototype implementation that, given a corpus, curates representative keywords, visualizes keywords and document embeddings via dimensionality reduction, allows interactive specification of keyword groups, and supports iterative refinement through system feedback. We evaluate KeySI through a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing user intent and improving embedding alignment.

</details>


### [157] [WaveformQA: Benchmarking LLM Temporal Reasoning on Digital Waveforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20638)
*Yichuan Liu,Daniel Cummings,Nick Vadlamudi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WaveformQA is an open-source benchmark with 360 questions across 8 categories for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms. Tests show LLMs struggle with complex temporal questions, and JSON representation outperforms VCD format.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs' ability to perform temporal reasoning over digital waveform data is largely unexplored, yet this is a critical bottleneck in design verification. Existing benchmarks focus on HDL code generation and use waveforms only as supplementary context.

Method: Created WaveformQA benchmark with 360 programmatically generated questions across 8 difficulty categories targeting multi-signal correlation and event ordering. Waveforms generated from open-source design implementations. Evaluated frontier LLMs and compared JSON vs VCD waveform representations.

Result: LLMs achieve reasonable accuracy on simple queries but performance degrades on complex temporal and multi-step questions due to context window limitations and reasoning difficulties. Event-time JSON representation improves reasoning accuracy over VCD format.

Conclusion: WaveformQA provides an open-source, extensible framework for evaluating and improving LLM temporal reasoning on digital waveforms, with future potential for new question categories and waveform sources.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and reasoning, yet their ability to perform temporal reasoning over digital waveform data remains largely unexplored. Although reasoning over digital waveforms is a critical bottleneck in design verification, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate hardware description language (HDL) code generation and use waveforms only as supplementary context. This paper presents WaveformQA, an open-source question-answering benchmark for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms. The benchmark comprises 360 questions with programmatically generated ground truths across eight categories of varying difficulty, including questions targeting multi-signal correlation and event ordering. Waveforms are generated from open-source design implementations, ensuring reproducibility and grounding the benchmark in real hardware behavior. Evaluation of frontier LLMs reveals that while models achieve reasonable accuracy on simple queries, performance degrades due to context window limitations and reasoning difficulties on complex temporal and multi-step questions. In addition, we show that an event-time JSON representation of waveforms improves LLM reasoning accuracy versus the standardized value change dump (VCD) format. The open-source framework supports extending to new question categories and importing new waveform sources, enabling researchers to rapidly prototype temporal reasoning experiments.

</details>


### [158] [NVIDIA-labs OO Agents: Native Python Object-Oriented Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20709)
*Paul Furgale,Severin Klingler,James Nolan,Matt Staats,Gaia Di Lorenzo,Elisa Martinez Abad,Christian Schüller,Razvan Dinu,Alessio Devoto,Pascal Berard,Gal Kaplun,Elad Sarafian,Riccardo Roveri,Leon Derczynski,Ricardo Silveira Cabral*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NOOA is a Python framework where agents are defined as Python objects—methods become actions, fields are state, docstrings are prompts, and type annotations are contracts. It unifies agent and developer programming models, enabling standard software practices (testing, tracing, refactoring) for agent development. The paper presents the programming model, identifies six combined design ideas, and shows strong benchmark results on SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench, and ARC-AGI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional agent development is fragmented across prompt templates, tool schemas, callback code, and workflow graphs, lacking a unified, software-engineering-friendly interface.

Method: Agents are implemented as Python objects: methods = LLM actions, fields = state, docstrings = prompts, type annotations = contracts. Methods with "..." body are LLM-driven; methods with normal bodies remain deterministic. Agent-specific capabilities (context, events, memory, LLM loops) are exposed via Pythonic APIs.

Result: Demonstrates effective performance on SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and ARC-AGI-3 benchmarks, showing current models can use this interface effectively.

Conclusion: NOOA unifies agent and developer programming models, making agent development testable, traceable, refactorable, and improvable like standard software. The paper identifies six model-facing ideas combined for the first time on a single surface.

Abstract: Traditional agent development is split across prompt templates, tool schemas, callback code, and workflow graphs. We present NVIDIA Object-Oriented Agents (NOOA), a model-agnostic Python framework for building reliable AI agents. NOOA takes a simpler approach: an agent is a Python object. Its methods are the actions the model can take, fields are its state, docstrings are its prompts, and its type annotations are contracts. A method whose code body consists of "..." is completed at runtime by an LLM-driven agent loop, while methods with normal bodies remain standard deterministic Python. This gives developers and agents the same interface, so agent behavior can be tested, traced, refactored, and improved just like other software.
  This paper makes three contributions. (1) We present the agent-as-a-Python-object programming model and the design principles behind it. Where Python has existing abstractions, we adopt them directly. Agent-specific capabilities--context, events, state rendering, long-term memory, and validated LLM loops--are exposed through simple Pythonic APIs, so both developers and agents share one familiar programming model. (2) We identify six model-facing ideas that NOOA is, to our knowledge, the first to combine on a single surface: typed input/output, pass-by-reference over live objects, code as action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs for context and events. We find the community already converging on several of these ideas--often as experimental or partial features--and present the comparison to encourage further adoption. (3) We demonstrate that current models use this interface effectively, both in targeted capability tests and on agentic and reasoning benchmarks such as SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 and ARC-AGI-3.

</details>


### [159] [ArbiGraph: Arbitrarily Scalable Verifiable Task Graphs for Evaluating Context Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20764)
*Pavel Golikov,Evgenii Opryshko,Gennady Pekhimenko,Mark C. Jeffrey*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ARBIGRAPH is a benchmark generator that evaluates how well tool-assisted language agents handle extended reasoning workflows by composing tasks into graphs with varying complexity, revealing significant accuracy degradation (up to 33.3%) on complex dependent tasks compared to isolated tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate LLM agents on single tasks or simple chains, failing to capture failures in retaining, updating, composing, and discarding context across extended multi-step reasoning workflows.

Method: ARBIGRAPH creates controllable task graphs where each node is a natural-language problem with an executable Python solver, connected via typed intermediate states (scalar/list values). Task graphs vary in length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value type, with exact automatic verification.

Result: On a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent, accuracy drops by up to 33.3% on branching chains of dependent math tasks compared to isolated tasks, demonstrating substantial degradation on complex dependent workflows.

Conclusion: ARBIGRAPH exposes reasoning failures invisible in single-task evaluation, highlighting the need for benchmarks that test compositional, multi-step reasoning in tool-assisted language agents.

Abstract: We introduce ARBIGRAPH, a benchmark generator for evaluating whether tool-assisted language agents can retain, update, compose, and discard task-relevant context across extended reasoning workflows. ARBIGRAPH represents each task as a natural-language problem with an executable Python solver, and composes tasks through typed intermediate states, instantiated here as scalar and list values. This design enables controllable task graphs whose length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value type can be varied while preserving exact automatic verification. We instantiate ARBIGRAPH with math, GSM-style word-problems, and Python-tracing task categories, and evaluate a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent across four topologies. The results show high accuracy on isolated tasks but substantial degradation on more complex dependent tasks: accuracy drops by up to 33.3% on branching chains of dependent math tasks. This shows that ARBIGRAPH exposes failures that are not visible from single-task evaluation alone. Our code, generated datasets, and evaluation results are available at https://github.com/pavelgolikov/ArbiGraph.git

</details>


### [160] [The Human-AI Substitution Principle: When will you be replaced by AI in your organization?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20781)
*Bonny Banerjee,Shreya Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents the Human--AI Task Allocation (HAT) model, an analytical framework for studying when and under what structural conditions AI replaces human employees in hierarchical organizations. It introduces the Human--AI Substitution Principle, showing that AI adoption can cause abrupt workforce transitions, hybrid organizations, and flatter hierarchies, with middle management being particularly vulnerable to automation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a formal analytical model that addresses the fundamental organizational and economic question of when human employees will be replaced by AI, moving beyond anecdotal or empirical observations to establish rigorous theoretical foundations for understanding AI-driven workforce transformation.

Method: An analytical model (HAT) that formally encodes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling, incorporating risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk to derive conditions for human--AI substitution.

Result: The Human--AI Substitution Principle provides a precise condition for AI replacement of human labor. Key findings include: abrupt workforce transitions, hybrid human--AI organizations, flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control, elevated middle-management vulnerability to automation, and a skill threshold determining highly skilled worker vulnerability.

Conclusion: The HAT model unifies automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a coherent theory of AI-driven organizational transformation, offering structural insights for workforce planning and organizational redesign.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming organizations, raising a fundamental organizational and economic question: when will a human employee be replaced by AI? We present an analytical model for studying Human--AI Task Allocation (HAT) in hierarchical organizations. A central feature of the HAT model is that it formally encodes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling. The HAT model allows us to derive how risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk jointly determine when, where, why, and under what structural conditions human--AI replacement occurs. A key result is the Human--AI Substitution Principle, which provides a precise condition --- grounded in the formal asymmetry assumption --- under which AI replaces human labor. Building on this result, we show that AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions, hybrid human--AI organizations, including cases where risk heterogeneity sustains human and AI roles without requiring a minimum-human-fraction constraint, and flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control. The HAT model identifies structural conditions under which middle-management roles exhibit elevated vulnerability to automation, and shows that the vulnerability of highly skilled workers depends on a skill threshold shaped by organizational depth, baseline costs, and risk differentials. More broadly, the paper connects automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a unified theory of AI-driven organizational transformation.

</details>


### [161] [Refusal-Gated Decoding: Preserving Refusal Behavior Under High-Temperature Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20791)
*Phillip Howard,Xin Su,Allen Roush,Manikandan Ravikiran,Amir Abdullah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: High-temperature sampling increases LLM diversity but weakens safety guardrails. The authors propose an efficient sequential decoding method that preserves greedy decoding refusal behavior at high temperatures (91-99% preservation) with minimal latency overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of existing solutions for maintaining LLM refusal behavior under high-temperature sampling (higher entropy regime), despite high-temperature sampling increasing diversity and the importance of maintaining model safety.

Method: A sequential decoding approach that preserves a model's greedy decoding refusal response at high temperatures while incurring minimal additional latency.

Result: The approach preserves 91-99% of greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets without compromising high-temperature response quality for safe prompts.

Conclusion: Refusal behavior can be maintained efficiently for applications requiring high-temperature sampling, enabling both diversity and safety.

Abstract: High-temperature sampling is one of the primary mechanisms for increasing diversity in LLMs. Recent advances in truncation-based sampling techniques have helped mitigate drawbacks of high-temperature sampling such as neural text degeneration, thereby enabling greater diversity in LLM outputs without sacrificing coherence. However, increasing the entropy of the token probability distribution via high temperatures has also been shown to weaken model guardrails by reducing the model's refusal response in the presence of harmful prompts. Despite the potential benefits of high-temperature sampling and the importance of maintaining model safety, there is a lack of existing solutions for maintaining the refusal behavior of LLMs under a higher entropy regime. To address this gap, we systematically study how temperature influences refusal behavior in LLMs and propose an efficient sequential decoding approach which preserves a model's greedy decoding refusal response at high temperatures while incurring minimal additional latency. Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach preserves 91-99% of the greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets without compromising the model's high-temperature response for safe prompts. Our work demonstrates how refusal behavior can be maintained in an efficient manner for applications which require high-temperature sampling.

</details>


### [162] [Profiling Lightweight Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20806)
*Tomohiro Harada,Enrique Alba,Gabriel Luque*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a PTME (Precision, Time, Memory, Energy) framework for profiling lightweight LLMs in resource-constrained environments, finding that static proxies like parameter count or FLOPs fail to predict precision, and that multi-dimensional Pareto analysis reveals deployment configurations hidden by single-metric evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM efficiency evaluations rely on proxy descriptors (parameter count, FLOPs) decoupled from task precision, which are inadequate for guiding real-world deployment in resource-constrained edge and mobile environments where energy, time, and memory directly affect usability.

Method: A PTME-based experimental framework that jointly measures Precision, execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption via direct hardware-level measurements, applied to lightweight LLMs on a controlled desktop platform under edge-class resource envelopes using benchmarks for code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding.

Result: Static proxy descriptors approximate inference cost well but fail to predict precision. Tightening resource envelopes increases cost without affecting precision, penalizing larger models most. No single model dominates all PTME dimensions; Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments.

Conclusion: Selecting lightweight LLMs by size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone can select the wrong deployment candidate. PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost, providing practical guidance for model selection under different resource constraints.

Abstract: Lightweight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed locally on personal computers and are expected to play a growing role in resource-constrained edge and mobile environments. In such settings, energy consumption, execution time, and memory usage directly affect practical usability, yet existing evaluations of LLM efficiency largely rely on proxy descriptors such as parameter count or FLOPs, often decoupled from task precision. This paper introduces a PTME-based experimental framework for the precision-aware profiling of lightweight LLM inference, jointly measuring Precision, execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption through direct hardware-level measurements. The methodology is applied to a representative set of lightweight LLMs executed locally under edge-class resource envelopes on a controlled desktop platform, using benchmarks spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding. We find that static proxy descriptors approximate inference cost well but fail to predict precision. Tightening the resource envelope increases cost without affecting precision, amplifying execution time more strongly than energy and penalizing larger models the most. Moreover, no single model dominates across all PTME dimensions, and a Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations that would be hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments, providing practical guidance for selecting models under different resource envelopes. These results show that selecting lightweight LLMs by size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone can select the wrong deployment candidate; PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost.

</details>


### [163] [Enhancing Explainable Cardiac Diagnosis with Guide-Grounded Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20814)
*Hai-Nam Duy Vuong,Duy-Anh Bui,Trong-Nghia Nguyen,Kim-Ngan Thi Nguyen,Trang Mai Xuan,Tien-Cuong Nguyen,Van-Dem Pham,Thien Van Luong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a guide-grounded multimodal framework for ECG report generation that injects a distilled clinical interpretation guide into the multimodal LLM pipeline, improving BERTScore from 0.818 to 0.953 on PTB-XL while reducing hallucinations and enhancing clinical plausibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical deployment of deep learning for ECG assessment is constrained by poor interpretability and hallucination risks of LLMs. Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM frameworks produce explanations that are only weakly grounded in established diagnostic criteria, reducing trustworthiness and reproducibility.

Method: A CNN and Grad-CAM produce class probabilities and heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. Authoritative ECG textbooks/guidelines are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, injected as a fixed knowledge block. A multimodal LLM is conditioned on the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the guide to generate structured diagnostic reports.

Result: On the full PTB-XL test set, guide grounding improves semantic quality and perceived consistency while preserving competitive classification performance. Average BERTScore of generated impressions increased from 0.818 to 0.953 relative to the CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline.

Conclusion: Injecting a distilled interpretation guide into multimodal prompting reduces hallucinations and enhances clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, bringing explainable cardiac diagnosis closer to real-world deployment.

Abstract: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac as- sessment, yet clinical deployment of deep learning models remains con- strained by limited interpretability and the hallucination risk of large language models (LLMs). Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM frameworks can generate ECG reports, but their explanations are often only weakly grounded in established diagnostic criteria, reducing trust- worthiness and reproducibility. We propose a guide-grounded multimodal framework that explicitly anchors report generation in curated clinical knowledge. A convolutional neural network (CNN) and Grad-CAM first produce class probabilities and class-specific heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. In parallel, authoritative ECG textbooks and guideline materials are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, which is injected as a fixed knowledge block for every sample. Conditioned on the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the in- jected guide, a multimodal LLM generates structured diagnostic reports with guideline-consistent terminology and criteria usage. Experiments on the full PTB-XL test set demonstrate that guide grounding improves se- mantic quality and perceived consistency of generated reports while pre- serving competitive classification performance. In particular, our method increases the average BERTScore of generated impressions from 0.818 to 0.953 relative to a strong CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, indicat- ing closer alignment with reference reports. These findings suggest that injecting a distilled interpretation guide into the multimodal prompting pipeline offers a practical pathway to reduce hallucinations and enhance the clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, bringing ex- plainable cardiac diagnosis closer to real-world deployment.

</details>


### [164] [Efficient and Interpretable Body-Based Emotion Recognition with Lightweight Temporal Convolutional Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20820)
*Christian Arzate Cruz,Stefanos Gkikas,Houshyar Asadi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) achieve competitive body-based emotion recognition accuracy compared to graph-based models while using 79% fewer parameters and 12.5× lower latency, with interpretability analysis revealing upper-body motion as the strongest regional cue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Body-based emotion recognition is important for real-time affective systems, but graph-based skeleton models are computationally expensive; this paper investigates whether lightweight TCNs can serve as efficient and interpretable alternatives.

Method: Evaluated a family of TCN models on DIEM-A dataset against a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline, using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency metrics. Analyzed body-region contributions via region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency.

Result: G-TSG achieves highest mean performance, but TCN-Base is within 1.58 accuracy points and 1.25 macro-F1 points while using 79.18% fewer parameters and ~12.5× lower latency. Upper-body motion provides strongest standalone regional cue; body region usefulness varies across emotions; different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior.

Conclusion: Lightweight TCNs can support efficient body-based emotion recognition while providing practical insight into how motion cues contribute to classification.

Abstract: Body-based emotion recognition is important for real-time affective systems, but graph-based skeleton models can be computationally expensive. This paper studies whether lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can provide an efficient and interpretable alternative for body-based emotion classification. We evaluate a family of TCN models on DIEM-A and compare them with a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Although G-TSG achieves the highest mean performance, TCN-Base remains within $1.58$ accuracy points and $1.25$ macro-F1 points while using $79.18\%$ fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by approximately $12.5\times$. We also analyze body-region contributions using region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency. The results show that upper-body motion provides the strongest standalone regional cue, that the usefulness of body regions varies across emotions, and that different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior. These findings suggest that lightweight TCNs can support efficient body-based emotion recognition while also providing practical insight into how motion cues contribute to classification.

</details>


### [165] [Auditing Provenance Sensitivity in LLM Agent Action Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20827)
*Junchi Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents' actions can be influenced by unauthorized (untrusted) evidence even when authorized evidence is available. In 450 controlled tasks, trusted vs. untrusted evidence variants produced different actions in 5.4% of competing cases and 1.7% of supporting cases, with unauthorized competition retained in ~2.4% of comparisons under controlled degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents process mixed-source contexts (user requests, tool outputs, memory, untrusted text) where relevant evidence may not be authorized to determine decisions. The paper aims to audit whether untrusted evidence improperly influences agent actions despite the presence of authorized evidence.

Method: Target-specific authorization audit: holding task, proposition, position, and policy fixed while varying only the proposition's source authority. Tests behavior when valid evidence is weakened, with context-subset interactions as secondary localization diagnostic. Evaluated across 450 controlled next-action tasks and multiple open-weight LLM families.

Result: Trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4% of competing cases vs. 1.7% of supporting cases. Unauthorized competition retained in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4% of comparisons (95% CI: 2.1-3.0%). Models respond to textual source-authority cues but this does not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing actions.

Conclusion: LLM agents remain vulnerable to unauthorized evidence influencing decisions despite recognizing source-authority cues. The rates are controlled stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence, but indicate a systematic vulnerability in agentic decision-making.

Abstract: LLM agents choose tools and arguments from context that mixes user requests, tool outputs, retrieved records, memory, and untrusted text. Evidence can be relevant without being authorized to determine a decision, so a correct action need not be grounded only in permitted evidence. We introduce a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors separately for each tool and argument target. Its primary test holds the task, proposition, position, and policy fixed while changing only the proposition's source authority. We then test behavior when valid evidence is weakened and use context-subset interactions as a secondary localization diagnostic. Across 450 controlled next-action tasks and multiple open-weight LLM families, trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4 percent of competing cases versus 1.7 percent of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition is retained in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4 percent of comparisons, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 2.1 to 3.0 percent. These are controlled stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence. The models respond to textual source-authority cues, but this does not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing their actions.

</details>


### [166] [Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20848)
*Junchi Liao,Jiawen Deng,Fuji Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A behavioral audit of evidence use in medical LLMs reveals that while most evidence interactions are clinically plausible, accuracy metrics can hide failures—especially with negated/absent findings—motivating role-aware evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diagnostic accuracy alone does not assess whether medical LLMs appropriately used case evidence, motivating a finer-grained audit of evidence utilization.

Method: Decompose patient information into evidence units, score diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets, mine low-order interactions, separate interaction discovery from failure assignment via robustness checks and clinical review.

Result: Faithful support and differential conflict/cancellation dominate interaction strength; invalid/shortcut cases concentrate in negated/absent findings and clinically local evidence; accuracy hides candidate evidence-use failures.

Conclusion: Accuracy can mask evidence-use failures, motivating role-aware audits for medical LLM evaluation.

Abstract: Medical LLMs are often evaluated by whether they select the correct diagnosis, but diagnostic accuracy alone does not show whether the model used the case evidence appropriately. We present a behavioral audit of evidence use in medical diagnosis. For each case, we decompose patient information into evidence units, score candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets, and mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins. Because medical evidence is diagnosis-relative, the audit separates interaction discovery from failure assignment: large or negative interactions can reflect plausible differential diagnosis, while suspicious interactions require robustness checks and clinical review. We evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase. Across datasets, faithful support and differential conflict or cancellation account for most interaction strength, showing that many evidence interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures. In a DDXPlus-focused blinded five-reviewer 130-item enriched review sample, invalid or shortcut-like cases concentrate in negated or absent findings and clinically local evidence. These results show that accuracy can hide candidate evidence-use failures and motivate role-aware audits for medical LLM evaluation.

</details>


### [167] [Code Monitor Red Teaming for Public-Test-Passing Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20852)
*Junchi Liao,Jiawen Deng,Fuji Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies whether weaker LLM verifiers can identify hidden bugs in LLM-generated code that has passed public tests. The authors introduce Code Monitor Red Teaming, a protocol with a public-check information boundary, and instantiate it as CodeMonitorBench. Across 71,000 candidates, 43,677 pass public tests but 23,081 fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers miss most hidden bugs at 5% FPR, and adversarial overfitting pressure degrades verifier performance. A GLM-5.1 verifier partially recovers the gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Visible (public) tests for LLM-generated code are insufficient to certify specification correctness. There is a need to understand whether weaker LLM verifiers can detect residual hidden bugs after code passes public tests, mimicking a real-world deployment monitoring scenario.

Method: The authors propose Code Monitor Red Teaming, a protocol that fixes a public-check information boundary while varying generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capabilities. It is instantiated as CodeMonitorBench, covering function-level, data-science, and workflow code tasks.

Result: Out of 71,000 generated candidates, 43,677 pass public tests, and 23,081 of those fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers miss most hidden bugs at a 5% false-positive rate. Adversarial public-test-overfit pressure reduces verifier AUROC and increases low-FPR miss rates. A GLM-5.1 verifier partially recovers performance under the same evidence boundary.

Conclusion: Weak verifiers have limited effectiveness for detecting hidden bugs after code passes public tests. Remaining misses are a mix of verifier failures and M1 evidence limits, as shown by an inferability audit. The protocol provides a robust framework for stress-testing verifier performance.

Abstract: Visible tests are a common gate for LLM-generated code, but passing them does not certify specification correctness. We study a deployment-like monitoring problem: after code has passed public tests, can a weaker LLM verifier identify the residual hidden bugs? We introduce Code Monitor Red Teaming, a monitor-red-teaming protocol that fixes a public-check information boundary while varying generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capability. We instantiate it as CodeMonitorBench, spanning function-level, data-science, and workflow code. Across 71,000 generated candidates, 43,677 pass public tests and 23,081 of those fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers improve with scaffolding and model family, but still miss most hidden bugs at 5% false-positive rate. As a robustness stress test, adversarial public-test-overfit pressure lowers verifier AUROC and raises low-FPR miss rates in most cells. A GLM-5.1 verifier recovers part of the gap under the same evidence boundary; an inferability audit shows that remaining misses mix verifier failures with M1 evidence limits.

</details>


### [168] [Is Deep Research Reliable? Misleading Knowledge Induces False Conclusions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20891)
*Pengyu Zhu,Lijun Li,Longju Yang,Sen Su*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MisKnow-Agent, a framework for generating misleading knowledge to test Deep Research agents, finding that misleading information can propagate through long-horizon workflows and cause false conclusions in final reports, with current defenses insufficient to fully prevent this.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep Research agents extend LLMs into long-horizon workflows (planning, retrieval, synthesis, report generation), but their reliability in open information environments is underexplored. A key concern is whether misleading knowledge can propagate through these workflows and be adopted as false conclusions in final reports.

Method: The authors propose MisKnow-Agent, a framework that generates misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles, producing 5,933 quality-controlled instances based on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. They conduct extensive experiments on open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents to evaluate vulnerability to misleading knowledge.

Result: Limited exposure to misleading knowledge induces false-conclusion adoption in final reports, revealing a broad reliability vulnerability. Search-enabled verifier models consistently identify instances as misleading during focused corpus validation, yet the same instances are adopted during long-horizon research, indicating a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use.

Conclusion: All evaluated defenses (pre- and post-research) mitigate but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption. Reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation abilities.

Abstract: Deep Research agents extend LLM-based assistants into long-horizon workflows involving planning, retrieval, evidence synthesis, and report generation, yet their reliability in open information environments remains underexplored. A key concern is whether apparently credible but factually misleading knowledge encountered in such environments can propagate through these workflows and be adopted as false conclusions in final reports. To study this failure mode, we introduce MisKnow-Agent, a framework for constructing and validating misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks. MisKnow-Agent generates misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles, yielding 5,933 quality-controlled instances built on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. Extensive experiments across open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents show that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can induce false-conclusion adoption in final reports, revealing a broad reliability vulnerability in current Deep Research agents. Although search-enabled verifier models consistently identify the retained instances as misleading during focused corpus validation, the same instances can still be adopted during long-horizon research, revealing a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use. Finally, we evaluate pre- and post-research defenses, both individually and in combination, finding that all three configurations mitigate but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption. Our findings suggest that reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both the model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation abilities.

</details>


### [169] [Source-Prior-Driven Selective Adaptation for Efficient Diffusion Model Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20913)
*Yi Xiong,Yuan-Yuan Cheng,Xiao-Ming Fu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A source-prior-driven selective adaptation method for fine-tuning diffusion models that identifies parameters minimally impacting general generation via static masking, then applies structured updates, achieving superior adaptation-retention trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods handle the trade-off between target-specific generation improvement and degradation of pretrained model's broad generative capability only implicitly, lacking explicit control over which parameters to adapt.

Method: (1) Learn a static mask to explicitly identify parameters that have minimal impact on general generative capability; (2) Construct structured update strategies for the selected subset of parameters, guided by source-prior knowledge.

Result: The proposed method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off than existing strong baselines in fine-tuning diffusion models.

Conclusion: Explicitly identifying and selectively updating parameters with minimal impact on general generation, using structured strategies, effectively balances target adaptation and retention of pretrained capabilities in diffusion model fine-tuning.

Abstract: Fine-tuning large diffusion models for new domains or styles involves a trade-off: improving target-specific generation often degrades the pretrained model's broad generative capability. Existing full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods typically handle this trade-off only implicitly. In this work, we propose a novel source-prior-driven selective adaptation method to efficiently fine-tune diffusion models, achieving a favorable trade-off. Our method relies on two key observations: (1) the loss of general generative capability is highly inconsistent across pretrained parameters, and (2) parameters that have a relatively small impact on the model's general generative capability remain structurally inconsistent across layers and parameter types. Motivated by these observations, we first learn a static mask to explicitly identify parameters better suited for downstream adaptation, and then construct structured update strategies for the selected subset. Experiments show that our method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off than existing strong baselines.

</details>


### [170] [Traceable Scholarship: Page Anchors and Ariadne's Thread for Humanistic Inquiry in the Age of Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20916)
*Deyu Jing*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Traceable Scholarship as a normative framework for AI-assisted humanistic research, introducing page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, and AIH-Infra—a three-layer reference implementation—to ensure verifiable, source-grounded scholarly output from generative AI, demonstrated via a Kant Akademie-Ausgabe case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI produces fluent but often unverifiable scholarly text lacking explicit sources, page numbers, and editions, creating a dangerous illusion of established explanation. The deep risk is not mere factual error but the appearance of validity without traceability, threatening the public and refutable nature of humanistic research.

Method: The paper situates Traceable Scholarship across three knowledge infrastructure revolutions (print, digital, generative AI) and introduces: page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE marker, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract. It presents AIH-Infra, a three-layer reference implementation comprising Contexture (document structuring), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway).

Result: A case study on a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base demonstrates how traceability supports retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading in AI-assisted humanistic research.

Conclusion: Traceability is not merely a software feature but the fundamental condition under which humanistic research can remain public and refutable in the age of generative AI. The page anchor serves as Ariadne's thread through the labyrinth of generative fluency, leading scholars back to sources.

Abstract: Generative AI lets large language models produce scholarly-looking text within seconds, yet fluency does not equal valid explanation. The deepest risk is not factual error alone but the appearance that an explanation is already established without clear sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence. We liken the page anchor to Ariadne's thread: within the labyrinth of generative fluency, it is the thread that leads the scholar back to the source. This paper proposes Traceable Scholarship as the minimum normative condition for AI-assisted humanistic research, situating it across the three revolutions of knowledge infrastructure: print, digital, and generative AI. We introduce page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract, and present AIH-Infra as a three-layer reference implementation: Contexture (document structuring), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). A case study on a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base illustrates how traceability supports retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading. Traceability is not a software feature; it is the condition under which humanistic research can remain public and refutable in the age of generative AI.

</details>


### [171] [OPOD: On-Policy Omni Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20918)
*Tong Zhao,Yuyang Hu,Reed Li,Yu Lu,Haibo Shi,Yutao Zhu,Zhicheng Dou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPOD routes student responses to modality-specific teachers, using selective probability-based guidance and independent influence adjustment, achieving state-of-the-art omni-modal performance across 12 benchmarks while discarding specialists after training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training a single omni-modal model on pooled multimodal data often underperforms modality-specific specialists, and on-policy distillation with multiple teachers can cause competing guidance that improves one modality at the expense of others.

Method: OPOD routes each student response to the matching text/image/audio teacher; applies teacher guidance only where teacher probability > student probability; adjusts each modality teacher's influence independently; and evaluates both the final answer and reasoning correctness.

Result: Across 12 benchmarks and 3 backbone sizes, OPOD achieves best average scores (70.8, 51.7, 46.2), exceeding strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, 1.7 points. On 30B model, outperforms base and pooled post-trained model on all 12 benchmarks, ranks 1st/2nd on 11 even vs. specialists.

Conclusion: Coordinating modality-specific teachers via OPOD is an effective way to improve a shared omni-modal model while maintaining cross-modal balance, producing a single deployable model after discarding specialists.

Abstract: Omni-modal models can handle text, images, and audio in one system, but improving all of these abilities together remains difficult. Training a single model on pooled multimodal data often fails to match models specialized for individual modalities. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a way to combine such specialists: the student generates a response, and a teacher evaluates that same response, so the student learns directly from behaviors it actually produces. Yet using several teachers can introduce competing guidance and improve one modality at the expense of another. We present On-Policy Omni Distillation (OPOD), which routes each student response to the matching text, image, or audio teacher. OPOD keeps teacher guidance only on tokens where the teacher assigns a higher probability than the student, adjusts the influence of each modality teacher independently during training, and asks the routed teacher to assess both the final answer and whether the reasoning supports the correct answer. Across twelve benchmarks and three backbone sizes, OPOD achieves the best average score at every scale, reaching 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2 and exceeding the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On the 30B model, it outperforms both the base model and a counterpart post-trained jointly on pooled multimodal data on all twelve benchmarks, and ranks first or second on eleven even when the individual specialists are included. The specialists are discarded after training, leaving one deployable omni-modal model. These results show that coordinating modality-specific teachers is an effective way to improve a shared model while maintaining cross-modal balance.

</details>


### [172] [Representing Entity Importance in AI Knowledge Systems: A Dual-Signal Framework of Audience Evaluation and Structural Authority](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20925)
*Shen Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes and empirically validates a dual-signal representation of entity importance for AI knowledge systems, separating audience evaluation (ratings) from structural authority (PageRank), and demonstrates they are non-redundant with only 10-34% overlap, advocating for preserving distinct importance signals for task-aware AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI knowledge systems need entity importance for tasks like retrieval and reasoning, but traditional approaches compress importance into a single score from human feedback or graph structure, potentially losing critical distinctions needed for different tasks.

Method: The framework uses a dual-signal representation with audience-evaluation (IMDb ratings) and structural-authority (Wikipedia PageRank) dimensions. It aligns entities via Wikidata and evaluates 482 movie entities with 13,690 directed relationships using Spearman correlation and overlap analysis.

Result: Weak correlation between dimensions (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Top-10 overlap is only 10%, top-100 overlap is 34%, with entity-level divergence in both directions, confirming non-redundancy.

Conclusion: Audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals and should not be collapsed into a single importance score. AI systems should preserve distinct signals for task-aware selection or aggregation.

Abstract: AI knowledge systems require representations of entity importance for retrieval, recommendation, evidence selection, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. Yet importance is often reduced to a single score derived from either human response or graph structure. Such compression may discard distinctions that matter when an AI system must choose among entities for different tasks. This study introduces an interpretable dual-signal representation in which each entity is characterized by an audience-evaluation dimension and a structural-authority dimension.
  The framework is evaluated using movie entities as an empirical validation domain. IMDb non-commercial datasets provide a rating-based audience ranking, Wikidata supports entity alignment, and English Wikipedia hyperlinks form the knowledge network on which PageRank estimates structural authority. Experiments on 482 entities and 13,690 directed relationships reveal a statistically significant but weak association between the two dimensions (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Their overlap is only 10% in the top 10 and 34% in the top 100, while entity-level divergence occurs in both directions.
  The results show that audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals and should not automatically be collapsed into a single scalar notion of importance. The contribution is not a new ranking algorithm or learned embedding, but a minimal knowledge-representation framework and an empirical test of its dimensional necessity. The findings support task-aware AI knowledge systems that preserve distinct importance signals before applying context-specific selection or aggregation.

</details>


### [173] [SciExplore: Evaluating Autonomous Agents from Scientific Navigation to Information Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20926)
*Yinhao Tang,Youqing Fang,Yanan Sun,Wenran Liu,Weiming Zhang,Bin Liu,Kuikun Liu,Wenwei Zhang,Kai Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SciExplore is a new benchmark evaluating LLMs and agents on scientific information-seeking and reasoning across 103 expert-curated tasks in four complexity levels, revealing that current models perform poorly, especially on complex structured synthesis tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on general-domain retrieval or static QA, failing to assess capabilities needed in realistic scientific research workflows involving heterogeneous sources and complex reasoning.

Method: SciExplore includes 103 expert-curated tasks across four types (database navigation, ambiguous retrieval, missing reference completion, cross-source synthesis) spanning ten+ disciplines, testing abilities from entity-level to domain-level synthesis.

Result: Over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and agents evaluated; performance degrades sharply with increasing task complexity, with extremely low accuracy on the most challenging structured synthesis tasks.

Conclusion: Current LLMs and agents have significant limitations in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios, highlighting major performance gaps as tasks grow more complex.

Abstract: Scientific research involves complex information-seeking and reasoning workflows across heterogeneous sources. However, existing benchmarks primarily emphasize general-domain retrieval or static scientific question answering, and therefore fail to assess key capabilities required in realistic scientific research workflows. We introduce SciExplore, a benchmark designed to evaluate scientific information-seeking and reasoning capabilities of LLMs and agents. SciExplore comprises four task types covering 103 expert-curated tasks across more than ten scientific disciplines: scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source structured knowledge synthesis, which probe progressively higher-level abilities from entity-level reasoning and document-level identification to evidence-level grounding and domain-level synthesis. We evaluate over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents on SciExplore, revealing substantial performance gaps with performance degrading sharply as task complexity increases and extremely low accuracy on the most challenging structured synthesis tasks. These results highlight significant limitations of current models and agents in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.

</details>


### [174] [Clustered Edge Intelligence: Beyond Just Convergence of Edge Computing and AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20937)
*Chinmaya Kumar Dehury,Boris Sedlak,Alaa Saleh,Ilir Murturi,Lauri Loven,Satish Narayana Srirama,Praveen Kumar Donta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI), a visionary framework that treats derived intelligence as a first-class, independently manageable entity across the edge-cloud continuum, addressing the gap in existing edge intelligence research which lacks such an intelligence-centric approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Edge Intelligence research focuses only on using AI for edge resource management and deploying lightweight AI models on edge devices, but lacks an intelligence-centric framework where derived intelligence is treated as a first-class, independently manageable entity that can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications.

Method: The authors introduce Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI), a three-layer architecture designed to make intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity that can be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed across the distributed edge-cloud continuum.

Result: The paper presents a three-layer CEI architecture and examines enabling technologies and research dimensions including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

Conclusion: CEI provides a visionary intelligence-centric approach that shifts focus from data and lightweight AI model deployment to treating derived intelligence itself as a first-class manageable entity, enabling sharing, reuse, and dynamic clustering across heterogeneous edge environments.

Abstract: We are moving from an information age to the age of intelligence. A decade, or possibly less than that, data will not be the gold anymore rather the derived intelligence out of the data and the information we posses from the edge of the network. Existing Edge Intelligence research focuses mainly on two directions: using AI for edge resource management and deploying lightweight AI models on edge devices. However, existing edge computing research lacks an intelligence-centric framework in which derived intelligence is treated as a first-class, independently manageable entity that can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications. To address these research gaps, we introduced Clustered Edge Intelligence, a visionary intelligence-centric approach. The aim of CEI is to make intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity that can be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed across the distributed edge-cloud continuum. We present a three layer CEI architecture and examine enabling technologies and research dimensions, including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

</details>


### [175] [From Scalars to Time Series: Rethinking Implicit Neural Representations for Time-Varying Volumetric Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20970)
*Weihan Zhang,Xuan Zhao,Yenwen Peng,Yuqi Chen,Jun Tao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes reformulating INR training for time-varying volumetric data from coordinate-wise sampling to sequence-level supervision over spatial time series, eliminating the need for dense spatiotemporal sampling, reducing training cost, improving reconstruction quality, and showing compatibility with mixture-of-experts architectures for enhanced capacity allocation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional INR training for time-varying volumetric data relies on dense spatiotemporal coordinate sampling, which is computationally expensive and inefficiently leverages temporal structure. The authors aim to reduce this cost while improving reconstruction quality by rethinking the sampling paradigm.

Method: Instead of coordinate-wise scalar supervision, the data is represented as a collection of spatially indexed time series, and INRs are trained with sequence-level supervision per spatial location, learning each location from its full temporal evolution. This is further combined with mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures to handle heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

Result: The sequence-level reformulation eliminates the need for dense spatiotemporal sampling, consistently improves reconstruction quality, and significantly reduces training cost. The MoE instantiation further improves quality over both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods.

Conclusion: Dense spatiotemporal sampling is unnecessary for learning time-varying fields; sequence-level supervision over spatial time series is more efficient and effective. The approach is compatible with various INR architectures and benefits from mixture-of-experts for heterogeneous dynamics.

Abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) for time-varying volumetric data are typically trained using dense sampling over spatiotemporal coordinates, where each observation corresponds to a single point in space and time. This coordinate-wise formulation requires extensive sampling during optimization, leading to high computational cost and inefficient use of temporal structure. In this work, we revisit this design choice and show that dense spatiotemporal sampling is not necessary for learning time-varying fields. Instead, we represent the data as a collection of spatially indexed time series and train INRs using sequence-level supervision over each spatial location, rather than coordinate-wise scalar samples. This reformulation eliminates the need for dense spatiotemporal sampling and instead learns each spatial location from its full temporal evolution in a structured manner. We demonstrate that this representation is compatible with a range of existing INR architectures and consistently improves reconstruction quality, while significantly reducing training cost. Furthermore, we show that this formulation can be combined with mixture-of-experts architectures, and that our MoE instantiation further improves reconstruction quality compared to both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods, providing a stronger capacity allocation under heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

</details>


### [176] [Beyond Independent Optimization: Compression, MoE Routing, and Quantization Interactions in Multimodal Edge Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20981)
*Jay Gor,Karm Dave,Akshita Abrol,Rajesh Gupta,Sudeep Tanwar,Zhengkui Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper reviews efficient multimodal inference techniques (visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, MoE routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment) and argues they must be treated as interdependent, not independent, optimizations due to cross-component interactions. It introduces Temporal Routing Consistency for video MoE diagnostics and highlights open research directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficient multimodal inference is increasingly constrained not just by model quality or FLOPs, but by the cost of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy constraints. The authors argue that existing techniques are often treated independently, ignoring crucial cross-component interactions.

Method: The paper reviews recent advances in efficient vision-language and multimodal LLMs, organizing the literature around interactions between visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, MoE routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment, and hardware-aware benchmarking. It identifies key design trade-offs and introduces Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models.

Result: The paper identifies key interactions: visual token compression alters downstream feature distributions and MoE routing; routing behavior affects expert utilization and quantization sensitivity; quantized router logits influence expert assignment; KV-cache policies determine retained multimodal evidence; hardware constraints transform computational savings into memory/communication bottlenecks. Key trade-offs include accuracy vs. token budget, static vs. adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency vs. expert collapse, and low-bit inference vs. modality-specific degradation.

Conclusion: The paper introduces Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models and highlights open directions: routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence.

Abstract: Efficient multimodal inference is increasingly constrained not only by model quality or FLOP count, but also by the cost of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy constraints. This paper reviews recent advances in efficient vision-language and multimodal large language models, covering visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment, and hardware-aware benchmarking. We argue that these techniques cannot be treated as independent optimizations. Visual token compression alters downstream feature distributions and MoE routing decisions, routing behavior affects expert utilization and quantization sensitivity, quantized router logits influence expert assignment, KV-cache policies determine retained multimodal evidence, and hardware constraints often transform computational savings into memory and communication bottlenecks. We organize the literature around these interactions and identify key design trade-offs, including accuracy versus token budget, static versus adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency versus expert collapse, and low-bit inference versus modality-specific degradation. Finally, we introduce Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models and highlight open research directions in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence.

</details>


### [177] [GuardianAgentBench: Where Agents Fail and How to Guard Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20982)
*Vishal Ishwar Naik,Chenyu Xu,Donna Dong,Hussein Hassan,Abhishek Pradhan,Ofer Mendelevitch,Tallat Shafat,Humayun Irshad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GABench is a 580-scenario benchmark across six domains for evaluating LLM agent safety, revealing that even the best models achieve only 74.8% accuracy, with guardrails recovering 19.9% of failures at 0.5% false positive rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents increasingly operate autonomously with tools and external environments, ensuring their safe and reliable behavior becomes critical, necessitating a systematic benchmark for safety evaluation.

Method: GABench includes 580 scenarios across six domains evaluated on LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara frameworks, with multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Guardrail-based defenses are compared against system-prompt-based defenses.

Result: Strongest model achieves 74.8% accuracy. Two failure regimes identified: stronger models under-call tools, weaker models mis-select/over-call tools. Performance degrades with tool-set size and turn depth. Guardrails recover 19.9% of failures at 0.5% false positive rate.

Conclusion: Execution-time structural intervention (guardrails) improves safety without disrupting correct agent behavior, consistently outperforming system-prompt-based defenses.

Abstract: As large language model agents increasingly operate autonomously with access to tools and external environments, ensuring their safe and reliable behavior becomes critical. We present GuardianAgentBench (GABench), a benchmark of 580 scenarios across six domains evaluated on three production-ready frameworks: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara. The benchmark incorporates rigorous multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Experiments with six state-of-the-art models reveal that even the strongest configuration achieves only 74.8% overall accuracy and expose two distinct failure regimes: stronger models under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades monotonically with both tool-set size and sequential turn depth, with long-horizon planning proving the steeper bottleneck. Our guardrail implementation consistently outperforms system-prompt-based defenses across all models, recovering 19.9% of failures at a false positive rate of just 0.5%. These results demonstrate that execution-time structural intervention improves safety without disrupting correct agent behavior.

</details>


### [178] [Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning: Attribution-Guided Repair and Knowledge Reuse for Structured Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20999)
*Zibin Lin,Shengli Zhang,Taotao Wang,Yihan Xia,Deen Ma,Guofu Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WML is a method that localizes failures in agent workflows to specific nodes/mechanisms, optimizes Skills via provenance-aware patching, and achieves high accuracy on SpreadsheetBench and WikiTableQuestions while reducing cost on Compiler-Supported50.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Skill optimizers cannot jointly identify where a workflow failure occurs, which mechanism caused it, and how to adapt third-party Skills for local reuse.

Method: WML consists of Node–Mechanism Attribution (locating failure node, mechanisms, and edit target) and a six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop that selects provenance/scope-aware knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates, and stores verified outcomes.

Result: SpreadsheetBench: 90.33±1.53 / 74.67±3.51 Hard Accuracy (DeepSeek/Qwen3.6-Flash); WikiTableQuestions: 84.00±2.00 / 83.00±2.00 Denotation Accuracy; Compiler-Supported50: highest hard-PASS rate and lowest cost per successful task with reduced tokens/calls.

Conclusion: WML effectively resolves workflow failures by attributing them to specific mechanisms and applying targeted Skill patches, achieving strong performance and cost efficiency across benchmarks.

Abstract: Agent Skills package reusable procedural knowledge as external artifacts for frozen language-model agents, yet existing optimizers do not jointly resolve where a failure occurs in a workflow, which mechanism caused it, and how relevant knowledge from third-party Skills should be reused locally. We introduce Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning (WML). Its Node--Mechanism Attribution identifies the failed workflow node, implicated mechanisms, and smallest valid edit target, routing single-mechanism defects to L3 resources and relational defects across mechanisms to L2 composition protocols. A six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop then selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified outcomes in optimizer-side memory. On SpreadsheetBench, WML reaches 90.33 +/- 1.53 and 74.67 +/- 3.51 Hard Accuracy with DeepSeek and Qwen3.6-Flash, respectively; without additional optimization, the learned Skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00 +/- 2.00 and 83.00 +/- 2.00 Denotation Accuracy. On Compiler-Supported50, WML attains both the highest hard-PASS rate and the lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution sharply reduces tokens and calls relative to a direct SkillAgent while retaining most of its successful tasks. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/xiaolin9595/workflow-localized-mechanism-learning.

</details>


### [179] [Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21000)
*Hyuk Lim,Seunghyun Yoon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Naju (Native Adaptive Junction Unit) decouples forget gate and write gain in recurrent state-space models to achieve both long-range retention and active overwriting, outperforming Mamba and remaining competitive with Transformers while maintaining linear complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-sequence memory tracking requires opposing capabilities: near-lossless retention of old bindings over long horizons and active overwriting of stale ones.
