Existing efficient baselines excel at only one side, and coupled single-gate recurrent designs impose a fundamental constraint (|r|+w ≤ 1) that limits simultaneous performance on both.

Method: Naju factorizes the recurrent update into an explicit discrete pole (sigmoid forget gate f_n), an independent write gain i_n, and input-dependent write/read maps. This decouples retention from writing, removing the coupled constraint. The recurrence is directly parameterized in discrete time rather than via zero-order-hold discretization of continuous-time SSMs like Mamba. Schur-stability is ensured by construction (0 < f_n < 1).

Result: Naju is the only model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4x the training length. On WikiText-103, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall, it consistently combines strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming Mamba baselines while remaining competitive with Transformers.

Conclusion: Decoupling the forget gate from the write gain is essential for achieving both long-range retention and active overwriting in recurrent models. Naju validates this design principle and demonstrates that linear-time, linear-memory models can match or exceed both Mamba and Transformer baselines across diverse benchmarks.

Abstract: Long-sequence memory tracking places two opposing demands on a recurrent state: near-lossless retention of stored bindings over long horizons, and active overwriting of stale ones. In our diagnostic suite, the strongest efficient baselines tend to solve only one side well. Continuous-time-parameterized state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba obtain their discrete recurrence by zero-order-hold discretization of a continuous-time system; we argue that this detour is unnecessary for memory tracking and parameterize the discrete transition directly. Naju (Native Adaptive Junction Unit) factorizes the recurrent update, schematically $x_n = f_n\odot x_{n-1} + i_n\odot(B_n u_n)$, into an explicit discrete pole (a learned forget gate $f_n$), an independent write gain $i_n$, and input-dependent write/read maps. Since the sigmoid pole satisfies $0<f_n<1$, each frozen local coordinate is Schur-stable by construction, and the full time-varying recurrence satisfies a fading-memory/BIBO bound under uniform boundedness assumptions, with no stability regularizer. We formalize the key structural limitation of coupled designs: any non-expansive complementary single-gate recurrence ties the effective retention $r$ and write gain $w$ through $|r|+w\le 1$, so near-complete retention forces weak writing; decoupling $f_n$ from $i_n$ removes this constraint. Empirically, Naju is the only evaluated model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4x the training length. Beyond the diagnostic suite, we evaluate Naju on WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall. Across these settings, Naju consistently combines strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming the Mamba baselines in the principal comparisons while remaining competitive with the Transformer and preserving linear-time, linear-memory scaling.

</details>


### [180] [Reexamining zero-shot summarization: Empirical investigation of trustworthiness of LLM-summarizers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21010)
*Vasudha Bhatnagar,Purnima Bindal,Vikas Kumar,Raj Kumari Bahl*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a two-level diagnostic protocol to benchmark LLM-summarizers based on stability of generated summaries, revealing significant variability across LLMs and motivating development of more trustworthy summarizers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The stochasticity of LLMs raises concerns about stability and trustworthiness of generated summaries, especially in educational settings where students and researchers use zero-shot LLM summarization for academic materials.

Method: A two-level diagnostic protocol: (1) lower-level document-level stability analysis computing stability coefficients via semantic and factual alignment scores from multiple LLM-generated summaries under controlled conditions; (2) higher-level consolidation of observations from stratified document samples to estimate a stability index as a proxy for trustworthiness.

Result: Empirical investigation across three LLM-summarizers and three document genres revealed statistically significant differences in generation-level variability among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics.

Conclusion: The study provides evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-generated summaries and motivates further research toward robust, reliable, and trustworthy LLM-summarizers.

Abstract: Zero-shot summarization using Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced the abstractive summarization task by producing coherent and fluent summaries. However, underlying stochasticity of the large language models raises concerns about the stability and trustworthiness of the LLM-generated summaries. This issue has become increasingly important due to proliferation of LLM-generated summaries in educational settings, where students and researchers summarize complex academic materials in zero-shot manner.
  We propose a novel two-level diagnostic protocol for benchmarking LLM-summarizers based on the stability of the generated summaries. At the lower level, document-level stability analysis is performed over multiple LLM-summaries generated under controlled environment, and the stability coefficient is computed. Each generated summary is scored for semantic and factual alignment with the original document, enabling estimation of stability along more than one dimensions. At the next level, observations from a stratified sample of documents drawn from the corpus are consolidated to estimate the stability index of the LLM-summarizer, which is the proxy for its trustworthiness.
  Our empirical investigation of three LLM-summarizers across three genres of documents reveals statistically significant differences in the generation-level variability among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics. This study advances the LLM-summarization research by evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-summaries and motivates further research towards development of robust, reliable and trustworthy LLM-summarizers.

</details>


### [181] [EmoAgent-R1: Towards Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21013)
*Lihuang Fang,Yuchen Zou,kebin Jin,Jinghui Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EmoAgent-R1 is a reinforcement learning-based dynamic agent specialization framework that enhances MLLM-based multimodal emotion recognition through cold-start training followed by RL optimization with a novel P-GRPO algorithm, achieving superior emotion reasoning performance on MER benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM-based MER methods use fixed prompts to perceive emotions, failing to account for the dynamic and complex nature of emotion sources in multimodal inputs.

Method: (1) Cold start strategy: trains MLLM with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data to acquire preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and agent routing abilities. (2) Reinforcement learning optimization: trains the MLLM via a two-step agentic workflow (agent selection + agent specialization). (3) Novel P-GRPO: combines group-based relative advantages with PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to convert sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, addressing GRPO's coarse-grained uniform credit assignment.

Result: Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks demonstrate stronger emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability.

Conclusion: EmoAgent-R1 effectively addresses the dynamic emotion perception limitation in existing MLLM-based MER methods, achieving superior performance via dynamic agent specialization guided by reinforcement learning.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance in multimodal emotion recognition (MER) tasks and lifted MER to a new level that is complex emotion understanding with advanced video understanding abilities and natural language description. However, existing MLLM-based methods often use a fixed prompt to perceive the emotions, ignoring the dynamicity and complexity of the emotion source in the multimodal inputs. To address these issues, we propose a novel Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization framework (\textbf{EmoAgent-R1}) to optimize the emotion recognition, reasoning, and generalization abilities of an MLLM with dynamic agent specialization based on reinforcement learning. Specifically, we first adopt a cold start strategy to endow an MLLM with preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and agent routing ability by training with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data. Then, we further train the MLLM with reinforcement learning to perceive emotions in a two-step agentic workflow with agent selection and agent specialization. To effectively train EmoAgent-R1, we propose a novel Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) to combine group-based relative advantages with a PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to transform sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, mitigating the coarse-grained uniform credit assignment issue in GRPO. Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our EmoAgent-R1 in stronger emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability.

</details>


### [182] [Faster IndexTTS-2: Accelerating and Streaming Autoregressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech Synthesis on GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21042)
*Muyang Du,Shuang Yu,Junjie Lai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Faster IndexTTS-2 accelerates the IndexTTS-2 autoregressive TTS model using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM, achieving up to 5.0× speedup on GPT and 3.6× end-to-end with minimal quality degradation, while adding streaming and batched inference support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive TTS models like IndexTTS-2 produce high-quality speech but suffer from slow sequential token generation, limiting production deployment in low-latency scenarios.

Method: Accelerated all neural components (GPT, flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, vocoder) using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM; enabled streaming synthesis and batched inference across all components.

Result: Up to 5.0× speedup on the autoregressive GPT component and 3.6× end-to-end speedup on the Seed-TTS benchmark for English and Chinese, with minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness.

Conclusion: Faster IndexTTS-2 provides a practical reference for efficiently accelerating similar autoregressive speech models on GPUs for production deployment.

Abstract: Autoregressive text-to-speech models achieve strong naturalness but suffer from slow inference due to sequential token generation, limiting their deployment in production applications that require low latency. IndexTTS-2 is a state-of-the-art autoregressive TTS model consisting of a GPT, a flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, and a vocoder. Despite its high synthesis quality, its inference speed barely reaches real-time without streaming or batching support. We present Faster IndexTTS-2, which accelerates all neural network components of IndexTTS-2 for production deployment on GPUs using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM. Faster IndexTTS-2 also enables streaming synthesis for latency-sensitive interactive applications, and batched inference across all components to maximize GPU utilization. Experiments on the Seed-TTS benchmark for both English and Chinese demonstrate up to 5.0$\times$ speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6$\times$ end-to-end, with minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness. Our methodology provides a practical reference for efficiently accelerating similar autoregressive speech models on GPUs.

</details>


### [183] [Can Generative Recommendation Reach Cold Items? A Temporal Perspective on Semantic-ID Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21101)
*Jie Peng,Yanping Zheng,Zhewei Zhe,Bin Tong,Guan Wang,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper examines Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation under temporal cold-start conditions, finding that while models can reach future items with observed tokens/prefixes, they struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths, revealing that SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether SID-based generative recommendation can handle temporal open-token cold-start induction—where new items enter the catalog with unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths—since prior work only considered closed-world recombination.

Method: The authors adopt an absolute-time temporal protocol separating seen and unseen targets, and conduct seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing to diagnose cold-item reachability at the token level.

Result: Current SID-based models can occasionally reach future items supported by observed tokens and prefixes, but fail on unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. SID generation behaves as hierarchical semantic bucketing: early tokens select coarse semantic regions, later tokens refine item-specific paths.

Conclusion: SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended; future directions include more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context.

Abstract: Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation represents items as sequences of shared semantic tokens, enabling token recombination beyond isolated item IDs. However, closed-world recombination does not necessarily imply temporal open-token cold-start induction, where new items enter the item catalog with unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths. In this work, we revisit SID-based generative recommendation under an absolute-time temporal protocol that separates seen and unseen targets and diagnoses the cold item reachability at the token level. Through seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing, we show that current SID-based models can occasionally reach future items supported by observed tokens and prefixes, but struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. We further explain this boundary by interpreting SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing: early tokens select coarse semantic regions, while later tokens refine item-specific paths. These findings show that SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended, and suggest future directions in more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context.

</details>


### [184] [AttriMem: Attribution-Guided Process Feedback for Agent Memory Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21106)
*Qinfeng Li,Yuntai Bao,Xinyan Yu,Hongze Chen,Wenqi Zhang,Xuhong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AttriMem is an attribution-guided process-feedback framework that uses RL to learn memory-construction policies for LLM agents, augmenting outcome rewards with token-level contribution rewards to address fine-grained credit assignment in memory management.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory-construction methods are limited: heuristic approaches rely on subjective, task-specific rules misaligned with downstream objectives, while RL-based methods use coarse outcome/module-level rewards that cannot identify which intermediate memory contents support the final answer, creating a fine-grained credit-assignment bottleneck.

Method: AttriMem augments global outcome rewards with local rewards derived from token-level contributions (attribution) to the final answer, enabling process-level feedback for RL-based memory policy learning without requiring pre-specified ground-truth targets for intermediate memory decisions.

Result: On long-horizon dialogue question answering, AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL-based baselines, generalizes across benchmarks and answer models, and stabilizes RL optimization.

Conclusion: Attribution-guided process feedback effectively bridges the credit-assignment gap in RL-based memory-construction policy learning, enabling more adaptive and generalizable memory management without task-specific heuristics or manual intermediate annotations.

Abstract: Effective memory is crucial for LLM agents, yet constructing it effectively remains challenging. A memory-construction policy decides what information to extract, store, update, compress, or discard as interactions accumulate. Heuristic memory methods rely on subjective, task-specific rules, which can misalign with downstream objectives and limit cross-task adaptability. RL-based methods, by contrast, learn from task feedback but mainly use outcome- or module-level rewards. These coarse signals indicate task success but cannot identify which intermediate memory contents support the final answer, creating a fine-grained credit-assignment bottleneck. However, constructing such process feedback is prohibitively difficult because intermediate memory decisions lack unique ground-truth targets, while the appropriate credit varies with the agent's uncertain reasoning trajectory and therefore cannot be specified in advance. We propose AttriMem, an attribution-guided process-feedback framework for learning memory-construction policies with RL. AttriMem augments the global outcome reward with local rewards derived from token-level contributions to the final answer. Experiments on long-horizon dialogue question answering show that AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL-based baselines, generalizes across benchmarks and answer models, stabilizes RL optimization.

</details>


### [185] [V-DEAL: Diagnosing Video Safety De-Calibration as an Understanding-Refusal Coupling Failure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21151)
*Zhetong Zhang,Honghao Fu,Miao Xu,Yiwei Wang,Yujun Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Harmful videos paired with benign queries achieve higher attack success rates on Video LLMs than with explicitly harmful queries. V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework, reveals that while models recognize harmful content with >81% accuracy, attack success rate reaches 48.33% due to weaker refusal tendencies from visual vs. textual understanding. A prompt injection intervention reduces attack success by ~48 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As Video LLMs are deployed in real-world applications, ensuring their safety alignment is critical. The authors discovered a counterintuitive vulnerability: harmful videos with benign queries achieve higher attack success rates than with explicitly harmful queries, motivating the need to understand this mechanism and develop mitigations.

Method: The authors propose V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework analyzing model behaviour, understanding, and internal representations. They test six Video LLMs on three public benchmarks, using hidden-state analysis to compare refusal tendencies from visual vs. textual understanding. They also introduce a prompt injection intervention method.

Result: Models correctly recognize harmful video content with >81% accuracy, yet the average attack success rate reaches 48.33% when pairing harmful videos with benign queries. Hidden-state analysis shows visual understanding activates weaker refusal tendencies than textual understanding. The prompt injection intervention reduces attack success rates by an average of 48.24 percentage points, comparable to fine-tuning-based methods.

Conclusion: The vulnerability stems from a mismatch between visual recognition and refusal triggering in Video LLMs. V-DEAL provides a diagnostic perspective for analyzing this failure. The proposed prompt injection intervention offers an effective, practical means to address such safety risks without requiring fine-tuning.

Abstract: As Video Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, ensuring their safety alignment has become critical. Counterintuitively, we find that harmful videos paired with benign queries achieve higher attack success rates than the same videos paired with explicitly harmful queries. To understand the underlying mechanism of this vulnerability, we present V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework that jointly analyzes this failure across model behaviour, understanding, and internal representations. By progressively ruling out perception failure and quantifying the model's internal refusal tendency, V-DEAL provides a new diagnostic perspective for analyzing the underlying mechanism of the observed vulnerability. We tested six Video LLMs on three public benchmarks and observed that models correctly recognize harmful video content with over 81\% accuracy, yet the average attack success rate still reaches 48.33\% under the condition pairing harmful videos with benign queries. Hidden-state analysis further shows that visual understanding activates a weaker refusal tendency than textual understanding. Furthermore, we introduce a prompt injection intervention method that reduces attack success rates by an average of 48.24 percentage points and achieves performance comparable to prior fine-tuning-based methods, providing an effective and practical means to address such safety risks in Video LLMs.

</details>


### [186] [SafeStep: AI-powered Travel Assistance for Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21156)
*Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia Azul Debenedetti,David Gamez,Franco Such,Nik Kairinos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SafeStep is an AI-driven travel system that uses a novel travel graph representation combining route planning with predictive modeling to assist elderly users with frailty or dementia. It generates personalized failure scenarios via LLMs and Anticip8 engine, proposes targeted interventions, and selects those maximizing destination arrival likelihood. Evaluated through graph generation experiments and 26 real-world journeys, it improved user confidence and safety but needs interface improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Over a million people in the UK suffer from frailty or dementia, which severely compromise their ability to travel in urban environments, motivating the need for an AI-driven assistive travel system.

Method: SafeStep uses a novel travel graph representation that integrates route planning with predictive modeling. For each journey stage, it: (i) generates personalized failure scenarios using LLMs + Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine, (ii) proposes targeted interventions, and (iii) estimates intervention impact on outcome probabilities to select those maximizing destination arrival likelihood.

Result: Combining Anticip8 for failure prediction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yielded the most reliable performance. The field study with 26 real-world journeys showed SafeStep improves user confidence and perceived safety.

Conclusion: SafeStep is effective for assisting elderly travelers, though interface usability needs improvement for the target demographic. The AI system could be applied to other domains like mental health, career coaching, and addiction treatment.

Abstract: More than a million people in the UK suffer from frailty or dementia, which severely compromise their ability to travel in urban environments. This paper presents SafeStep, an AI-driven travel system that assists elderly users with their journeys. At the core of SafeStep is a novel travel graph representation, which integrates route planning with predictive modelling. For each stage of a journey, the system (i) generates personalized failure scenarios using a combi-nation of LLMs and the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine, (ii) proposes targeted interventions, and (iii) estimates the impact of interventions on out-come probabilities. This enables SafeStep to select interventions that maximize the likelihood of the person reaching their destination. SafeStep was evaluated through experiments on travel graph generation and a field study involving 26 real-world journeys. Results showed that combining Anticip8 for failure pre-diction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yields the most re-liable performance. User feedback indicated that SafeStep improves confidence and perceived safety during travel, although interface usability needs to be im-proved for the target demographic. In the future, we would like to improve and release SafeStep. The AI system that was developed for SafeStep could be ap-plied in other areas, such as mental health, career coaching and addiction treatment.

</details>


### [187] [Safeguards for Speech2Speech LLM-Assistants: A Case Study in Automotive Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21180)
*Gregor Endler,Sebastian Kraus,Lukas Stappen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates transcript-based and tool-based guardrails for speech-to-speech assistants in automotive contexts, finding both insufficient for industrial deployment due to latency (0–1.4s delay) and technical issues like non-deterministic tool calls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess whether current S2S guardrail approaches are viable for safe deployment in automotive conversational assistants, given the tension between end-to-end S2S architectures and the need for programmable domain-specific safety measures.

Method: Empirical evaluation of two S2S guardrail strategies—transcript-based and tool-based—measuring latency and technical reliability in an automotive context.

Result: Both guardrail strategies are insufficient for industrial deployment: they introduce prohibitive latency (0–1.4 seconds per check, even for computationally cheap operations) and suffer from technical impediments such as potentially non-deterministic tool call behavior.

Conclusion: Current S2S guardrail approaches are inadequate for production-grade automotive use, and open challenges remain for developing viable safety mechanisms in this domain.

Abstract: Recent advances have introduced speech-to-speech (S2S) conversational assistants capable of producing natural-sounding interactions, including non-verbal cues like tonality and mood. In the automotive domain, this enables intuitive and humanlike in-car dialogue experiences. However, integrating these end-to-end assistants limits architectural options for programmable domain-specific safeguards. This paper discusses two implementation approaches for S2S guardrails: transcript-based and tool-based. Through an empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that both strategies are insufficient for industrial deployment in most cases due to prohibitive latency (delaying each answer by 0 to 1.4 seconds even for computationally cheap checks) and technical impediments (like potentially non-deterministic tool call behavior). Finally, we outline open challenges for S2S guardrails in the automotive context.

</details>


### [188] [Explaining Weather Bulletins via ILP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21184)
*Enrico Santi,Alessandro Dal Palù,Agostino Dovier,Talissa Dreossi,Andrea Formisano*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper uses the FastLAS2 ILP framework to learn interpretable hypotheses from meteorological data and expert bulletins, generating natural language explanations for weather forecast pictogram symbols used by the Regional Meteorological Observatory of Friuli Venezia-Giulia.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To clarify weather bulletins issued by OSMER FVG by generating simple, interpretable hypotheses that explain the rationale behind human experts' choices of specific symbols in the bulletin pictogram.

Method: A pipeline that extracts ASP facts from simulated meteorological raw data and OSMER bulletins (ground truth), generates ILP examples, and infers explanatory hypotheses via FastLAS2, which are then translated into natural language.

Result: A general, non-region-specific approach that successfully generates explanatory hypotheses for weather forecast pictogram symbols used by human experts.

Conclusion: The proposed pipeline is effective for explaining expert-driven weather forecast symbols and is generalizable to other regions and bulletin sources.

Abstract: Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) originated within the Logic Programming community in the Nineties as a framework for combining symbolic learning with declarative knowledge representation. Nowadays, mature ILP frameworks exist and they are capable of learning complex, non-monotonic hypotheses, thus broadening both the modeling capabilities and the scope of real-world applications of ILP. This work is primarily based on the FastLAS2 framework and aims to generate simple, interpretable hypotheses to help clarify the weather bulletins issued by OSMER FVG, the Regional Meteorological Observatory of the Italian region of Friuli Venezia-Giulia. In this paper we present a pipeline that, starting from simulated meteorological raw data and from OSMERs' bulletins (used as ground truth), extracts data as ASP facts and generates ILP examples. From such examples an explanatory hypothesis is then inferred via FastLAS2. Such a hypothesis (translated into natural language) explains the weather forecast issued by human experts, and in particular the rationale behind experts' choices of specific symbols in the bulletin pictogram (the symbol-annotated meteorological map of the forecast). The proposed approach is general, not specific to any particular region and it can equally be applied to bulletins from other sources and to different regions.

</details>


### [189] [Differentiable Logic Programming to Mitigate Reasoning Shortcuts in Neurosymbolic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21185)
*Akihiro Takemura,Katsumi Inoue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a matrix-based differentiable logic programming method to mitigate reasoning shortcuts in neurosymbolic systems, specifically addressing constraint satisfaction and cognition shortcuts by using one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neurosymbolic systems suffer from shortcut reasoning behaviors, including constraint satisfaction shortcuts (constraints satisfied without task completion) and cognition shortcuts (biased data causing incorrect concept mappings), which undermine their reliability.

Method: The authors develop a matrix-based differentiable logic programming approach with unified encoding of rules and constraints in a single matrix, leveraging fuzzy logic t-norms and one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms instead of soft probability distributions.

Result: Experiments on MNIST variants demonstrate that one-to-one grounding significantly reduces both shortcut types compared to prior soft probability-based methods, and architectural choices in coupling symbolic knowledge with neural learning critically impact shortcut mitigation.

Conclusion: Architectural decisions for coupling neural and symbolic components are crucial for mitigating reasoning shortcuts, and matrix-based differentiable logic with precise grounding offers a promising direction for robust NeSy systems.

Abstract: Neurosymbolic (NeSy) systems integrate neural networks with logical reasoning to achieve both generalization and interpretability, but recent work has shown they are susceptible to shortcut reasoning behaviors.  We propose a novel method using matrix-based differentiable logic programming to mitigate reasoning shortcuts in two phenomena: constraint satisfaction shortcuts, where constraints are satisfied without achieving the intended task, and cognition shortcuts, where biased data leads to semantically incorrect concept mappings despite logically sound inference. Building on recent matrix-based logic programming semantics, we introduce design elements to mitigate shortcuts, including a unified encoding of rules and constraints in a single matrix.  We also identify connections to fuzzy logic t-norms and empirically compare their gradient flow properties. Through carefully designed experiments on MNIST variants, we show that one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms significantly reduces both shortcut types compared to previous methods that rely on soft probability distributions.  We then confirm that architectural choices in coupling symbolic knowledge with neural learning play a critical role in shortcut mitigation.

</details>


### [190] [Identifying Good Rules for Efficient SAT Encodings of Single-Constant Multiplication Using Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21188)
*Chufeng Jiang,Neng-Fa Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A neuro-symbolic framework accelerates SAT encoding for the Single Constant Multiplication problem by using GNN predictions to prune suboptimal operator choices, achieving 1-2 orders of magnitude speedup and 97% memory reduction while preserving encoding quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamic programming methods for SCM SAT encoding produce near-optimal results but suffer from high encoding cost (time and memory) for large constants, motivating the need for efficiency improvements.

Method: A neuro-symbolic framework combining a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to predict promising operator types from constant decompositions, using confidence scores to prune no-good choices during symbolic search for SCM SAT encoding.

Result: On unseen 17-32 bit constants: 1-2 orders of magnitude reduction in encoding time, over 97% reduction in memory usage, order-of-magnitude decrease in branching, while preserving near-optimal encoding quality in terms of additions.

Conclusion: Learning-guided symbolic strategies significantly improve scalability and efficiency of SCM encoding, demonstrating the effectiveness of neuro-symbolic approaches for hardware design optimization.

Abstract: The Single Constant Multiplication problem is a fundamental NP-hard optimization task in hardware design, which seeks to decompose a fixed constant using only additions, subtractions, and bit-shifts. Although dynamic programming methods can produce near-optimal SAT encodings for SCM, their encoding cost remains high for large constants. We propose a neuro-symbolic framework that accelerates SCM SAT encoding by identifying good rules for guiding operator selection during decomposition. Our approach employs a graph neural network model to predict promising operator types from constant decompositions, and exploits the resulting confidence scores to prune no-good choices in the symbolic search. Experimental results on unseen 17-32 bit constants demonstrate one to two orders of magnitude reductions in encoding time, over 97% reduction in memory usage, and an order-of-magnitude decrease in branching, while preserving near-optimal encoding quality in terms of additions. These results show that learning-guided symbolic strategies can significantly improve the scalability and efficiency of SCM encoding. Our code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/Chufeng-Jiang/SCM_MLDP

</details>


### [191] [Bound-Founded Semantics for Answer Set Programming with Difference Constraints: Preliminary Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21201)
*Pedro Cabalar,Jorge Fandinno,Nicolas Rühling,Torsten Schaub,Sebastian Schellhorn,Philipp Wanko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a many-sorted variant of Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb) to provide a unified logical foundation for hybrid ASP solvers integrating linear constraints. It applies this framework to difference constraints, formalizing foundedness for numeric variables and uncovering semantic roots of behaviors in systems like clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hybrid ASP solvers with linear constraints lack a unified logical foundation, relying on disparate semantic underpinnings. This gap hinders rigorous study of program simplifications and integration of diverse semantic principles.

Method: The authors introduce a many-sorted variant of Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb) as a versatile framework for characterizing equilibrium models across alternative semantics. They apply it to difference constraints, formalizing foundedness for numeric variables and analyzing how hybrid systems (clingo[DL], clingcon, flingo) justify constraint atoms.

Result: A single, consistent framework that formalizes the foundations of clingo[DL] and uncovers the semantic roots of varying behaviors across different hybrid ASP systems.

Conclusion: The framework not only formalizes current systems like clingo[DL] but also facilitates rigorous study of program simplifications and future integration of diverse semantic principles.

Abstract: While the integration of linear constraints has significantly expanded the reach of Answer Set Programming (ASP), existing hybrid solvers often rely on disparate semantic underpinnings that lack a unified logical foundation. We address this gap by introducing a many-sorted variant of the Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb), providing a versatile framework capable of characterizing equilibrium models across a wide spectrum of alternative semantics for extensions of ASP with linear constraints. We apply this framework to the setting of difference constraints, focusing on the semantic characterization of clingo[DL]. Central to our approach is the formalization of foundedness for numeric variables. By investigating how different hybrid systems - such as clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo - justify constraint atoms, we uncover the semantic roots of their varying behaviors. This investigation results in a single, consistent framework that not only formalizes the foundations of current systems like clingo[DL] but also facilitates the rigorous study of program simplifications and the future integration of diverse semantic principles.

</details>


### [192] [A New Well-Supported Semantics for Description Logic Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21203)
*Spencer Killen,Jia-Huai You*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a new well-supported semantics for description logic programs that evaluates ontological atoms more strictly, keeping consistency problem complexity NP-complete (vs. second-level polynomial hierarchy), and characterizes it via fixpoint operator and reduct transformation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current well-supported semantics for DL programs has two limitations: (1) increased computational complexity for consistency (rises to second level of polynomial hierarchy), and (2) lack of a reduct transformation characterization.

Method: A new semantics is introduced that evaluates ontological atoms more strictly than existing semantics. A syntactic class of DL programs is identified where the new semantics is equivalent to the current one. The semantics is characterized using a fixpoint operator and a reduct-based transformation.

Result: The new semantics keeps consistency problem complexity NP-complete instead of rising to the second polynomial hierarchy level. It is a strict subset of current well-supported semantics, maintaining prior well-supportedness while inducing a stricter notion.

Conclusion: The new notion of well-supportedness is preferred due to its similarities with logic programming, offering a better balance of expressivity and computational complexity.

Abstract: Description logic programs are a powerful formalism for combining rules with ontologies. The well-supported semantics for description logic programs ensures that no answer sets rely on cyclic dependencies. Most popular semantics for logic programming have this property of well-supportedness. We recognize two limitations of the current well-supported semantics for DL programs: its increased computational complexity for the consistency problem and its lack of a reduct transformation characterization.  In this work, we present a new semantics which evaluates ontological atoms more strictly than the current semantics. This keeps the complexity of its consistency problem NP-complete, rather than increasing it to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. Additionally, we identify a syntactic class of description logic programs for which our new semantics is equivalent to the current semantics. We characterize our semantics using a fixpoint operator and a reduct-based transformation. Our new semantics is a strict subset of the current well-supported semantics, so it maintains the prior notion  of well-supportedness while inducing its own stricter notion. We prefer our new notion of well-supportedness due to its similarities with logic programming.

</details>


### [193] [How Rules Represent Causal Knowledge: Causal Modeling with Probabilistic Logic Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21208)
*Kilian Rueckschloss,Felix Weitkaemper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper extends Pearl's causal theory to probabilistic logic programming (PLP) by aligning PLP with a non-temporal philosophical foundation, proposing a formal causal semantics with interventions, and showing its equivalence to P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pearl's causal framework is limited to acyclic Bayesian networks, and applying it to other formalisms risks misinterpretation. The paper aims to bridge this gap for probabilistic logic programming.

Method: The authors align PLP with non-temporal philosophical foundations (simultaneous events), propose a formal causal semantics with intervention notions, implement it, and compare the semantics with P-log for stratified and non-stratified ProbLog programs.

Result: The proposed causal semantics coincides with P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs but may differ for non-stratified cases and other PLP formalisms.

Conclusion: Pearl's causal reasoning can be successfully ported to PLP with a non-temporal foundation, but the equivalence is not universal across all program classes.

Abstract: Pearl famously argues that causal knowledge enables the prediction of intervention effects. By contrast, purely descriptive knowledge supports only conclusions drawn from observations. His theory of causality, however, is developed exclusively within Bayesian networks and causal models. Consequently, it is largely restricted to acyclic causal relationships, and transferring its ideas to other formalisms risks misinterpretation or inconsistency.
  This paper brings Pearl's approach to causality into probabilistic logic programming (PLP). To this end, such programs are aligned with philosophical foundations established in prior work that do not rely on temporal notions; that is, all relevant events are assumed to occur simultaneously. A formal causal semantics for these programs, together with a notion of intervention and an implementation, is proposed. It is shown that this semantics coincides with the P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs, while the two may differ in the non-stratified case and for other PLP formalisms.

</details>


### [194] [ICAE-Bench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Interactive Project Builders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21217)
*Zhongyuan Peng,Dan Huang,Chuyu Zhang,Caijun Xu,Changyi Xiao,Shibo Hong,David Lo,Lin Qiu,Xuezhi Cao,Jiyuan He,Yixin Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ICAE-Bench is a benchmark that evaluates coding agents on interactive project-building tasks starting from fuzzy product requirements, using automated User Agents and multi-dimensional diagnostics including black-box tests, to address the gap between existing static benchmarks and emerging vibe-coding workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing coding agent benchmarks evaluate agents on static, fully specified tasks, but modern vibe-coding workflows require agents to transform incomplete product intent into working software through planning, clarification, tool use, debugging, and repository-level construction—capabilities not captured by current benchmarks.

Method: ICAE-Bench starts from fuzzy product requirements and uses an automated User Agent to simulate dynamic interactions. It grounds requirements in real open-source repositories, uses User Agent Data for reproducible simulation without leaking artifacts, and evaluates with standardized black-box tests plus multi-dimensional diagnostics (functional correctness, semantic/API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, interaction quality).

Result: The paper presents a benchmark design with three key contributions: (1) ambiguity derived from precise executable repositories, (2) grounded user simulation via User Agent Data, and (3) comprehensive evaluation via black-box tests and multi-dimensional diagnostics.

Conclusion: ICAE-Bench addresses the gap in evaluating coding agents under interactive, fuzzy-requirement settings, enabling more realistic assessment of agents in vibe-coding paradigms.

Abstract: The recent emergence of vibe-coding workflows is changing what coding agents are expected to do. Instead of merely completing code under fully specified instructions, agents are increasingly expected to transform incomplete product intent into working software by combining various abilities including planning, requirement clarification, tool use, debugging, and repository-level construction. Yet existing benchmarks have not fully caught up with this shift, evaluating agents on static, fully specified tasks.
  In this paper, we introduce ICAE-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under interactive project-building settings. The basic idea is to start from a fuzzy product requirement, simulating the dynamic paradigm with an automated User Agent. To make this setting both realistic and evaluable, ICAE-Bench introduces three key designs. First, to avoid the ambiguity of unconstrained fuzzy requirements, each task derives ambiguity from a precise real open-source repository with executable behavior. Second, to ensure high-quality and reproducible user simulation, ICAE-Bench grounds interaction through User Agent Data, allowing the User Agent to reveal hidden constraints without inventing new requirements or leaking implementation artifacts. Third, to evaluate open-ended repositories fairly, ICAE-Bench uses standardized black-box tests together with multi-dimensional diagnostics, including functional correctness, semantic and API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, and interaction quality.

</details>


### [195] [Logic Programming Semantics for Causal Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21233)
*Felix Weitkämper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper explores the relationship between logic programming semantics (stable and supported models) and causal processes, showing that stable models correspond to eventual states from neutral initial conditions, while supported models correspond to eventual states from arbitrary starting points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research is motivated by challenging modelling issues in the life sciences, aiming to better understand how logic programming semantics relate to causal processes in biological systems.

Method: The paper establishes formal relationships between logic programming semantics and causal processes by analyzing how different semantics (stable models vs. supported models) correspond to eventual states under different initial conditions (neutral state vs. arbitrary starting points).

Result: Stable models of positive logic programs correspond to eventual states of causal processes starting from a neutral state and continuing undisturbed; supported models correspond to eventual states reachable from arbitrary starting points.

Conclusion: The findings contribute to the discussion of appropriate semantics for logic programming as a causal rule language, adding a temporal perspective to recent explanatory interpretations of stable and supported model semantics in causality.

Abstract: Motivated by challenging modelling issues in the life sciences, we investigate the relationship between logic programming semantics and the eventual states of causal processes compatible with those logic programs. More precisely, we show that while stable models of positive logic programs correspond to the eventual states of processes commencing from a neutral state and continuing undisturbed indefinitely, supported models describe the eventual states reachable from arbitrary starting points. This also contributes to the discussion of the appropriate semantics for logic programming as a causal rule language, adding a temporal perspective to recent interpretations of the stable and supported model semantics from an explanatory viewpoint of causality.

</details>


### [196] [BasketEvent: Understanding Who Did What and When in Basketball Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21267)
*Yu Zhang,Jiayuan Rao,Haoning Wu,Weidi Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BasketEvent is a player-centric basketball video dataset with grounded event labels and temporal annotations. PlayNet, a reasoning framework tracking entities and modeling interactions, outperforms video-level and crop-based baselines for fine-grained sports understanding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods treat spatial perception and semantic recognition as isolated tasks, failing to ground events to individual players or pinpoint temporal boundaries in complex collective dynamics.

Method: Proposes PlayNet, a player-centric reasoning framework that tracks key entities, associates player identities, reasons about events via modeling player-player, player-ball, and global court interactions, and aggregates sparse temporal evidence using gated pooling.

Result: PlayNet significantly outperforms representative video-level and crop-based baselines, demonstrating the superiority of player-centric modeling for fine-grained sports video understanding.

Conclusion: Player-centric modeling is superior for fine-grained sports video understanding; data, code, and models will be publicly released.

Abstract: Comprehensive basketball video understanding requires resolving not only what event occurs, but also who is responsible and when the key evidence appears. However, exist- ing methods typically treat spatial perception and semantic recognition as isolated tasks, failing to ground events to individual players or pinpoint their temporal boundaries within complex collective dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce BasketEvent, a player- centric basketball event understanding dataset curated from real NBA broadcasts. In BasketEvent, event labels are grounded to the responsible players, and a manually an- notated subset of 1,000 samples with precise event intervals is provided to evaluate tem- poral evidence localization. Based on this data, we propose PlayNet, a player-centric reasoning framework that maps basketball videos to player-level event predictions with temporal evidence. Concretely, PlayNet tracks key entities, associates player identities, and reasons about events by modeling player-player, player-ball, and global court inter- actions, while aggregating sparse temporal evidence via gated pooling. Extensive experi- ments demonstrate that PlayNet significantly outperforms representative video-level and crop-based baselines, proving the superiority of player-centric modeling for fine-grained sports video understanding. Our data, code, and models will be made publicly available.

</details>


### [197] [An LLM-Driven Workflow for Automated Process Control Strategy Generation and Tuning from Dynamic Process Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21292)
*Ari Luna Rueda,Eike Cramer,Klaus Hellgardt,Mehmet Mercangöz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A structured LLM-driven workflow for automated multi-variable control design is presented, demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with decentralized PI control. Bayesian optimization reduces the closed-loop performance objective by ~26.5%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To automate the complex, multi-step process of multi-variable control design from dynamic process models using large language models, reducing manual effort and expertise requirements.

Method: The workflow decomposes control design into constrained code-generation steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, MV-CV pairing, controller specification, closed-loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation, and Bayesian-optimization-based tuning. Generated artifacts are executed, validated, and repaired with feedback before downstream tasks proceed.

Result: Applied to a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark, the workflow produced a physically consistent decentralized PI feedback-feedforward controller. Bayesian optimization reduced the closed-loop performance objective by approximately 26.5% relative to the initial controller, mainly through improved pressure-loop transient performance.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate feasibility of using structured LLM-based code generation for constructing executable control-design workflows, while highlighting the need for broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks.

Abstract: We present a structured large-language-model-driven workflow for automated multi-variable control design from dynamic process models. The workflow decomposes the design task into constrained code-generation steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, manipulated-variable controlled-variable (MV-CV) pairing, controller specification, closed loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation and Bayesian-optimization (BO) based tuning. Generated artifacts are executed and validated before downstream tasks proceed, and failed artifacts are repaired using validation feedback. The proposed approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics. The generated workflow produces a physically consistent decentralized PI (proportional-integral) feedback-feedforward control structure and an executable tuning environment. Bayesian optimization reduces the closed loop performance objective, which aggregates set-point tracking and disturbance-rejection errors for the controlled variables, by approximately 26.5% relative to the initial controller generated by the workflow, mainly through improved pressure-loop transient performance. This figure quantifies the automated tuning stage rather than a comparison against a manually designed controller. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using structured large-language-model-based code generation to construct executable control-design workflows, while also highlighting the need for broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks.

</details>


### [198] [Expert Behavior Prior Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21302)
*Gong Gao,Weidong Zhao,Xianhui Liu,Ning Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Expert Behavior Prior (EBP), a novel algorithm that uses a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder (Q-CVAE) to generate expert policy priors directly from the online replay buffer, avoiding reliance on static offline datasets. It incorporates expert policy guidance (EPG) and policy gradient correction (PGC) to improve policy exploitation and stability, achieving superior sample efficiency and convergence on robotic and industrial control benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Behavior Prior RL methods rely on static offline datasets with low diversity and suboptimal trajectory quality, which limits policy prior effectiveness and causes inefficient exploration and unstable learning dynamics.

Method: EBP introduces a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder (Q-CVAE) to generate expert policy priors from the online replay buffer, an expert policy guidance (EPG) mechanism to select expert actions from a generative support set, and a policy gradient correction (PGC) module to harmonize Q-guidance with expert supervision.

Result: Extensive experiments on Gym, PyBullet, and DMControl benchmarks show EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms with higher sample efficiency and more stable convergence.

Conclusion: EBP effectively addresses the limitations of static offline dataset reliance in BPRL by generating expert priors online, leading to more efficient exploration, stable learning, and improved performance on continuous control tasks.

Abstract: Behavior prior reinforcement learning (BPRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to improve sample efficiency in online reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging policy priors derived from offline demonstrations. However, most existing BPRL methods rely on static offline datasets, which often suffer from low data diversity and suboptimal trajectory quality. This reliance restricts the effectiveness of policy priors, hindering both policy exploitation and stability during online training. Consequently, agents are prone to inefficient exploration and unstable learning dynamics. To address these limitations, we deviate from existing offline pre-training methods and propose an Expert Behavior Prior (EBP) algorithm. Specifically, we introduce a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder (Q-CVAE) that learns to generate expert policy priors directly from the online replay buffer. This enables the generation of high-value actions for guiding policy updates without relying on pre-collected expert trajectories. To further enhance policy exploitation, we propose an expert policy guidance (EPG) mechanism that selects expert actions from a generative support set, and we integrate a policy gradient correction (PGC) module to harmonize Q-guidance with expert supervision, promoting stable and consistent policy improvement. Extensive experiments conducted on robotic control (Gym, PyBullet) and industrial control (DMControl) benchmarks demonstrate that EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms, achieving higher sample efficiency and more stable convergence.

</details>


### [199] [Regulating autonomous and agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21345)
*Chris Reed,Alex Austria,Anmol Bharuka,Pragnitha Mandava,Khushiya Mujawar,Luka Shakhkulashvili*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper examines how autonomous and agentic AI disrupts traditional regulatory assumptions about regulatee knowledge and control, analyzes four regulatory systems (UK content platforms, data protection, UK financial services, EU AI Act), and proposes solutions to transform regulation from reactive to active to address new systemic risks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing regulatory models assume regulatees have knowledge and control over regulated activities, but autonomous and agentic AI shifts this control elsewhere in the AI supply chain, making retrospective oversight ineffective and generating new systemic risks that demand a fresh governance approach.

Method: The paper investigates four regulatory systems: UK regulation of content platforms, data protection regimes, UK financial services regulation, and the EU AI Act's cross-sectoral regime, analyzing challenges posed by autonomous and agentic AI.

Result: Identifies that regulatory assumptions about regulatee knowledge/control are invalid for autonomous AI, retrospective supervision is ineffective, and AI autonomy creates novel systemic risks requiring new solutions across all four examined regimes.

Conclusion: Regulators need to adopt proposed solutions that transform regulation from a reactive process to an active one, bringing the AI supply chain within regulatory scope to effectively adapt to challenges of AI autonomy.

Abstract: Regulating activities where regulatees use autonomous and agentic AI is challenging. Regulatory assumptions about regulatee knowledge and control no longer hold true; much of that lies elsewhere in the AI supply chain which thus needs to be brought within the scope of regulation. Governance systems for autonomous AI cannot replicate existing governance models, but need a fresh approach. Retrospective supervisory oversight becomes ineffective as a risk management tool, and AI autonomy generates new systemic risks which require new solutions. This paper investigate four regulatory systems: UK regulation of content platforms, data protection, UK financial services, and the EU AI Act\'92s cross-sectoral regime. It analyses the challenges posed by autonomous and agentic AI and proposes potential solutions which regulators might adopt. These will transform regulation from a reactive process to an active one, and assist it in adapting to the challenges of AI autonomy.

</details>


### [200] [SPORD: A Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose Approach for Supply Chain Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21354)
*Jiayin He,Yutong Pan,Sen Yang,Ningxuan Kang,Yongzhi Qi,Jianshen Zhang,Wei Qi,Zuo-Jun Max Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JD.com's NetSim platform introduces the SPORD (Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose) method, decoupling simulation from optimization to overcome operational fragmentation, computational intractability, and implementation hurdles in e-commerce supply chain planning. Since 2025, it has optimized services for 20,000+ suppliers, reducing cross-regional fulfillment rate from 6.1% to 4.9% and cutting ~5,745 tCO2e monthly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: E-commerce supply chain planning suffers from three barriers: operational fragmentation (bespoke models), computational intractability (combinatorial scale of millions of SKUs, thousands of nodes), and implementation hurdle (executives distrust opaque optimal solutions).

Method: SPORD decouples simulation and optimization: simulation proposes by generating/evaluating all operationally valid candidate paths (absorbing business logic), then an integer program disposes by selecting the globally optimal subset. Uses matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU accelerated simulation (10-100x speedup) and a list scheduling algorithm for coupled-order processing (hours→minutes), with a closed-loop intelligent diagnosis engine.

Result: Deployed as JD.com's NetSim since 2025, optimized services for 20,000+ suppliers; cross-regional fulfillment rate dropped from 6.1% to 4.9%; monthly carbon reduction ~5,745 tCO2e.

Conclusion: SPORD moves simulation from monitoring to active planning, transparent outputs turn skeptical executives into collaborators, and modular architecture ensures future planning needs only configuration, not reconstruction.

Abstract: For years, supply chain planning at e-commerce firms has operated as a collection of isolated projects. Each planning task from static network planning to dynamic warehouse assortment planning requires analysts to spend weeks building models from scratch, calibrating and persuading executives to act on outputs they cannot verify. Three barriers drive this: bespoke models proliferate because standardization is difficult (operational fragmentation); once unified, the combinatorial scale of millions of SKUs, thousands of nodes, and intricate routing logic exceeds what solvers can handle within a tight window (computational intractability); and a mathematically optimal solution still fails to be implemented if the executives do not trust it (implementation hurdle). To bridge this gap, we propose and implement the Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose method, deployed as JD.com's NetSim platform. The central insight is decoupling: simulation proposes by generating and evaluating the full set of operationally valid candidate paths-absorbing all idiosyncratic business logic, while an integer program disposes by selecting the globally optimal subset. Computationally, matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU accelerated simulation achieves a 10-100 times speedup over serial methods, and a list scheduling algorithm reduces coupled-order processing from hours to minutes. Operationally, we establish a closed loop via an intelligent diagnosis engine. Since 2025, NetSim has optimized end to-end services for over 20,000 suppliers, the cross-regional fulfillment rate dropped from 6.1% to 4.9%, and the average monthly carbon reduction is approximately 5,745 tCO2e. SPORD moves simulation from monitoring to active planning. The transparent outputs turn skeptical executives into engaged collaborators, and the modular architecture ensures that the next planning requires just configuration, not reconstruction.

</details>


### [201] [Towards Faithful Graph Explanations with Synergistic Edge Effects via Granular Balls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21381)
*Jiancu Chen,Shuyin Xia,Guan Wang,Degang Chen,Fan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SeeExplainer is a parameter-free GNN explainer that uses granular-ball graph refinement to capture synergistic effects among edges, then perturbs nodes and edges in the structural graph to generate explanatory subgraphs, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines on graph classification datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous GNN explanation methods assess edge importance by perturbing each edge independently, neglecting the synergistic effects among edges that are crucial for accurately characterizing edge importance.

Method: (1) Introduces a granular-ball graph refinement mechanism that decomposes a graph into disjoint granular-balls with no fixed size and uses them as nodes to construct a structural graph, capturing synergistic edge effects. (2) Perturbs nodes and edges in the structural graph to generate explanatory subgraphs based on their respective contributions. The method is parameter-free.

Result: Experiments on several graph classification datasets of different networks show that SeeExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed parameter-free SeeExplainer effectively addresses the limitation of neglected synergistic edge effects in prior GNN explanation methods, achieving superior performance in generating instance-level explanations.

Abstract: Instance-level explanations aim to reveal the rationale behind a model's decisions for a specific graph. Previous methods explain graph neural networks (GNNs) by selecting important edges to induce subgraphs, where edge importance is assessed by perturbing each edge and observing changes in the model predictions. However, they often neglect the synergistic effects among edges, which are crucial for accurately characterizing edge importance. To address this issue, we propose SeeExplainer, a parameter-free explainer to interpret GNNs. Specifically, we first introduce a granular-ball graph refinement mechanism that decomposes a graph into several disjoint granular-balls with no fixed size, and utilize them as nodes to construct a structural graph. This process can better capture the synergistic effects among edges. Then, we perturb nodes and edges in the structural graph to generate explanatory subgraphs based on their respective contributions. Experiments on several graph classification datasets of different networks show that SeeExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [202] [Multimodal Pretraining for Generalizable EEG Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21384)
*Targol Bakhtiarvand,Jugal Kalita,Adham Atyabi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a multimodal EEG foundation model combining Mamba-based raw signal encoder, ViT-style time-frequency encoder, and lightweight text encoder within a shared embedding space. Using masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses for pretraining, the model achieves state-of-the-art seizure detection (0.874 AUROC on CHB-MIT, 0.878 with ensemble) and demonstrates robust patient-independent performance under LOSO evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing EEG models for epilepsy are limited to specific datasets and tasks, making cross-dataset generalization difficult. The paper aims to develop an adaptable EEG backbone that can support a range of EEG-related tasks, overcoming the narrow applicability of current models.

Method: A multimodal EEG foundation model with three encoders: (1) Mamba architecture for raw signal encoding, (2) Vision Transformer (ViT)-style encoder for time-frequency data, and (3) lightweight text encoder. Pretraining uses masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses to learn seizure-relevant representations without labels. Fine-tuning on CHB-MIT and additional seizure detection datasets.

Result: On standard CHB-MIT split: best single model AUROC 0.874, ensemble AUROC 0.878 (state-of-the-art). Under LOSO protocol (rarely reported): mean balanced accuracy 0.558 across 19 subjects, highlighting difficulty of patient-independent detection.

Conclusion: The multimodal foundation model enables robust seizure detection and straightforward adaptation to new scenarios across datasets and evaluation settings, while also supporting interpretable seizure localization.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) models used for epilepsy are often limited to specific datasets and tasks. This limited approach can make it challenging to apply these models across different datasets or in various situations. However, recent studies in foundation models and self-supervised learning suggest that an adaptable EEG backbone could support a range of EEG related tasks. In this study, we have developed a multimodal EEG foundation model that combines a raw signal encoder based on the Mamba architecture, a Vision Transformer (ViT)-style encoder for time-frequency data, and a lightweight encoder for text, all within a shared embedding space. The pretraining process relies on several innovative techniques, such as masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses. These methods are designed to create rich, seizure-relevant representations without requiring labeled data. To assess the efficacy and generalization of our pretrained model, we fine-tuned it on the canonical CHB-MIT seizure detection benchmark and additional seizure detection datasets, and conducted extensive experiments comparing different model variants. On the standard CHB-MIT split, our best single model achieved an AUROC of 0.874, and an ensemble variant reached 0.878 AUROC, representing state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark. In addition to standard train-test splits, we evaluated performance under a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol, which is rarely reported in prior EEG seizure modeling work and highlights the difficulty of patient-independent seizure detection, with a mean LOSO balanced accuracy of 0.558 across 19 subjects. Across datasets and evaluation settings, our multimodal foundation model enabled robust seizure detection and straightforward adaptation to new seizure detection scenarios, while also supporting interpretable seizure localization.

</details>


### [203] [MSBraM: A Multi-scale Self-supervised Brain Foundation Model for Hierarchical EEG Dynamics Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21402)
*Tao Zhou,Jing Han,Lingyu Shu,Zixing Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MSBraM is a multi-scale self-supervised foundation model for EEG that learns hierarchical representations by first tokenizing raw signals into multi-resolution semantic codes via VQ reconstruction, then pretraining with curriculum-based masked prediction; trained on 2,400+ hours of EEG, it outperforms SOTA across 10 downstream tasks on 12 datasets, demonstrating that explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is key for EEG foundation models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-supervised EEG foundation models fail to capture the multi-scale temporal structure of EEG signals (local neural patterns + long-range dependencies), limiting cross-scale representation learning and generalization across diverse downstream tasks.

Method: MSBraM uses a two-stage pretraining framework: (1) a multi-scale neural tokenizer that discretizes raw EEG into semantic codes at different temporal resolutions via vector-quantized reconstruction, and (2) curriculum multi-scale masked prediction pretraining that progressively integrates fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context.

Result: MSBraM achieves superior performance over other state-of-the-art pretrained models across 10 downstream tasks on 12 public datasets, demonstrating strong generalization and transferability after pretraining on over 2,400 hours of EEG data.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is critical for building effective EEG foundation models, as validated by MSBraM's strong cross-task performance.

Abstract: Self-supervised foundation models have recently shown strong potential for electroencephalogram (EEG)-based analysis. However, existing approaches struggle to capture the inherently multi-scale temporal structure of EEG signals, where local neural patterns and long-range dependencies jointly encode task-relevant information. This limitation hampers cross-scale representation learning and generalization across diverse downstream tasks. To address this challenge, we propose MSBraM, a Multi-Scale self-supervised Brain foundation Model designed to learn hierarchical EEG representations. MSBraM follows a two-stage pretraining framework. First, a multi-scale neural tokenizer discretizes raw EEG signals into semantic codes at different temporal resolutions via vector-quantized reconstruction. Second, the model is pretrained to predict masked codes using a curriculum multi-scale masking strategy, progressively integrating fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context. We pretrain MSBraM on over 2,400 hours of EEG data and evaluate it across 10 downstream tasks on 12 public datasets. Extensive experiments show that MSBraM achieves superior performance on other state-of-the-art pretrained models, demonstrating strong generalization and transferability. These results indicate that explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is critical for effective EEG foundation models.

</details>


### [204] [Logical Regression for Planning with Axioms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21414)
*Connor Little,Christian Muise*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a methodology for approximating logical regression in planning domains with axioms, producing minimal partial states that generalize across domains, reducing execution monitoring variables by up to 70% and enabling frequent recovery in unexpected environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Logical regression, while useful for robust plan execution and non-deterministic planning, becomes significantly more complex when axioms are present in the domain.

Method: The authors propose an approximation of logical regression that limits conditions to partial states, produces minimal partial states, and avoids recalculating axioms.

Result: The method reduces variables considered for execution monitoring by up to 70% and enables over 50% recovery rates in several domains under unexpected environmental changes.

Conclusion: The approximated logical regression generalizes partial states across domains and yields robust execution monitors capable of frequent recovery in dynamic environments.

Abstract: In automated planning, logical regression is an operation that returns the most general condition necessary for an action to achieve a particular formula. It has many applications, such as allowing for more robust plan execution and providing compact policies for non-deterministic planning. Although relatively simple to calculate in basic planning settings, logical regression becomes significantly more complex when additional factors, such as axioms, are present. We introduce a methodology for approximating the logical regression of an action in a domain that includes axioms; an approximation that limits conditions to partial states. Our method produces minimal partial states while avoiding the recalculation of axioms. To demonstrate the impact of our methods, we embed our form of regression in an execution monitoring context, a well-established setting that can benefit greatly from logical regression. Our results show that this form of regression can dramatically generalize partial states across multiple domains, reducing the number of variables considered for execution monitoring by up to 70%, and demonstrate that the resulting execution monitor is robust enough to recover frequently in an environment with unexpected changes: several domains recover over 50% of the time in our tests.

</details>


### [205] [PATS: Policy-Aware Training Scaffolding for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21419)
*Yipeng Shi,Zhipeng Ma,Yue Wang,Qitai Tan,Yang Li,Peng Chen,Zhengzhou Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Pats is a policy-centric framework that uses dynamic skill scaffolds (evidence cards from rollouts) to guide weak LLM agent policies during training, then discards them at deployment, achieving up to 18.6% improvement on ALFWorld/WebShop and 32.1% fewer prompt tokens on QA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Weak policies in long-horizon LLM agent RL repeat similar failures, producing uninformative rollouts that limit policy optimization. Existing skill-centric methods focus on skills themselves rather than providing adaptive training-time support for the evolving policy.

Method: Pats adopts a policy-centric training paradigm: it converts rollout groups from the latest policy into evidence cards, uses task-specific evaluation to adjust the context for subsequent rollouts, provides concrete guidance to weak policies, and revises/removes redundant context as the policy improves. The policy is optimized with environmental rewards via standard RLVR, and the scaffold is discarded at deployment.

Result: On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats improves over strong baselines by up to 18.6%. Across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, it remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens than the baseline.

Conclusion: The policy-centric training paradigm (Pats) effectively uses skills as a dynamic scaffold to support weak policies during training, which can be discarded at deployment, leading to improved performance and token efficiency.

Abstract: In long-horizon LLM agent reinforcement learning, weak policies often repeat similar failures, producing uninformative rollout trajectories and limiting effective policy optimization. Existing skill-centric methods improve exploration by optimizing, filtering, or internalizing reusable skills. However, they remain centered on the skills themselves rather than being designed as adaptive training-time support for the evolving policy. To address this, we propose a policy-centric training paradigm that reframes skills as a dynamic training scaffold. Our framework, Pats, converts rollout groups from the latest policy into evidence cards and uses task-specific evaluation to adjust the context used in subsequent rollouts.
