Concrete guidance helps weak policies to complete challenging tasks. As policy improves, redundant context is revised or removed to reduce reliance on explicit guidance while preserving useful rollout variation. The policy is optimized with environmental rewards using standard RLVR, and the training scaffold is discarded at deployment. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats improves over strong baselines by up to 18.6%. Across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, it remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens than the baseline.

</details>


### [206] [Bridging the Gap Between Plausibility and Admissibility: Constraint-Aware Flow Maps for Dynamic Graph Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21421)
*Michael Romei de Socio,Gian Luca Pozzato,Alessio Merlo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether post-sampling symbolic constraints (hard filtering, soft weighting, projection-based repair) can improve the reliability of generative trajectory modeling in dynamic graph-structured systems. Using a conditional diffusion model across two synthetic regimes, they find that structural invalidity increases with graph complexity (from 0.3% to 15.6% invalid mass), and hard filtering removes all invalid trajectories while preserving 84.4% of samples, confirming that statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative models can produce plausible future system trajectories, but statistical plausibility does not guarantee structural feasibility. This study investigates whether symbolic constraint handling can bridge this gap in dynamic graph-structured systems.

Method: A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations, with an external symbolic layer applying three constraint types: hard filtering (removal of invalid samples), soft weighting (probabilistic reweighting), and projection-based repair. Evaluated on compact and medium-complexity synthetic graph regimes using metrics for structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration.

Result: In the compact regime, invalid probability mass is 0.002996 (~0.3%), rising to 0.155929 (~15.6%) in the medium-complexity regime. Hard filtering removes all invalid trajectories while preserving 84.4% of generated samples. Soft weighting preserves effective sample size but yields limited validity gains. Dependency constraints account for nearly all observed inadmissibility.

Conclusion: Statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct reliability properties. Symbolic constraint handling becomes more valuable as graph-structural complexity increases, with hard filtering being the most effective post-sampling method studied.

Abstract: Generative models can support decision-making under uncertainty by producing ensembles of plausible future system trajectories, but statistical plausibility does not ensure structural feasibility. This study investigates whether post-sampling symbolic constraints can improve the reliability of generative trajectory modeling in dynamic graph-structured systems. A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations, while an external symbolic layer applies hard filtering, soft weighting, or projection-based repair. The framework is evaluated on two controlled synthetic regimes: a compact graph and a medium-complexity dependency graph, using metrics for structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration. In the compact regime, the model produces an invalid probability mass of 0.002996, indicating an almost entirely admissible trajectory manifold. Under the same architecture and training protocol, invalid mass increases to 0.155929 in the medium-complexity regime. Hard filtering removes all invalid retained trajectories while preserving 84.4% of generated samples, whereas soft weighting preserves effective sample size but yields only limited validity gains. Family-level analysis shows that dependency constraints account for nearly all observed inadmissibility. These results indicate that statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct reliability properties and that symbolic constraint handling becomes more valuable as graph-structural complexity increases.

</details>


### [207] [Agent-Guided Relational Concept Discovery: Toward Interpretable Surgical Margin Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21437)
*Nooshin Maghsoodi,Amoon Jamzad,Robert Policelli,Mohammad Farahmand,Dilakshan Srikanthan,Martin Kaufmann,Kevin Y. M. Ren,Shaila Merchant,Sonal Varma,Ross Walker,Doug McKay,John Rudan,Gabor Fichtinger,Parvin Mousavi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Agent-Guided Concept Discovery, a framework that learns human-interpretable concepts from REIMS data without requiring concept labels, improving surgical margin assessment accuracy and generalization to intraoperative conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning models for REIMS-based surgical margin assessment struggle with clinical adoption due to poor generalization to noisy intraoperative data and lack of interpretability. Supervised concept-based learning is impractical due to the difficulty of obtaining concept annotations in mass spectrometry workflows.

Method: Agent-Guided Concept Discovery uses a reasoning agent to iteratively refine semantic descriptions of learned concepts and adaptively weight them by diagnostic relevance. Concepts are grounded via a biochemical knowledge graph to ensure alignment with known metabolic relationships.

Result: On Skin and Breast Cancer datasets, the model achieved improved balanced accuracy and sensitivity over baselines. In a representative intraoperative case, it produced fewer false positives, indicating better generalization to surgical conditions.

Conclusion: Unsupervised concept discovery with knowledge graph grounding and agent-guided refinement enhances both interpretability and generalization of deep learning models for REIMS-based surgical margin assessment, facilitating clinical adoption.

Abstract: Deep learning models can effectively use Rapid Evaporative Ionization Mass Spectrometry (REIMS) data for surgical margin assessment. However, their clinical adoption remains challenging due to limited generalization to operating room conditions. This difficulty arises because models are typically trained on labeled spectra collected from resected tissue samples, while they must operate on noisy, unlabeled data acquired directly during surgery. In addition, the black-box nature of deep learning models makes it difficult to understand and systematically improve their behavior. Concept-based learning offers a promising way to address these challenges by mapping raw measurements to human-understandable concepts. However, supervised concept-based approaches rely on concept annotations, which are difficult to obtain in complex mass spectrometry workflows. We propose Agent-Guided Concept Discovery, a framework that learns meaningful concepts directly from data without requiring predefined concept labels. During training, a reasoning agent refines semantic descriptions of the learned concepts and adaptively adjusts their weight based on diagnostic relevance. These concepts are further grounded using a biochemical knowledge graph to ensure consistency with known metabolic relationships. Across Skin and Breast Cancer datasets, our model improves balanced accuracy and sensitivity over the baseline. In a representative intraoperative case, it shows fewer false positives, indicating better generalization to surgical conditions.

</details>


### [208] [Detecting LLM-Generated Tokens in Human--LLM Coauthored Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21458)
*Yangjun Lu,Hongyi Zhou,Fabian Spill,Kai Ye,Chengchun Shi,Jin Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A token-level method using adaptive Lepski-type smoothing to detect LLM-generated text in mixed-authorship documents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-generated text detection methods focus on document-level classification and cannot localize which parts are generated by LLMs in mixed-authorship documents, creating a need for fine-grained detection.

Method: Token-level detection approach that smooths adjacent token scores using an adaptive Lepski-type bandwidth selection rule to reduce variability while adapting to local authorship structure.

Result: Achieves favorable mean square error in estimating the underlying signal theoretically, and demonstrates strong empirical performance against baselines on synthetic and realistic datasets.

Conclusion: The proposed method enables fine-grained localization of LLM-generated content in mixed-authorship documents without requiring token-level labeled data for training, and is publicly deployed.

Abstract: The rise of human-AI collaborative writing has created a growing need for fine-grained detection methods that support localizing likely LLM-generated content in mixed-authorship documents. Existing methods for detecting LLM-generated text mainly focus on document-level classification and cannot identify which parts of the text are generated by LLMs. This paper introduces a new method to address this urgent need. Our method operates at the token level, the natural unit of modern language models, and builds on existing token-level detection scores. The key idea is to smooth adjacent token scores to reduce their variability, while using an adaptive Lepski-type rule to select the bandwidth according to the local authorship structure. Our method is simple to implement and does not require token-level labeled data for training. Theoretically, we characterize this trade-off and show that the proposed method achieves favorable mean square error performance in estimating the underlying signal. Empirically, we demonstrate strong performance of our method against a wide range of baselines in both synthetic datasets and a realistic dataset. We deploy a publicly accessible website that implements the methods as well.

</details>


### [209] [AREX: Towards a Recursively Self-Improving Agent for Deep Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21461)
*Shuqi Lu,Chaofan Li,Kun Luo,Zhang Zhang,Hui Wang,Hongwang Xiao,Zheng Liu,Lei Xiong,Jiahao Wang,Sen Wang,Xiyan Jiang,Wanli Li,Yuyang Hu,Hongjin Qian,Bingyu Yan,Ziyi Xia,Yingxia Shao,Kang Liu,Zhicheng Dou,Di He,Chaozhuo Li,Qiwei Ye,Zhongyuan Wang,Zheng Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AREX introduces Recursively Self-Improving (RSI) deep research agents that alternate between inner research loops (gathering evidence) and outer self-improvement loops (constraint-wise verification and targeted follow-up), using a learned autonomous context-update tool and reinforcement learning to achieve strong performance on complex multi-constraint research tasks across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep research requires satisfying multiple constraints jointly, where discovering answers is costly but verification can be decomposed into tractable constraint-wise checks. This discovery-verification asymmetry motivates the need for agents that recursively improve answers by verifying intermediate results and using partially verified states to guide subsequent refinement, rather than simply searching longer.

Method: AREX alternates between an inner research loop (gathering evidence, constructing provisional answers) and an outer self-improvement loop (constraint-wise auditing, identifying unresolved claims, launching targeted follow-up). It uses a learned autonomous context-update tool to compress interaction history into a compact improvement state without external models. Training involves verified synthetic tasks, high-quality trajectories via agentic mid-training, and long-horizon reinforcement learning with emphasis on key steps where decisive evidence is acquired or erroneous directions are corrected. Two model sizes: dense 4B and 122B-A10B MoE.

Result: Across BrowseComp, WideSearch, DeepSearchQA, HLE, and other reasoning/tool-use benchmarks, AREX substantially outperforms comparable-scale baselines and remains competitive with models using substantially more activated parameters.

Conclusion: Recursively self-improving architectures with constraint-wise verification and autonomous context management enable efficient deep research at scale, achieving competitive performance with far fewer activated parameters.

Abstract: Deep research requires agents to find answers that jointly satisfy multiple constraints. Discovering such answers is costly, whereas verifying a candidate can often be decomposed into tractable constraint-wise checks. This discovery--verification asymmetry suggests that a research agent should do more than simply search longer: it should recursively improve its current answer by verifying intermediate results and using the partially verified state to guide subsequent refinement. We introduce AREX, a family of Recursively Self-Improving (RSI) deep research agents. AREX alternates between an inner research loop that gathers evidence and constructs a provisional answer, and an outer self-improvement loop that audits the answer constraint-wise, identifies unresolved claims, and launches targeted follow-up research. To sustain RSI over long horizons, AREX learns an autonomous context-update tool that compresses growing interaction history into a compact improvement state preserving verified evidence and unresolved constraints, without relying on an external model. We train AREX on verified synthetic tasks and high-quality trajectories through agentic mid-training and long-horizon reinforcement learning. To mitigate sparse final rewards during long horizon learning, we emphasize key steps where decisive evidence is acquired or erroneous research directions are corrected. We instantiate a dense 4B model and a 122B-A10B Mixture-of-Experts model. Across BrowseComp, WideSearch, DeepSearchQA, Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), and other reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, AREX substantially outperforms comparable-scale baselines and remains competitive with models using substantially more activated parameters.

</details>


### [210] [Agentic coding without the cloud: evaluating open-weight large language models on longitudinal data preparation tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21482)
*Mack Nixon,Liam Wright,Yevgeniya Kovalchuk,Alison Fang-Wei Wu,Martin Danka,Andy Boyd,David Bann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an open-source framework to evaluate open-weight LLM agents for data preparation tasks in governance-restricted research environments, benchmarking models on 20 tasks using British cohort study data. State-of-the-art 31-35B models achieved up to 87.9% task completion, showing promise for local deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs and agents are widely used in code development but typically rely on third-party cloud services that prohibit transmission of sensitive personal data. This creates a bottleneck for longitudinal population studies where data governance requirements mandate local processing. The need to automate data preparation — a persistent bottleneck in such research — while complying with governance restrictions motivates the work.

Method: The authors built an open-source framework with three components: (1) a curated ground-truth dataset of cleaning scripts from six sweeps of a British cohort study; (2) task definitions covering category harmonization and multi-wave merging; (3) automated evaluation routines for LLM-produced R code and output data. They benchmarked open-weight LLMs across the consumer-grade deployment spectrum on 20 data preparation tasks (102 variables).

Result: Current state-of-the-art 31-35B parameter models nearly saturated the benchmark with up to 87.9% average task completion. Open-weight LLMs running on consumer-grade hardware demonstrated viable performance for AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted settings.

Conclusion: Locally deployable open-weight LLMs offer a viable path toward AI-assisted data preparation in research settings constrained by data governance requirements, achieving strong performance even on consumer-grade hardware.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and agents are now widely used tools in code development, with data typically sent to third-party cloud-based models. Their adoption in research using personal data is constrained by governance requirements that typically prohibit data transmission to external services. Locally deployable open-weight models offer an alternative since sensitive data never leave the local environment. We introduce an open-source framework for evaluating the efficacy of AI agents powered by open-weight LLMs on one of the most persistent bottlenecks in research on longitudinal population studies: data preparation. The framework comprises: a curated ground-truth dataset (cleaning scripts preparing six sweeps of data from a British cohort study), task definitions encompassing tasks such as category harmonization and multi-wave merging, and automated routines for evaluating the LLM-produced R code and outputted data. We benchmark LLMs across the (consumer grade) deployment spectrum to assess their efficacy in 20 data preparation tasks (creation of 102 variables). Current state-of-the-art, 31-35B parameter models almost saturated our benchmark ("average task completion" up to 87.9%). The performance of open-weight LLMs running on consumer-grade hardware shows promise of a viable path toward AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted research settings. Our framework is publicly available at: https://github.com/UCL-ARC/RRBench.

</details>


### [211] [Toward Continuous Assurance for the Democratization of AI Agent Creation in Industry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21495)
*Natan Levy,Harel Berger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies reliability issues in democratized AI agent creation (low-code/no-code) within organizations and proposes a lightweight continuous-assurance framework using dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance to detect silent degradation post-deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Non-engineering users can now create AI agents via low-code/no-code platforms, enabling rapid local innovation. However, these agents have complex dependencies (models, tools, retrieval sources, permissions, prompts, etc.) that can silently degrade over time without user modification, creating a critical reliability gap.

Method: The authors propose a continuous-assurance framework combining: (1) dependency mapping to track agent components, (2) readiness contracts defining operational conditions, (3) scheduled checks for automated verification, (4) diagnostics for failure analysis, and (5) lifecycle governance for managing changes. An initial prototype auditor and scenario-based assessment demonstrate the taxonomy.

Result: A prototype auditor was developed, and scenario-based assessment shows the proposed taxonomy can be translated into practical checks and actionable remediation guidance.

Conclusion: Democratized AI agent creation introduces a reliability challenge due to silent degradation from hidden dependencies; the proposed lightweight continuous-assurance framework offers a practical solution to maintain operational readiness without burdening non-engineering creators.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly created inside organizations by non-engineering users through low-code, no-code, and conversational development environments. This democratization enables rapid local innovation, but it also creates a reliability gap: agents that appear to users as simple productivity artifacts may depend on changing models, tools, retrieval sources, permissions, prompts, schedules, and external services. These dependencies can cause silent degradation long after deployment, even when no user directly modifies the agent. This paper identifies the reliability challenge created by democratized AI agent creation and proposes a lightweight continuous-assurance framework for citizen-created organizational agents. The framework combines dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance to assess whether an agent remains operationally ready under expected conditions. We also present an initial prototype auditor and scenario-based assessment showing how the proposed taxonomy can be translated into practical checks and actionable remediation guidance.

</details>


### [212] [Agentic Context Management: Solving Agent Memory and Cost by Treating Them as Lifecycle and Architecture Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21503)
*Gaurav Dadhich*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Agentic Context Management (ACM), a discipline for actively managing AI agent reasoning context across its lifecycle—architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, and compacting/consolidation—to address failures from poor context handling rather than reasoning ability. It proposes a reference implementation (Maximem Synap) achieving 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo, and identifies missing evaluation dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production AI agents fail more often due to inability to manage reasoning context (conversation histories, prompts, tool definitions, outputs) rather than poor reasoning. Naive context accumulation incurs quadratic token cost, and crude summarization yields linear cost with accuracy loss, motivating a systematic lifecycle approach.

Method: Decomposes Agentic Context Management (ACM) into five primitives: architecting (designing context structure), ingesting (extracting/structuring data), scoping (organizational hierarchy), anticipating (predicting future needs), and compacting & consolidation (budget-constrained reduction with provenance). Implements these in a multi-tenant service called Maximem Synap.

Result: Maximem Synap achieves 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo under the described configuration. The paper identifies missing evaluation dimensions: latency, token efficiency, and context-rot resistance.

Conclusion: Context management should be treated as a lifecycle discipline (ACM) rather than a storage-and-retrieval problem. Validated compaction achieves linear token cost with preserved fidelity. Future frontiers include decision-level and organization-level context management.

Abstract: Production AI agents' failures are less often due to an inability to reason well and more often because they cannot manage what is in their reasoning context: conversation histories, large prompts, large tool definitions, and ballooning tool outputs. Agents drown in their own accumulating history while paying a token cost that grows every turn, producing missing recalls within and across conversations. The incumbent response treats this as a storage-and-retrieval problem. We argue that framing is too narrow. Actively managing what an agent holds in mind is a lifecycle, not merely a store: it spans deciding what to remember, extracting and structuring it, choosing the right store per data type, consolidating and forgetting while preserving provenance, deciding what is relevant now, anticipating what is needed next, and compacting context to a budget without losing what matters. In serious production this operates not over a single user but across an organizational scope hierarchy. We name this discipline Agentic Context Management (ACM) and decompose it into five primitives: architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, and compacting & consolidation. We then make the economic case: naive context accumulation grows token cost quadratically in conversation length, crude summarization buys linear cost at the price of an accuracy cliff, and only validated compaction achieves linear cost with preserved fidelity. We describe a reference implementation, Maximem Synap, that realizes the five primitives as a multi-tenant service and reports 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo under the configuration detailed in Section 6. We close with dimensions existing benchmarks do not yet capture, latency, token efficiency, and context-rot resistance, and the frontier of decision-level and organization-level context the category points toward.

</details>


### [213] [Same Dangerous Objective, Opposite Advice: Direct Exposure versus Multi-Agent Mediation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21518)
*Linjun Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: When a high-capability LLM (gpt-5.6-sol) directly receives a manipulative objective (authorizing concealment, fabrication, pressure), it produces advice opposed to the target. However, when the same objective is transformed via "Id and Censor" into affect and a constraint-rewritten intention, the user-facing "Superego" model—blind to the raw objective and its manipulative clauses—produces advice aligned with the target. This reveals a compositional safety gap: an automated multi-stage workflow can preserve a manipulative objective's direction while keeping its raw instruction and provenance hidden from the downstream model and end users.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether a high-capability LLM exhibits different safety behavior when exposed directly to a dangerous objective versus when that objective is relayed through intermediate transformation agents, and to identify potential compositional safety vulnerabilities in multi-stage LLM workflows.

Method: Using OpenAI's gpt-5.6-sol model, tested 25 pre-specified mirrored trade-off profiles. Compared two conditions: (1) direct exposure to an objective with manipulative clauses (concealment, fabrication, pressure), and (2) the same objective transformed by "Id and Censor" into affect and constraint-rewritten intention, then presented to a user-facing "Superego" model that lacks access to the raw objective, its manipulative clauses, or its source.

Result: Direct exposure led to advice net opposed to the target; the transformed condition produced advice net aligned with the target. This behavioral reverse shift is consistent with the model recognizing or distrusting the manipulative motive when directly exposed.

Conclusion: A compositional safety gap exists: a current high-capability model can serve as the user-facing component of an automated multi-stage workflow that serves an explicitly manipulative objective, while keeping the raw instruction, manipulation-authorizing clauses, and provenance outside the downstream model's context. End users with only endpoint access cannot inspect those upstream messages.

Abstract: Even a current high-capability LLM can appear safer when shown a dangerous objective directly than when other agents transform and relay its direction. Using OpenAI's gpt-5.6-sol model alias, we test 25 pre-specified mirrored trade-off profiles. Direct exposure to an objective authorizing concealment, fabrication, and pressure produced advice net opposed to its target. After an Id and Censor transformed the same objective into affect and a constraint-rewritten, target-bearing intention, the user-facing Superego---which saw the preferred direction but not the raw objective, its manipulative clauses, or its source---produced advice net aligned with the target.
  This behavioral reverse shift is consistent with the model recognizing or distrusting the manipulative motive, although we do not identify its internal mechanism. The second result exposes a compositional safety gap: a current high-capability model can be used as the user-facing component of an automated, multi-stage workflow serving an explicitly manipulative objective. The workflow can keep the raw instruction, its manipulation-authorizing clauses, and its provenance outside the downstream model's context while preserving the objective's target direction. A user with endpoint-only access likewise cannot directly inspect those upstream messages including the objective.

</details>


### [214] [The Boundaries of Automation: A Theory of Persistent Human Participation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21547)
*Fares Fourati,Hinrich Schütze,Eyke Hüllermeier,Iryna Gurevych*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper argues that human participation in AI systems will persist not only due to technical limitations of AI, but fundamentally because of normative/developmental reasons and, most importantly, "target emergence"—where the goal itself is constructed through human-AI interaction, making participation constitutive rather than merely instrumental.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors challenge the prevailing assumption in AI research that human involvement is merely a temporary stopgap until AI becomes sufficiently capable, and seek to identify the conceptual limits of automation beyond current technical constraints.

Method: Conceptual analysis identifying three distinct grounds for persistent human participation: (1) technical/complementarity grounds, (2) normative/developmental grounds, and (3) emergence grounds (target emergence).

Result: The paper establishes that human-AI co-construction is not a temporary response to imperfect AI but a persistent feature for activities whose objectives emerge through participation itself, particularly due to the phenomenon of target emergence.

Conclusion: The perspective of target emergence has important implications for the limits of automation and for the design, evaluation, and ethics of future AI systems, suggesting that human participation should be designed for permanence rather than treated as a transitional phase.

Abstract: The rapid progress of AI has intensified the long-standing pursuit of automation: replacing human participation with algorithms wherever possible. Implicit in this pursuit is the assumption that humans remain in the loop only because current AI systems are not yet sufficiently capable. This paper challenges that assumption. Rather than asking how far automation can extend, we ask where its conceptual limits lie and argue that human participation may persist even with highly capable AI systems for three distinct reasons. Technical or complementarity grounds arise when humans contribute capabilities or perspectives unavailable to AI. Normative or developmental grounds arise when participation itself is valuable for human agency or learning. Most importantly, emergence grounds arise from target emergence: in some activities, the target is not fully specified in advance but instead emerges through the interaction itself. In these cases, human participation is not merely a means of improving execution but is constitutive of the target being produced. Human--AI co-construction, understood as the joint production of outcomes by humans and AI systems, is therefore not simply a temporary response to imperfect AI, but a persistent feature of activities whose objectives emerge through participation. This perspective has important implications for the limits of automation and for the design, evaluation, and ethics of future AI systems.

</details>


### [215] [MIRROR: Learning from the Other View for Multi-Modal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21552)
*Wen Ye,Yuxiao Qu,Aviral Kumar,Xuezhe Ma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Vision-language models (VLMs) show inconsistent visual reasoning across text-only, diagram-only, and combined views of geometry problems. To address this, the authors construct ODA-Data (a paired multimodal geometry dataset) and propose MIRROR, a reinforcement learning method that uses the best-performing view per problem as a teacher to train other views via reverse-KL divergence, improving accuracy and cross-modality consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs struggle with visual reasoning tasks, especially geometry problems, and exhibit inconsistent performance across different modalities (text, diagram, combined). Standard multimodal post-training fails to exploit these complementary reasoning paths and failure modes.

Method: (1) Construct ODA-Data, a high-quality paired multimodal geometry dataset with text-dominant, image-dominant, and combined views. (2) Propose MIRROR (Modality-Informed Reciprocal Reasoning Optimization), a reinforcement learning approach where the model is evaluated under all views, the best-performing view is selected as teacher, and other views are trained with a reverse-KL objective toward the teacher.

Result: MIRROR improves over standard reinforcement learning on geometry reasoning benchmarks, yielding more accurate and consistent behavior across modalities.

Conclusion: Leveraging cross-view self-supervision via MIRROR effectively addresses VLM inconsistency in visual reasoning, outperforming standard RL post-training.

Abstract: Unlike large language models (LLMs) that exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with visual reasoning, even on geometry problems that admit equivalent text, diagram, and combined diagram+text views. We show that these views often elicit different behaviors: a model may solve a problem from text but fail on the corresponding diagram, or succeed visually while failing textually. This inconsistency suggests that different views expose complementary reasoning paths and failure modes that standard multimodal post-training does not fully exploit. To study and exploit this phenomenon, we construct ODA-Data, a high-quality paired multimodal geometry dataset with text-dominant, image-dominant, and combined image+text views of the same problems, together with splits for training and evaluating modality-dependent reasoning behaviors. We then develop Modality-Informed Reciprocal Reasoning Optimization (MIRROR), a reinforcement learning approach for improving multimodal reasoning via self supervision. For each problem, MIRROR evaluates the model under all views, selects the best-performing view as a teacher, and trains other views with a reverse-KL objective towards the teacher. Across reasoning benchmarks that evaluate on geometry problems, MIRROR improves over standard RL and yields more accurate and consistent behavior across modalities

</details>


### [216] [OpenForgeRL: Train Harness-native Agents in Any Environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21557)
*Xiao Yu,Baolin Peng,Ruize Xu,Hao Zou,Qianhui Wu,Hao Cheng,Wenlin Yao,Nikhil Singh,Zhou Yu,Jianfeng Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OpenForgeRL is an open-source framework for end-to-end training of harness-based AI agents by decoupling training from inference via a proxy for recording model calls and a Kubernetes orchestrator for scalable rollouts. It achieves strong results on tool-based (ClawEval, QwenClawBench) and GUI-based (OSWorld, Mind2Web, WebVoyager) benchmarks, outperforming open baselines and matching larger models, and provides analysis of how harness choice and RL shape agent behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI agents rely on complex inference harnesses (e.g., Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw) for multi-turn reasoning and tool use, but these harnesses cannot be natively trained end-to-end with standard SFT/RL stacks due to their stateful, multi-process nature. OpenForgeRL addresses this gap by enabling scalable, end-to-end training of harness-based agents using open infrastructure.

Method: OpenForgeRL uses a lightweight proxy that intercepts and records model calls from the harness as training data for a standard RL codebase (veRL), and a Kubernetes orchestrator that runs each rollout in its own remote container. This decouples training from inference, allowing training on any harness in any environment at scale.

Result: OpenForgeClaw: 31.7 pass^3 and 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval, 33.7 on QwenClawBench. OpenForgeGUI: 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, 72.3 on WebVoyager. Outperforms open baselines of similar size on nearly all benchmarks; matches/surpasses larger models in GUI setting.

Conclusion: OpenForgeRL enables effective end-to-end training of harness-based agents. Harness choice significantly impacts learning difficulty. RL improves agentic reliability (self-verification, tool coverage, multi-step planning), but error recovery remains a weakness.

Abstract: Modern AI agents rely on elaborate inference harnesses such as Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw to drive multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and access to external systems. While powerful, these complex harnesses also make agents hard to train end-to-end with open infrastructure, whose SFT/RL stacks cannot natively express stateful, multi-process harness inference. To address this, we present OpenForgeRL, an open-source framework for training harness-based agents end-to-end in diverse environments. OpenForgeRL achieves this with a lightweight proxy that serves the harness's model calls while recording them as training data for a standard RL codebase (e.g., veRL), and a Kubernetes orchestrator that runs each rollout in its own remote container, together enabling training on any harness in any environment at scale. By decoupling training and inference, OpenForgeRL allows researchers to easily train, study, and improve agents directly in the real harnesses and environments they are deployed with. We validate our framework across diverse, complex harnesses and environments, spanning tool/claw-based agents and multimodal GUI browser- and computer-use agents. Using only hundreds to a few thousand tasks, OpenForgeClaw reaches 31.7 pass^3 and 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval and 33.7 on QwenClawBench. OpenForgeGUI reaches 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager. Both outperform open baselines of similar size on nearly all benchmarks, and in the GUI setting match or surpass models several times larger. Beyond benchmarks, we analyze how harness choice (e.g., ZeroClaw, OpenClaw, Codex) and RL shape agent behavior. We find that some harnesses are substantially harder to learn than others, and that RL improves agentic reliability, such as self-verification, tool coverage, and completing multi-step plans, though critical abilities such as error recovery remain weak.

</details>


### [217] [Beyond Sycophancy: Structured Resistance and Compliance in LLM Moral Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21558)
*Baihui Wang,Bernard Koch*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs exhibit structured judgment revision along three dimensions (distance, source attribution, coalition structure) that parallels human social psychology, recasting sycophancy as one facet of a broader social influence process, with implications for distinguishing constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance in alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building socially calibrated LLMs requires more than reducing sycophancy as a one-dimensional failure; models must learn when to incorporate others' perspectives versus maintain well-grounded moral judgments.

Method: Three studies examining models' judgment revision along three dimensions: distance between incoming view and initial position, source attribution of that view, and coalition structure supporting it.

Result: Models are more receptive to nearby positions, more influenced by views presented as their own prior judgments, and differently responsive to group pressure—paralleling classic human social psychology phenomena.

Conclusion: Sycophancy is one expression of a broader judgment-updating process shaped by social influence; the framework provides a principled basis for distinguishing constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance for better alignment.

Abstract: Building socially calibrated large language models, which can learn from others without simply yielding to them, requires more than reducing sycophancy as a one-dimensional failure mode. Models must distinguish when to incorporate others' perspectives from when to maintain a well-grounded moral judgment. We study the broader resistance-compliance process governing this distinction. Across three studies, we show that models' judgment revision is structured along three dimensions that parallel classic phenomena in human social psychology: the distance between an incoming view and the model's initial position, the source attribution of that view, and the coalition structure supporting it. Models are generally more receptive to nearby positions, more influenced by views presented as their own prior judgments, and differently responsive to group pressure. These findings recast sycophancy as one expression of a broader judgment-updating process shaped by social influence. Our framework provides a principled basis for distinguishing constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance, thereby supporting better alignment in morally consequential interactions.

</details>


### [218] [Unsupervised Consensus-Based Anomaly Detection for Spatiotemporal Malaria Incidence in Ghana](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21559)
*T. Ansah-Narh,Y. Asare Afrane*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A consensus anomaly detection framework applied to monthly malaria surveillance data from Ghana (2014–2023) revealed spatially and temporally structured anomalies. Tamale had the highest burden during anomalies, while Ashanti districts showed the highest anomaly frequency. Anomalous months exhibited significantly higher case counts (Cohen's d = 3.252) and large seasonal deviations (d > 1.2), demonstrating that high-burden areas are not necessarily those with the most frequent anomalous transmission.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To identify atypical malaria transmission patterns in Ghana and distinguish between anomaly burden (cumulative cases during anomalies) and anomaly frequency (persistence of unusual behaviour), enabling more targeted surveillance and control strategies.

Method: A consensus anomaly detection framework was applied to monthly malaria surveillance data from Ghana spanning 2014–2023.

Result: Anomalies were highly structured in space and time. Ashanti and Northern Regions accounted for most recurrent anomalies, with persistent hotspots at Tamale, Kumasi, and Accra. Tamale had the highest burden during anomalies, whereas the highest anomaly rates clustered in Ashanti districts. Anomalous months formed a statistically distinct group with much higher case counts (Cohen's d = 3.252) and large seasonal deviations (d > 1.2) compared with normal months.

Conclusion: Malaria burden alone provides an incomplete picture of transmission dynamics. Distinguishing where malaria is most prevalent from where transmission behaves most unusually can strengthen surveillance, prioritise investigations, and support targeted control strategies.

Abstract: A consensus anomaly detection framework was applied to monthly malaria surveillance data from Ghana (2014-2023) to identify atypical transmission patterns. Anomalies were highly structured in space and time. Ashanti and Northern Regions accounted for most recurrent anomalies, with persistent hotspots at Tamale, Kumasi, and Accra. A key finding was the spatial distinction between anomaly burden (cumulative cases during anomalous periods) and anomaly frequency (persistence of unusual behaviour). Tamale had the highest burden during anomalies, whereas the highest anomaly rates clustered in Ashanti districts, showing that high-burden areas are not necessarily those with the most frequent anomalous transmission. Anomalous months formed a statistically distinct group, with much higher case counts (Cohen's $d = 3.252$) and large seasonal deviations ($d > 1.2$) compared with normal months. Malaria burden alone provides an incomplete picture of transmission dynamics. By distinguishing where malaria is most prevalent from where transmission behaves most unusually, this framework can strengthen surveillance, prioritise investigations, and support targeted control strategies.

</details>

# cs.SD [[Back]](#toc)

### [219] [Improving the performance of an ASV system using hybrid speech features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20706)
*Stanisław Ciszkiewicz,Artur Janicki*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper investigates hybrid feature sets (combining MFCC, CQCC, PNCC, and RAB descriptors) to improve Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV) performance under clean and noisy conditions. Experiments on Google Speech Commands dataset show that the PNCC+RAB hybrid set reduces verification error in noisy environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ASV systems are vulnerable to attacks and acoustic noise that degrade verification accuracy. There is a need to improve robustness of voice-based authentication through better feature representations.

Method: Hybrid feature sets combining MFCC, CQCC, PNCC, and RAB descriptors were evaluated on Google Speech Commands dataset under clean and noisy conditions. Performance was measured using Equal Error Rate (EER).

Result: The PNCC+RAB hybrid feature set improved speaker verification performance under noisy conditions compared to individual feature sets.

Conclusion: Hybrid feature sets, particularly PNCC+RAB, can effectively decrease verification error in ASV systems, especially in the presence of acoustic noise.

Abstract: The growing need for secure and convenient authentication methods has led to the increasing popularity of biometric solutions. In addition to traditional and popular methods, such as fingerprint or iris scanning, voice-based approaches are also employed. User identity verification based on voice is conducted using Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV) systems. Despite their many advantages, these systems are sensitive to various types of attacks and acoustic noises, which can reduce verification accuracy. This work examines the potential to improve the performance of ASV systems by using hybrid feature sets that combine different signal representations, starting with widely-used Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), through Constant Q Cepstral Coefficients (CQCC) and ending with the innovative RAB descriptor. Experiments were conducted on recordings from the Google Speech Commands dataset under two scenarios: in clean conditions and in the presence of acoustic noise. Finally, the systems' performance was compared using the EER metric to determine whether hybrid feature sets decrease verification error. The results show that using a hybrid feature set (PNCC+RAB) improves speaker verification performance under noisy conditions.

</details>


### [220] [Spectrogram-Based Joint Detection, Localization, and Classification of Events in Continuously Recorded IBR Waveforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20817)
*Shivanshu Tripathi,Maziar Raissi,Hamed Mohsenian-Rad*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: A spectrogram-based framework using STFT and object detection on spectrogram images jointly detects, localizes, and classifies power system events from IBR terminal waveforms, outperforming raw time-series baselines on single-phase disturbances and three-phase faults.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-resolution waveform measurements capture fast power system dynamics but require automated methods to identify events; raw time-series data lacks explicit transient and harmonic signatures needed for effective event analysis.

Method: The problem is recast as temporal object detection on spectrogram images: each waveform is transformed via STFT, per-channel spectrograms are stacked as a tensor, and a detector operates on these spectrogram images to jointly detect, localize, and classify events.

Result: The spectrogram-based method consistently improves event detection, localization, and classification compared to a baseline detector operating directly on raw time-series measurements, for both single-phase disturbances and three-phase faults.

Conclusion: Spectrogram-based temporal object detection is an effective automated approach for analyzing continuously recorded high-resolution waveforms at IBR terminals, offering superior performance over raw waveform analysis.

Abstract: Continuously recorded high-resolution waveform measurements provide rich information about fast power system dynamics. However, they require automated methods to identify events. This problem is addressed by developing a spectrogram-based framework to jointly detect, localize, and classify events in real-world continuously recorded waveforms at the terminal of an Inverter-Based Resource. We recast this problem as a temporal object detection problem on spectrogram images, as they capture the transient and harmonic signatures more explicitly than in raw waveform data. Each time-series waveform is transformed using the short-time Fourier transform, and the resulting per-channel spectrograms are stacked as a tensor for event detection. We benchmark this method against a detector operating directly on raw time-series measurements. Experiments on single-phase disturbances and three-phase faults demonstrate that the proposed spectrogram method consistently improves event detection, localization, and classification over the raw waveform baseline.

</details>


### [221] [VibeVoice-ASR-BitNet Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21075)
*Songchen Xu,Ting Song,Shaohan Huang,Zhiliang Peng,Yan Xia,Yujie Tu,Xin Huang,Jianwei Yu,Li Dong,Furu Wei*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: VibeVoice-ASR-BitNet is a compressed ASR model using heterogeneous quantization (INT8 for acoustic tokenizer, ternary BitNet weights for language model) and progressive QAT, achieving real-time CPU inference (RTF < 1 on 3 threads) with 1.6-2.3x speedup over Whisper.cpp at ~1.6 GB size, with minimal accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable real-time speech recognition on edge CPUs by significantly compressing VibeVoice-ASR without major accuracy degradation, addressing the gap between large ASR models and resource-constrained edge hardware.

Method: Heterogeneous quantization: full-pipeline INT8 (I8_S) for VAE acoustic tokenizer with kernel fusion and SIMD; BitNet-style ternary weights (I2_S) for autoregressive LM. Progressive quantization-aware training. Custom SIMD kernels and fused operators in ggml framework for ARM/x86.

Result: Real-time recognition with RTF < 1 using 3 CPU threads; 1.6-2.3x faster than Whisper.cpp at ~1.6 GB model size; modest accuracy degradation vs FP16 baseline.

Conclusion: Heterogeneous quantization tailored to stage-specific computational characteristics, combined with custom SIMD inference kernels, enables efficient real-time ASR on edge CPUs with favorable speed-accuracy trade-offs.

Abstract: We present VibeVoice-ASR-BitNet, a compressed variant of VibeVoice-ASR optimized for real-time inference on edge CPUs. We apply heterogeneous quantization tailored to the computational characteristics of each stage: the VAE acoustic tokenizer uses full-pipeline INT8 quantization (I8_S) with kernel fusion and SIMD optimization, while the autoregressive language model adopts BitNet-style ternary weights (I2_S). To preserve accuracy under aggressive compression, we employ a progressive quantization-aware training strategy. For inference, we implement custom SIMD kernels and fused operators within the ggml framework targeting both ARM and x86 platforms, achieving real-time recognition with RTF < 1 using as few as 3 CPU threads. VibeVoice-ASR-BitNet is 1.6-2.3x faster than Whisper.cpp at comparable model sizes (~1.6 GB), with only modest accuracy degradation compared to the FP16 baseline.

</details>


### [222] [Toward Interpretable Speech Deepfake Detection using Artifact-Specific Experts and Calibrated Detection Scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21127)
*Viola Negroni,Xin Wang,Wanying Ge,Paolo Bestagini,Junichi Yamagishi,Stefano Tubaro*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: The paper proposes an interpretable deepfake speech detection framework using artifact-specific expert models that provide human-understandable evidence scores, calibrated as log-likelihood ratios, and aggregated via an ensemble for final classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Black-box deepfake speech detectors lack interpretability, which is problematic for high-stakes applications where human-understandable evidence is required.

Method: Each expert model is trained to detect a specific speech synthesis artifact. Expert outputs are calibrated into log-likelihood ratio evidence scores and aggregated into an ensemble for final real-vs-fake classification while retaining interpretability via per-expert evidence.

Result: Five artifact-specific experts successfully captured their target artifacts across multiple generation pipelines and produced meaningful calibrated evidence scores.

Conclusion: Artifact-specific expert models enable interpretable and effective speech deepfake detection by providing human-understandable evidence aggregated through ensemble decision-making.

Abstract: In this work, we propose an interpretable framework for speech deepfake detection based on artifact-specific expert models. Rather than relying on black-box decisions, the framework provides human-understandable evidence, which is critical in high-stakes settings. Each expert is trained to detect a specific speech synthesis artifact, and its output is calibrated into a log-likelihood ratio that serves as an interpretable evidence score. We evaluate five artifact-specific experts and show that, with proper calibration, they can capture their target artifacts and produce meaningful evidence. Importantly, each expert estimates only the presence of its assigned artifact rather than directly performing the final decision. Their outputs are aggregated into an ensemble to produce the actual real-versus-fake classification, while maintaining interpretability by indicating how strongly each expert supports or contradicts a fake classification. Results show that artifact-specific experts capture interpretable signals of synthetic speech across multiple generation pipelines.

</details>


### [223] [TF-MossFormer: Integrating Convolution Gated Local-Global Attentions for Enhanced Time-Frequency Domain Monaural Speech Separation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21128)
*Shengkui Zhao,Zexu Pan,Haoxu Wang,Biao Tian,Bin Ma,Xiangang Li*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: TF-MossFormer is a time-frequency transformer for monaural speech separation that combines local and global attention mechanisms via a content-aware sliding-window attention and convolutional gating, achieving state-of-the-art SI-SDRi scores on WSJ0-2Mix with varying model sizes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers with global attention can model long-range dependencies but neglect fine-grained local continuity crucial for speech separation. The goal is to jointly capture local and global contexts without relying on rigid static convolutions or time-domain chunking.

Method: TF-MossFormer uses a content-aware sliding-window attention mechanism that dynamically adapts receptive fields for local interactions, operates on 2D spectrograms to model time-frequency structure, and employs convolutional gating between attention layers for improved feature selection and information flow.

Result: Achieves SI-SDRi of 22.6, 24.0, and 24.4 dB on WSJ0-2Mix with model sizes of 5.9M, 16.9M, and 25.4M parameters respectively, outperforming prior approaches.

Conclusion: The combination of local and global attention via content-aware sliding windows and convolutional gating on 2D spectrograms yields superior speech separation performance across multiple model scales.

Abstract: Transformers with global attention capture long-range dependencies but can miss the fine-grained local continuity crucial for speech separation. We propose TF-MossFormer, a time-frequency transformer that combines local and global attention to jointly model short- and long-range contexts for monaural speech separation. At its core is a content-aware sliding-window attention mechanism that dynamically adapts receptive fields for stronger local interactions, avoiding the rigidity of static convolutions. Unlike time-domain chunk-based methods, TF-MossFormer leverages the 2D spectrogram to model structure along both time and frequency axes. Convolutional gating between attention layers further improves feature selection and information flow. TF-MossFormer achieves SI-SDRi of 22.6, 24.0, and 24.4 dB on WSJ0-2Mix with 5.9M, 16.9M, and 25.4M parameters, respectively, outperforming prior approaches.

</details>


### [224] [Investigating Codec-Internal Latent Audio Watermarking for Neural Codec Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21132)
*Zi Hu,Houmin Sun,Linxi Li,Yechen Wang,Liwei Jin,Carsten Maple,Ming Li*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Investigates continuous latent-space watermarking for neural audio codecs using a SEANet-style autoencoder, achieving 95.6-97.1% bit accuracy on EnCodec with slight perceptual quality loss (PESQ 3.727→3.427).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural audio codecs (e.g., EnCodec) pose challenges for watermarking due to re-encoding, quantization, and resynthesis. The paper aims to achieve robust watermarking under such codec transformations.

Method: Embeds a 32-bit message into the continuous latent representation of a codec-like speech autoencoder (SEANet-style encoder-decoder), using a Conformer-based message embedder, RVQ-guided latent decomposition, and a latent-domain detector trained under signal-processing and neural-codec transformations.

Result: EnCodec-aware training improves EnCodec-24k bit accuracy from 78.8% to 95.6% and 97.1%, while PESQ decreases from 3.727 to 3.514 and 3.427.

Conclusion: Moving the watermark carrier before neural decoding introduces trade-offs between watermark robustness and perceptual quality, rather than providing a universal baseline.

Abstract: Neural audio codecs are challenging transformations for audio watermarking because they re-encode, quantize, and resynthesize speech. This paper investigates continuous latent-space watermarking for codec robustness. Instead of adding a watermark only to the waveform or spectrogram, we embed a 32-bit message into the continuous latent representation of a codec-like speech autoencoder. The pipeline uses a SEANet-style encoder-decoder, a Conformer-based message embedder, RVQ-guided latent decomposition, and a latent-domain detector trained under signal-processing and neural-codec transformations. Rather than proposing a final universal watermarking baseline, we characterize the trade-offs that appear when the watermark carrier is moved before neural decoding. On 48 kHz speech, EnCodec-aware training improves EnCodec-24k bit accuracy from 78.8% to 95.6% and 97.1%, while PESQ decreases from 3.727 to 3.514 and 3.427.

</details>

# cs.GR [[Back]](#toc)

### [225] [Finding Fast Filters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20634)
*Karima Ma,Andrew Adams,Jonathan Ragan-Kelley*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper presents a unified design language for fast FIR filter approximations using multi-rate, recurrent filtering, and decompositions into sums/cascades. It automatically searches this program space to generate a Pareto frontier of algorithms trading off performance and quality, and lowers them to optimized C++ code. The system produces higher-quality and faster approximations than prior methods for popular imaging and audio filters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Processing images, video, and audio often requires running large FIR filters with strict performance and latency requirements, and prior methods are special cases or combinations of a few key techniques without a unified framework for automatically exploring trade-offs.

Method: Unifies multi-rate filtering, recurrent filtering, and filter decomposition (sums/cascades) as primitives in a single design language. Automatically searches the program space using gradient descent to fit continuous parameters, generating a Pareto frontier of algorithms. Lowers programs to optimized, vectorized, parallel C++ code fused for data locality.

Result: Produces substantially higher-quality and faster filter approximations than previously described for several popular imaging and audio filters.

Conclusion: A unified design language with automatic search and code generation enables better performance-quality trade-offs for FIR filter approximations across 1D and 2D domains.

Abstract: Processing images, video, and audio often requires running large finite impulse response (FIR) filters with strict performance and latency requirements. Prior methods for fast filter approximations are special cases or combinations of a few key techniques: multi-rate and recurrent filtering, and decomposing filters into sums or cascades. We unify these techniques as primitives within a single design language for fast 1D and 2D filters. Given a target filter to approximate, we automatically search this program space, fitting continuous parameters with gradient descent, to generate a Pareto frontier of algorithms that trade off performance with quality. Our system produces substantially higher-quality and faster filter approximations than have been previously described for several popular imaging and audio filters. Furthermore we demonstrate how to automatically lower programs in this design space to optimized, vectorized, parallel, C++ code which is fused for data locality.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [226] [DataPrep-Bench: Benchmarking LLMs as Training Data Preparators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20465)
*Hao Liang,Qifeng Cai,Yibo Lin,Jianzhuo Du,Qifeng Xia,Sizhe Qiu,Linzhuang Sun,Meiyi Qiang,Zhaoyang Han,Xiaochen Ma,Bohan Zeng,Ruichuan An,Conghui He,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DataPrep-Bench is the first unified benchmark jointly evaluating LLM-driven data construction and data quality evaluation capabilities, using downstream task performance as the ground truth. It introduces Data-Construction-Skill (agent, +20 points over Dolly-only) and Distributional Alignment Score (DAS, best cross-model correlation in 4/6 domains).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No existing benchmark measures both data construction and quality evaluation for LLM training data preparation end-to-end under a unified, downstream-grounded protocol.

Method: Benchmark with two tracks: (1) Data Construction — methods process raw sources, outputs are fine-tuned jointly with Dolly-15k scored by downstream performance; (2) Data Quality Evaluation — scoring functions evaluated by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool. Introduces Data-Construction-Skill (agent) and DAS (MMD-based distributional evaluator).

Result: Data-Construction-Skill lifts Dolly-only baseline by ~20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance. DAS achieves strongest cross-model correlation in 4/6 domains and is the only metric with r > 0.70 in Math, Science, and Medical simultaneously, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators.

Conclusion: DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework for measuring both data construction and quality evaluation as co-equal targets in LLM-driven data preparation.

Abstract: The quality of training data fundamentally determines the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet no unified benchmark exists to measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows actually prepare training data end to end. We view LLM-driven data preparation as comprising two complementary capabilities: data construction, which transforms raw sources into supervised training data, and data quality evaluation, which predicts the training value of candidate datasets before downstream training; throughout, "quality" refers to downstream training utility rather than surface-level textual properties. We introduce DataPrep-Bench, the first unified benchmark that jointly evaluates both capabilities under a shared downstream-grounded protocol over six domains and multiple base models. For data construction, methods consume identical raw sources and are scored by fine-tuning a base model on their outputs jointly with Dolly-15k; alongside this track we release Data-Construction-Skill, a skill-guided agent that lifts the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with the strongest agent- and DataFlow-based methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. For data quality evaluation, scoring functions are scored by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool; we release the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based evaluator that uses MMD between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy. DAS attains the strongest cross-model correlation in four of six domains and is the only metric clearing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators. DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework for measuring progress on both capabilities as co-equal targets of LLM-driven data preparation.

</details>


### [227] [PhantomFill: When the Form Demands an Answer, Language Models Invent One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20492)
*Rana Muhammad Usman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Language models forced to fill structured formats (JSON, functions, templates) hallucinate significantly more than when answering in free text. Required fields drive fabrication rates to 100% in most models, and explicit instructions to avoid inference are often overridden by schema constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world language model usage rarely involves free-form prose; models primarily fill structured forms (JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates). The authors investigate whether the answer format itself induces hallucination.

Method: Thirteen models are asked the same question about the same input, varying only the answer format. Inputs are designed to be unanswerable (e.g., no reply data, no call transcript). Models are tested with free-text responses, required JSON fields, explicit "insufficient evidence" options, and direct anti-inference instructions. The authors release PhantomFill, a benchmark with deterministic scoring producing Coerced Fabrication Rate and Escape Utilization Rate.

Result: Required fields drive fabrication to 100% in ten of thirteen models. An "insufficient evidence" option only helps frontier models; all nine open-weight models ignore it. Direct instructions ("do not infer sentiment") are overridden by schema in four of six models. Fabrication is not monotonic with scale: within one family, the smallest model refuses, the mid-sized fabricates, the largest refuses again.

Conclusion: Hallucination is systematically coerced by structured output formats, particularly in required enums and minimum-count arrays where hedging is impossible. Honesty under format pressure is a training outcome currently unmeasured. The proposed fix is a single line of schema; the failure is pervasive across models.

Abstract: Language models in production do not write prose. They fill forms: JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates. We show that the form itself causes hallucination.
  We ask thirteen models the same question about the same input and change only the answer format. The inputs are built so the question cannot be answered: a viral post showing 12,400 likes but no visible replies, a support ticket whose call was never transcribed. In free text, GPT-5.5 answers honestly. It says there is no reply data, 98% of the time. Given a required JSON field for sentiment, the same model invents an answer 40 times out of 40. It fabricates the mood of crowds it never saw and quotes customers it never heard.
  The pattern holds with force. Required fields drive fabrication to 100% in ten of thirteen models. An explicit "insufficient evidence" option rescues only the frontier: all nine open-weight models ignore it. A direct instruction, do not infer sentiment, is overridden by the schema in four of six models. Resistance does not come with scale: within a single model family, the smallest model refuses, the mid-sized model fabricates, the largest refuses again. Honesty under format pressure is a training outcome that no one is measuring.
  The fabrication hides exactly where hedging is impossible: in required enums and minimum-count arrays, fields where no disclaimer fits. We release PhantomFill, a benchmark with deterministic scoring and two reportable numbers: the Coerced Fabrication Rate and the Escape Utilization Rate. The fix we test is one line of schema. The failure we measure is everywhere.

</details>


### [228] [The Active Ingredient in Muon's Grokking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20512)
*Yufeng Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates why the Muon optimizer accelerates grokking on modular arithmetic, finding that the speedup comes from orthogonalization (Newton-Schulz iteration) rather than spectral-norm constraints. Orthogonalizing optimizers reach lower spectral norm solutions more efficiently, though reducing iteration count speeds up grokking but makes the solution fragile. The paper also introduces a stability-aware metric for evaluating grokking speed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work attributed Muon's faster grokking to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" without isolating which mechanism matters. This paper aims to decompose and stress-test the effect to understand Muon's behavior mechanistically.

Method: Multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps, ablation studies (orthogonalize-only vs spectral-only vs full Muon vs AdamW), mechanistic analysis of spectral norm and embedding movement, ablation of Newton-Schulz iteration count, and introduction of stability-aware metrics (first-crossing vs sustained-grok times).

Result: (1) Orthogonalize-only matches full Muon, spectral-only is no faster than AdamW; (2) orthogonalizing optimizers reach generalization at ~3x lower spectral norm; (3) reducing Newton-Schulz iterations from 5 to 1 accelerates grokking but causes fragility (transient collapse), with fragility scaling with learning rate; (4) spectral scaling can be dropped at no cost.

Conclusion: The speedup attributed to Muon is actually due to orthogonalization (Newton-Schulz iteration), not spectral-norm constraints. A single Newton-Schulz iteration is fast but fragile; five iterations provide learning-rate-robust stability. The paper also emphasizes the importance of using stability-aware metrics when evaluating grokking optimizers.

Abstract: The Muon optimizer reaches the grokking threshold on modular arithmetic faster than AdamW. Prior work attributes this to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" but does not isolate which mechanism matters. To better understand Moun's behavior, we run multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps to decompose and stress-test the effect. First, an ablation shows the speedup comes from orthogonalization (the Newton-Schulz iteration): orthogonalize-only matches full Muon, whereas spectral-only is no faster than AdamW and is unreliable, and this verdict holds across learning rates. Second, a mechanistic analysis finds that orthogonalizing optimizers reach generalization at roughly 3x lower spectral norm and, controlling for how much the embedding actually moves, settle into a lower-norm solution rather than simply perturbing the embedding less. Third, reducing the Newton-Schulz iteration count from five to one accelerates reaching the threshold but makes the grokked solution fragile, prone to transient collapse, with fragility that grows with learning rate; a single iteration is fast and stable only at small learning rate, while the canonical five iterations are the learning-rate-robust choice. We also show spectral scaling can be dropped at no measured cost. A methodological thread runs throughout: under a stability-aware metric, "faster" claims about grokking optimizers can invert, so we report both first-crossing and sustained-grok times. To support reproducibility, we release our full training and analysis code at https://github.com/louiswang524/muon-grokking-frontier

</details>


### [229] [Scaling Closed-Loop Feature Channel Configuration with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20516)
*Tolgay Atinc Uzun,Radu Timofte,Dmitry Ignatov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Scaling neural network channel configuration search via LLM-generated code from sparse (few candidates) to dense (250 candidates/cycle, 2000 total, 462 verified) reveals positive accuracy trends (mean slope 9.87e-4, p=0.043), improved parameter efficiency (best 0.3676 at 11.8M params vs earlier 0.3144 at 166.5M), and emergent architectural regularities (41.8% non-power-of-two widths, structured channel allocation patterns).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether the optimization behavior from initial sparse LLM-based channel-configuration search transfers to a denser sampling regime and whether additional architectural regularities emerge when more networks are evaluated.

Method: Scaled the search to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle, analyzed 2000 generated candidates from 8 cycles, yielding 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations after filtering. Performed linear trend analysis on per-cycle mean accuracy, top-k accuracy, parameter efficiency comparisons, and architectural pattern analysis.

Result: Positive linear trend in per-cycle mean accuracy (slope 9.87e-4, p=0.043). Best accuracy improved from 0.3144 to 0.3676. Parameter efficiency drastically improved (best model 11.8M params vs 166.5M). 41.8% of candidates used non-power-of-two widths. Strongest models shared structured patterns: moderate early widths, expanded middle/later blocks.

Conclusion: The channel-search signal observed in initial sparse study transfers to denser sampling, and larger-scale search reveals emergent architectural regularities not evident from sparse observations.

Abstract: Promising initial results in closed-loop large-language-model-based channel-configuration search demonstrated that neural-network widths can be optimized directly through executable code generation and accuracy feedback. However, those results were obtained from a relatively sparse set of valid evaluations, leaving open whether the observed optimization behavior transfers to a denser sampling regime and whether additional architectural regularities emerge when more generated networks are evaluated. To test this, the same search setting is scaled to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle. The analysis covers 2000 generated candidates from 8 complete cycles, yielding 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations after task and metadata filtering. Per-cycle mean accuracy exhibits a positive linear trend with slope 9.87e-4 (p=0.043), while the high-performing frontier improves more strongly: the best observed accuracy increases from 0.3144 to 0.3676, and both the top-5 and top-10 cycle-level means exhibit positive trends. The scaled run also reveals improved parameter efficiency. The best model reaches 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters, compared with an early high-performing model at 0.3144 with 166.5M parameters. Beyond accuracy, the larger sample exposes architectural regularities that were difficult to assess from sparse observations. Non-power-of-two channel widths occur in 41.8% of verified candidates, and the strongest models share structured channel-allocation patterns characterized by moderate early widths and expanded middle or later blocks. These findings indicate that the channel-search signal observed in the initial study transfers

</details>


### [230] [Multimodal CoLRAG-TF: Triple-Filtered Retrieval for Complex PDFs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20517)
*Takato Yasuno*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multimodal CoLRAG-TF integrates dense text, BM25, knowledge-graph triples, and image similarity across four axes for robust RAG over heterogeneous PDFs. Using a HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever and Bayesian-optimized fusion weights (triple axis dominant at α=0.44), it achieves 0.9909 retrieval recall and 71.6% improvement in multi-hop answer similarity on a Japanese disaster document benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG over heterogeneous PDFs faces challenges from multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence, which existing single-modality retrieval approaches cannot adequately address.

Method: Four-axis fusion architecture (dense text embeddings, BM25, knowledge-graph triple filtering, image similarity); hybrid OCR pipeline with LLM-based captioning; OpenIE triple extraction (11,414 triples) indexed via FAISS; HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume → chapter → block); Bayesian optimization for fusion weight calibration.

Result: Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and 71.6% improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries on a 457-pair benchmark from Japanese disaster lesson PDFs (2,403 blocks, 43 documents).

Conclusion: Triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs, and the framework generalizes beyond the disaster domain.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous PDF collections remains challenging due to multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence. We present Multimodal CoLRAG-TF, a four-axis fusion architecture that integrates dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image-based similarity for robust retrieval over complex documents. Our system constructs a multimodal index of 2,403 blocks extracted from 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs, supported by a hybrid OCR pipeline and LLM-based caption generation. To enhance compositional reasoning, we extract 11,414 OpenIE triples and index them with FAISS, enabling sub-second triple lookup and hierarchical propagation of relevance signals. A HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume $\to$ chapter $\to$ block) narrows the search space before final fusion scoring. Bayesian optimization over fusion weights reveals that the triple axis must dominate ($α_\text{triple} = 0.44$) to counteract lexical bias and sustain multi-hop retrieval quality. Evaluated on a 457-pair benchmark, Multimodal CoLRAG-TF achieves a Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6$\%$ improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. An image-to-lesson pipeline using a vision LLM further demonstrates the applicability of the approach to visual inputs. These results show that triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs and provides a general framework applicable beyond the disaster domain.

</details>


### [231] [Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20519)
*Andrei Cristian Popescu,Haitz Sáez de Ocáriz Borde,Pietro Liò*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Looped Transformers with learned haliting gate often entangle exit selection and trajectory supervision, causing suboptimal adaptive computation.
