The paper disentangles these, showing fixed-prior depth supervision yields better trajectories, and simple post-hoc confidence readouts match or outperform learned gates. Joint gate training primarily harms trajectory formation, not gate expressivity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learned halting in looped Transformers entangles exit selection (readout) with trajectory formation (supervision weighting). This entanglement can degrade adaptive-compute performance, and prior work often treats gate learning as the sole problem without distinguishing these two factors.

Method: Systematic diagnostic evaluation across synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic, binary parity) and large-scale Ouro-1.4B/2.6B checkpoints. Compares fixed-prior depth supervision vs. learned gates, and evaluates post-hoc confidence readouts (linear, MLP) on frozen trajectories to isolate trajectory vs. readout effects.

Result: Fixed-prior depth supervision produces difficulty-aware trajectories with useful stopping signals. Simple post-hoc confidence readouts match or outperform learned linear/MLP gates. Failure in joint gate training stems from trajectory induction, not limited gate expressivity. In Ouro, ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal; average exit depth reductions translate to practical latency savings.

Conclusion: Adaptive depth in looped Transformers should be reframed as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, not gate learning alone. This distinction has been implicit in prior learned-halting work.

Abstract: Looped Transformers increase test-time computation by repeatedly applying a shared recurrent block. Learned halting objectives in looped Transformers typically use a single exit distribution both as the inference-time stopping rule and as the training-time weighting of per-depth losses. This entangles exit selection with trajectory formation: the gate not only chooses which recurrent state to use, but also determines how strongly each intermediate state is supervised. Consequently, poor adaptive-compute performance can arise from the readout, the induced trajectory, or their interaction. We study adaptive depth in looped Transformers through this trajectory--readout lens, across controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic and binary parity) and large-scale Ouro-1.4B and 2.6B checkpoints. We find that fixed-prior depth supervision, which shapes the trajectory without an input-dependent halting policy, produces difficulty-aware trajectories whose intermediate states expose useful stopping signals, and that simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or outperform learned linear and MLP gates. Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes the failure: it appears to stem mainly from the trajectory induced by joint gate training rather than from limited gate expressivity. The same pattern is present in Ouro evaluations, where pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal, and measured latency confirms that the resulting reductions in average exit depth translate into practical inference-time savings. Our systematic diagnostic evaluation reframes adaptive depth in looped Transformers as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, rather than gate learning alone, highlighting a distinction that prior learned-halting work has often left implicit.

</details>


### [232] [Generative Bayesian Filtering for State Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20521)
*Lei Cao,Sihang Feng,Jixin Yan,Tao Sun,Naichen Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GBF replaces restrictive linear-Gaussian observation models with pretrained CVAE generative models for Bayesian filtering, formulating measurement update as score-based posterior sampling for improved state estimation in nonlinear, high-dimensional systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical filtering methods (e.g., Kalman filters) rely on simple observation models like linear-Gaussian, which cannot capture nonlinear and heterogeneous patterns in high-dimensional sensor signals.

Method: GBF uses pretrained conditional variational autoencoders (CVAE) as observation models, performs Bayesian prediction-update recursion where measurement update is a posterior sampling problem combining dynamical prior with CVAE-induced likelihood, then transforms it into a score-based sampling problem.

Result: Experiments on synthetic datasets, manufacturing system monitoring, and arrhythmia diagnosis show improved state estimation accuracy and robustness over baseline approaches.

Conclusion: GBF provides a flexible filtering framework that inherits generative model flexibility and ensemble-based uncertainty quantification, outperforming classical methods on nonlinear, high-dimensional filtering tasks.

Abstract: The state of a dynamic system evolves over time, switching among several latent modes that govern its observable behavior. Filtering methods infer the latent state from observations. Classical filtering approaches, including Kalman filters, typically rely on simple observation models, such as linear-Gaussian models, that are incapable of characterizing the increasingly nonlinear and heterogeneous patterns in high-dimensional sensor signals. To tackle the challenge, we propose Generative Bayesian Filtering (GBF), a filtering framework that replaces restrictive observation models with pretrained conditional generative models parametrized by conditional variational autoencoders (CVAE). For online inference, GBF performs a Bayesian prediction-update recursion in which the measurement update is formulated as a posterior sampling problem that combines the dynamical prior with the CVAE-induced likelihood. The resulting filtering problem is then transformed into a score-based sampling problem, which naturally inherits the flexibility from generative models and the uncertainty quantification capabilities from ensembling. Experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world applications involving manufacturing system monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis demonstrate that GBF improves state estimation accuracy and robustness relative to baseline approaches.

</details>


### [233] [Do Active SAE Feature Planes Carry More Holonomy? A Preregistered Reversal in Gemma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20522)
*Larry Richards*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper tests whether holonomy concentrates on active sparse-autoencoder feature planes in Gemma 2 2B, finding that active-feature planes carry less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls, falsifying the prediction in reverse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To empirically test the "semantic-concentration prediction" — specifically whether holonomy (a measure of geometric curvature) localizes to active SAE feature planes in the residual stream of a language model.

Method: Holonomy was measured at the final-token layer-12 to layer-13 residual-stream readout by transporting a local frame around small loops using restricted-Jacobian transport, normalizing by area. The experiment was preregistered with predefined materiality, analysis, and verdict rules. Three plane types were compared: active-feature, mixed-feature, and random.

Result: Active-feature planes carried less holonomy than mixed-feature controls (adjusted log contrast -0.29439, 95% CI [-0.43989, -0.14889]). A magnitude-only explanation was unsupported. The three-way ordering was undefined due to failed common support. Post-freeze diagnostics validated the area law, bounded matched-center displacement, and identified transport distortion as a live confound.

Conclusion: The semantic-concentration prediction was falsified in reverse — meaning does not suppress holonomy. The result is a narrow, auditable operational reversal; the causal mechanism remains open with multiple alternatives (activation-strength geometry, feature engagement, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, manifold proximity, transport shear).

Abstract: This paper tests whether holonomy concentrates on active sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature planes in Gemma 2 2B, a concrete operationalization of the broader semantic-concentration prediction. Holonomy is measured at the final-token layer-12 to layer-13 residual-stream readout by carrying a local frame around small loops using the instrument's restricted-Jacobian transport rule, then normalizing the resulting rotation by enclosed area. The design, materiality threshold, analysis, and verdict rules were preregistered and frozen before the analysed measurements were inspected. The prediction was falsified in reverse: active-feature planes carried less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls, with an adjusted log contrast of -0.29439 and 95% interval [-0.43989, -0.14889]. A magnitude-only explanation was not supported in this design, while the three-way ordering across random, mixed-feature, and active-feature planes was undefined at matched magnitude because common support failed. Post-freeze diagnostics at the same readout supported the area law on a small validation subset, bounded matched-center displacement under a simple paired regression, and identified transport distortion as a live mechanism or confound. The result is therefore a narrow, auditable operational reversal, not a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. The cause remains open, with activation-strength geometry, degree of feature engagement, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, activation-manifold proximity, and transport shear as live alternatives.

</details>


### [234] [Uncertainty-Aware Trust Estimation for Multi-LLM Systems via Structured Expert Judgement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20529)
*Jiawei Zheng,Jiazhen Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes using Cooke-style log weighting (adapted from structured expert judgment) for aggregating predictions from multiple LLMs, which estimates and calibrates expert reliability via context-aware calibration questions rather than treating all models as equally trustworthy. This approach outperforms naive aggregation under heterogeneous and contaminated expert panels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM ensemble aggregation methods assume all models are equally trustworthy, overlooking differences in uncertainty quality. This assumption fails for heterogeneous LLMs with varying reliability and capability, making naive aggregation vulnerable to unreliable or adversarial experts.

Method: Formulates multi-LLM aggregation as uncertainty-aware trust estimation by adapting structured expert judgment from decision theory. Uses context-aware calibration questions to estimate expert reliability and employs Cooke-style log weighting that penalises overconfident incorrect predictions and favours well-calibrated experts.

Result: Evaluated on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels. Aggregation methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings, but Cooke weighting becomes critical under heterogeneity and contamination, achieving superior accuracy-reliability balance and robustness to unreliable experts.

Conclusion: Multi-LLM aggregation requires not just combining predictions, but calibrating trust under uncertainty. Cooke-style weighting effectively addresses the challenges of heterogeneous and contaminated LLM ensembles.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) ensembles are increasingly used to improve reliability by combining predictions from multiple LLMs. However, existing aggregation methods typically assume that all models are equally trustworthy, overlooking differences in uncertainty quality. This assumption is poorly suited to heterogeneous LLMs, whose reliability and capability vary significantly, making naive aggregation vulnerable to unreliable or adversarial experts. In this work, we formulate multi-LLM aggregation as a problem of uncertainty-aware trust estimation. We adapt structured expert judgment from decision theory, using context-aware calibration questions to estimate expert reliability based on the quality of its probabilistic predictions. Specifically, we employ Cooke-style log weighting, which penalises overconfident incorrect predictions and favours well-calibrated experts. We evaluate our approach on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels. Results show that while aggregation methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings, Cooke weighting becomes critical under heterogeneity and contamination. It achieves a superior accuracy-reliability balance and remains robust when unreliable experts are introduced. These findings suggest that Multi-LLM aggregation requires not just combining predictions, but calibrating trust under uncertainty.

</details>


### [235] [CLOE: Christoffel Loss Autoencoder for Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20530)
*Léa Billet,Louise Travé-Massuyès,Elodie Chanthery,Alexandre Gaffet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CLOE combines an autoencoder with a Christoffel Function-based detector for semi-supervised anomaly detection, using a novel loss function guided by the Christoffel Function to improve representation learning for high-dimensional data, achieving superior performance with minimal hyperparameter tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semi-supervised anomaly detection is important in fields like process monitoring, healthcare, and finance, but lightweight methods struggle with high-dimensional data and require careful hyperparameter tuning. Christoffel Function-based methods are attractive for their simplicity and theoretical foundation but suffer from poor scalability to high-dimensional settings.

Method: CLOE combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with a Christoffel Function-based detector applied in the latent space. It introduces a novel loss function that leverages the Christoffel Function to guide representation learning toward better capturing the support of the normal data distribution. It also proposes a principled detection threshold setting procedure and an efficient strategy to tune the single remaining hyperparameter.

Result: Experiments on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks show CLOE achieves superior performance compared to existing methods while preserving the lightweight and low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function-based approaches.

Conclusion: CLOE effectively addresses the scalability limitation of Christoffel Function-based methods to high-dimensional settings, maintaining their simplicity (at most one hyperparameter) and theoretical foundation while achieving state-of-the-art anomaly detection performance.

Abstract: Semi-supervised anomaly detection plays a key role in diverse fields such as process monitoring, healthcare, and finance. However, lightweight methods often struggle with high-dimensional data and typically require careful tuning of multiple hyperparameters. Among existing approaches, Christoffel Function--based methods are attractive due to their simplicity, requiring at most a single hyperparameter. They also benefit from a well-established theoretical foundation that yields several interesting results for data science. However, their main limitation is poor scalability to high-dimensional settings. In this paper, we introduce CLOE, a new method that combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with a Christoffel Function--based detector applied in the latent space. To better align representation learning with anomaly detection, we design a novel loss function that leverages the Christoffel Function to guide the autoencoder toward representations that better capture the support of the normal data distribution. We further propose a principled procedure to set the detection threshold and an efficient strategy to tune the single remaining hyperparameter. Experiments on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that CLOE achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, while preserving the lightweight and low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function--based approaches.

</details>


### [236] [Position: Stop Reactively Patching Your Model Every Time and Start Proactive Test-Driven AI Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20532)
*Nadine Chang,Maying Shen,Jialiang Wang,Rafid Mahmood,Jose M. Alvarez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This position paper argues that current reactive AI flywheels (which patch models based on observed user errors) are limited because they ignore broader system context, fail to prevent future edge cases, and struggle with long-tail error distributions. The authors propose a proactive test-driven flywheel that maps feedback data to task objectives via a "test space," and mathematically prove it achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reactive AI flywheels, commonly used for maintenance, suffer from three key limitations: (1) they ignore the broader context of errors within system objectives, (2) they fail to preempt potential future edge cases, leading to unnecessary iterative cycles, and (3) collecting remaining errors becomes statistically difficult due to the long-tail nature of open-world use-cases.

Method: The paper advocates for a proactive test-driven flywheel that introduces a "test space" to technically map feedback data to task objectives, shifting from reactive to proactive maintenance. The authors mathematically prove that the proactive approach achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations compared to the reactive flywheel.

Result: Mathematical proof that a proactive test-driven flywheel achieves superior long-term scaling (better performance with fewer iterations) than the reactive counterpart.

Conclusion: A proactive test-driven flywheel is necessary to overcome the limitations of reactive flywheels and move toward more generalizable AI systems. The proposed "test space" enables mapping feedback to objectives, fundamentally evolving the maintenance paradigm from reactive to proactive.

Abstract: Many modern AI systems are designed to operate under diverse, open-ended, use-cases. To help generalize deployed systems, many deployed-system maintenance pipelines use a reactive AI flywheel that observes emerging feedback from user behavior (errors) and patches the model accordingly. However, when used as the primary maintenance mechanism, these flywheels often ignore the broader context of these errors within the system's objectives, failing to preempt potential future edge cases, which leads to more unnecessary flywheel iterations. Also, it is statistically increasingly difficult to collect remaining errors due to the long-tail nature of open-world use-cases. This position paper argues that a proactive test-driven flywheel is required to address reactive flywheel's limitations and to approach a generalizable system. We advocate for creating a "test space" to technically map feedback data to task objectives, evolving the flywheel from reactive to proactive. We augment our position by mathematically proving a proactive one achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations than the reactive flywheel.

</details>


### [237] [Grounding Investor Views: Neural Predicates in the Black-Litterman Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20533)
*Marcos Florencio*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural predicates provide a structured, probabilistic, and differentiable framework for generating Black-Litterman views (pick matrix P, return vector q, uncertainty matrix Ω) from financial data, replacing subjective investor input with interpretable, end-to-end learnable view generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Portfolio construction under the Black-Litterman model requires subjective and difficult-to-scale manual specification of views on asset returns and uncertainty estimates.

Method: Neural predicates process structured financial data through a compositional hierarchy, producing probability distributions over market stances that are mapped to the Black-Litterman parameters (P, q, Ω), with view confidence derived from predicate output distributions for data-driven uncertainty elicitation.

Result: The approach is interpretable (any portfolio weight can be traced back through the predicate's logical chain) and fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end learning.

Conclusion: Neural predicates offer a formal, scalable, and data-driven alternative to subjective view specification in the Black-Litterman model, combining interpretability with differentiability for end-to-end portfolio optimization.

Abstract: Portfolio construction under the Black-Litterman model requires investors to specify views on asset returns alongside explicit uncertainty estimates -- a process that remains largely subjective and difficult to scale. We propose a formal approach in which neural predicates serve as a structured, probabilistic mechanism for view generation. In our formulation, structured financial analysis data is processed through a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates whose outputs -- probability distributions over market stances -- are mapped to the pick matrix $\mathbf{P}$, the view return vector $\mathbf{q}$, and the view uncertainty matrix $\boldsymbolΩ$ of the Black-Litterman model. View confidence is derived from predicate output distributions, providing a data-driven alternative to subjective uncertainty elicitation. The resulting approach is interpretable, in the sense that any portfolio weight can be traced back through the predicate's logical chain to the underlying data, and fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end learning.

</details>


### [238] [A Graph Neural Network approach to zero-shot Digital Twins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20535)
*Alicia Tierz,Icíar Alfaro,David González,Elías Cueto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Zero-Shot Digital Twins, a framework combining real-time visual perception with a geometry-agnostic, physics-informed reasoning engine (Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network) that enforces energy conservation and entropy production. It uses closed-loop data assimilation via deep segmentation and optical flow to correct simulations, demonstrating extreme generalization across viscoelastic beam deformations and viscous fluid sloshing on unseen geometries without retraining, achieving ~25 ms/frame real-time performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional Predictive Digital Twins are geometrically rigid and require extensive retraining or fine-tuning when the physical domain or boundary conditions change, limiting their adaptability to dynamic real-world scenarios.

Method: The framework uses a Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network (GNN) based on a metriplectic thermodynamic formalism for local energy conservation and entropy production. An auxiliary GNN infers unobservable fields from sparse visual boundaries. Real-time closed-loop data assimilation is achieved via deep segmentation networks and sparse optical flow to track deformations and free-surface boundaries, correcting autoregressive simulation rollout and eliminating numerical drift.

Result: The framework demonstrates extreme generalization across two distinct physical regimes (viscoelastic beam deformation and viscous fluid sloshing) on novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining, operating within real-time latency budgets of approximately 25 ms per frame, with latent mechanical variables projected via Augmented Reality.

Conclusion: Zero-Shot Digital Twins enable physically accurate simulations on unseen geometries without retraining, bridging the sim-to-real gap through continuous visual assimilation and achieving real-time performance for adaptive digital twin applications.

Abstract: Traditional Predictive Digital Twins often remain geometrically rigid, requiring extensive retraining or fine-tuning whenever the underlying physical domain or boundary conditions change. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel framework for \textit{Zero-Shot Digital Twins} that seamlessly couples real-time visual perception with a geometry-agnostic, physics-informed reasoning engine. At the core of our architecture is the Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network architecture, a Geometric Deep Learning solver grounded in a metriplectic thermodynamic formalism that enforces energy conservation and non-negative entropy production locally through graph message passing. The framework integrates an auxiliary Graph Neural Network to infer unobservable fields (such as stress tensors or velocity and energy distributions) directly from sparse initial visual boundaries, mitigating numerical start-up transients. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, we implement a continuous closed-loop data assimilation mechanism; the pipeline tracks macroscopic deformations and free-surface fluid boundaries in real-time using deep segmentation networks combined with sparse optical flow, dynamically correcting the autoregressive simulation rollout and eliminating numerical drift. To test the validity of our approach, we demonstrate the extreme generalization capabilities of our approach across two disparate physical regimes: the large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and the non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid. In both scenarios, the unified framework instantiates physically accurate simulations on novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining, operating well within real-time latency budgets (approximately 25 ms per frame) and enabling the direct projection of latent mechanical variables via Augmented Reality.

</details>


### [239] [ReliableTableQA:How Much Supervision Does Reliability Annotation Need?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20537)
*Huei-Chung Hu,Hsin-Tai Wu,Koyo Kobayashi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReliableTableQA is a framework for training LLMs to assess statistical reliability of tabular QA results. With a 10-category taxonomy and a program-first data pipeline generating 50K examples, they show that a small SFT set (200 examples) achieves near-perfect reliability flagging (F1 0.98, UCAR zero), while GRPO only helps when SFT is under-trained and provides no benefit once SFT is adequate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tabular QA systems answer confidently even when computed results are statistically unreliable (e.g., due to small samples, wide confidence intervals, confounding), which can mislead real enterprise analytics. Quantified as Unreliable Confident Answer Rate (UCAR), this problem motivates the need for structured reliability annotation of tabular QA outputs.

Method: (1) A ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10) covering hazards like small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch; (2) a program-first data pipeline using context-free grammar over public retail schemas to generate 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits; (3) controlled experiments comparing SFT and GRPO across varying training set sizes.

Result: 200 SFT examples raise reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98, parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, drive UCAR to zero, and generalize to unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on H&M). GRPO only helps when SFT is under-trained (+0.06-0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples) and provides no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate, confirmed across hard compound-flag slices, exact-match metrics, and OOD evaluation.

Conclusion: Statistical reliability annotation for tabular QA is primarily a data-efficiency problem solvable with modest SFT data. GRPO's benefits are limited to low-data regimes; once SFT reaches adequacy, GRPO provides no added value. This delineates precisely when reinforcement fine-tuning does and does not pay off.

Abstract: We introduce ReliableTableQA, a framework for training an LLM to annotate the statistical reliability of tabular QA results, not whether the query is answerable, but whether the computed answer is statistically meaningful. In real enterprise analytics, a syntactically correct SQL query can return a value that is based on too small a sample, has an excessively wide confidence interval, or is too confounded to support action. Existing systems answer confidently in all such cases, a failure we quantify as the Unreliable Confident Answer Rate (UCAR). We contribute (1) a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10) covering hazards such as small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch; (2) a program-first data pipeline that generates 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas, with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits; and (3) a controlled study of how much supervision calibrated reliability annotation actually requires. We find that a small, schema-stratified SFT set is remarkably sufficient: 200 examples raise reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98 and parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, drive UCAR to zero, and yield a model that generalizes to an unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on held-out H&M). Against this strong SFT baseline, GRPO, commonly assumed to be essential, helps only when SFT is under-trained (+0.06-0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples, in- and out-of-distribution) and provides no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate, a null result we confirm across a hard compound-flag slice, a strict exact-match metric, and out-of-distribution evaluation. Our findings reframe reliability annotation as a data-efficiency problem and delineate precisely when reinforcement fine-tuning does and does not pay off.

</details>


### [240] [Codec-Gauge: Learning Compression-Friendly Gauges for Transformer KV Caches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20538)
*Yitao Jiang,Yaoqing Yang,Luyang Zhao,Muhao Chen,Devin Balkcom*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Codec-Gauge introduces post-training learned orthogonal channel transforms that reorient KV-cache coordinates to concentrate energy in low-frequency components, improving compression fidelity by 44% average KL divergence reduction across models without altering weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context Transformer inference relies on KV-cache compression, but the channel basis of key/value vectors significantly affects how faithfully a fixed compression backend preserves model behavior. Existing methods overlook optimizing this coordinate geometry.

Method: Codec-Gauge is a post-training cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms. It uses a frequency-distribution objective combining a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss with a smooth rate proxy to concentrate KV energy in low-frequency codec-facing layouts. Evaluated using actual compression/decompression with measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring.

Result: Across six models at 3, 4, and 6 bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by 44.0% on average vs. raw coordinates, outperforming random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls. Improvements hold for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Validated on a 27B model with long-context task prompts and serial storage/timing measurements.

Conclusion: Cache-coordinate geometry is established as a practical post-training variable for improving compression fidelity without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.

Abstract: Long-context Transformer inference increasingly relies on KV-cache compression or quantization. Prior rotation and transform-coding results suggest that the channel basis of each key/value vector affects how faithfully a fixed backend preserves model behavior. We introduce Codec-Gauge, a post-training cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing compression and quantization backends. Its frequency-distribution objective combines a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss with a smooth rate proxy to concentrate KV energy in low-frequency codec-facing layouts. We evaluate actual compression and decompression using measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring. Across six models at $3$, $4$, and $6$ bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by $44.0\%$ on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls. The same gauges improve quality preservation for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Experiments on a 27B model and long-context task prompts reproduce the quality trend, while serial storage and timing measurements validate the implemented compressed-cache paths. These results establish cache-coordinate geometry as a practical post-training variable for improving compression fidelity without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.

</details>


### [241] [Leveraging Biokinetic Knowledge Priors for Data-Scarce Bioprocess Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20539)
*Kyunghoon Hur,Eunjung Jeon,Hyun Woo Kim,Gyubok Lee,Seongjun Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents the first systematic study of injecting biokinetic ODE knowledge into neural networks for biomanufacturing, showing that both data-level (pre-training on simulated ODE curves) and architecture-level (embedding ODE inside decoder) priors outperform no-prior baselines across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species. The key finding is that these two approaches are substitutable, making simulation pre-training a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning has had limited impact on biomanufacturing due to data scarcity—bioreactor experiments are costly, time-consuming, and rarely shared publicly. However, the domain is rich in prior knowledge in the form of biokinetic ODE models, yet how to inject this knowledge into neural networks has not been systematically studied.

Method: The authors systematically compare two approaches for injecting ODE knowledge into neural networks: (1) a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves, and (2) an architecture-level prior that embeds the ODE directly inside the decoder. Both are evaluated against no-prior baselines across 11 datasets spanning 7 microbial species.

Result: Both ODE-informed priors consistently outperform no-prior baselines across all 11 datasets and 7 microbial species. The central finding is that the two approaches are substitutable—a generic decoder pre-trained on simulation matches the performance of a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data.

Conclusion: Simulation pre-training offers a simple, data-efficient recipe for applying deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity, as it achieves equivalent performance to architecturally complex bio-structured models without requiring architectural modifications.

Abstract: While deep learning has accelerated drug discovery, its impact on biomanufacturing has been considerably more limited. The reason is data scarcity. Bioreactor experiments are high-cost, take days to weeks, and are rarely shared in public form, leaving each research work with only a handful of experiments. The domain itself, however, is rich in prior knowledge. Biokinetic ordinary differential equation (ODE) models have described microbial growth for decades, yet how to inject this knowledge into a neural network has not been studied systematically. We present the first systematic study of how to inject this ODE knowledge into a neural network, comparing a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves against an architecture-level prior that embeds the ODE inside the decoder. Both consistently outperform no-prior baselines across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species. Our central finding is that the two are substitutable. A generic decoder pre-trained on simulation matches a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data. Simulation pre-training therefore offers a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity.

</details>


### [242] [From Atoms to Entropy: Optimal Noise Allocation for Diffusion Training in the Convex Regime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20540)
*Luca Ambrogioni,Giulio Franzese,Alberto Foresti,Gabriel Raya,Bac Nguyen,Georgios Batzolis,Yuhta Takida,Naoki Murata,Chieh-Hsin Lai,Yuki Mitsufuji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops a statistical framework for optimizing noise-level allocation in diffusion model training, showing that optimal schedules are atomic (concentrated on finitely many noise levels) under convexity/PL assumptions, and proposing a square-root entropy rate scheduling rule that closely tracks the optimum in neural-network settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current noise schedules for diffusion models are based on heuristics or empirical tuning despite their critical importance to training efficiency. The authors aim to provide a principled statistical framework to determine which noise levels to train on and how much.

Method: The authors develop a general statistical framework studying asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation. They analyze two regimes: (1) fully coupled regime with convexity/PL assumptions, showing atomic minimizer solutions; (2) independent-learner regime with feature-noise decoupling, where random-matrix analysis yields a proxy: sampling density ∝ √(generative entropy rate). They test predictions on Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, and MNIST.

Result: Optimized schedules are consistently finite-support (atomic) across controlled settings. The smooth entropic proxy closely tracks the atomic optimum in neural-network models but breaks down in the fully coupled parametric case. In larger-scale experiments, square-root entropy scheduling substantially improves training efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with EDM-style heuristics on continuous images.

Conclusion: The square-root entropy rate scheduling provides a principled, computationally tractable alternative to heuristic noise schedules, with strong theoretical grounding and empirical validation across both discrete and continuous domains.

Abstract: How should a diffusion model decide which noise levels to train on, and how much? Despite the importance of this choice, current noise schedules are based largely on heuristics or empirical tuning. Here, we develop a general statistical framework for studying asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation in diffusion training. Our first main result concerns the fully coupled regime, where information can spread between different time points. Under convexity or Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type assumptions, we show that the optimized training schedule admits an atomic minimizer, concentrated on finitely many noise levels. Our second main result specializes this framework to an idealized independent-learner regime, intended to model temporal specialization in neural networks. Under an additional feature-noise decoupling condition, a random-matrix analysis leads to an information-theoretic proxy: the decoupled sampling density is proportional to the square root of the generative entropy rate, the rate at which conditional entropy grows along the forward process. We test these predictions in controlled settings where the coupled objective can be optimized directly, including Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, and MNIST. In these settings, the optimized schedules are consistently finite-support, while the smooth entropic proxy closely tracks the atomic optimum in neural-network models and breaks down mainly in the fully coupled parametric case, as the theory suggests. We then evaluate the entropic schedule in larger-scale experiments, where full schedule optimization is currently intractable. The results indicate that square-root entropy scheduling can substantially improve training efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with standard EDM-style heuristics on continuous images.

</details>


### [243] [HypNO: A Graph-Based Neural Operator with Physics-Informed Message Passing for Hyperbolic Conservation Laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20541)
*Dimitrije Ždrale,Cassie An Jeng,Katie Wang,Sonia Vanier,Alexandre Bayen,Hossein Nick Zinat Matin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HypNO is a graph-based neural operator that uses physics-informed message passing on space-time graphs to solve scalar hyperbolic conservation laws, demonstrating accurate shock-capturing predictions on traffic-flow models LWR and ARZ.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a neural operator that can accurately handle hyperbolic conservation laws with shocks and discontinuities, which are challenging for existing operator-learning methods due to simultaneous global transport and shock formation.

Method: HypNO operates on a space-time graph of finite-volume cells using adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing that respects upwinding and entropy admissibility near shocks.

Result: HypNO accurately predicts solution snapshots across a range of initial conditions and captures shocks/discontinuities on LWR and ARZ traffic-flow models.

Conclusion: HypNO effectively addresses shock-capturing in hyperbolic conservation laws via graph-based neural operators with physics-informed message passing.

Abstract: We introduce HypNO, a graph-based neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws. HypNO operates directly on a space-time graph of finite-volume cells and uses adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing to respect upwinding and entropy admissibility near shocks. We benchmark the architecture on the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) and Aw-Rascle-Zhang (ARZ) traffic-flow models, a stress test for operator-learning methods because of their simultaneous global transport and shock formation. HypNO predicts solution snapshots accurately across a range of initial conditions while capturing the shocks and discontinuities of the solution.

</details>


### [244] [Improving Access to Essential Medicines via Decision-Aware Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20542)
*Angel Tsai-Hsuan Chung,Jatu Abdulai,Patrick Bayoh,Lawrence Sandi,Francis Smart,Hamsa Bastani,Osbert Bastani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A decision-aware machine learning framework with multi-task learning and catalytic priors was deployed in Sierra Leone to allocate essential medicines, resulting in a 19% increase in consumption in treated districts, and was subsequently scaled nationwide to cover an estimated 2 million women and children under five.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficient and equitable allocation of scarce essential medicines in LMICs is critical but hindered by limited high-quality data, making traditional data-driven approaches infeasible.

Method: Proposed a decision-aware ML framework using multi-task learning for sample efficiency and catalytic priors for equitable allocation; deployed as a staggered nationwide decision support tool in Sierra Leone.

Result: Econometric evaluation showed an estimated 19% increase in consumption of allocated products in treated districts; the tool was scaled nationwide, covering ~2 million women and children under five.

Conclusion: Machine learning methods can improve efficiency at very low cost in resource-constrained global health settings.

Abstract: A critical challenge in healthcare systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) is the efficient and equitable allocation of scarce resources, particularly essential medicines. This problem is complicated by limited high-quality data, which restricts the applicability of traditional data-driven techniques. We propose a novel decision-aware machine learning framework for essential medicines allocation, which additionally leverages multi-task learning to ensure sample efficiency and catalytic priors to ensure equitable allocation. In collaboration with the Sierra Leone national government, we performed a staggered, nationwide deployment of our system as a decision support tool. Our econometric evaluation finds an estimated 19% increase in consumption of allocated products in treated districts, demonstrating its efficacy at improving access to essential medicines. Our tool was subsequently scaled nationwide, covering an estimated 2 million women and children under five. Our work demonstrates how machine learning methods can improve efficiency at very low cost in resource-constrained global health settings.

</details>


### [245] [When RLVR Shrinks the Reasoning Boundary: Diagnosing Pass@k Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20543)
*Todd Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RLVR training can improve one-shot accuracy but degrade pass@k performance by losing rare correct trajectories in boundary prompts. The paper diagnoses this as an absence-of-evidence failure and proposes Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) to preserve base-model coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand and diagnose why RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards) causes pass@k inversion—where a model solves fewer distinct problems at large sampling budgets after training than its base model—and to propose a fix for this failure mode.

Method: Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA): a simple method that sharpens prompts with sufficient frozen-base correct evidence and anchors risky prompts to the base distribution. Applied with GRPO on Omni-MATH-Test and MATH500.

Result: Across three seeds, PBA improves both Pass@1 and high-budget coverage over matched GRPO. A 3000-prompt controlled study confirms that ordinary GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts while PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories.

Conclusion: Reasoning post-training should consider not only optimization strength but also which prompts are safe to optimize. The pass@k inversion risk extends beyond math to vision-language agents using repeated attempts checked by external tools/verifiers.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve one-sample accuracy while making a model worse under repeated sampling. We study this pass@k inversion: after training, the policy may solve fewer distinct problems than its base model at large $k$. The failure concentrates on boundary prompts, where the base model contains rare correct trajectories that are recoverable by sampling but too sparse to reliably appear in finite RLVR rollout groups. We argue that a two-mode account explains this as an absence-of-evidence failure: rare correct trajectories may disappear before RLVR samples and reinforces them often enough. The main contribution is this diagnostic and mechanistic framing. Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) is a deliberately simple proof-of-concept: sharpen prompts with sufficient frozen-base correct evidence, and anchor risky prompts to the base distribution. Across three training seeds on Omni-MATH-Test, with MATH500 as a secondary high-coverage validation benchmark, PBA improves both \PassK{1} and high-budget coverage over matched GRPO. A 3000-prompt regime-controlled diagnostic study is consistent across seeds with the expected signature: ordinary GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts, while PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories. We use mathematical verifiers as a controlled testbed for verifier-guided optimization; the same pass@k inversion risk applies to ECCV-relevant vision-language agents when repeated visual, spatial, or chart-reasoning attempts are checked by external tools or verifiers. Reasoning post-training should decide not only how strongly to optimize, but which prompts are safe to optimize.

</details>


### [246] [Conflict Resolution under Degraded Surveillance in Air Corridors Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20547)
*Esrat Farhana Dulia,Syed Arbab Mohd Shihab,Caleb Adams,Ruben Del Rosario*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Deep Q-Network-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework is developed for decentralized conflict resolution among heterogeneous aircraft (sUAVs and eVTOLs) in a structured 3D corridor, addressing noisy, delayed, or unavailable surveillance. Trained policies were evaluated across 90 traffic/separation scenarios, showing that loss-of-separation events increase with density but are mostly resolved within 1s. Six Pareto-optimal configurations reveal safety-capacity trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable safe Advanced Air Mobility operations by developing a conflict resolution framework that works under degraded surveillance conditions (noise, delay, incompleteness, or temporary unavailability of information).

Method: Deep Q-Network-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with separate policies for two aircraft categories (sUAVs and eVTOLs), using local observations and a 14-action space (maintaining course, turning, vertical maneuvering, landing, speed control). Simulation includes aircraft dynamics, energy use, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind disturbance, actuator/model uncertainty.

Result: Loss-of-separation frequency and duration increase with traffic density and minimum separation thresholds, but most events resolve within 1s. Under safe conditions, agents maintain motion ~79% of the time. During conflicts: turning 33%, maintaining motion 29%, speed control 25%, vertical maneuvers 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations identified.

Conclusion: The framework supports simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance conditions, revealing trade-offs between safety and corridor capacity.

Abstract: Safe Advanced Air Mobility operations require aircraft to maintain separation when surveillance information is noisy, delayed, incomplete, or temporarily unavailable. This study develops a Deep Q-Network-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework for decentralized conflict resolution among heterogeneous small unmanned aerial vehicles and electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft operating within a structured three-dimensional corridor. Separate policies are trained for the two aircraft categories using local observations and a 14-action space that includes maintaining course, turning, vertical maneuvering, landing, and speed control. The simulation incorporates aircraft-specific dynamics, energy use, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind disturbance, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty. The trained policies are evaluated across 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds. Loss-of-separation frequency and duration generally increase with traffic density and separation requirements, although most events are resolved within 1s. Under safe conditions, agents maintain their motion approximately 79% of the time. During conflicts, turning accounts for 33% of actions, followed by maintaining motion at 29%, speed control at 25%, and vertical maneuvers at 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations reveal trade-offs between safety and corridor capacity. The framework supports the simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance conditions.

</details>


### [247] [SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20548)
*Mikail Khona,Aditya Vavre,Boxiang Wang,Deyu Fu,Hao Wu,Mike Chrzanowski,Bryan Catanzaro,Dheevatsa Mudigere,Jeff Pool,Michael Lightstone,Mohammad Shoeybi,Mostofa Patwary,Nima Tajbakhsh,Tijmen Blankevoort*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper enhances SOAP and Muon optimizers for large-scale LLM pretraining, introducing stability fixes for SOAP (per-step QR orthogonalization, improved preconditioning), demonstrating consistent superiority over AdamW on multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens, and presenting a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM that hides communication and avoids approximations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Higher-order optimizers (Muon, SOAP) offer faster convergence than AdamW, but their computational cost and numerical stability challenges have limited adoption at scale. The authors aim to overcome these practical challenges for large-scale LLM pretraining.

Method: (1) Identified instabilities in SOAP at large batch sizes; proposed per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning strategies to eliminate loss spikes. (2) Conducted unified empirical study of SOAP, Muon, and AdamW using update-RMS matching for fair learning rate transfer. (3) Empirically evaluated orthogonalization quality of Muon. (4) Introduced a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM that balances memory, hides communication, and avoids approximations to optimizer computations. (5) Built system-level improvements to accelerate layer-wise implementation.

Result: On multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens, SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW. At batch sizes up to 100M tokens for next-token prediction, these optimizers maintain training stability and quality while AdamW degrades.

Conclusion: The proposed enhancements make higher-order optimizers practical and stable for large-scale LLM pretraining. The authors release a codebase (Emerging-Optimizers) to support the research community.

Abstract: Higher-order optimizers such as Muon and SOAP offer faster convergence than AdamW, but their computational cost and numerical stability challenges have limited adoption at scale. In this work, we adapt and enhance preconditioned gradient methods to overcome the practical challenges of large-scale LLM pretraining. We first identify instabilities in SOAP at large batch sizes and propose algorithmic modifications including per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning strategies that eliminate loss spikes and enable stable training in these regimes. We then present a unified empirical study of SOAP, Muon, and AdamW using update-RMS matching to ensure fair learning rate transfer across optimizers. As part of this analysis, we empirically evaluate the orthogonalization quality of Muon. Our experiments on multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens reveal that SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW at the scales we tested. Notably, at batch sizes of up to 100M tokens for next-token prediction, these optimizers maintain training stability and quality while AdamW degrades. To enable efficient training at large scale, we introduce a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM. Our implementation balances memory and hides communication while avoiding approximations to the optimizer computations, thus retaining their convergence benefits. Additionally, we identify and build specific system-level improvements to further accelerate our layer-wise implementation. To support the research community, we release a codebase that contains emerging algorithms for optimization: https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Emerging-Optimizers

</details>


### [248] [SevDiff: Severity-Conditioned Diffusion for Long-Tail Conflict Trajectory Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20549)
*Eni Solomon Laughter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SevDiff is a severity-conditioned diffusion model that generates vehicle interaction trajectories with a specified Time-to-Collision (TTC) value, achieving high hit-rate accuracy for low TTC targets (0.5-1.5 s) with graceful degradation at higher TTC values, addressing the rarity of critical conflict events in ADAS evaluation datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Trajectory datasets for ADAS evaluation are biased toward routine driving and lack rare but critical vehicle-to-vehicle conflict events. Existing generative methods condition on scene-level properties (spatial goals, agent structure, adversarial objectives) but cannot accept a target TTC value as input and produce it within measurable error, limiting the ability to systematically generate conflict events of specific severity.

Method: SevDiff uses a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) conditioned on a scalar TTC target value. It is trained on 468 interaction windows from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset (1,041 vehicles, 822,691 observations). Performance is evaluated via a hit-rate metric measuring how often generated trajectories match the requested minimum TTC within ±0.5 s tolerance.

Result: 100% hit-rate within ±0.5 s for TTC targets of 0.5-1.5 s; 97-99% at 2.0-2.5 s; graceful degradation to 39% at TTC = 5.0 s. Maximum out-of-range rate of 4.7% across 12 kinematic features; no negative speed or gap values in >96.5% of samples. Degradation pattern is physically interpretable as conditioning signal strength relative to training prior.

Conclusion: SevDiff enables precise, measurable control over generated conflict severity via TTC conditioning, providing a precision characterization of the generator's capabilities rather than a binary pass/fail. This supports systematic evaluation of ADAS systems on rare but high-cost conflict events.

Abstract: Trajectory datasets used in ADAS evaluation are heavily biased toward routine driving; genuine vehicle-to-vehicle conflict events are rare, and the rarer the event, the higher the cost when an ADAS system fails to handle it. Existing generative approaches address this imbalance by conditioning on scene-level properties - spatial goals, agent structure, or natural-language adversarial objectives - but none can accept a target Time-to-Collision (TTC) value as input and be held to producing it within a measurable error. This paper introduces SevDiff, a severity-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that accepts a requested minimum TTC value as a scalar conditioning signal and generates paired vehicle interaction trajectories whose realized conflict severity matches the request, evaluated through a hit-rate metric. Trained on 468 interaction windows extracted from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset (1,041 vehicles, 822,691 observations after smoothing), SevDiff achieves 100% hit-rate within +/-0.5 s for TTC targets of 0.5-1.5 s and 97-99% at 2.0-2.5 s, with graceful degradation to 39% at TTC = 5.0 s. Generated kinematic features are physically plausible, with a maximum out-of-range rate of 4.7% across 12 features and no negative speed or gap values in more than 96.5% of samples. The hit-rate degradation pattern is physically interpretable as the strength of the conditioning signal relative to the training prior, making it a precision characterization of the generator rather than a pass/fail result.

</details>


### [249] [Beyond SBDD: Geometric Deep Learning in Polypharmacology and Multi-target Drug Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20550)
*Tianming Han,Zhijie Pan,Wenchi Ge,Qi Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This review positions geometric deep learning (GDL) as a transformative approach for polypharmacology-based drug design, enabling rational structure-driven discovery of multi-target ligands through invariant and equivariant neural architectures, structure-conditioned generative models, and multimodal integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The traditional "one drug, one target" SBDD paradigm fails for multifactorial diseases (cancer, neurodegeneration) due to compensatory signaling and drug resistance. Polypharmacology offers synergistic benefits, but rationally designing ligands that simultaneously satisfy geometric constraints across multiple targets remains a major computational bottleneck.

Method: The review systematically surveys GDL architectures (invariant graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models), analyzes three core dimensions: (1) shared binding pocket characterization via geometric embeddings, (2) multi-target bioactivity prediction via heterogeneous graph fusion, and (3) de novo dual-target ligand generation—with emphasis on structure-conditioned generative algorithms combining diffusion models and reinforcement learning.

Result: GDL enables autonomous resolution of geometric conflicts between competing binding sites through structure-conditioned generative algorithms; multimodal omics integration and geometric benchmarking infrastructures are critical for model validation.

Conclusion: The paradigm shifts from serendipitous drug discovery to rational, structure-driven polypharmacological molecular engineering, providing a structured guide for next-generation therapeutic design.

Abstract: The traditional "one drug, one target" paradigm of structure-based drug design (SBDD) frequently proves inadequate for treating multifactorial diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders, owing to compensatory signaling pathways and the emergence of drug resistance. While polypharmacology offers a synergistic therapeutic strategy, the rational design of ligands capable of simultaneously satisfying the geometric constraints imposed by multiple targets remains a major computational bottleneck. This review positions geometric deep learning (GDL) as a powerful integrative approach to overcome these limitations. We systematically survey GDL architectures ranging from invariant graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models that harness non-Euclidean molecular data to capture intrinsic three-dimensional (3D) structural interdependencies. We critically analyze GDL applications across three core dimensions, including the characterization of shared binding pockets via geometric embeddings, multi-target bioactivity prediction through heterogeneous graph fusion, and de novo generation of dual-target ligands. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging structure-conditioned generative algorithms that integrate diffusion models with reinforcement learning to autonomously resolve complex geometric conflicts between competing binding sites. Furthermore, we evaluate the pivotal role of multimodal omics integration and specialized geometric benchmarking infrastructures in validating these models. By synthesizing these methodological advances, this review elucidates the paradigm shift in drug discovery from serendipitous exploration to rational, structure-driven polypharmacological molecular engineering, thereby providing a clear, structured guide for navigating the complexities of next-generation therapeutics.

</details>


### [250] [SenCos-GEM: SENet-Calibrated and Law-of-Cosines-Constrained Geometry-Enhanced Molecular Representation for Property Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20551)
*Tianming Han,Li Zhang,Qi Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SenCos-GEM is a molecular representation learning framework that uses physics-guided geometric consistency (law-of-cosines constraints) and SE-module-based dynamic feature modulation to improve 3D molecular property prediction, achieving SOTA results on FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, and QM9 with error reductions of 12.9%, 5.3%, and 8.2% respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SSL methods for molecular representation learning lack explicit physical constraints, are susceptible to geometric noise from coarse force fields during pre-training, and overlook dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation, leading to catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer.

Method: SenCos-GEM employs a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to derive high-fidelity 3D spatial priors, integrates lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules as task-specific adapters in the backbone, and uses a dual-modulation prediction head combining FiLM and SENet for dynamic feature recalibration.

Result: Achieves SOTA on MoleculeNet benchmarks, with relative error reductions of 12.9% (RMSE) on FreeSolv, 5.3% (RMSE) on Lipophilicity, and 8.2% (MAE) on QM9. Also demonstrates superior stereoisomer discrimination and conformational perturbation sensitivity.

Conclusion: SenCos-GEM is a significant breakthrough in accurate molecular property prediction, offering robust spatial modeling and improved generalization through physically constrained pre-training and dynamic feature modulation.

Abstract: Effective molecular representation learning is crucial for accurate molecular property prediction. Recently, numerous self-supervised learning (SSL) approaches leveraging 3D GNNs have been developed to capture comprehensive 3D structural information for drug discovery. However, existing methods lack explicit physical constraints and are highly susceptible to geometric noise induced by coarse empirical force fields during large-scale pre-training.Furthermore, they overlook dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer. To address these limitations, we introduce SenCos-GEM, a novel explicitly decoupled geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework that incorporates SENet-calibrated and law-of-cosines-constrained enhancements. SenCos-GEM employs a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to derive high-fidelity and mathematically invariant 3D spatial priors. In addition, lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules are integrated into the backbone as task-specific adapters, while a dual-modulation prediction head combines Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) and SENet mechanisms to enable dynamic feature recalibration. SenCos-GEM demonstrates highly competitive performance across diverse classification and regression tasks on MoleculeNet benchmark, establishing new state-of-the-art results specifically on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks, such as FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, and QM9, achieving relative error reductions of 12.9% (RMSE), 5.3% (RMSE), and 8.2% (MAE), respectively. Moreover, our model exhibits superior capability in distinguishing stereoisomers and discriminating conformational perturbations, underscoring its robust spatial modeling performance. Collectively, SenCos-GEM represents a significant breakthrough in accurate molecular property prediction.

</details>


### [251] [Thermodynamic Weight Decay: Exploring Grokking Acceleration via Attention Specific Heat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20552)
*Chitraansh Pandey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces CvAdamW, a variant of AdamW that monitors attention logit variance (specific heat Cv) to detect and accelerate the grokking phenomenon (delayed generalization) in neural networks. It shows Cv peaks reliably before generalization transitions and uses this signal to dynamically adjust weight decay, achieving grokking at epoch 2802 where baseline never groks on modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grokking wastes thousands of training epochs and is notoriously unpredictable. The authors aim to understand and accelerate this delayed generalization by drawing an analogy between Transformer attention and thermodynamic systems.

Method: The authors: (1) treat variance of attention logits as specific heat Cv, showing it peaks before generalization; (2) introduce CvAdamW that monitors Cv online and dynamically scales weight decay when a phase transition is detected; (3) identify and fix three failure modes (initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, slingshot blinding) using a memorization gate and EMA shock absorber; (4) propose a scale-invariant z-score reformulation to remove task-specific hyperparameters.

Result: On modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97), CvAdamW achieves grokking at epoch 2802 within a 4000-epoch budget where baseline never groks. Across 10 paired seeds, the cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166 epochs; Wilcoxon p=0.049, Cohen's d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8 of 10 seeds. Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds.

Conclusion: Neural networks may expose detectable precursors (Cv peaks) of impending generalization transitions, and a physically motivated, proportional intervention can facilitate generalization within a fixed compute budget. The thermodynamic analogy proves practically useful for optimization.

Abstract: Grokking -- the delayed generalization of neural networks long after they have memorized their training data -- wastes thousands of training epochs and is notoriously unpredictable. Building on the recent result that Transformer attention is formally isomorphic to a thermodynamic system, we treat the variance of attention logits as a specific heat Cv and show that its peak reliably precedes the generalization transition. We introduce CvAdamW, a drop-in AdamW variant that monitors Cv online and injects thermal energy by dynamically scaling weight decay when a phase transition is detected. Through a strictly iterative development process we identify three failure modes -- initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, and slingshot blinding -- and resolve them with a memorization gate and an exponential-moving-average shock absorber. On modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97), CvAdamW enables grokking at epoch 2802 in a 4000-epoch budget where the baseline never groks. We further propose a scale-invariant z-score reformulation that removes task-specific hyperparameters, and evaluate it across 10 paired seeds. A paired analysis shows the cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166 epochs; Wilcoxon p=0.049, Cohen's d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8 of 10 seeds; on this single task Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds. Our results indicate that neural networks may expose detectable precursors of impending generalization transitions, and that a physically motivated, proportional intervention can facilitate generalization within a fixed compute budget. Code and data are public.

</details>


### [252] [Double-Scoring: Reliable Extraction of Strong Lottery Tickets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20555)
*Bryce A. Christopherson,Jack Baretz,Darian Colgrove,Salah Dandan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies layerwise sparsity selection as a bottleneck in strong lottery ticket extraction and proposes double-scoring, an augmented score-space method that replaces sparsity search with optimization over enlarged score tensors, substantially improving performance over edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Strong lottery ticket hypothesis suggests that random networks contain accurate subnetworks without weight training, but reliable extraction remains difficult. The authors identify layerwise sparsity selection as a central bottleneck in existing frozen-weight score-training methods like edge-popup.

Method: The authors introduce double-scoring, an augmented score-space parameterization that replaces layerwise sparsity search with optimization over enlarged score tensors. They prove fixed-density masking in this augmented space preserves access to all original-coordinate masks, and show the method is interpretable as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network.

Result: Double-scoring substantially improves strong-ticket extraction over fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines, outperforms rewound sparse-training topologies, and shows markedly lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablations confirm gains are tied to augmented score-space competition inducing effective original sparsity, not merely additional trainable parameters.

Conclusion: The augmented score-space competition is the key mechanism driving improvement, not just additional parameters. Double-scoring offers a more robust approach to strong lottery ticket extraction.

Abstract: The lottery ticket hypothesis proposes that large random neural networks contain sparse subnetworks that can match the performance of dense models after comparable training. A stronger version asserts that sufficiently overparameterized random networks contain subnetworks that are already accurate before any weight training. Existing theory establishes that such strong lottery tickets exist, but reliable extraction remains difficult. We revisit edge-popup, a frozen-weight score-training method for extracting strong tickets, and identify layerwise sparsity selection as a central bottleneck. We introduce double-scoring, an augmented score-space parameterization that replaces a layerwise sparsity search with optimization over enlarged score tensors. We prove that fixed-density masking in an augmented score space preserves access to all original-coordinate masks, and we show that the resulting method can be interpreted as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network. In controlled experiments, double-scoring substantially improves strong-ticket extraction over fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines, improves on the performance of rewound sparse-training topologies, and exhibits markedly lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablations show that the gain is not merely due to additional trainable score parameters, but is tied to the augmented score-space competition that induces the effective original sparsity.

</details>


### [253] [Monkey King Bang: A Unified Scientific Multimodal Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20557)
*Hesen Chen,Xinyu Su,Xiaomeng Yang,Yuetan Lin,Zixiong Yang,Junyi An,Fenglei Cao,Yifeng Jiao,Yunqi Zhang,Yuan Cheng,Zhiyu Tan,Hao Li,Libo Wu,Yuan Qi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MKB is a unified multimodal AI model for scientific discovery that covers six branches (DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, medical images) using a shared Transformer backbone with modality-tailored components, achieving competitive understanding and generation across domains while retaining general capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific discovery is shifting from isolated disciplines to multi-domain reasoning, but existing AI systems are either specialized for individual domains or limited to text-based unification, lacking the ability to handle diverse scientific inputs, produce modality-native outputs, and support joint reasoning across domains.

Method: MKB uses a shared Transformer backbone with modality-tailored encoders, adapters, and decoders for six scientific branches. Training follows a two-stage modality-then-language curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality-specific components with the frozen backbone; Stage 2 consolidates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora.

Result: MKB achieves competitive scientific understanding on biological and molecular benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely retains the general capabilities of its Qwen3-VL backbone.

Conclusion: Shared-backbone models with modality-tailored components can provide a promising foundation for future cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration.

Abstract: Scientific discovery is increasingly shifting from isolated disciplines to multi-domain reasoning, and AI for science faces a similar transition. Existing systems are either specialised for individual domains or unify scientific data mainly through text tokenisation and prompt-based interfaces, limiting their ability to handle diverse scientific inputs, produce modality-native outputs, and support joint understanding, reasoning, and generation across scientific domains. We introduce MKB, a unified scientific multimodal model for both understanding and generation, built around a shared Transformer backbone and modality-tailored encoders, adapters, and decoders. MKB covers six scientific branches, including DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, and medical images, and supports native outputs such as biological sequences, molecular strings, meteorological fields, and segmentation masks. Training follows a two-stage modality-then-language curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality-specific components with the frozen backbone, and Stage 2 consolidates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora. Experiments show that MKB achieves competitive scientific understanding across biological and molecular benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely retains the general capabilities of its Qwen3-VL backbone. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed paradigm, suggesting that shared-backbone models with modality-tailored components can provide a promising foundation for future cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration. The model and code are publicly available at https://github.com/Shanghai-Academy-of-AI-For-Science/MKB and https://huggingface.co/sais-org/MKB.

</details>


### [254] [StabilityBench: Benchmarking Instability in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20558)
*Emma Kondrup,Zachary Yang,Anne Imouza,Reihaneh Rabbany*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: StabilityBench is a benchmark operator that converts static single-turn queries into multi-turn interaction histories by injecting realistic user simulations (demographic proxies or sycophantic baits), revealing that LLM performance is consistently unstable under these conditions across four benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation protocols rely on static, single-turn benchmarks that fail to capture real-world variability and context dependence in conversational AI deployments, especially in high-stakes settings like healthcare or government services.

Method: The authors propose StabilityBench, a model-agnostic benchmark operator that transforms single-turn queries into multi-turn interaction histories by injecting realistic user simulations (demographic proxies or sycophantic baits) while preserving original task intent, then evaluate nine LLMs across four benchmarks (mathematical reasoning, health QA, and safety).

Result: Model performance is consistently unstable under user simulation injections, with considerable performance degradations on three out of four benchmarks studied.

Conclusion: Static evaluations have important limitations, motivating more realistic evaluation settings. StabilityBench-Mini is proposed as a cost-preserving variant that samples across diversification axes for more realistic evaluation without increased costs.

Abstract: AI Assistants are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, such as healthcare or government services. Yet their real-world behavior remains poorly understood due to strong context dependence. Current evaluation protocols follow a defense-in-depth paradigm with compounding layers of safeguards, ranging from traditional benchmarks to live or adversarial testing. Such benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, limiting their ability to capture real-world variability in conversational settings. We propose StabilityBench, a principled, general and model-agnostic benchmark operator that transforms single-turn benchmark queries into multi-turn interaction histories. StabilityBench augments existing benchmarks by injecting realistic user simulations, through demographic proxies or sycophantic baits, while preserving original task intent.
