We apply StabilityBench to four benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, health question-answering and safety, and evaluate nine large language models under these conditions. Our results show that model performance is consistently unstable under these injections, with considerable performance degradations on three out of four benchmarks studied. These highlight important limitations of static evaluations and motivate more realistic evaluation settings. To this end, we propose StabilityBench-Mini: a size-preserving variant of StabilityBench that samples across diversification axes, enabling more realistic evaluation without increasing costs.

</details>


### [255] [Joint Utilization of Geospatial and census proxies for Autoencoder-Assisted Downscaling (JUGAAD) of socioeconomic indicators in India](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20559)
*Aditya Dutt,Paul Gader,Aditya Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JuGAAD is a deep learning framework that combines Indian census and survey data to predict socioeconomic indicators at high resolution by addressing scale mismatches through village-cluster tessellation, autoencoder compression, and regression mapping.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the scale mismatch between census data (fine-grained geographic coverage) and survey data (coarse, infrequent socioeconomic indicators), enabling high-resolution poverty and food security monitoring in developing nations.

Method: Three-step framework: (1) Census and geospatial data are averaged into intermediate village-cluster-scale tessellations; (2) An autoencoder compresses high-dimensional NSSO survey data into a low-dimensional latent representation; (3) A regression model maps upscaled census/geospatial data to this latent representation, then applied to fine-grained census data for high-resolution predictions.

Result: The method predicts socioeconomic indicators at fine scales with strong accuracy, validated against ground-truth district-level NSSO indicators.

Conclusion: JuGAAD effectively bridges the scale mismatch between census and survey data, producing reliable high-resolution socioeconomic predictions for developing regions.

Abstract: Monitoring poverty and food security indicators is imperative for addressing socioeconomic challenges in developing nations. A limitation is mismatches in scale between data sources: census data provide geographic coverage, while socioeconomic indicators are derived from infrequently conducted surveys at coarse resolutions, posing a methodological challenge. This study introduces a deep learning framework, JuGAAD, using Indian census and survey data from 2001 and 2011 as a case study. We employ a three-step process: census and geospatial data are averaged into intermediate village-cluster-scale tessellations to reduce noise and regularize administrative boundary changes; an autoencoder compresses high-dimensional National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) data into a low-dimensional latent representation; and a regression model maps upscaled census and geospatial data to this representation. This function is applied to fine-grained census data to generate high-resolution predictions, validated against ground-truth district-level NSSO indicators. Results confirm the methodology predicts socioeconomic indicators at fine scales with strong accuracy.

</details>


### [256] [Chronofy: A Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture for Information Validity in Time-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20560)
*Muntaser Syed,Marius Silaghi,Sheikh Abujar,Sharun Akter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Chronofy is a three-layer neuro-symbolic framework (TLDA) that embeds temporal validity into RAG systems by using dedicated temporal subspaces in embeddings, learnable exponential decay in retrieval, and Signal Temporal Logic robustness for reasoning, reducing temporal hallucination where outdated facts corrupt LLM outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RAG systems treat all retrieved facts as equally valid regardless of temporal provenance, causing temporal hallucination—plausible but obsolete facts corrupting outputs. A clinical lab reading from yesterday is actionable, but the same reading from six months ago is noise.

Method: Three-layer Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture: (1) dedicated temporal subspace in Matryoshka embeddings making fact age structurally irremovable; (2) learnable exponential decay functions in graph-based retrieval, with decay coefficient grounded in Bayesian decision theory; (3) Signal Temporal Logic robustness functions evaluating temporal validity of retrieved knowledge, enforcing the possibilistic weakest-link principle.

Result: Evaluated on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, TimE temporal QA benchmark, and domain-specific sensitivity analysis; explicit temporal decay modeling improves retrieval precision, reduces temporal hallucination, and enables principled data re-acquisition triggers.

Conclusion: Explicit temporal decay modeling in RAG systems improves retrieval precision and reduces temporal hallucination, enabling principled data re-acquisition when temporal context is insufficient.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems retrieve and integrate external knowledge to ground large language model (LLM) outputs. However, current RAG architectures treat all retrieved facts as equally valid regardless of temporal provenance, leading to temporal hallucination, where plausible but obsolete facts corrupt the output. A clinical lab reading from yesterday is actionable; the same reading from six months ago is noise. We present Chronofy, a three-layer neuro-symbolic framework implementing the Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture (TLDA) that embeds temporal validity directly into the representation, retrieval, and reasoning layers of RAG systems. Layer 1 reserves a dedicated temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings to make fact age structurally irremovable from the representation. Layer 2 integrates learnable exponential decay functions into graph-based retrieval, where the decay coefficient $β_j$ is grounded in Bayesian decision theory as an approximation of twice the latent process mean-reversion rate. Layer 3 applies Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness functions to evaluate the temporal validity of retrieved knowledge, not LLM output confidence, and enforces the possibilistic weakest-link principle to bound output confidence by the most decayed evidence in the reasoning chain. We evaluate Chronofy on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, the TimE temporal QA benchmark, and a domain-specific sensitivity analysis, demonstrating that explicit temporal decay modeling improves retrieval precision, reduces temporal hallucination, and enables principled data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient.

</details>


### [257] [CT-Merging: Consensus Directions and Task-Level Scaling for LoRA Adapter Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20561)
*Keumseo Ryum,Joonhyuk Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CT-Merging is a LoRA-aware adapter merging algorithm that constructs a consensus basis from shared SVD subspaces and assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on DC-Merge CLIP benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SVD-based LoRA merging methods suffer from a mismatch between inherited coefficients (which preserve component order with high rank correlation) and the coefficients induced by task updates, as their magnitudes differ substantially on a fixed merged basis.

Method: CT-Merging estimates consensus directions from average task subspace projectors and assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales. It uses repeated support across task SVD subspaces to construct a common basis, reducing reliance on rank-wise SVD magnitudes after direction construction.

Result: CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy on the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, improving over DC-Merge by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 using KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

Conclusion: CT-Merging effectively addresses the coefficient magnitude mismatch in LoRA merging by using consensus directions and RMS scaling, leading to state-of-the-art multi-task adapter performance.

Abstract: LoRA adapters provide an efficient way to specialize a pretrained model for many downstream tasks, but deploying one adapter per task requires adapter storage and task selection at inference time. Model merging addresses this issue by combining independently trained adapters into one multi-task adapter. Recent SVD-based LoRA merging methods mainly focus on constructing shared or task specific directions, while the coefficients assigned to the final directions are often directly from the original task SVD. On a fixed merged basis, inherited coefficients preserve component order with high rank correlation, yet their magnitudes differ substantially from the coefficients induced by the task updates. To address this mismatch, we propose CT-Merging, a LoRA-aware merging algorithm that estimates consensus directions from average task subspace projectors and assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales in the final update. CT-Merging uses repeated support across task SVD subspaces to construct the common basis, while reducing reliance on rank wise SVD magnitudes after direction construction. On the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy compared to state-of-the-art merging methods and further improves over DC-Merge by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

</details>


### [258] [AI-Driven Surrogate Models for Predicting Electrode-Scale Discharge Behavior in Lithium-Ion Batteries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20577)
*Mengda Xing,Jean-Marie Lagniez,Alejandro Franco*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a Swin3D Transformer-based deep learning surrogate pipeline with Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE) and Temporal Encoding that predicts spatiotemporal discharge dynamics in lithium-ion batteries from volumetric data, outperforming point cloud baselines while reducing computational costs by orders of magnitude.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physics-based simulations of electrode-scale discharge behavior in lithium-ion batteries are essential but computationally prohibitive, motivating the need for efficient surrogates.

Method: A deep learning surrogate pipeline based on Swin3D Transformer, integrating Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE) for spatial feature representation in complex electrode geometries and a Temporal Encoding module for nonlinear time-series evolution.

Result: The pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud baselines in prediction accuracy on an Electrochemical Simulation dataset and reduces computational overhead by orders of magnitude.

Conclusion: The proposed method provides a scalable and efficient framework for high-throughput battery design and optimization.

Abstract: Physics-based simulations are essential for understanding the electrode-scale discharge behavior of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) but suffer from prohibitive computational costs. To address this, we introduce a novel deep learning surrogate pipeline based on the Swin3D Transformer to predict spatiotemporal discharge dynamics directly from volumetric data. Our approach integrates two key innovations: Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE), which enhances spatial feature representation by adapting to the complex geometry of electrode microstructures, and a specialized Temporal Encoding module to capture non-linear timeseries evolution. Experimental validation on an Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset demonstrates that our pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud baselines in prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed method reduces the computational overhead by orders of magnitude, providing a scalable and efficient framework for high-throughput battery design and optimization.

</details>


### [259] [Fisher Widths: Local Learning Geometry and Anisotropic Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20578)
*Vu Khac Ky*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies primal Fisher width and inverse-Fisher width on statistical manifolds. The Fisher width measures local parameter fluctuations under Fisher geometry (learning), while the inverse-Fisher width captures anisotropic Gaussian measurement effects (recovery). A key result is that the product of these widths is bounded below by the squared Euclidean width, implying Fisher anisotropy cannot reduce both complexities simultaneously.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand Gaussian-width complexity on statistical manifolds through two complementary geometric functionals—primal Fisher width (induced by Fisher metric) and inverse-Fisher width (induced by inverse Fisher metric)—and their distinct statistical roles in learning and recovery.

Method: The authors define Fisher width $w_G(T)=w(G^{1/2}T)$ and inverse-Fisher width $w_{G^{-1}}(T)=w(G^{-1/2}T)$. For Fisher-regular losses, they prove the scale $w_G(H_r)/\sqrt{n}$ is attained on small Fisher balls. For sparse recovery, they derive two-sided estimates for statistical dimension and support-sensitive recovery bounds. A sharp inequality $w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T) \geq w(T)^2$ is proved.

Result: (1) For Fisher-regular losses, $w_G(H_r)/\sqrt{n}$ scale is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls. (2) Two-sided estimate for statistical dimension in inverse-Fisher width recovery, with support-sensitive estimates and curvature-dependent ordering of supports. (3) Sharp inequality $w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T) \geq w(T)^2$ holds for any common compact coordinate set $T$.

Conclusion: Fisher anisotropy can transfer complexity between primal and inverse geometries, but cannot reduce both widths relative to the Euclidean baseline, establishing a fundamental trade-off in statistical complexity.

Abstract: We study Gaussian-width complexity on statistical manifolds through a pair of functionals: the primal Fisher width $w_G(T) = w(G^{1/2}T)$, induced by the Fisher metric, and the inverse-Fisher width $w_{G^{-1}}(T) = w(G^{-1/2}T)$, induced by the inverse Fisher metric. The two widths play complementary statistical roles.
  On the learning side, the Fisher width measures the size of local parameter fluctuations in the geometry induced by the Fisher information. For Fisher-regular losses, we prove that the scale \(w_G(H_r)/\sqrt n\) is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls.
  On the recovery side, the inverse-Fisher width captures the effect of anisotropic Gaussian measurements whose covariance is determined by the inverse Fisher information. For sparse recovery, the resulting geometry depends not only on sparsity but also on the position of the active coordinates in the Fisher spectrum. We obtain a two-sided estimate for the corresponding statistical dimension, together with support-sensitive recovery estimates and a natural ordering of supports with different curvature profiles.
  Finally, we establish a sharp relation between the primal and inverse-Fisher widths. On any common compact coordinate set $T$, they satisfy \[ w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T)\geq w(T)^2. \] Thus, Fisher anisotropy may transfer complexity from one geometry to the other, but cannot reduce both widths relative to the Euclidean scale.

</details>


### [260] [Bayesian uncertainty estimation improves clinical decision making in medical AI agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20582)
*Frederik Hauke,Patrick Wienholt,Christiane Kuhl,Dyke Ferber,Jakob Nikolas Kather,Sven Nebelung,Daniel Truhn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Monte Carlo dropout provides epistemic uncertainty signals that improve error detection (AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77) in chest X-ray classification, but its clinical utility depends on communicating it as a binary error-risk flag rather than raw scores (reducing confident misdiagnoses from 8.5% to 2.7%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical image analysis models lack reliable confidence measures, limiting their use in ambiguous or atypical cases where knowing model uncertainty is critical for safe clinical deployment.

Method: Applied Monte Carlo dropout to a multi-task chest-radiograph classifier (8 thoracic findings, 137,593 training images) to estimate epistemic uncertainty. Tested uncertainty signal's value in a 2x2 factorial experiment comparing raw scores vs. binary error-risk flag delivery to a clinical-decision-support agent.

Result: Epistemic uncertainty tracking improved error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 (Δ+0.023, CI [+0.014, +0.033]). Binary error-risk flag delivery cut confident misdiagnoses from 8.5% to 2.7%, while raw scores did not yield the same benefit.

Conclusion: Epistemic uncertainty carries decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its practical value depends critically on how it is communicated to downstream decision-support agents.

Abstract: Machine learning models for medical image analysis typically lack a reliable measure of confidence, limiting their use in ambiguous or atypical cases. Here we show that Monte Carlo dropout, applied to a multi-task chest-radiograph classifier (eight thoracic findings, 137,593 training images), provides an epistemic uncertainty signal that tracks generalisation across training-set scales and flags confident yet error-prone predictions. Adding this signal to the point prediction raised error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 ($Δ$AUROC +0.023, 95% CI [+0.014, +0.033]). In a controlled 2x2 factorial experiment, a clinical-decision-support agent exploited this uncertainty only when it was delivered as a binary error-risk flag rather than as raw scores, cutting confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%. Epistemic uncertainty estimation thus carries decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its value for downstream agents depends on how it is communicated.

</details>


### [261] [Exact ReLU realization of affine one-dimensional refinement iterates via residual memory and offset frames](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20586)
*Boldsaikhan Bolorkhuu,Tsogtgerel Gantumur*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proves that vector-valued affine refinement operators with finitely supported masks and piecewise linear inputs admit exact fixed-width ReLU network realizations of depth O(n) for M ≥ 3, using a residual memory controller and offset frames to handle noninvertible dynamics and forcing terms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To extend the homogeneous realization theorem for affine refinement operators (with forcing term B ≠ 0) and construct exact ReLU network representations with bounded width and linear depth.

Method: Introduces a residual memory controller that converts noninvertible residual dynamics into an injective skew-product, enabling exact backward replay of residual states for Horner-type evaluation. Offset frames align forcing atoms away from residual seams, and complementary loop readouts recover exact values.

Result: For M ≥ 3, every finite affine iterate W^nγ admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization with depth O(n). For M=2, the construction applies with ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. Stage-dependent extensions for finite-dimensional continuous piecewise linear spans are also proven.

Conclusion: The affine refinement operator can be exactly represented by a ReLU network of fixed width and linear depth, with the residual memory controller resolving the noninvertibility issue. The result covers arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing for M ≥ 3, and yields linear-depth upgrades for various recursive constructions.

Abstract: We study vector-valued affine refinement operators of the form [
(Wγ)(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}} A_jγ(Mt-j)+B(t), ]
with finitely supported matrix mask and compactly supported continuous piecewise linear input and forcing data. Building on the homogeneous realization theorem for (B\equiv 0), we prove that, for (M\ge 3), every finite affine iterate (W^nγ) admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization whose depth is (O(n)).
  The main new ingredient is a residual memory controller. It replaces the noninvertible residual dynamics by an injective skew-product and permits exact backward replay of the residual states required by a Horner-type evaluation of the affine forcing sum. Offset frames align the forcing atoms away from residual seams, allowing complementary loop readouts to recover their values exactly. The remaining branch-selection ambiguity occurs only where the accumulated affine state has already vanished.
  For (M\ge 3), the result applies to arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing terms. For (M=2), the same construction applies to ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. We also prove a stage-dependent extension for forcing terms in a fixed finite-dimensional continuous piecewise linear span and record the resulting linear-depth upgrade for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.

</details>


### [262] [Detecting Neural Network Failures through Spectral Analysis of Internal Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20590)
*Arunan J*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies Spectral Drift — frequency-domain instability in internal neural network activations that correlates with misclassifications — and proposes Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN), a lightweight framework using STFT, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to detect failures via spectral monitoring. SDNN achieves 79% AUROC on CIFAR-10, outperforming confidence-based methods by ~25-30 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current confidence-based failure detection methods (e.g., MaxSoftmax, Energy Score) struggle because misclassification-indicative spectral instability emerges in internal activations but becomes masked at the output layer. The authors aim to exploit this hidden spectral signature for more reliable detection.

Method: SDNN monitors spectral dynamics across network depth using Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to extract multi-scale spectral features from internal activations. A lightweight detector network (5% parameter overhead) is trained via curriculum learning on progressively challenging distributions: natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations.

Result: On CIFAR-10, SDNN achieves 79.0±25.3% AUROC across three seeds, substantially outperforming MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%) by ~25-30 percentage points. Ablation studies confirm wavelet decomposition and statistical features contribute consistently, while STFT's role remains unclear.

Conclusion: Spectral analysis of internal activations is a promising direction for neural network reliability, revealing diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches. The high variance (±25.3%) suggests room for improving stability, and the unclear contribution of STFT warrants further investigation.

Abstract: Neural network misclassifications exhibit characteristic spectral instability in internal activations that is invisible at the output layer. This phenomenon is identified and formalized as Spectral Drift -- the frequency-domain distance between consecutive layer activations -- with empirical validation showing that failures exhibit significantly higher drift than correct predictions (1.9% increase, p<0.001). This spectral signature emerges during internal processing but becomes masked in final outputs, explaining why confidence-based detection methods struggle.
  This work introduces Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN), a framework that monitors spectral dynamics across network depth using Short-Time Fourier Transform, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to capture multi-scale spectral features. A lightweight detector network (5% parameter overhead) learns to identify failure-indicative patterns via curriculum learning on progressively challenging distributions: natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations.
  Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that SDNN achieves 79.0 +/- 25.3% AUROC across three seeds, substantially outperforming confidence-based baselines including MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%) by approximately 25-30 percentage points. Ablation studies reveal that wavelet decomposition and statistical features make consistent contributions, while STFT's role remains unclear. This work establishes spectral analysis of internal activations as a promising direction for neural network reliability, revealing diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches.

</details>


### [263] [STeMP: Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20592)
*Jan Linnenbrink,Jakub Nowosad,Marvin Ludwig,Anna Frederike Jablotschkin,Fabian Schumacher,Teja Kattenborn,Hanna Meyer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: STeMP is a standardized protocol for transparent reporting and guidance in spatio-temporal machine-learning modeling, featuring a structured three-section format, an R-package with a web app, and automated warnings for common pitfalls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine-learning spatio-temporal models are widely used in environmental research but lack standardized reporting protocols, leading to issues with trust, transparency, and comparability. The authors aim to fill this gap.

Method: The protocol STeMP is structured into three sections (Overview, Model, Prediction) covering metadata, predictors, evaluation, software, and workflow elements. It is hosted on GitHub with an R-package featuring a web application for manual or semi-automated protocol filling and warnings for common pitfalls.

Result: STeMP provides standardized reporting and guidance for spatio-temporal modeling, with semi-automated protocol filling and automatic detection of common pitfalls to assist authors and reviewers.

Conclusion: STeMP enables trust, transparency, and comparability in spatio-temporal machine-learning modeling through a standardized protocol and open-source tooling, with community contributions encouraged via GitHub.

Abstract: Spatio-temporal machine-learning modelling is an important tool in environmental research. However, machine-learning models are highly sensitive to both the characteristics of the training data, such as its distribution, and methodological choices, including the cross-validation strategy. Each decision has impact and implications on the model itself as well as the estimation of the model quality and applicability for certain purposes. Taking into account the large role of machine-learning based maps of the environment in science and their transfer into practice, transparent reporting of spatio-temporal models, ideally using standardized model protocols, is essential to enable trust, transparency and comparability. However, such protocols are currently lacking for spatio-temporal modelling.
  We propose STeMP (Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol) to fill this gap by serving two purposes: standardized reporting to understand the model functioning as well as providing guidance during the modelling process by pointing at critical decisions and parameters. The protocol is structured in three sections: Overview, Model and Prediction. The Overview section contains metadata, while the Model and Prediction sections go into detail, describing predictors, evaluation and software, and further relevant elements of the modelling workflow.
  The protocol definition is hosted on GitHub and accompanied by an R-package (https://github.com/LOEK-RS/STeMP). The R-package contains a web application that can be used to fill the protocol either manually or in a semi-automated way from provided modelling objects. Warnings are returned from the protocol when common pitfalls are encountered, which may help authors as a guide through the modelling process but also support reviewers in the assessment of modelling studies. Via GitHub, incorporation of contributions and feedback from the community is encouraged.

</details>


### [264] [When Does Recurrence Become an Algorithm? Convergence Selection in Weight-Tied Looped Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20594)
*Tong Zhang,Junhao Hu,Yun Peng,Tao Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A weight-tied looped transformer learns a linear computation frontier (v ~ n_train/T_train) that determines how many positions it can solve per loop; training contracts set the speed, test-time loops can rescue late positions, and the model's architecture prior (not expressivity) selects serial vs. parallel algorithms. Group order, not circuit complexity, creates learning walls, and mechanisms are portable across budgets. A new convergence-time scaling analysis reveals dynamics invisible to standard fixed-point instruments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand when and how weight-tied looped transformers implement actual algorithms, specifically investigating the relationship between training budget, computation frontier, architectural choices, and learning dynamics on group word problems.

Method: Controlled experiments on group word problems with weight-tied looped transformers, analyzing the "budget law" (v ~ n_train/T_train), comparing untied vs. tied architectures, testing circuit complexity vs. group order hardness, and introducing convergence-time scaling as a diagnostic instrument validated with damage cones.

Result: (1) A linear computation frontier v ~ n_train/T_train (exponent 0.98±0.04, R²=0.99) governs positions solved per loop. (2) Weight tying flips algorithm selection from parallel to serial frontier. (3) NC1-completeness is not costly (A5 generalizes), but group order creates deadlocks (S5's 120×120 operator). (4) Mechanisms are portable across budgets but not mandatable via input schedule.

Conclusion: Weight-tied looped transformers implement algorithms with a predictable computation frontier determined by training budget; standard instruments fail to capture these dynamics, but convergence-time scaling provides causal, predictive insights invisible to fixed-point analyses.

Abstract: When does a weight-tied looped transformer -- one block applied T times -- implement an actual algorithm? We answer with four findings from controlled populations on group word problems. (1) The budget law: free training installs a linear computation frontier, a mechanism that solves v positions per loop, whose speed is priced by the training contract: v ~ n_train/T_train (exponent 0.98 +/- 0.04, R^2=0.99), exactly unity under T=n training. SGD selects a frontier matching the minimum the contract demands; granting more test-time loops than ever trained rescues late positions at fixed input length, yielding a principled halting rule T* = ceil(n / v-hat). (2) Architecture prior, not expressivity, picks the algorithm: standard-depth transformers learn parallel scans on this family; weight tying flips the selection to the serial frontier, even when positional addressing for a log-depth scan is supplied. At matched depth and parameters, untied models extrapolate worst and fail to learn A5 at all. (3) The walls are not where circuit complexity says: NC1-completeness costs nothing (A5 generalizes fully), while group order does (S5's 120x120 operator deadlocks joint learning) -- and an operator-first curriculum dissolves the wall in every seed. (4) Mechanisms are portable, not mandatable: warm-starting across budget contracts transfers the algorithm in every seed, re-pricing its speed, while imposing seriality through the input schedule fails where free training succeeds. These results are invisible to standard instruments, which provably saturate at the fixed points trained loops converge to. We introduce a head instrument, the convergence-time scaling tau(n,i), validate it causally via damage cones whose slope reproduces v, and show in-distribution head measurements predict out-of-distribution fate where tail metrics do not. Results replicate on the public easy-to-hard benchmark.

</details>


### [265] [Are Single-Token Sparse Autoencoder Features Causally Necessary? Layer-Depth and SAE-Family Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20596)
*Seonglae Cho,Zekun Wu,Kleyton Da Costa,Rishi Kalra,Ilham Wicaksono,Adriano Koshiyama*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analyzes 3.9M sparse autoencoder features across six models and three SAE families, finding that single-token features cluster tightly in decoder space, concentrate in early layers, and produce significant causal effects when ablated. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects, and interpretability claims are sensitive to training methodology rather than just activation function or scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether the causal roles of SAE features are stable across different SAE families, using single-token features as a diagnostic case where ground truth permits direct comparison.

Method: Analyzed 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families using zero-ablation at full layer depth, measuring logit reductions, feature clustering, and target token rank recovery.

Result: Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space, concentrate in early layers, and yield significant logit reductions in 178/208 full-layer conditions. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects. Target token rank recovers to within 2x baseline 96-98% of the time after ablation.

Conclusion: Cross-family interpretability claims are sensitive to training methodology, not just activation function or scale. Training recipe is the residual candidate for explaining causal differences.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are used to interpret and steer large language models, yet whether a feature's causal role is stable across SAE families remains untested. Single-token features that activate on one vocabulary item provide the diagnostic case where ground truth permits direct comparison. We analyze 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families using zero-ablation at full layer depth. Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers (Layer 0 in GPT2-Small; L0-L4 in Gemma). Ablating them yields Benjamini-Hochberg-significant logit reductions in 178 of 208 full-layer conditions, with depth controlling whether damage cascades downstream or shapes the output directly. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects: on the same base model, GemmaScope and BatchTopK features remain causally anchored, while LlamaScope features are locally redundant. The target token's rank recovers to within 2x baseline 96-98% of the time after the same ablation, and a controlled activation-function comparison reverses sign within the same model, leaving training recipe as the residual candidate. Cross-family interpretability claims are therefore sensitive to training methodology, not just activation function or scale.

</details>


### [266] [One Round Is All You Need: Analytic Federated Learning for Task-Heterogeneous Multi-Label Medical Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20641)
*Afsaneh Mahanipour,Hana Khamfroush*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity, using closed-form operations instead of iterative gradient optimization, achieving convergence in at most two communication rounds and outperforming FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC and 13.24 AUC points on ChestXray14.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing gradient-based FL methods struggle under task heterogeneity (each institution labels only its own expertise subset) because they require hundreds of communication rounds to converge and suffer from systematic false-negative bias due to missing class labels.

Method: Replaces iterative gradient optimization with three closed-form operations: (1) balanced label projection to neutralize class-imbalance bias; (2) per-class absolute aggregation law to independently assemble optimal ridge-regression classifiers from annotating clients' sufficient statistics; (3) optional analytic pseudo-label refinement using a confidence-filtered teacher classifier to propagate missing-class knowledge.

Result: Outperforms state-of-the-art FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC and 13.24 AUC points on ChestXray14 under four progressively severe missing-class configurations, requiring at most two communication rounds.

Conclusion: The proposed analytic framework effectively handles task heterogeneity in federated multi-label medical image classification with drastically reduced communication overhead and superior accuracy.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple clinical institutions to collaboratively train a shared disease classifier without centralizing patient data. In practice, however, each institution annotates only the pathologies within its area of expertise, so the federation operates under task heterogeneity: each client holds labels for a strict subset of the target disease categories while the remaining classes are entirely unobserved at that site. Existing gradient-based FL methods fail under this setting because they require hundreds of communication rounds to converge and because missing class labels introduce systematic false-negative bias that the model cannot correct without a principled mechanism. We propose an analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity. The proposed method replaces iterative gradient optimization with three closed-form operations: a balanced label projection that neutralizes class-imbalance bias by normalizing positive and negative contributions to equal total mass; a per-class absolute aggregation law that independently assembles the optimal ridge-regression classifier for each disease category from the sufficient statistics uploaded by its annotating clients; and an optional analytic pseudo-label refinement round that propagates missing-class knowledge from a confidence-filtered teacher classifier to non-annotating clients. The entire procedure requires at most two communication rounds, irrespective of the degree of task heterogeneity or the number of participating clients. Experiments on ChestXray14 under four progressively severe missing-class configurations demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art federated multi-label method FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points, while reducing the communication.

</details>


### [267] [Scaling Interpretable Transformers with Parity Bottleneck Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20652)
*Andrew Mack,Kraig Yuheng Tou,Mark Henry,Zhengxun Wu,Lauren Greenspan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The ParityTransformer introduces a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) that replaces learned over-complete bases with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary, enabling efficient and interpretable sparse representations at GPT-2 scale without prohibitive memory costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training models with interpretable-by-construction internal representations has been impractical because per-layer over-complete bottlenecks are prohibitively expensive in memory and compute, unlike post-hoc sparse autoencoders (SAEs) which recover features after training.

Method: A Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) uses a parameter-free algebraic dictionary with deterministic incoherence guarantees, combined with a hardware-aware hierarchical sparse bottleneck via multi-level mixture-of-experts to close the cost gap between sparse and dense training.

Result: ParityTransformers match or outperform post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks, and exceed them on feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions.

Conclusion: This is a step toward training models whose internal representations are interpretable by design rather than recovered post-hoc, as features surviving the sparse bottleneck are native to the model's forward pass.

Abstract: Language models are thought to exhibit the phenomenon of superposition, representing many more features than dimensions in their residual streams. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to recover such features post-hoc, but training models that are interpretable by construction has remained impractical, as a per-layer over-complete bottleneck is prohibitively expensive in both memory and compute. To overcome this issue, we introduce the ParityTransformer, a GPT-2-scale architecture whose intermediate representations are efficient and wide / sparse by design. At each layer, a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) replaces a learned over-complete basis with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary, providing a deterministic incoherence guarantee and eliminating the memory requirements that have prevented per-layer interpretable bottlenecks at scale. A DPB is a hierarchically structured sparse bottleneck which efficiently enforces sparsity using a multi-level mixture-of-experts approach: a hardware-aware implementation that closes the cost gap between activation sparse and dense training to a manageable interpretability tax. Empirically, ParityTransformers perform at least as well as post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks, while out-performing on measures of feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions. Because subsequent computation acts only on features that survive the sparse bottleneck, the ParityTransformer's features are native to the model's forwards pass by construction, addressing the question of whether SAEs probe features the model actually uses during computation. We see this as a step toward training models whose internal representations are interpretable by design rather than recovered post hoc.

</details>


### [268] [SalesLoop: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Sales Lead Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20655)
*Chenyu Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SalesLoop is a reinforcement learning framework for CRM lead ranking that bridges offline-online gaps via a performance-aware reward and Discriminative GRPO, achieving significant production lifts (e.g., +4.7% cumulative lift, p=0.047) validated by a 160-day A/B test at a New Energy Vehicle manufacturer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High offline accuracy of CRM lead ranking models often fails to translate to production due to three fundamental gaps: offline-online metric mismatch, pointwise-listwise objective misalignment, and temporal distribution drift.

Method: SalesLoop uses a reinforcement learning closed-loop framework with (1) a performance-aware reward that weights conversion outcomes by ranking position and conversion velocity, and (2) Discriminative GRPO, a listwise optimization objective adapting Group Relative Policy Optimization to discriminative ranking models.

Result: NDCG@K +7.9%, P@K +15.8% over static baseline. 160-day production A/B test: cumulative lift +4.7% (p=0.047) and +8.7% (p=0.002). Top-10% recall 44.1%; high-intent leads surfaced at 2.3× conversion rate vs. specialist baselines.

Conclusion: SalesLoop effectively closes the offline-online gap for lead ranking in CRM, demonstrating statistically significant and practically meaningful improvements in a real-world production environment.

Abstract: Lead ranking in Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems faces a persistent challenge: models achieving high offline accuracy often underperform in production. We identify three fundamental gaps responsible for this disconnect: offline-online metric mismatch, pointwise-listwise objective misalignment, and temporal distribution drift. To address these gaps, we propose SalesLoop, a reinforcement learning framework that establishes a closed feedback loop between model predictions and real-world business outcomes. Our approach introduces (1) a performance-aware reward that encodes conversion outcomes weighted by ranking position and conversion velocity, and (2) Discriminative GRPO, a listwise optimization objective that adapts Group Relative Policy Optimization to discriminative ranking models.
  SalesLoop improves NDCG@K by +7.9\% and P@K by +15.8\% over the strongest static baseline. A 160-day production A/B test at a New Energy Vehicle manufacturer, spanning 16.5M leads and 280 sales specialists across two provincial markets, validates statistically significant cumulative lift of +4.7\% ($p=0.047$) and +8.7\% ($p=0.002$). In production, the ranking backbone achieves Top-10\% recall of 44.1\% and surfaces high-intent leads at $2.3\times$ the conversion rate of specialist baselines.

</details>


### [269] [Adaptive Multi-Horizon Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20656)
*Manoosh Samiei,Doina Precup,Paul Masset*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a multi-horizon reinforcement learning approach that adaptively selects and combines temporal horizons, replacing fixed discount factors with flexible temporal discounting for improved adaptation to changing environments and task switches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Biological agents exhibit flexible temporal discounting, but standard RL uses a fixed discount factor, which limits adaptability in complex, changing environments and requires manual tuning.

Method: A multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines multiple temporal horizons, enabling automatic adjustment of discount factors without manual tuning.

Result: The approach identifies effective discount factors across MiniGrid environments and performs well in continual settings with three sequentially changing tasks.

Conclusion: Adaptive temporal discounting improves parameter efficiency and enhances adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems.

Abstract: Effective decision-making in complex and changing environments requires balancing short-term and long-term consequences. In reinforcement learning (RL), this trade-off is typically controlled through a fixed discount factor, which imposes a single exponentially discounted temporal horizon. However, biological agents exhibit flexible and adaptive temporal discounting, suggesting that effective planning requires multiple timescales. Here, we propose a multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines temporal horizons, enabling robust adaptation to changes in reward structure without manual discount-factor tuning. This flexibility makes the method particularly suitable for continual learning scenarios involving task switches and varying environmental configurations. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach identifies effective discount factors across a range of MiniGrid environments, including continual settings composed of three sequentially changing tasks. These results suggest that adaptive temporal discounting can improve parameter efficiency and enhance adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems.

</details>


### [270] [End-to-End Learning of Safe Optimal Feedback Control in High Dimensions with Control Barrier Function Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20674)
*Xingjian Li,Kelvin Kan,Deepanshu Verma,Krishna Kumar,Stanley Osher,Samy Wu Fung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a scalable method for end-to-end training of high-dimensional controllers with hard safety constraints using control barrier functions (CBFs), overcoming prior computational bottlenecks by combining operator splitting with Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB), and demonstrates effectiveness on multi-agent systems with up to 1200 state dimensions and 400 control dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior approaches to incorporating CBF-based safety filters into end-to-end policy training were limited to low-dimensional systems (≤16 state dimensions) due to computational and differentiation bottlenecks in the quadratic-program-based optimization layer.

Method: Combines operator splitting with Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) to enable scalable end-to-end training through the CBF safety filter optimization layer, with theoretical justification via nonsmooth analysis.

Result: Successfully scales to high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state dimensions up to 1200 and control dimensions up to 400, far exceeding prior limits of ~16 state dimensions.

Conclusion: The proposed approach enables end-to-end training of high-dimensional safety-critical controllers with hard safety guarantees, dramatically expanding the applicability of CBF-based methods.

Abstract: We consider the problem of learning high-dimensional semi-global feedback controllers under hard safety constraints enforced by control barrier functions (CBFs). Incorporating CBFs into end-to-end policy training requires embedding a quadratic-program-based safety filter as an optimization layer, but computational and differentiation bottlenecks have largely restricted prior approaches to low-dimensional systems, typically with at most 16 state dimensions. We address this limitation by combining operator splitting with the recently developed Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) method to enable scalable end-to-end training while preserving hard safety guarantees through the CBF safety filter. We justify this training methodology theoretically using nonsmooth analysis techniques and demonstrate its effectiveness on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state and control dimensions up to 1200 and 400, respectively.

</details>


### [271] [Explanation-Based Runtime Verification for Trustworthy ML-driven Optical Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20675)
*Omran Ayoub,Carlos Natalino,Ali Al Housseini,Felix Foschum,Philipp Morger,Tiziano Leidi,David Hock,Paolo Monti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes explanation-based runtime verification that uses XAI to assess ML decision soundness in optical networks before execution, demonstrating on lightpath QoT classification that it intercepts erroneous decisions while maintaining high automation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As ML models are increasingly integrated into optical network control loops, incorrect decisions can directly impact service quality and network stability. Ensuring reliability of individual ML decisions at deployment time is critical but challenging.

Method: Explanation-based runtime verification that evaluates explanation coherence and physics grounding consistency at runtime using XAI techniques. The approach defers or rejects ML decisions flagged as uncertain before they execute in the network control loop.

Result: On a lightpath quality of transmission (QoT) classification use case, the explanation-based verification approach intercepts a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving high automation rate.

Conclusion: Explanation-based runtime verification is an effective approach for enhancing ML reliability in optical network automation by using model explanations to detect unsound decisions before they impact the network.

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) models are increasingly integrated into optical network automation frameworks to support tasks such as failure management, performance monitoring and resource allocation. In these environments, ML-driven predictions may be directly coupled with control-plane actions where incorrect decisions can immediately impact service quality, resource efficiency, and network stability. As automation levels increase, ensuring the reliability of individual decisions at deployment time becomes a critical requirement. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques have emerged to improve transparency by highlighting the factors influencing ML predictions. In addition to identifying influential features, they provide insights into the underlying reasoning process of the model, revealing how different input variables contribute to the final outcome and how feature interactions shape the decision boundary. In this work, we introduce explanation-based runtime verification, an approach that exploits model explanations to assess the soundness of individual ML decisions before they are executed in the network control loop. The proposed approach evaluates explanation coherence and physics grounding consistency at runtime, enabling the system to defer or reject decisions flagged as uncertain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a representative use case of lightpath quality of transmission classification. Experimental results show that explanation-based verification can intercept a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving high automation rate.

</details>


### [272] [Attribution Markets: A Fisher-Market Formulation for Fractional Credit Assignment Between Planned Tasks and Performed Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20694)
*Salavat Ishbulatov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formulates the bridge between planned task budgets and logged action durations as a quasi-linear Fisher market, introduces a satiation-threshold fixed point extension with convergence guarantees, and proposes an entropy-regularized generalization robust to affinity noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing personal and organizational planning systems use an exclusive, all-or-nothing link between planned task budgets and logged actions, which misses genuinely related but unlinked effort and falsely reports stalls on active goals.

Method: The problem is formulated as a quasi-linear Fisher market where planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers, performed actions are divisible goods, and valuations come from fused text/structural/temporal signals. A concave completion utility with satiation-threshold fixed point is introduced; entropy-regularized generalization unifies the sharp market with optimal transport.

Result: The market yields conservation, hard budget cap, and provable junk filter theorems. The satiation-threshold fixed point has existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under diagonal dominance, validated on random/adversarial instances. The de-circularized benchmark reveals the sharp zero-entropy market is more noise-sensitive; the entropy-regularized variant with a noise-adaptive rule resolves this.

Conclusion: The proposed entropy-regularized Fisher market bridges planning and logging systems robustly, with connections to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms.

Abstract: Personal and organizational planning systems maintain two records that drift apart: what was planned (a task's effort budget) and what was done (a logged action's duration and description). Existing systems bridge them with an exclusive, all-or-nothing link that strands genuinely related but unlinked effort and reports false stalls on active goals. We formulate the bridge as a quasi-linear Fisher market: planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers, performed actions are divisible goods, and a fused text/structural/temporal signal sets each buyer's valuation. Two market instruments - a seller reserve price and a buyer cash option - yield conservation, a hard budget cap, and a provable junk filter as theorems. We extend the market with a concave completion utility discounting progress as a task nears its plan; standard convergence theory for the market's algorithm does not transfer here, resolved by a satiation-threshold fixed point with existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under an explicit diagonal-dominance condition, validated empirically on random and adversarial instances. A de-circularized, multi-seed benchmark - observed affinity corrupted independently of the scored ground truth - surfaces a genuine weak spot: the market's sharp, zero-entropy equilibrium is more sensitive to affinity noise than entropy-regularized optimal transport's permanently smoothed one. We resolve this with a one-parameter entropy-regularized generalization unifying the two, plus a noise-adaptive rule for its regularization strength. We report full reproducibility parameters, discuss limitations candidly, and relate the result to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms.

</details>


### [273] [CEDAR: Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20696)
*Mohammad Fesanghary*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CEDAR is a constraint-based method for discovering lagged causal edges in sparse autoregressive time series, using residualized distance correlation screening and targeted conditional-independence tests, achieving O(d²) CI tests with edge-level interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable efficient and interpretable lagged causal discovery in sparse time series, particularly when data are scarce and variables exhibit strong lag-1 self-dynamics.

Method: CEDAR screens candidate cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation, then applies two targeted conditional-independence tests per significant candidate, accepting at most one lag per ordered pair. A stable MCI pruning step removes indirect edges, and optional deterministic C-nodes adjust for trend-like nonstationarity.

Result: In sparse regimes, CEDAR requires only O(d²) CI tests after screening while retaining edge-level interpretability.

Conclusion: CEDAR is most effective when data are scarce and variables exhibit lag-1 self-dynamics; methods with richer conditioning sets become preferable as T grows or when higher-order autoregressive or simultaneous multi-lag effects are common.

Abstract: We propose CEDAR (Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes), a constraint-based method for lagged causal edge discovery in sparse autoregressive time series. CEDAR screens candidate cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation, then applies two targeted conditional-independence tests per significant cross-variable lag candidate and accepts at most one lag per ordered pair. A stable MCI pruning step removes indirect edges, and optional deterministic C-nodes adjust for specified trend-like nonstationarity. In sparse regimes where few lags survive screening, CEDAR requires $O(d^2)$ CI tests after screening while retaining edge-level interpretability. CEDAR is most effective when data are scarce and variables exhibit lag-1 self-dynamics; methods with richer conditioning sets become preferable as $T$ grows or when higher-order autoregressive or simultaneous multi-lag effects are common.

</details>


### [274] [Perspective Latents as an Architectural Condition for Causal Emergence in Active Inference Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20708)
*Hongju Pae*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In an active inference agent with fast/slow latent architecture, Integrated Information Decomposition (Φᵣ) concentrates in the slow global latent g. Its magnitude is mainly architectural and decreases with learning; meaningful effects only appear at the atom-compositional level (decoupling flips sign, becomes regime-invariant; downward causation tracks regimes). Thus scalar Φᵣ is not a direct index of learned integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate how reward-free predictive organization in active inference relates to information-theoretic signatures of causal emergence (Φᵣ), which prior work in RL agents showed grows with training and tracks reward improvement.

Method: An active inference agent with two-layer latent architecture (fast perception z, slow global g driven by prediction error, decoupled from policy gradients) is tested in a reward-free regime-switching protocol; Φᵣ is measured at aggregate and atom-compositional levels.

Result: Φᵣ concentrates in g; aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. At atom-compositional level, decoupling flips from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant, while downward causation carries regime-dependent adjustment.

Conclusion: The slow global latent g is the architectural locus of Φᵣ-relevant temporal organization in active inference; scalar Φᵣ should not be interpreted as a direct index of learned integration.

Abstract: A recent line of work measures causal emergence in reinforcement learning agents through Integrated Information Decomposition, reporting that $Φ_r$ grows with training and tracks reward improvement. For active inference, this raises the question of how reward-free predictive organization relates to such information-theoretic signatures. I test this within an active inference agent whose architecture separates a fast perception latent $z$ from a slow global latent $g$, where $g$ is driven by prediction error and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. In a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol, $Φ_r$ concentrates in $g$; its aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. The substantive effect of learning becomes legible only at the atom-compositional level: decoupling flips sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant under environmental change, while downward causation carries the regime-dependent adjustment. These results identify $g$ as the architectural locus of $Φ_r$-relevant temporal organization in an active inference agent, and argue against reading scalar $Φ_r$ as a direct index of learned integration.

</details>


### [275] [LLMs Get Lost in Evolving User Intent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20734)
*Jihoon Tack,Philippe Laban,Jennifer Neville*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLMs struggle to track and act on evolving user intent in multi-turn conversations, despite strong performance in static, single-turn settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLMs are predominantly evaluated in single-turn, fully-specified settings, but real user interactions are dynamic—users disclose, revise, and reshape intent as conversations unfold. The gap between static evaluation and dynamic collaboration remains unexplored.

Method: The authors introduce a framework that converts static, single-turn tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations where user intent evolves incrementally (revealed, revised, or redirected) across turns, while preserving original evaluation protocols to reuse existing benchmarks without new annotations.

Result: Strong performance in static settings does not transfer to evolving-intent settings, with substantial performance drops observed consistently across multiple tasks and model families.

Conclusion: Today's LLMs do not faithfully track and act on evolving user intent, revealing a fundamental capability gap invisible to static evaluation but critical for future collaborative agents.

Abstract: As LLMs become more capable, they are increasingly deployed as collaborative agents, taking on user-delegated tasks through iterative interaction. Yet genuine interaction is inherently dynamic: users rarely specify their intent upfront, instead disclosing, revising, and reshaping it as the conversation unfolds. Despite this, LLMs are still predominantly evaluated or trained in single-turn, fully-specified settings, leaving open a fundamental question: how well do LLMs track and act on user intent as it evolves over the course of a conversation? To study this, we introduce a framework that transforms static, single-turn tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations in which the user's intent evolves across turns--incrementally revealed, revised, and at times redirected mid-conversation--while preserving each task's original evaluation protocol, enabling existing benchmarks to be reused as controlled testbeds without new annotation. Across multiple tasks, we surface a consistent phenomenon: strong static-setting performance does not transfer to the evolving-intent setting, with substantial drops across model families. Our findings point to a fundamental gap: today's LLMs do not yet faithfully track and act on the user's evolving intent, a capability invisible to static evaluation yet critical for future collaborative agents.

</details>


### [276] [Cardinality-Decomposed Loss: Matching Training Objectives to Relation Structure in Heterogeneous Recommendation Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20737)
*Parul Maheshwari,Amulya Paruchuri,Yiqing Zou,Alireza Sahami Shirazi,Farhad Farahani,Prakhar Mehrotra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Graph Neural Networks for recommendation systems suffer from a silent failure where BPR loss causes attribute embeddings to collapse to near-random geometry, hurting downstream tasks. The authors propose Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL) combining CE and BPR, showing that the two losses compete in shared parameter space, and demonstrate improved attribute discriminability across five datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard recommendation systems using GNNs on heterogeneous bipartite graphs apply a single loss (BPR) across all relations, which works for recommendation but silently collapses attribute embeddings to near-random geometry, polluting user node embeddings and degrading downstream tasks like personalization and segmentation. This failure is invisible to standard ranking metrics.

Method: Proposes Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL) that combines Cross Entropy (CE) for one-to-one attribute relations and BPR for one-to-many preference relations, showing the two losses compete in the shared encoder parameter space. A lambda parameter navigates the trade-off between ranking and attribute discriminability, governed by two graph properties: semantic alignment and topology leakage.

Result: CDL consistently improves discriminability in attribute embeddings across five datasets (MovieLens-1M, Last.fm-360K, PayPal Audience Factory, BookCrossing, Yelp). Ranking (NDCG) improves when attributes carry meaningful preference signal but conflicts when correlation is weak. Dataset behavior is governed by semantic alignment (whether attribute predicts preferences) and topology leakage (whether graph connectivity already encodes it).

Conclusion: Using a single loss function for heterogeneous relations in recommendation GNNs causes silent failures in attribute embeddings. CDL decouples losses by cardinality to address this, with a tunable lambda parameter to navigate the trade-off between ranking and attribute quality based on dataset-specific graph properties.

Abstract: Graph Neural Networks trained on heterogenous bipartite graphs form a common basis in recommendation systems. These graphs often express relations that vary in cardinality, for example, user-item preferences are one-to-many and user-attribute features are one-to-one. Traditionally, a unique loss function is applied for all of the network components which is often Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR). While BPR works well for the recommendation task, we find that it causes attribute embeddings to collapse to near-random geometry -- a silent failure that leaves standard ranking metrics largely unaffected and therefore invisible to conventional evaluation. This in turn pollutes user node embeddings, which are shaped by both edge types simultaneously, hurting downstream tasks like personalization, segmentation, etc. Here we propose a Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL) that combines both Cross Entropy (CE) and BPR to enable the model to collectively optimize for relations across cardinalities. We confirm this CE-BPR conflict by showing the two losses compete in the shared encoder's parameter space. We evaluate CDL on five datasets spanning two structural configurations -- one-to-one attributes on user nodes (MovieLens-1M, Last.fm-360K, PayPal Audience Factory, BookCrossing) and on item nodes (Yelp) -- and find that CDL consistently improves discriminability in attribute embeddings. We also show that ranking (NDCG) improves when attributes carry meaningful preference signal, but conflicts with it when the correlation is weak. We use a lambda parameter to navigate this trade-off, and a lambda-sweep reveals that dataset behavior is governed by two graph properties -- semantic alignment and topology leakage. Semantic alignment measures whether the attribute predicts preferences, while topology leakage measures whether the graph's connectivity already encodes it.

</details>


### [277] [Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion for Trustworthy Multi-Omics Multimodal Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20742)
*Mohammad Raahemi,Ali Sekhavati,Alireza Maleki,Hamid Nasiri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ACE is a multimodal fusion framework that enhances trustworthiness by generating complementary modalities from intra-modality correlations and employing a dual-level confidence mechanism to adaptively reweigh modalities and estimate a global trust score. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on four multi-omics datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal learning improves medical prognosis but suffers from poor performance under noisy/uninformative data streams. Existing fusion approaches lack dynamic data quality assessment and trustworthy confidence scores, hindering deployment in safety-critical settings.

Method: ACE (1) generates new complementary modalities from intra-modality correlations to enhance the multimodal space, then (2) employs a dual-level confidence mechanism that adaptively reweighs modalities by reliability before fusion and estimates a global trust score over the fused final decision.

Result: ACE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in both classification performance and confidence calibration across four challenging multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, ROSMAP).

Conclusion: ACE provides a more stable and robust data fusion method that facilitates multimodal learning in high-stakes problems by improving trustworthiness through adaptive confidence weighting.

Abstract: Multimodal learning is a robust approach to improve predictive performance in applications such as medical prognosis. However, the clinical applicability of models that use multimodal learning is hampered by their poor performance under noisy or uninformative data streams. Present fusion approaches often lack robust mechanisms for the dynamic assessment of data quality and for the provision of a trustable confidence score on the final prediction. This dissuades their deployment in safety-critical settings. To address these limitations, we introduce Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion (ACE), a novel framework to enhance the trustworthiness of multimodal fusion models. ACE first enhances the multimodal space by generating new, complementary modalities from intra-modality correlations. It then employs a dual-level confidence mechanism that (1) adaptively reweighs all modalities by their reliability before fusion and (2) estimates a global trust score over the fused, final decision. To evaluate ACE, we used four challenging multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, and ROSMAP). ACE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in both classification performance and confidence calibration. Our framework provides a more stable and robust data fusion method that facilitates the use of multimodal learning in addressing high-stakes problems.

</details>


### [278] [GaugeQuant: Online Learning of Quantization-Optimal Bases from LLM Symmetries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20757)
*Miguel P. Bento,João Seabra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GaugeQuant uses LogSumExp regularization during training to break internal symmetries in Transformers, reducing activation outliers for better quantization without calibration data or overhead, significantly improving perplexity under low-bit quantization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers possess internal continuous symmetries that cause activation outliers, degrading quantization performance. Existing post-training quantization methods require calibration datasets and frozen models. GaugeQuant aims to leverage training-time symmetry breaking to improve quantization without these requirements.

Method: Introduces a LogSumExp term to the loss function that breaks internal symmetries, selecting a basis minimizing activation outliers. A stop-gradient operator ensures only rotation matrices are updated, leaving the language modeling objective unaltered.

Result: With LLaMA-2 7B under W4A4 quantization (group size 128), perplexity drops from 8.22 to 6.73. Under W4A16, perplexity drops from 11.16 to 5.45. Achieves performance comparable to post-training methods that require frozen models and calibration datasets.

Conclusion: GaugeQuant effectively reduces quantization-induced perplexity degradation without calibration data, quantization simulation, or significant training overhead, providing a lightweight in-training solution that competes with post-training quantization methods.

Abstract: Transformers are known to have internal continuous symmetries that leave outputs invariant, while modifying quantization. GaugeQuant leverages this in-training by introducing a LogSumExp term to the loss that breaks the symmetries, thus selecting a basis that minimizes activation outliers. A stop-gradient operator ensures that only rotation matrices are updated, yielding the language modeling objective completely unaltered. Our requires no specific calibration data, no quantization simulation, and adds negligible training overhead. With the LLaMA-2 7B model under W4A4 quantization with group size 128, perplexity drops from 8.22 to 6.73, competing with post-training methods that require frozen models and calibration datasets. Under W4A16, perplexity drops from 11.16 to 5.45. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/gauge-quant.

</details>


### [279] [Memory-Computation Tradeoffs in Semi Amortized Parametric Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20769)
*Shijie Pan,Agustin Castellano,Zeyu Shen,Enrique Mallada*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies amortized parametric optimization, analyzing how much offline memory is needed to guarantee ε-accuracy under a fixed online computation budget (K steps of projected gradient descent). For strongly convex objectives, matching upper/lower bounds are established; for convex objectives with β-growth, near-matching bounds and a phase transition are identified. The framework quantifies the memory cost of acceleration and identifies key drivers: online optimizer convergence rate and Lipschitz sensitivity of the solution map.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a general theoretical understanding of the tradeoff between offline information (memory) and online computation in learning-enabled decision systems, specifically quantifying how much offline data is needed to achieve desired accuracy under fixed online compute budget.

Method: The paper frames the problem as amortized parametric optimization: offline stores solved instances, online retrieves a warm start and runs K steps of projected gradient descent. A nonparametric predictor built from offline solutions is analyzed for smooth convex parametric optimization over a compact domain. Theoretical analysis establishes upper and lower bounds for μ-strongly convex objectives and convex objectives with β-growth condition (β>2).

Result: For μ-strongly convex objectives: matching upper and lower bounds on memory needed for ε-accuracy given K online iterations. For convex objectives with β-growth (β>2): near-matching bounds and a phase transition where additional memory provides no benefit beyond a certain K. The framework quantifies memory cost of acceleration, identifying convergence rate of online optimizer and Lipschitz sensitivity of solution map as key quantities. Experiments on parameterized ridge regression confirm predicted tradeoffs.

Conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for the memory-computation-accuracy tradeoff in amortized optimization, with matching or near-matching bounds for convex and strongly convex objectives, and identifies conditions under which offline memory can accelerate online computation.

Abstract: Learning-enabled decision systems often use offline data or computation to reduce online compute cost. Despite the empirical success of such approaches, there is limited general understanding of how much offline information is needed to achieve a desired accuracy under a fixed online computation budget. We study this question through the lens of amortized parametric optimization: an offline phase stores a finite memory of solved problem instances, and an online phase produces a solution to a new instance by retrieving a warm start and applying $K$ steps of projected gradient descent. We analyze this setup for smooth convex parametric optimization over a compact domain, using a nonparametric predictor built from the stored offline solutions. For $μ$-strongly convex objectives, we establish matching upper and lower bounds on the memory required to guarantee $\varepsilon$-accuracy under a fixed online iteration budget $K$. For convex objectives satisfying a $β$-growth condition ($β>2$), we obtain near-matching bounds and identify a phase transition in $K$ beyond which additional memory provides no benefit. We further provide a general proof framework that (i) explicitly quantifies the memory cost of acceleration---how much offline memory is required to achieve a prescribed speedup over the unaided online optimizer---and (ii) identifies two key quantities driving this cost: the convergence rate of the online optimizer and the Lipschitz sensitivity of the solution map to the problem parameter. Experiments on parameterized ridge regression confirm the predicted memory--computation--accuracy tradeoffs.

</details>


### [280] [Toward Mechanistic Interpretability of an AI Foundation Model Fine-Tuned for Atmospheric Chemistry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20778)
*Jason Y. Hu,Ivan Higuera-Mendieta,Patrick Obin Sturm,Makoto M. Kelp*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates what Microsoft's Aurora weather forecasting foundation model has learned about atmospheric chemistry when fine-tuned for air quality prediction. Through controlled chemical perturbations, analysis of internal representations, and sparse autoencoders, the authors find that while Aurora captures first-order ozone-nitrogen relationships, it fails to enforce consistent chemical constraints, relaxes localized emission features, and its internal representations remain organized around meteorology rather than chemistry. The study provides a framework for evaluating whether AI forecasting systems genuinely learn physical mechanisms or exploit statistical patterns, arguing that composition forecasts should be judged by internal mechanisms, not just benchmark skill.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Weather forecasting foundation models fine-tuned for air quality prediction are increasingly used, but high forecast skill does not reveal whether these models have learned physical/chemical mechanisms or simply exploit statistical regularities in training data. Understanding the internal mechanisms is crucial as these models are positioned to inform environmental policy decisions.
