Method: The authors examine Microsoft's Aurora model by (1) imposing controlled chemical perturbations on forecasts and testing against known photochemical relationships, (2) examining internal representations that generate forecasts, and (3) using sparse autoencoders to identify internal components that causally control chemical forecasts.

Result: Aurora captures a first-order ozone response to reactive nitrogen but does not enforce chemical constraints expected in process-based models. It generates chemically inconsistent combinations of related species, relaxes localized emission features like wildfire plumes toward background, and its internal representations remain largely organized around meteorology inherited during pretraining with little chemistry-specific structure. Sparse autoencoders reveal internal components causally controlling chemical forecasts but these do not map cleanly onto individual atmospheric processes.

Conclusion: AI forecasting systems should be judged not only by benchmark skill but also by their internal mechanisms. The work provides a framework for testing whether such models genuinely learn atmospheric chemistry from reanalysis data.

Abstract: Weather forecasting foundation models (FMs) are increasingly fine-tuned to predict air quality, offering fast global pollution forecasts at lower computational cost than conventional chemical transport models. These FMs are typically trained on reanalysis data and generate forecasts through autoregressive rollout. They do not explicitly represent governing physical or chemical processes. Therefore, high forecast skill does not reveal whether a model has learned physical mechanisms or exploits statistical regularities in its training data. Here, we present the first study of what a FM fine-tuned for atmospheric chemistry has learned by examining Microsoft's Aurora model. We impose controlled chemical perturbations on its forecasts and test them against known photochemical relationships. We then examine the internal representations that generate these forecasts. We find that Aurora captures a first-order ozone response to reactive nitrogen but does not enforce the chemical constraints that a process-based model encodes. It generates chemically inconsistent combinations of related species and relaxes localized emission features such as wildfire plumes toward background. Internally, its representations remain largely organized around the meteorology inherited during pretraining, with little structure specific to chemistry. Using sparse autoencoders, we identify internal components that causally control the chemical forecast but do not map cleanly onto individual atmospheric processes. This work provides a framework for testing whether AI forecasting systems learn atmospheric chemistry from reanalysis data. As these models are increasingly positioned to inform environmental policy decisions, we argue that composition forecasts should also be judged by their internal mechanisms rather than by benchmark skill alone.

</details>


### [281] [Synthetic minority data is redundant or invalid: a data-dependent validity theory and a de-biased test](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20787)
*Ahmad B. Hassanat,Ahmad S. Tarawneh,Ghada A. Altarawneh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper reveals that the standard validity check for synthetic minority data in class-imbalanced learning is fundamentally flawed (circular validation), proposes a de-biased estimator that uses withheld real data, proves that validity depends on class overlap rather than generation method, and shows that across 91 methods, no synthetic data generation approach meaningfully improves over trivial baselines while maintaining validity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard check for synthetic minority examples in class-imbalanced learning is circular—synthetic points are evaluated against the same data that generated them—leading to an illusion of validity that masks invalidity in 96-99% of cases.

Method: The paper develops a de-biased validity estimator that scores synthetic points against withheld real data, establishes that validity is a population quantity determined by class overlap (not generation method), and audits 91 synthetic generation methods across three classifiers on medical and financial datasets.

Result: The classical test underestimates true invalidity in 96-99% of method-by-imbalance-ratio cells. No generator clears both bars of validity and information gain; improvements over baselines are below 0.01 median F1 (within decision threshold noise), and most damage calibration. Even a generator engineered to pass the classical check fails under the de-biased audit.

Conclusion: Class overlap sets an invalidity floor that no faithful generator can escape, making oversampling redundant where classes separate and invalid where they overlap. The burden of proof is flipped: synthetic minority data must now demonstrate both validity and information gain on the data at hand.

Abstract: For two decades, the standard remedy for class-imbalanced learning has been to fabricate synthetic minority examples, and the standard evidence of their validity has been a check that cannot fail: synthetic points are scored against the very data that generated them. We de-bias the check. Validity becomes a population quantity -- the probability that a synthetic point truly belongs to the minority class -- with a consistent estimator that scores synthetic points against withheld real data. Where held-out ground truth is available, the classical test underestimates true invalidity in 96-99% of method-by-imbalance-ratio cells, while the de-biased estimator tracks it closely. We prove validity is a property of the data, not the method: class overlap sets an invalidity floor no faithful generator escapes, making oversampling redundant where classes separate and invalid where they overlap. Across 91 methods, three classifiers, and datasets spanning medicine and finance -- including a generator engineered to pass the classical check -- none clears both bars: gains over the best trivial baseline are noise-thin (median below 0.01 F1, a decision threshold's reach), and most damage calibration. We release the audit as a pip-installable test and flip the burden of proof: synthetic minority data must now demonstrate, on the data at hand, both validity and information gain.

</details>


### [282] [Memoir: Should a Model Write to Its Memory While It Thinks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20792)
*Jaber Jaber,Osama Jaber*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Memoir combines fast memory, slow parameters, variable-depth recurrence, and a future-latent energy objective. On procedural associative recall, the read-only pondering arm (0.6557) outperformed the coupled rewriting arm (0.5203) at 240 steps, but both reached 1.0000 by 960 steps, indicating a learning-speed penalty rather than a capability ceiling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test the riskiest coupling in the Memoir architecture: whether having each pondering iteration rewrite the same fast-tier memory it reads degrades performance.

Method: Compared two 81,738-parameter arms (coupled vs. read-only pondering) on procedural associative recall with key interference, matched on compute, data, optimizer, schedule, and seeds. Used 12 seeds at 240 steps and 8 seeds at 960 steps.

Result: At 240 steps: coupled recall 0.5203 [0.4522, 0.5883], read-only recall 0.6557 [0.5953, 0.7160], paired difference 0.1354 (t=3.23, 95% CI [0.0431, 0.2277], 10/12 seeds). At 960 steps: both 1.0000. Kernel restructuring reduced delta-rule forward time from 0.907 ms to 0.351 ms.

Conclusion: The coupling imposes a learning-speed penalty, not a capability ceiling. The predicted failure of energy signal corruption did not occur; energy margin grew and held. Longer convergence on a non-saturating task remains unmeasured.

Abstract: Memoir combines per-sample fast memory, shared slow parameters, variable-depth latent recurrence, and a future-latent energy objective. We test its riskiest coupling: each pondering iteration may rewrite the fast tier that the same iteration reads. On procedural associative recall with key interference, we compare a coupled arm against an otherwise identical read-only pondering arm. Both arms contain 81,738 parameters, including 76,362 trainable parameters, and use matched declared forward multiply-accumulate counts, data, optimizer, schedule, and seeds. After 240 training steps across 12 seeds, coupled recall is 0.5203 with a 95 percent interval of [0.4522, 0.5883], while read-only recall is 0.6557 with [0.5953, 0.7160]. The arms are paired per seed, and the read-only lead of 0.1354 gives a paired t of 3.23 on 11 degrees of freedom with a 95 percent interval of [0.0431, 0.2277] on the difference, winning on 10 of 12 seeds. After 960 steps across 8 seeds, both arms reach 1.0000, so the measured effect is a learning-speed penalty at a fixed budget, not a demonstrated capability penalty. That longer control is ceiling limited, leaving convergence on a non-saturating task unmeasured. A predicted failure in which memory rewriting corrupts the energy signal did not occur: the energy margin grew and held. Kernel restructuring also reduced delta-rule forward time from 0.907 ms to 0.351 ms on the stated device. Code and evidence are available at https://github.com/RightNow-AI/Memoir

</details>


### [283] [External Clustering Validation by the Homogeneity-Parsimony Trade-off](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20799)
*Andreas Tiffeau-Mayer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces normalized homogeneity and parsimony scores for clustering evaluation, built on the information bottleneck principle without rewarding lossy compression, showing monotonicity under cluster refinement and unifying commonly used evaluation criteria via information-theoretic, set-matching, and pair-based frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scalar clustering metrics often obscure the fundamental trade-off between being informative about class labels and avoiding unnecessary fragmentation. The authors aim to quantify this trade-off explicitly.

Method: The authors develop normalized homogeneity and parsimony scores based on the information bottleneck principle (modified to not reward lossy compression). They extend beyond Shannon entropies to derive set-matching and pair-based counterparts, proving monotonicity under cluster refinement.

Result: The scores vary monotonically under cluster refinement (proved mathematically). The pair-based setting recovers the ROC of binary classifiers. The framework unifies commonly used evaluation criteria and demonstrates utility for feature selection and algorithm comparison, identifying Pareto-optimal solutions.

Conclusion: Jointly considering homogeneity and parsimony scores clarifies clustering operating points and enables principled evaluation of clusterings, unifying existing criteria under a coherent information-theoretic framework.

Abstract: Scalar metrics are often used to evaluate clusterings against known classes, but they can obscure a fundamental trade-off: clusterings should be informative about class labels while avoiding unnecessary fragmentation. Here we describe normalized scores of cluster homogeneity and parsimony that quantify this trade-off. These scores build on the information bottleneck principle, modified to not reward lossy compression. We show by example and mathematical proof that our definitions of these scores have the intuitive property of varying monotonically under cluster refinement in contrast to related proposals. Extending the information-theoretic framework beyond Shannon entropies, we furthermore derive set-matching and pair-based counterparts of the homogeneity and parsimony scores. These unify commonly used evaluation criteria and show that, in the pair-based setting, the homogeneity-parsimony trade-off recovers the receiver operating characteristic of binary classifiers. We demonstrate the framework's utility for feature selection and algorithm comparison, illustrating how considering scores jointly can clarify clustering operating points and identify Pareto-optimal solutions.

</details>


### [284] [New Complexity-Theoretic Frontiers of Tractability for Neural Network Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20811)
*Cornelius Brand,Robert Ganian,Mathis Rocton*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes new polynomial-time algorithms for optimally training neural networks with ReLU and linear activations, pushing beyond prior tractability boundaries. For ReLU networks, the authors show tractability when hidden neurons have out-degree 1. For linear networks, they identify the first non-trivial polynomial-time solvable class under a novel data throughput condition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite neural networks' fundamental role, the computational complexity of optimally training them remains poorly understood. While lower bounds have tightened recently for linear and ReLU activations, progress on identifying polynomial-time tractable architectures has been limited.

Method: The authors develop novel algorithmic upper bounds for optimally training neural networks. For ReLU networks, they analyze architectures where hidden neurons have out-degree 1. For linear networks, they introduce a "data throughput condition" that characterizes a polynomially solvable class.

Result: - For ReLU networks: polynomial-time tractability for all architectures with hidden neuron out-degree 1, improving upon the prior algorithm by Arora, Basu, Mianjy and Mukherjee.
- For linear networks: identification of the first non-trivial polynomial-time solvable class via a novel data throughput condition.

Conclusion: The results push the boundaries of tractability for training neural networks to optimality, expanding the known classes of architectures that can be solved in polynomial time for both ReLU and linear activation functions.

Abstract: In spite of the fundamental role of neural networks in contemporary machine learning research, our understanding of the computational complexity of optimally training neural networks remains incomplete even when dealing with the simplest kinds of activation functions. Indeed, while there has been a number of very recent results that establish ever-tighter lower bounds for the problem under linear and ReLU activation functions, less progress has been made towards the identification of novel polynomial-time tractable network architectures. In this article we obtain novel algorithmic upper bounds for training linear- and ReLU-activated neural networks to optimality which push the boundaries of tractability for these problems beyond the previous state of the art. In particular, for ReLU networks we establish the polynomial-time tractability of all architectures where hidden neurons have an out-degree of $1$, improving upon the previous algorithm of Arora, Basu, Mianjy and Mukherjee. On the other hand, for networks with linear activation functions we identify the first non-trivial polynomial-time solvable class of networks by obtaining an algorithm that can optimally train network architectures satisfying a novel data throughput condition.

</details>


### [285] [Robust Asynchronous Q-Learning under Reward and State Corruption via Batching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20822)
*Sreejeet Maity,Aritra Mitra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes BR-Async-Q, a robust Q-learning algorithm that uses batch partitioning and robust estimation to defend against adversarial corruption of both rewards and state observations, achieving near-optimal error bounds and the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous Q-learning under such threats.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the problem of learning optimal policies in harsh environments where an adversary can corrupt both reward signals and state observations (Huber contamination model), filling the gap of robustness guarantees for asynchronous Q-learning under dual-source corruption.

Method: The algorithm, BR-Async-Q, is an epoch-based robust Q-learning approach with two key ideas: (i) partitioning the online data stream into batches to reduce variance, and (ii) constructing robust estimates of the Bellman optimality operator using the batched data.

Result: Proves a high-probability ℓ∞ error bound matching vanilla Q-learning up to a small additive term scaling with the corruption fraction; achieves minimax optimal dependence on corruption fraction when only rewards are corrupted.

Conclusion: This work provides the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous Q-learning under both reward and state corruption, with minimax optimal performance in the reward-only corruption setting.

Abstract: Motivated by reinforcement learning in harsh environments, we consider the problem of learning an optimal policy subject to adversarially corrupted feedback. Specifically, at each time-step, an adversary can perturb both the reward and state observations of the learner following the Huber contamination model. To defend against such data corruption, we propose {\texttt{BR-Async-Q}}: a novel, epoch-based, robust \(Q\)-learning algorithm built upon two key ideas: (i) partitioning the online data stream into batches to reduce variance, and (ii) constructing robust estimates of the Bellman optimality operator using such batched data. We prove a high-probability $\ell_\infty$ error bound for {\texttt{BR-Async-Q}} that matches that for vanilla \(Q\)-learning, up to a small additive term that scales with the fraction of corrupted samples. To our knowledge, this provides the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous \(Q\)-learning subject to both reward and state corruption. Furthermore, when only rewards are corrupted, the dependence of our algorithm's bound on the corruption fraction is minimax optimal.

</details>


### [286] [Beyond Heavy Log Curation: Perplexity-Based APT Detection via Unsupervised, Context-Augmented Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20832)
*Shoya Otsu,Kei Suzuki,Toshiaki Koike-Akino,Jing Liu,Ye Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CAPTAIN is a perplexity-based APT detection method that uses pre-trained language models with minimal preprocessing, encoding temporal context via a Q-Former-style bridge and smoothing filters, achieving competitive performance with lower engineering overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: APTs are hard to detect due to the sparse attack signals in massive logs, and existing ML approaches require heavily curated training data and complex preprocessing pipelines that demand significant domain expertise and engineering cost.

Method: CAPTAIN uses pre-trained language models with minimal, domain-agnostic preprocessing; encodes recent history via an encoder + Q-Former-style bridge to inject compact context tokens into the decoder, computing perplexity with temporal context; and applies smoothing filters to the perplexity time series for stability.

Result: CAPTAIN competes with strong existing baselines on APT-oriented benchmarks and remains robust under substantially less curated inputs.

Conclusion: Reducing reliance on complex preprocessing lowers development and operational costs while maintaining detection performance, making APT detection more scalable and accessible.

Abstract: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) remain difficult to detect because only a small fraction of events in large-scale logs are attack-related, and investigation is expensive and hard to scale. Prior machine-learning approaches can reduce analyst workload, but they often rely on heavily curated training data and sophisticated preprocessing pipelines. Building and maintaining such pipelines require substantial domain expertise and engineering cost. Motivated by insights from a study of a strong APT detection baseline, we propose CAPTAIN (Context-Augmented Perplexity-based Threat Activity log detectIoN), a perplexity-based detector that leverages general, pre-trained language models with minimal, domain-agnostic preprocessing, enabling robust scoring of long, minimally processed log entries. CAPTAIN encodes recent history with an encoder model and a Q-Former-style bridge, then injects the compact context tokens into the decoder input so that perplexity reflects temporal context. To improve stability, CAPTAIN additionally applies smoothing filters to the perplexity time series. Across APT-oriented benchmarks, CAPTAIN competes with strong existing baselines and remains robust under substantially less curated inputs, that reduces the development and operational cost of advanced log preprocessing.

</details>


### [287] [Offline RL with Hierarchical Action Chunking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20834)
*Ahad Jawaid*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HiQC combines high-level latent planning with low-level action chunking to enable unbiased k-step value backups for offline goal-conditioned RL, achieving tighter value error bounds and state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline goal-conditioned RL struggles with long-horizon tasks due to the curse of horizon, where value estimation errors compound through bootstrapped Bellman backups. Existing hierarchical methods suffer from myopic low-level controllers and biased value estimates.

Method: HiQC proposes a hierarchical framework with high-level latent planning and low-level action chunking, where the low-level critic is conditioned on temporally extended action sequences to perform unbiased k-step value backups.

Result: Theoretically, HiQC achieves a tighter bound on value error under bounded per-backup error compared to standard hierarchy or flat chunking. Empirically, it achieves the highest aggregate performance on OGBench, with largest gains on long-horizon navigation like humanoid-giant.

Conclusion: Dual decomposition of horizon at both planning and execution levels (latent planning + action chunking) effectively mitigates the curse of horizon in offline goal-conditioned RL.

Abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning general-purpose policies from static datasets. However, scaling these methods to long-horizon tasks remains a challenge due to the curse of horizon, where value estimation errors can compound through long chains of bootstrapped Bellman backups. Existing hierarchical approaches mitigate this by decomposing tasks into subgoals, yet they often rely on low-level controllers that suffer from myopic execution and biased value estimates. In this work, we propose Hierarchical Implicit Q-Chunking (HiQC), an offline goal-conditioned RL algorithm that combines high-level latent planning with low-level action chunking. By conditioning the low-level critic on temporally extended action sequences, HiQC enables unbiased k-step value backups, compressing the horizon at both the planning and execution levels. We theoretically demonstrate that this dual decomposition results in a tighter bound on value error under a bounded per-backup error model compared to standard hierarchy or flat chunking alone. Empirically, HiQC achieves the highest aggregate performance among the compared methods on the OGBench suite, with its largest gains on long-horizon navigation tasks such as humanoid-giant.

</details>


### [288] [Multilevel Graph Wavelet Compressed Sensing with Scale-Aware Neural Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20857)
*Amirhossein Nouranizadeh,Sarang Rajendra Patil,Alan John Varghese,Varsha Narayanan,Amit Chakraborty,Mengjia Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GWCS is a learning-based framework that compresses graph signals (e.g., PDE simulation data on meshes) by sparsely representing them in the wavelet domain using spectral graph wavelet transform, combining a multilevel importance sampler for coefficient selection with a scale-aware GNN for reconstruction, achieving high fidelity and substantial compression over benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific ML methods (neural operators, PINNs) require large volumes of simulated data, making data preparation and model training expensive. Existing compression methods for graph signals (e.g., sampling methods, graph autoencoders) have limitations in reconstruction fidelity and compression ratio.

Method: GWCS: (1) Apply spectral graph wavelet transform to represent graph signals as wavelet-domain coefficients; (2) Use a nonparametric multilevel importance sampler to retain high-energy coefficients per scale for a given compression ratio; (3) Employ a scale-aware graph neural network to reconstruct the signal from the sparse coefficients.

Result: Evaluated on synthetic graph signals and four PDE simulation datasets (Turbulent Radiative Layer, Viscoelastic Instability, Kolmogorov Flow, Dynamic Stall). Outperforms graph signal sampling methods and graph autoencoder baselines in both reconstruction fidelity and data compression.

Conclusion: GWCS provides an effective offline compression framework for graph-structured simulation data, enabling substantial data reduction while maintaining high reconstruction quality, which can lower the cost of data preparation for scientific ML applications.

Abstract: Scientific machine learning methods such as neural operators and physics-informed neural networks have advanced engineering applications and inverse problems, but their training typically requires large volumes of simulated data. This makes data preparation and model training expensive. We propose Graph Wavelet Compressed Sensing (GWCS), a learning-based framework for offline compression of graph signals by representing them as sparse, interpretable wavelet-domain representations using the spectral graph wavelet transform. The framework combines a nonparametric multilevel importance sampler, which retains high-energy wavelet coefficients within each scale for a given compression ratio, with a scale-aware graph neural network that reconstructs the signal from the sparse coefficients. We evaluate the proposed framework on synthetic approximately band-limited graph signals over random graphs and four PDE simulation datasets over meshes, which include Turbulent Radiative Layer, Viscoelastic Instability, Kolmogorov Flow, and Dynamic Stall. We compare against graph signal sampling methods and graph autoencoder baselines. Results demonstrate that the framework achieves high reconstruction fidelity and substantial data compression compared to existing benchmarks.

</details>


### [289] [Position Bias is Hidden Behind Ceiling Effects: A Permutation Diagnostic for LLM Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20864)
*Hiroki Tamba*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Position bias in multiple-choice LLM evaluation is statistically detectable only within a 60-95% base-accuracy Goldilocks zone; outside this band, it is either confounded by processing-load dominance or compressed by ceiling effects. Standard MMLU places frontier models above this band, meaning absence of detectable bias should be interpreted as "not measurable" rather than "unbiased."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing position-bias measurements rely on single answer-order shuffles, which confound bias signals with content-level noise and sampling stochasticity. The field lacks a rigorous, statistically grounded method to detect and characterize position bias in multiple-choice LLM evaluations.

Method: The author introduces inspect_permute, an inspect_ai extension that runs exhaustive answer-order permutations per question and reports chi-squared/Cramér V signatures with bootstrap confidence intervals. It is applied across four models (gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5, gemini-2.5-flash, grok-3) on five MMLU subjects (24,000 API calls, temperature-0), with falsifier predictions pre-registered via SHA-256 hash.

Result: Position bias is detectable only within a ~60-95% base-accuracy Goldilocks zone. Below it, processing-load dominance overwhelms subject-specific signal; above it, ceiling effects compress variance below chi-squared test resolution. Two mechanism types identified: monotone A-to-D decrease (processing_load, low-tier models) and non-monotone D-drop (content_ambiguity, narrow capability band). Frontier models on MMLU fall above this detection band.

Conclusion: Standard MMLU places frontier-tier models above the detection band, so absence of position-bias signal should be interpreted as "not measurable" rather than "unbiased." Together with arXiv:2606.26185, this work brackets the detectable region of position-bias measurement and enables verifiable formulation of the field's central question.

Abstract: Position bias in multiple-choice LLM evaluation is widely cited as a confound in capability comparisons, but published measurements rely on single answer-order shuffles whose results confound the bias signal with content-level noise and sampling stochasticity. I introduce inspect_permute, an open-source extension to the inspect_ai evaluation framework that runs exhaustive answer-order permutations per question and reports the chi-squared / Cramer V signature of position bias with bootstrap confidence intervals. I apply the tool across four vendors (gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5, gemini-2.5-flash, grok-3) on five MMLU subjects, 24,000 API calls under temperature-0 generation, with falsifier predictions pre-registered via a public SHA-256 hash before half the data was observed. Position bias turns out to be statistically detectable only within a roughly 60-95% base-accuracy Goldilocks zone. Below it, processing-load dominance swamps subject-specific signal; above it, ceiling effects compress the variance below the chi-squared test resolution. Detectable cells separate into two mechanism types: monotone A-to-D decrease (processing_load, in low-tier models) and non-monotone D-drop (content_ambiguity, in a narrow capability band). Standard MMLU places every frontier-tier model above the detection band, so absence of signal there should be read as not measurable, not unbiased. Together with the ceiling-effect characterisation in arXiv:2606.26185, this work brackets the detectable region of position-bias measurement and makes the field central question askable in a verifiable form. Package, data, preregistration under MIT.

</details>


### [290] [TwistedMerge: Certified Higher-Order Diagnostics and Abstention for Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20887)
*Ting Gong,Shitan Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TwistedMerge is a certification pipeline for model merging that treats merging as a finite descent problem, using cycle consistency and cohomological tests to detect alignment obstructions, and abstains when certification fails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pairwise alignability between independently trained models does not guarantee globally consistent alignment, leading to hidden obstructions in model merging that naive averaging cannot detect.

Method: Formulates merging as a finite descent problem (checkpoints as local objects, alignment maps as transitions, cycle products as residuals); introduces TwistedMerge, a conservative certification pipeline with fixed-chart averaging, synchronization-removable gauge inconsistency, certified central obstruction, and nonabelian holonomy; applies four tests (inverse-consistency, coefficient-identification, centrality, closure) before promoting residuals to cohomology classes.

Result: Proves constant-edge no-go result, frozen-complex three-way and predeclared-family error-control theorems, and refinement test; removes planted neural alignment defect via cycle-consistent synchronization; recovers predicted non-coboundary and projective-rank behavior in controlled central systems; shows naive factor averaging is GLr-representation-dependent while global factor synchronization and dense-delta SVD are stable; finds no natural central or period-index class certified on natural checkpoint collections.

Conclusion: Cycle residuals do not predict merge degradation in natural settings; descent theory is positioned as a falsifiable certification and abstention framework for model merging.

Abstract: Model merging combines independently trained or fine-tuned models, but pairwise alignability does not imply globally consistent alignment. We formulate merging as a finite descent problem in which checkpoints are local objects, alignment maps are transitions, and cycle products are residuals. TwistedMerge is a conservative certification pipeline that separates fixed-chart averaging, synchronization-removable gauge inconsistency, a certified central obstruction on a specified comparison complex, and nonabelian holonomy. A residual is promoted to a cohomology class only after inverse-consistency, coefficient-identification, centrality, and closure tests; otherwise the method abstains and returns an ordinary or synchronized fallback. We prove a constant-edge no-go result, frozen-complex three-way and predeclared-family error-control theorems, and a refinement test for comparison-complex sensitivity. A planted neural alignment defect is removed by cycle-consistent synchronization, showing that a nonzero cycle score alone is not a higher obstruction. Controlled central systems recover the predicted non-coboundary and projective-rank behavior, while noisy estimates move from certification to abstention without false lifts on the tested controls. A trained low-rank-adapter audit shows that naive factor averaging depends on the chosen GLr representative, whereas global factor synchronization and dense-delta SVD are stable. On natural checkpoint collections, cycle residuals do not predict merge degradation and no natural central or period-index class is certified. The results position descent theory as a falsifiable certification and abstention framework.

</details>


### [291] [Information-Theoretically Secure Aggregation for Lightweight Federated Learning: Resilient to Dropouts and Adversaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20890)
*Hyeong-Gun Joo,Songnam Hong,Dong-Joon Shin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a lightweight, information-theoretically secure aggregation framework for sign-based federated learning that securely computes majority vote via single-round secure multiplication, achieving up to 99.5% reduction in online communication and 85.7% reduction in latency while providing robustness against dropouts and adversarial behaviors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sign-based FL methods (e.g., signSGD) reduce communication cost via one-bit gradients but are vulnerable to inference attacks, and existing secure aggregation schemes are incompatible or incur high overhead, motivating a need for a lightweight, secure aggregation framework tailored for sign-based FL.

Method: The framework uses (1) inverse-form exponent reduction to halve the effective majority vote polynomial degree, (2) single-round secure multiplication achieving linear offline complexity/storage with only single online communication, and (3) MDS-code-based decoding for robustness against dropouts and adversarial behaviors, all under honest-majority information-theoretic security.

Result: Online communication reduced by up to 99.5%, latency reduced by up to 85.7% compared to conventional approaches. Accuracy gains of up to 20.65% against dropouts and 10.74% against adversarial behaviors.

Conclusion: The proposed framework establishes a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, and information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based federated learning.

Abstract: On-device federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving and personalized model training on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and IoT nodes. To reduce communication cost, sign-based methods (e.g., signSGD) transmit one-bit gradients. However, exposing gradient signs makes them vulnerable to inference attacks, while existing secure aggregation schemes are often incompatible with such methods or incur significant computational and communication overhead. We propose a lightweight and information-theoretically secure aggregation framework tailored for sign-based FL. The framework securely computes the majority vote (MV) polynomial through single-round secure multiplication, ensuring end-to-end information-theoretic security under the honest-majority assumption while revealing only the final aggregated sign to the server. To enhance efficiency and scalability, we introduce two key techniques. First, inverse-form exponent reduction halves the effective MV polynomial degree, reducing both communication and computation costs. Second, we propose single-round secure multiplication, achieving linear offline complexity and storage with only a single online communication. Together, these techniques reduce online communication by up to 99.5% and latency by up to 85.7% compared to conventional approaches. Also, by leveraging inherent MDS-code-based decoding, the framework achieves robustness against both dropouts and adversarial behaviors, yielding accuracy gains of up to 20.65% and 10.74%, respectively. Overall, the proposed framework establishes a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, and information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based FL.

</details>


### [292] [HierarchicalDAEW: Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted Graph Convolution with Evidential Uncertainty for Multi-Section Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from H&E Histology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20896)
*Kritanu Chattopadhyay,Soumya Chatterjee,Ondrej Krejcar,Debotosh Bhattacharjee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HierarchicalDAEW is a dual-graph architecture for predicting spatially resolved gene expression from H&E histology, using domain-aware edge weighting and evidential uncertainty estimation, achieving state-of-the-art results across six human tissue sections.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spatial transcriptomics is costly and technically demanding, preventing routine clinical deployment. Current H&E-based prediction methods ignore tissue architecture and lack prediction trustworthiness quantification.

Method: Dual-graph architecture with (1) a spot-level graph using Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolution (Leiden clustering-based inter/intra/boundary domain edges) and (2) a gene-level graph fusing STRING-DB protein-protein interaction priors with tissue-specific co-expression via learned attention gating, plus evidential uncertainty estimation.

Result: Achieves strongest correlation with ground-truth expression across six human Visium sections and thirteen baselines, with gains holding under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls, plus better calibrated confidence intervals than Monte Carlo dropout.

Conclusion: Both domain-aware edge typing and hierarchical depth are necessary for improvement; calibrated uncertainty estimates enable identifying low-confidence predictions for pathologist review before clinical action.

Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics assays remain costly and technically demanding, restricting transcriptome-wide profiling to specialist settings and preventing routine clinical deployment. Predicting spatially resolved gene expression from H&E histology could close this gap, yet current methods largely ignore the underlying tissue architecture and rarely quantify how their predictions can be trusted. We introduce HierarchicalDAEW, a dual-graph architecture that addresses both gaps. On the spot graph, a Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolutional operator learns separate projections for inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges derived from Leiden clustering, allowing the model to treat tissue heterogeneity as an explicit structural signal rather than an implicit one. A second gene-level graph then fuses protein-protein interaction priors from STRING-DB with tissue-specific co-expression through learned attention gating, propagating predictions from a landmark gene set to a broader gene panel. Reliability is handled through evidential uncertainty estimation, which produces far better calibrated confidence intervals than Monte Carlo dropout under identical conditions. Across six human Visium sections spanning breast, colorectal, prostate, and cerebellar tissue, and against thirteen published baselines, HierarchicalDAEW achieves the strongest correlation with ground-truth expression, with gains that hold up under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls that rule out positional shortcuts. Ablations further confirm that both the domain-aware edge typing and the hierarchical depth are necessary to this improvement, and calibrated uncertainty estimates identify low-confidence predictions for pathologist review before clinical action.

</details>


### [293] [Multi-turn RL with Structural and Performance Aware Rewards for CUDA Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20908)
*Quazi Ishtiaque Mahmud,Nesreen K. Ahmed,Ali Jannesari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CudaPerf is a reinforcement learning framework that enhances LLM-based CUDA code generation by combining execution-based rewards with structural code-aware rewards (memory coalescing, occupancy, arithmetic intensity, synchronization patterns). It uses offline pairwise ranking and online RL training with iterative refinement, achieving up to 5x speedup and 17% correctness improvements over strong baselines like Qwen-3-32B and CUDA Agent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RLVR approaches for code generation rely only on outcome-based signals (correctness, speedup) and overlook performance-critical structural properties of programs, limiting their ability to generate optimized code.

Method: CudaPerf employs a two-stage reflective RL framework: (1) offline pairwise ranking module that learns to distinguish strong vs weak program candidates via contrastive comparisons, and (2) online RL training that jointly optimizes correctness, performance, and structural efficiency via a unified reward signal incorporating verifiable execution rewards and structural code-aware rewards (memory coalescing, occupancy, arithmetic intensity, synchronization patterns). It also uses iterative refinement with execution feedback.

Result: CudaPerf achieves up to 5x and 3.32x improvements in speedup, and 17% and 7% improvements in correctness on C to CUDA and PyTorch to CUDA transformations respectively, outperforming Qwen-3-32B and CUDA Agent baselines.

Conclusion: Incorporating structural code-aware rewards alongside execution-based signals significantly improves LLM-generated CUDA code quality in both correctness and performance.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful technique to enhance the reasoning capacity of LLMs for optimized code generation. However, existing RLVR approaches primarily rely on outcome-based signals such as correctness and speedup, overlooking performance-critical structural properties of programs that are essential for generating optimized code. In this work, we propose CudaPerf, a reflective RL framework that incorporates both verifiable execution rewards and structural code-aware rewards derived from parallelization features (e.g., memory coalescing, occupancy, Arithmatic Intensity, and synchronization patterns). CudaPerf operates in two stages: (1) an offline pairwise ranking module that learns to distinguish strong and weak program candidates via contrastive comparisons, and (2) an online RL training phase that jointly optimizes for correctness, performance, and structural efficiency through a unified reward signal. To further enhance learning, CudaPerf utilizes iterative refinement using execution feedback enabling progressive improvement of generated candidates. We also introduce a dataset comprising 2.9k C to CUDA and 1k PyTorch to CUDA programs, each paired with diverse input configurations and multiple CUDA implementations encompassing diverse optimization strategies. CudaPerf is evaluated across multiple benchmarks comprising both C to CUDA and PyTorch to CUDA transformations. Empirical findings suggest that CudaPerf significantly outperforms strong baselines, including Qwen-3-32B (for C to CUDA) and CUDA Agent (for PyTorch to CUDA) by achieving up to 5X & 3.32X improvements in speedup, and 17% & 7% improvements in correctness, respectively.

</details>


### [294] [Three-Pronged Spectral Control for Federated Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20914)
*Shiva Raj Pokhrel,Dipsan Bhattarai,Anwar Walid*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRISHUL is a spectral-control framework for federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning that uses shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases, nuclear norm proximal shrinkage, and concave water filling budget allocation to improve robustness under non-IID client heterogeneity, outperforming federated LoRA baselines across vision and language benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated PEFT (e.g., LoRA) suffers from fragile performance under non-IID client heterogeneity because clients learn spectrally misaligned update subspaces, leading to high-variance aggregation and poor global transfer.

Method: TRISHUL employs three key components: (1) shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases for algebraically exact aggregation of compact core updates, (2) nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress high-rank spectral components before upload, and (3) concave water filling budget rule for non-uniform allocation of adaptation heads across layers based on pretrained layer capacity.

Result: Across CIFAR-100, SVHN, 20 Newsgroups, MRQA, and GLUE with LLaMA3.2-1B, TRISHUL improves convergence, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines, with greater gains under stronger heterogeneity, while adding negligible computation and no extra per-round communication.

Conclusion: TRISHUL provides an effective spectral-control approach for robust federated PEFT under data heterogeneity, though it does not provide formal privacy guarantees itself.

Abstract: Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables communication-efficient adaptation of large pretrained models on decentralized edge data, but it remains fragile under non-IID client heterogeneity. In low-rank adaptation (LoRA), different clients may learn locally useful but spectrally misaligned update subspaces, causing high-variance aggregation and poor global transfer. We propose TRISHUL, a spectral-control framework for robust federated PEFT. TRISHUL follows the FL no-raw-data-sharing setting but does not itself provide formal privacy guarantees. TRISHUL uses shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases to obtain algebraically exact aggregation of compact core updates, applies nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress client-specific high-rank spectral components before upload, and allocates adaptation heads non-uniformly across layers using a concave water filling budget rule derived from pretrained layer capacity. Because shrinkage is performed only on small core matrices, TRISHUL adds negligible computation and no extra per-round communication over the underlying multi-head PEFT protocol. Across vision and language benchmarks, including CIFAR-100, SVHN, 20 Newsgroups, MRQA, and GLUE with LLaMA3.2-1B, TRISHUL improves convergence, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines, with greater gains under stronger heterogeneity.

</details>


### [295] [Best-of-Evidence: Best-of-N Selection under Partial Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20950)
*Cenwei Zhang,Teng Fang,Yuxia Wang,Derek Li,Bryan Dai,Lei You*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BoE extends BoN selection to vision-language tasks where only partial verification is possible, using signed factor graphs and evidence allocation to improve selection under limited verification budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BoN assumes reliable whole-response verification, which fails in vision-language tasks where only partial verification (e.g., checking specific findings, spans, values, regions, or relations) is possible. The same claim may also appear across candidates with opposing stances, creating contradictions.

Method: BoE keeps the candidate pool fixed, represents reusable claims via a signed candidate–factor graph, and allocates a limited budget to evidence actions that can influence the final selection. Includes a score-based controller where zero budget recovers standard BoN.

Result: Theoretically shows residual evidence capacity limits evidence-driven gains and that shared factor queries achieve O(log K) vs Θ(K) query separation. Experiments on four medical VQA settings show BoE improves fixed-pool selection and rescues some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant.

Conclusion: BoE is a principled framework for inference-time selection under partial verification. It improves upon BoN but faces limits from channel quality and candidate generation, preventing universal gains.

Abstract: BoN improves model outputs by sampling several candidates and selecting one with a proxy score, but it assumes that complete candidates can be evaluated reliably. Many vision-language tasks instead provide only partial verification: a finding, span, value, region, or relation may be checkable even when no dependable whole-response verifier exists. Moreover, the same claim may recur across candidates with opposing stances, allowing one observation to support part of the pool and contradict another. We introduce Best-of-Evidence (BoE), an inference-time selection framework that keeps the BoN candidate pool fixed, represents reusable claims with a signed candidate--factor graph, and allocates a limited budget to evidence actions that can change the final choice. BoE formalizes selection under partial verification and provides a practical score-based controller, with the zero-budget case recovering the underlying BoN decision. Theoretically, we show that residual evidence capacity limits any evidence-driven improvement and that shared factor queries can achieve an O(log K) versus Θ(K) query separation in a factor-code model. Common-ledger experiments on four medical VQA settings show that BoE can improve fixed-pool selection and rescue some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant, while also revealing the channel-quality and candidate-generation limits that prevent universal gains.

</details>


### [296] [The Weight of Silence: A Causal Case for Weights Over the Scratchpad in Latent Chess Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20952)
*Ishan S. Kshirsagar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper tests whether latent reasoning in language models functions as an active inference-time scratchpad after reinforcement learning (RL). Training a chess model through latent reasoning + RL, they find that RL improves legality (48%→61%) and eliminates checkmate confabulation, but causal interventions show the model does not rely on latent thought content—only exact-zero ablation causes collapse, and RL adds robustness to disruption rather than reliance on thoughts. This challenges the assumption that latent thoughts are actively consulted during inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing causal analyses of latent reasoning are confined to math/logic tasks and only compare reliance within a single checkpoint, never before vs. after RL. The field's default assumption is that latent thoughts function as an actively consulted inference-time scratchpad, but this has not been directly tested under RL.

Method: Train a chess-playing model through a staged latent-reasoning curriculum followed by RL. Run a six-condition causal intervention suite (substituting noise, adding matched noise, ablations, exact-zero ablation) on the same model before and after RL to measure reliance on latent thought vectors.

Result: Legality climbs from 48% (pre-RL) to 61% (post-RL); checkmate confabulation eliminated. Substituting/adding noise leaves performance unchanged; ablations cause mild degradation; only exact-zero vectors cause collapse. Under exact-zero corruption, legality drops to 1% (pre-RL) vs 9% (post-RL). RL adds robustness to disruption, not reliance on thought content.

Conclusion: Latent thoughts do not function as an actively consulted inference-time scratchpad under RL. The principal effect of latent reasoning is shaping model parameters during training, not serving as an active reasoning mechanism during inference.

Abstract: Latent, or silent, reasoning lets language models carry out intermediate computation in continuous vector space instead of words, and is widely assumed to function as an internal scratchpad the model actively consults during inference. Whether that assumption survives reinforcement learning has not been tested directly: existing causal analyses of latent reasoning are confined to math and logic tasks, and compare a model's reliance on its thoughts within a single checkpoint, never before and after an RL stage. We train a chess-playing model through a staged latent-reasoning curriculum followed by reinforcement learning, and find legality climbs monotonically to 61% (from a 48% pre-RL baseline) while checkmate confabulation is eliminated entirely. To locate this gain, we run a six-condition causal intervention suite on the same model before and after RL: substituting or adding matched noise to the latent thought vectors leaves performance unchanged, ablating them causes only mild degradation, and only exact-zero vectors cause collapse. This robustness gap is itself the finding: under exact-zero corruption, legality collapses to 1% pre-RL versus 9% post-RL, a gap that survives correction for testing across the full battery; milder conditions trend similarly without independently reaching significance. RL appears to add robustness to disruption, not reliance on thought content. These results push back against the field's default assumption that latent thoughts function as an actively consulted inference-time scratchpad, and instead indicate latent reasoning's principal effect here is shaping the model's parameters during training. We also demonstrate a working RL gain in chess, a domain outside the math and logic settings where multiple groups report the same latent-reasoning-plus-RL recipe failing to improve accuracy over SFT.

</details>


### [297] [ADABORD: a novel AdaBoost approach for ordinal classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21003)
*Rafael Ayllón-Gavilán,Francisco José Martínez-Estudillo,David Guijo-Rubio,César Hervás-Martínez,Pedro A. Gutiérrez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ADABORD is an AdaBoost-based framework for ordinal classification that incorporates ordinal information via an ordinal Gini splitting criterion in decision trees and the absolute ranked probability score as the error function, significantly outperforming seven state-of-the-art methods on the largest OC benchmark, especially on datasets with five or more classes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ordinal classification approaches often fail to fully leverage the ordinal structure of classes, treating the problem as nominal classification and thus losing performance potential.

Method: ADABORD extends AdaBoost by: (1) using decision trees with an ordinal Gini splitting criterion as base estimators; (2) employing the absolute ranked probability score (a measure accounting for both ordering and distance between classes) as the error function for updating sample weights and classifier weights in the ensemble.

Result: Extensive comparison against seven state-of-the-art methods on the TOC-UCO repository shows ADABORD significantly outperforms competing methods, particularly on datasets with five or more classes where ordinal structure is more pronounced. Statistical analysis supports the results.

Conclusion: ADABORD effectively leverages ordinal information through tailored base estimator and error function, achieving superior performance in ordinal classification. Code and protocols are publicly available for reproducibility.

Abstract: Ordinal Classification (OC) deals with classification tasks where the classes follow a natural order. Despite the progress in OC, many existing approaches fail to fully leverage the ordinal information, treating the problem as nominal classification and thereby losing performance potential. In this work, ADABORD, an AdaBoost framework specifically designed for ordinal classification problems, is introduced. The ordinal nature of the classes is incorporated into two key components of the well-known AdaBoost algorithm: 1) the base estimator, where decision trees with the ordinal Gini splitting criterion are proposed; 2) the error function used to update sample weights at each stage and the weights of the classifier in the final ensemble model, given by the absolute ranked probability score, a measure that accounts for both the ordering and the distance between classes. ADABORD is extensively compared against seven state-of-the-art methods on the TOC-UCO repository, the largest benchmark collection for OC to date. The experimental results, supported by statistical analysis, show that ADABORD significantly outperforms competing methods, particularly on datasets with five or more classes, where the ordinal structure becomes more pronounced. Source code, along with all experimental protocols, is publicly available to ensure reproducibility and facilitate future research in OC.

</details>


### [298] [Weight-norm Criticality: A Mechanism for Loss Spikes Induced by the Normalization and Weight Decay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21005)
*Xiaolong Li,Zhangchen Zhou,Zhi-Qin John Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies "weight-norm criticality" as an overlooked source of training instability in deep neural networks, caused by the interaction between normalization (scale-invariant components) and weight decay, which drives weight norms toward zero, increases loss landscape sharpness, and triggers loss spikes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing explanations of training instability focus primarily on learning-rate criticality (Edge of Stability), but fail to account for instability phenomena observed in practical deep network training, particularly loss spikes caused by weight decay interacting with normalization.

Method: The authors theoretically analyze the interaction between weight decay and scale-invariant components (from normalization), showing that increasing weight decay drives scale-invariant weight norms to zero, which increases loss landscape sharpness and destabilizes training. They derive testable predictions from this weight-norm criticality framework.

Result: The paper demonstrates that excessive weight decay pushes scale-invariant weight norms past a critical boundary, causing abrupt loss spikes. The proposed weight-norm criticality mechanism is empirically validated in networks with scale-invariant components.

Conclusion: Weight-norm criticality offers a new mechanistic understanding of loss spikes and explains why weight penalties improve generalization but cannot be made arbitrarily strong, as excessive decay destabilizes training.

Abstract: Most explanations of training instability focus on \emph{learning-rate criticality}, typically characterized by the Edge of Stability, beyond which optimization becomes unstable. We argue that, in practical deep neural network training, there is an additional and often overlooked \emph{weight-norm criticality}. This criticality is induced by the interaction between normalization (which introduces scale-invariant components) and weight decay (which persistently shrinks parameter norms). As the weight decay coefficient increases, the norms of scale-invariant weights are progressively driven toward zero. Meanwhile, the sharpness of the loss landscape increases rapidly, destabilizing the optimization dynamics and resulting in abrupt loss spikes. This perspective provides a rationale for why weight penalties can improve generalization yet cannot be made arbitrarily strong: excessive decay drives scale-invariant weight norms past a critical boundary and destabilizes training. Our work provides a new mechanistic understanding of loss spikes through the lens of \emph{weight-norm criticality}. Moreover, \emph{weight-norm criticality} yields testable predictions that we validate empirically in networks with scale-invariant components, providing empirical support for the proposed mechanism.

</details>


### [299] [Regularized Optimization on Grassmann Manifold: Theory, Algorithm and Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21039)
*Zhuan Liang,Zheng Zhai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a Regularized Projection Matrix Approximation (RPMA) framework for robust estimation of rank-K projection matrices, formulated as an optimization problem on the Grassmann manifold, with theoretical analysis of optimality and stability, and efficient Riemannian optimization algorithms, showing improved performance over spectral methods for community detection and clustering under noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spectral methods for community detection, clustering, and graph learning are widely used but their performance degrades substantially in the presence of noise, outliers, or model perturbations due to inaccurate spectral subspace estimation.

Method: Proposes RPMA, which extends classical spectral projection with a regularization term, formulated as an optimization problem on the Grassmann manifold of rank-K projection matrices. Derives first/second-order optimality conditions, analyzes local stability of regularized eigenspace and critical-point landscape. Develops a Riemannian gradient projection algorithm with backtracking line search and a more efficient Cayley-SMW gradient method avoiding repeated eigendecompositions.

Result: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that RPMA substantially improves recovery accuracy of projection matrices and consistently outperforms conventional spectral projection methods for community detection and clustering under noisy environments.

Conclusion: The regularized projection framework provides more robust, sparse, and interpretable subspace estimates, with theoretical guarantees and efficient algorithms, making it a superior alternative to classical spectral methods in noisy settings.

Abstract: Spectral methods are among the most widely used techniques for community detection, clustering, and graph learning. Their performance, however, critically depends on the accurate estimation of the underlying spectral subspace and can deteriorate substantially in the presence of noise, outliers, or model perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose a Regularized Projection Matrix Approximation (RPMA) framework for robust estimation of rank-$K$ projection matrices. RPMA extends classical spectral projection by incorporating a regularization term, producing projection estimates that are more robust, sparse, and interpretable. We formulate the proposed model as an optimization problem on the manifold of rank-$K$ projection matrices and exploit its geometric equivalence to the Grassmann manifold. Based on this manifold characterization, we derive the first- and second-order optimality conditions, establish the local stability of the regularized leading eigenspace, and characterize the stability of the critical-point landscape under sufficiently small regularization. To efficiently solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a Riemannian gradient projection algorithm with backtracking line search, together with a more efficient Cayley--Sherman--Morrison--Woodbury (Cayley--SMW) gradient method that avoids repeated eigendecompositions. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that RPMA substantially improves the recovery accuracy of projection matrices and consistently outperforms conventional spectral projection methods for community detection and clustering under noisy environments.

</details>


### [300] [Counterfactual Explainability Framework With CycleGAN And Counterfactual-Classifier Alignnment Score for Retinal Disease Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21068)
*Kritanu Chattopadhyay,Sayanjit Singha Roy,Soumya Chatterjee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CounterFundus is a CycleGAN-driven counterfactual explainability framework for retinal disease detection that generates disease-to-normal fundus image translations, providing clinically meaningful explanations via difference maps, and introduces CCAS to quantify spatial alignment between counterfactual explanations and classifier saliency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explainability of deep learning models for retinal disease detection remains a major bottleneck for clinical adoption, particularly when model decisions are not linked to clinically meaningful retinal regions.

Method: CounterFundus integrates EfficientNet-B5-based retinal disease detection with CycleGAN-driven counterfactual image translation. For each pathological image, it generates a healthy counterpart via the generator, producing difference maps to localize disease-associated changes. CCAS (Spearman correlation, binary IoU, pointing accuracy) quantifies spatial agreement between counterfactual maps and classifier saliency.

Result: EigenCAM-aligned evaluation shows counterfactual explanations spatially consistent with classifier-relevant retinal evidence across all CCAS dimensions. Ablation studies confirm CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation improves downstream classification performance.

Conclusion: CounterFundus establishes a clinically-grounded, explainable AI framework for retinal disease detection, addressing the explainability bottleneck by providing visually plausible counterfactual explanations that align with clinically meaningful regions.

Abstract: Automated detection of vision impairing retina-based ocular conditions from fundus images is important for early screening, timely referral and reducing dependency on specialist-only assessment, for which neural network-based deep learning (DL) models have been widely utilized. However, explainability of the DL frameworks remains a major bottleneck for clinical adoption, particularly when model decisions are not linked to retinal regions that are clinically meaningful. To address this issue, this study presents CounterFundus, a novel CycleGAN-driven counterfactual explainability framework, integrating EfficientNet-B5-based retinal disease detection with visually interpretable disease-to-normal fundus image translation. For each pathological image, the counterfactual yielded by the CycleGAN generator represents an estimated healthy counterpart and the resultant difference map is utilized to localize disease-associated retinal changes. Unlike conventional post-hoc saliency methods, CounterFundus provides counterfactual explanations through visually plausible disease-to-normal retinal translation. Thereafter, to quantify the spatial agreement between counterfactual difference maps and classifier saliency, the Counterfactual-Classifier Alignment Score (CCAS) is introduced, embedding Spearman correlation, binary IoU and pointing accuracy into a single assessment protocol. To this end, EigenCAM-aligned evaluation demonstrates that the generated counterfactual explanations remain spatially consistent with classifier-relevant retinal evidence across all CCAS dimensions. Along with that, ablation studies further confirm that CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation improves the downstream classification performance in fundus images, establishing CounterFundus as a clinically-grounded, explainable artificially intelligence (XAI) framework for retinal disease detection.

</details>


### [301] [From Evaluation to Optimisation: Hierarchy-Aware Training Signals for CWE Prediction in Python](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21069)
*Muntasir Adnan,Manile Srun,Carlos C. N. Kuhn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper validates that the ALPHA penalty, originally designed for evaluation, can also serve as an effective training signal. Supervised fine-tuning and dual-head classification regress below zero-shot baselines under distribution shift, while GRPO with a dense reward succeeds, achieving 27.9% penalty reduction and statistical parity with a 4.5x larger teacher model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To validate whether the taxonomy-aware ALPHA penalty, previously used only for evaluation, can effectively serve as a training signal for CWE-level vulnerability prediction in Python.

Method: Compared three delivery mechanisms: supervised fine-tuning, dual-head classification loss, and reinforcement learning (GRPO) with a dense reward derived from the normalized ALPHA penalty. Evaluated on the Security Hardening and Adversarial Testing (SVEN) dataset using Qwen2.5-Coder-7B.

Result: Supervised approaches regressed below the zero-shot baseline under distribution shift. GRPO reduced cumulative ALPHA penalty by 27.9% (greedy decoding) and 25.5% (sampled decoding, p=0.005), achieving statistical parity with a 4.5x larger zero-shot teacher model.

Conclusion: The value of a hierarchical penalty as a training signal depends largely on the directness of its delivery; direct reward-based methods (GRPO) outperform indirect supervised approaches.

Abstract: The original ALPHA benchmark introduced a taxonomy-aware penalty for evaluating CWE-level vulnerability prediction in Python and proposed that the penalty could theoretically also serve as a training signal. This paper provides that validation. We compare three delivery mechanisms: supervised fine-tuning, a dual-head classification loss, and reinforcement learning with a dense reward derived from the normalised penalty. We find that supervised approaches consistently regress below the zero-shot baseline under distribution shift, while GRPO succeeds. Our best policy reduces the cumulative ALPHA penalty of Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on Security Hardening and Adversarial Testing (SVEN) dataset by 27.9% under greedy decoding, and by 25.5% under sampled decoding(p = 0.005, Welch's t-test), reaching statistical parity with its 4.5x larger zero-shot teacher. We conclude that the value of a hierarchical penalty as a training signal depends largely on the directness of its delivery.

</details>


### [302] [Spectral Transformation for Layer-wise Global Rank Discovery in Federated LoRA for Vision Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21074)
*Hariharan Ramesh,Jyotikrishna Dass*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SpecTraL stacks client LoRA modules, applies orthonormal Householder Transformation in low-rank space to avoid dense reconstruction, and uses Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory to discover optimal global ranks without hyperparameter tuning, achieving better accuracy-communication trade-offs in federated ViT fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LoRA aggregation strategies in federated learning suffer from cross-term aggregation error (independent averaging of LoRA factors), increased download cost (heterogeneous rank concatenation), reinitialization lag and unstable convergence (merging into pretrained weights), or high server-side overhead (dense reconstruction or auxiliary models). The paper aims to resolve these fundamental limitations.

Method: SpecTraL stacks local LoRA modules from clients, performs orthonormal Householder Transformation directly in the low-rank latent space to eliminate dense reconstruction. It uses Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory to analytically separate global consensus signal from non-IID noise for optimal layer-wise global rank discovery. A padding-aware initialization framework lets clients incorporate residual LoRA dimensions without re-merging them into the pretrained base model.

Result: Experiments on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 over DomainNet and NICO++ demonstrate improved accuracy-communication trade-offs, reduced server computation, and elimination of hyperparameter search for rank selection.

Conclusion: SpecTraL provides a unified, mathematically consistent solution for LoRA aggregation in federated learning, addressing key limitations of prior approaches while achieving better performance and efficiency.

Abstract: Fine-tuning Vision Transformers (ViTs) with low-rank adapters (LoRA) promises better communication efficiency under federated setup, yet existing aggregation strategies face fundamental limitations. Independently averaging these LoRA factors is mathematically inconsistent, introducing cross-term aggregation error. In contrast, approaches that preserve heterogeneous client ranks by concatenating local adapters on the server substantially increase download cost and often require merging global LoRA updates into pretrained weights on the clients, causing reinitialization lag and unstable convergence. Other approaches further increase server-side overhead by reconstructing dense weight updates or training auxiliary models to refine aggregation error. In this work, we propose SpecTraL, spectral transformation for layer-wise global rank discovery, that resolves these challenges within a unified design. SpecTraL stacks local LoRA modules from clients and performs orthonormal Householder Transformation of the stacked adapters directly in the low-rank latent space, eliminating dense reconstruction of the global update and any auxiliary refinement on the server. By leveraging the Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory, SpecTraL analytically separates the global consensus signal from non-IID noise, discovering optimal layer-wise global ranks without manual hyperparameter tuning. To match local ranks in subsequent rounds, we introduce a padding-aware initialization framework that lets clients incorporate residual LoRA dimensions without re-merging them into the pre-trained base model. Experiments on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 over DomainNet and NICO++ demonstrate improved accuracy-communication trade-offs, reduced server computation, and elimination of hyperparameter search for rank selection. Our code is available at https://github.com/DASS-Lab-Group/SpecTraL

</details>


### [303] [Nipping the Butterfly Effect in the Bud: Self-Output Fine-Tuning for Autoregressive Weather Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21080)
*Yun-Ye Cai,Hsuan-Tien Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies that error growth in autoregressive DLWP is caused by a feedback loop between output errors and input distribution shifts, and proposes SOFT (Self-Output Fine-Tuning) to calibrate biased input distributions, achieving state-of-the-art long-horizon weather forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon weather forecasting using autoregressive DLWP suffers from rapidly growing prediction errors, and the underlying mechanisms of this error growth were not well understood.

Method: The paper provides theoretical and empirical analysis showing error growth stems from a feedback loop between output errors and input distribution shifts. They propose SOFT, a plug-and-play strategy that uses the model's own one-step predictions to fine-tune and calibrate the biased input distribution encountered at the first autoregressive step.

Result: SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon forecasting tasks, substantially reducing both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy, despite its simplicity.

Conclusion: The success of SOFT highlights the importance of reexamining the fundamental DLWP pipeline and represents a critical pipeline advance for atmospheric science.

Abstract: Long-horizon weather forecasting is a fundamental challenge in atmospheric science, for which autoregressive Deep Learning Weather Prediction (DLWP) has emerged as the primary paradigm. Although the autoregressive pipeline is highly scalable and flexible, its prediction errors grow rapidly over long forecasting horizons. In this work, we study this error growth phenomenon from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Our analysis reveals that the growth is driven by a feedback loop between output errors and input distribution shifts. Specifically, the autoregressive process amplifies small initial output errors, which progressively corrupt subsequent input distributions, echoing the butterfly effect in atmospheric science and ultimately deteriorating forecasting accuracy over longer horizons. Furthermore, we show that this distributional shift originates at the earliest stage of inference, with out-of-distribution signatures detectable as early as the first autoregressive step. To mitigate this issue, we propose \textbf{Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT)}, a plug-and-play strategy that leverages the model's own one-step predictions to calibrate the biased input distribution encountered at the first step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, despite its simplicity, SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon forecasting tasks and substantially reduces both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy. The success of SOFT highlights the importance of reexamining the fundamental pipeline of deep learning weather prediction, representing a critical pipeline advance for atmospheric science.

</details>


### [304] [CASC: Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering for Multivariate Spatiotemporal Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21088)
*Francis Ndikum Nji,Vandana Janeja,Jianwu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CASC is a novel deep subspace clustering framework that integrates U-Net adversarial clustering, FAConvLSTM, graph attention transformers, and two new loss functions (causal subspace preservation and dynamic temporal subspace evolution) to discover evolving causal-temporal regimes in multivariate spatiotemporal data, moving beyond correlation-driven static subspace clustering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep subspace clustering methods rely on geometric self-expressiveness, assume static subspace structures, and fail to capture causal dependencies, local spatial interactions, and long-range temporal dynamics in complex spatiotemporal systems like sea ice monitoring, disease spread, and neurodegeneration tracking.

Method: CASC combines a U-Net-inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers for spatiotemporal representation learning, a graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network for modeling local/global/long-range dependencies, and two novel objectives: Causal Subspace Preservation Loss (aligning self-expression with causal relationships) and Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss (capturing evolving subspaces and regime transitions).

Result: The framework transforms deep subspace clustering from a correlation-driven paradigm into a causal-temporal regime discovery framework, enabling the discovery of evolving latent regimes in high-dimensional spatiotemporal data.

Conclusion: CASC addresses key limitations of static geometric self-expressiveness by introducing causal and temporal evolution awareness into subspace clustering, making it suitable for nonstationary spatiotemporal environments.
