Abstract: Deep subspace clustering plays a critical role in applications involving multivariate spatiotemporal data, such as sea ice monitoring, disease spread analysis, and tracking neuro-degeneration over time. Despite recent advances, existing methods primarily rely on geometric self-expressiveness, assume static subspace structures, and often fail to capture causal dependencies, local spatial interactions, and long-range temporal dynamics inherent in complex spatiotemporal systems. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering (CASC) framework for discovering evolving latent regimes in high-dimensional spatiotemporal data. CASC integrates a U-Net-inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers to preserve spatial and temporal structure while learning robust latent representations. A graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network is introduced to jointly model local spatial relationships, global dependencies, and long-range temporal interactions. Furthermore, we propose two new learning objectives: (1) a Causal Subspace Preservation Loss that aligns self-expression coefficients with latent causal relationships, encouraging clusters to reflect underlying causal processes rather than simple feature similarity, and (2) a Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss that captures evolving subspace structures and temporal regime transitions in nonstationary environments. Together, these components transform deep subspace clustering from a correlation-driven paradigm into a causal-temporal regime discovery framework.

</details>


### [305] [Training Large Language Models for Self-Explanation Faithfulness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21090)
*Yeoktatt Cheah,María Pérez-Ortiz,Noah Y. Siegel,Oana-Maria Camburu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes using Reinforcement Learning to directly optimize the faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by converting faithfulness metrics (Phi-CCT) into an RL reward. Fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B show significant improvements in faithfulness (up to 0.664 in-distribution, 0.691 out-of-distribution) on tasks involving random-word and user-bias insertions, with some cross-intervention generalization observed, while ruling out reward gaming.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods evaluate faithfulness or use inference-time prompting to improve self-explanations, but lack a mechanism to directly optimize model parameters for generating faithful self-explanations. This paper bridges that gap.

Method: The authors modify existing faithfulness metrics (Phi-CCT) into an RL training objective with per-sample rewards. They experiment with two intervention types: random-word insertions and user-bias insertions. They fine-tune Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B using RL to optimize faithfulness directly.

Result: In-distribution Phi-CCT scores rose from near-zero to 0.664; out-of-distribution scores reached 0.691 on held-out tasks (e.g., StrategyQA). Cross-intervention generalization showed weak but interesting transfer (e.g., Llama3.1-8B trained on random-word insertions generalized to user-bias phrases). Reward gaming behaviors were ruled out via analysis.

Conclusion: Models can be trained to implicitly identify influential factors and disclose them, offering a scalable path toward reducing unfaithful reasoning in LLMs.

Abstract: We propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) method to directly optimize the faithfulness of self-explanations - the extent to which a model's generated reasoning accurately reflects its internal decision-making process. While existing work focuses on evaluating faithfulness or using inference-time prompting frameworks to improve an LLM's self-explanation's tractability, these approaches do not provide a mechanism to directly optimize a model's parameters to generate faithful self-explanations. We bridge this gap by modifying existing faithfulness metrics into an RL training objective. We investigate (1) if models can be trained to accurately detect factors that affect their decisions, and (2) whether RL can directly optimize for the disclosure of these factors thereby improving LLM self-explanations' faithfulness. We experiment with two intervention types: random-word insertions and user-bias insertions, using a per-sample reward derived from the Phi-CCT correlation metric. RL fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B show substantial improvements on the Phi-CCT faithfulness metric, with in-distribution scores rising from near-zero to as high as 0.664, and out-of-distribution scores reaching up to 0.691 on held-out tasks such as StrategyQA. Cross-intervention generalization is weaker but more interesting: a priori we would not expect a model trained only on random word insertions to generalize to user-bias phrases, yet Llama3.1-8B shows non-zero transfer in this direction. The reverse direction and Qwen3-8B do not replicate this, indicating model-dependent and setup-dependent effects we cannot yet explain. Lastly we analyze model behavior to rule out reward gaming behaviors that often plague RL training. Ultimately, we show that models can be trained to implicitly identify influential factors and disclose them, offering a scalable path toward reducing unfaithful reasoning in LLMs.

</details>


### [306] [A Polynomial Architecture-Attribution Co-Design Framework for Exact Aumann-Shapley Attribution in GNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21094)
*Bizu Feng,Zhimu Yang,Shuming Wang,Shaode Yu,Yuan Cheng,Xiaojun Qian,Zixin Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: APEX is a model-attribution co-design framework using Polynomial GIN (PolyGIN) to make Aumann-Shapley attributions for GNNs exactly computable via Gauss-Legendre quadrature, reducing evaluation cost while maintaining high attribution fidelity and predictive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Path-integral attribution methods (e.g., Integrated Gradients) for GNNs rely on finite-sample numerical approximations, requiring a trade-off between quadrature error and computational cost. This work aims to make the attribution integral exactly computable to eliminate this trade-off.

Method: The authors propose APEX, a co-design framework combining (1) PolyGIN—a GIN-style polynomial GNN where message-passing, normalization, and transformation preserve bounded multivariate polynomial forms for scalar scores; and (2) Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 2^{L-1} deterministic evaluation points to exactly evaluate the Aumann-Shapley path integral, thanks to bounded degree (≤ 2^L-1) derivatives.

Result: PolyGIN maintains competitive predictive performance on synthetic and real-world graph benchmarks. APEX achieves higher attribution fidelity than baselines and substantially reduces the number of path integral evaluations required.

Conclusion: Model-attribution co-design enables exact, efficient computation of Aumann-Shapley attributions for GNNs at both feature and node levels while preserving completeness.

Abstract: We study feature-level and node-level explanations for graph neural networks (GNNs) through the lens of Aumann-Shapley attribution. Path-integral methods such as Integrated Gradients provide an axiomatic formulation of attribution, but their practical use in deep GNNs typically relies on finite-sample numerical approximations to the path integral, requiring a trade-off between quadrature error and computational cost. This paper proposes APEX, a model-attribution co-design framework that makes the attribution integral exactly computable under a polynomial GNN architecture. The key component is PolyGIN, a GIN-style graph network whose message-passing, normalization, and transformation operations preserve a bounded multivariate polynomial form for scalar model scores, such as pre-softmax logits. We show that, for a PolyGIN with $L$ polynomial transformation blocks, the derivative along the attribution path has degree at most $2^L-1$. Therefore, Gauss--Legendre quadrature can evaluate the Aumann--Shapley path integral exactly, up to floating-point precision, with $2^{L-1}$ deterministic evaluation points. The resulting attributions can be computed at the feature level and then aggregated into node-level scores while preserving completeness. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graph benchmarks show that PolyGIN maintains competitive predictive performance, while the complete APEX framework achieves higher attribution fidelity than the compared baselines and substantially reduces the number of evaluations required for path integration.

</details>


### [307] [Smooth Neural Point Processes via B-Splines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21098)
*Michele Bellomo,Riccardo Ramaschi,Alberto Dolara,Tomaso Aste*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a neural temporal point process model that directly parametrizes the conditional intensity function using B-spline basis functions with neural-network-predicted coefficients, enabling exact NLL evaluation, flexible architectures, parallel training, and smoothness regularization, achieving better efficiency and accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural TPP models that allow exact NLL evaluation either model the compensator instead of the CIF, impose architectural constraints, or are computationally expensive due to sequential evaluation. The goal is to develop a model that directly parametrizes the CIF with exact NLL, full architectural flexibility, parallel training, and built-in smoothness regularization.

Method: The CIF is parametrized as a non-negative linear combination of B-spline basis functions, where the coefficients are predicted by a neural network. This allows exact evaluation of the NLL without numerical integration, supports parallel computation during training, and enables smoothness regularization via the integrated squared second derivative of the CIF.

Result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to reference neural TPP baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed B-spline-based neural TPP model offers a computationally efficient and accurate alternative to existing neural TPPs, with the advantages of exact NLL, architectural flexibility, parallelization, and smoothness regularization.

Abstract: Temporal point processes (TPPs) provide a general and flexible framework for modeling sequences of events in continuous time. Neural networks have been successfully employed to model TPPs in a highly expressive and data-driven way. Neural TPPs are typically trained via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL), which depends on both the conditional intensity function (CIF) and its integral over time, the compensator. Recent neural TPP approaches enable exact evaluation of the NLL without numerical integration. However, these methods typically model the compensator rather than the CIF directly, impose constraints on the neural network architecture, and are computationally expensive during training, as event contributions to the NLL are evaluated sequentially rather than in parallel. In this work, we propose a novel neural TPP model that directly parametrizes the CIF as a non-negative combination of B-spline basis functions, whose coefficients are predicted by a neural network. This formulation enables exact evaluation of the NLL, preserves full flexibility in the neural architecture, allows efficient parallelization during training, and naturally supports CIF smoothness regularization through the integrated squared second derivative. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to the reference neural TPP baseline.

</details>


### [308] [TOUR: A Trajectory-Level Unlearning Benchmark for Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21111)
*Chaofan Pan,Lingfei Ren,Xiangyu Jiang,Yanhua Li,Xuemei Cao,Xiangkun Wang,Hao Yu,Wei Wei,Xin Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TOUR is a benchmark for evaluating trajectory-level unlearning in offline RL, showing that common deletion baselines have environment-dependent privacy-utility behavior and that single-score auditing is insufficient for reliable conclusions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline RL agents trained on fixed trajectories need trajectory-level deletion when selected data must be removed after training, but evaluating such deletion is difficult because lower membership scores can reflect removal, residual memorization, or policy collapse.

Method: TOUR combines trajectory-level partitioning, matched non-member controls, retraining references, retained-performance anchors, and multi-attack privacy auditing across D4RL locomotion and AntMaze tasks.

Result: Common deletion baselines show environment-dependent privacy-utility behavior; retraining and fine-tuning often provide stronger retained-utility references than uniform GA+Refit; TrajDeleter is useful but not uniformly stronger; single likelihood-based membership scores can overstate deletion quality.

Conclusion: Conclusions about offline RL unlearning are not stable under single-score auditing; they depend on matched non-member construction, retraining-relative calibration, attack family, retained utility, and diagnostic scope.

Abstract: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents are trained on fixed behavioral trajectories, which makes trajectory-level deletion important when selected data must be removed after training. Evaluating such deletion is difficult because a lower membership score can reflect trajectory removal, residual memorization visible to another attack, or policy collapse that destroys useful behavior. We introduce Trajectory-level memOrization and Unlearning in offline RL (TOUR), a benchmark that combines trajectory-level partitioning, matched non-member controls, retraining references, retained-performance anchors, and multi-attack privacy auditing. Across D4RL locomotion experiments and an exploratory AntMaze extension, TOUR shows that common deletion baselines have environment-dependent privacy-utility behavior. Retraining and fine-tuning often provide stronger retained-utility references than uniform GA+Refit, while TrajDeleter remains a useful comparator but is not uniformly stronger under the same audit. Reference-model, threshold, deviation, equivalence, action-error, representation-based, and query-limited attacks further show that a single likelihood-based membership score can overstate deletion quality. In the evaluated settings, conclusions about offline RL unlearning are therefore not stable under single-score auditing. They depend on matched non-member construction, retraining-relative calibration, attack family, retained utility, and explicit scope for diagnostic architecture or component-level evidence.

</details>


### [309] [GlucoTune: A Unified Framework for Blood Glucose Preprocessing, Forecasting, and Benchmarking in Diabetes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21117)
*Davide Marelli,Giorgia Rigamonti,Mirko Paolo Barbato,Paolo Napoletano*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GlucoTune is a standardized, extensible framework for reproducible preprocessing, training, and evaluation of blood glucose time-series models, featuring configurable YAML pipelines, unified dataset wrappers, and a benchmarking leaderboard to address reproducibility and data-sharing challenges in type 1 diabetes research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Blood glucose preprocessing lacks standardized workflows and evaluation protocols, hindering reproducibility and fair comparison; privacy and licensing restrictions further prevent sharing of preprocessed datasets.

Method: GlucoTune provides configurable YAML-based preprocessing pipelines, unified interfaces for dataset integration and model implementation, a curated collection of forecasting methods, and a benchmarking leaderboard for systematic comparison.

Result: Demonstrated effectiveness through comprehensive experiments and validated usability via a user study.

Conclusion: GlucoTune enables reproducible, comparable, and extensible experimentation in blood glucose forecasting while circumventing data-sharing restrictions.

Abstract: Preprocessing blood glucose time-series data is a critical yet often overlooked step in developing data-driven methods for diabetes management, particularly for type 1 diabetes. The lack of standardized preprocessing workflows and evaluation protocols hinders reproducibility and complicates fair comparison across studies. These challenges are further exacerbated by data-sharing restrictions, as privacy and licensing constraints often prevent the redistribution of preprocessed medical datasets. To address these limitations, we present GlucoTune, a comprehensive and extensible framework for reproducible experimentation with blood glucose time-series data. The framework standardizes the entire experimental workflow, from preprocessing to model evaluation, enabling reproducible experiments directly from the original datasets. Reproducible preprocessing is achieved through configurable pipelines defined in portable YAML configuration files, ensuring consistent data handling without distributing sensitive preprocessed data. Beyond preprocessing, GlucoTune provides a unified interface for implementing, training, and evaluating blood glucose prediction models. The framework integrates public datasets through standardized wrappers and provides a curated collection of state-of-the-art blood glucose prediction and general time-series forecasting methods, while remaining readily extensible to additional datasets, preprocessing strategies, and forecasting models. To promote transparent and consistent evaluation, GlucoTune includes a benchmarking leaderboard that reports results across datasets, preprocessing configurations, and forecasting methods, enabling systematic comparison of experimental settings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GlucoTune through comprehensive experiments and assess its usability in a user study.

</details>


### [310] [Relative Value Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21120)
*Marc Höftmann,Jan Robine,Stefan Harmeling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Relative Value Learning (RV), a framework that directly learns value differences between state pairs via an antisymmetric function, replacing traditional absolute value estimation. It introduces a pairwise Bellman operator with contraction properties, derives multi-step targets and a policy-gradient estimator (R-GAE), and shows competitive performance with PPO on Atari benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard reinforcement learning critics estimate absolute state values V(s), but only value differences matter for control. This mismatch motivates directly learning relative values instead of absolute ones.

Method: The method uses an antisymmetric function Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j) to learn value differences. It defines a pairwise Bellman operator (proven as γ-contraction), develops 1-step, n-step, and λ-return targets, and derives a generalized advantage estimation variant (R-GAE) for unbiased policy gradients.

Result: Competitive performance on the Atari benchmark (49 ALE games) when integrated with PPO, compared to standard PPO with absolute critics.

Conclusion: Relative value estimation is an effective alternative to absolute critics in reinforcement learning, both theoretically grounded and empirically competitive.

Abstract: In reinforcement learning, critics typically estimate absolute state values $V(s)$, estimating how good a particular situation is in isolation. However, it turns out that only differences in value are relevant for control. Motivated by this, we propose Relative Value Learning (RV), a framework that learns value differences directly via an antisymmetric function $Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j)$. We introduce a pairwise Bellman operator and prove it is a $γ$-contraction with a unique fixed point equal to the true value differences, derive well-posed $1$-step, $n$-step and $λ$-return targets and reconstruct generalized advantage estimation from pairwise differences to obtain an unbiased policy-gradient estimator (R-GAE). Beyond theoretical results, we integrate RV with PPO and achieve competitive performance on the Atari benchmark (49 ALE games) compared to standard PPO, indicating that relative value estimation is an effective alternative to absolute critics.

</details>


### [311] [Demographically-Informed Heat-Mortality Risk Curves via Risk Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21131)
*Alex O. Davies,Eunice Lo,Rui Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RGNNs integrate census features with DLNMs via hierarchical GNNs to improve heat-related mortality risk prediction, achieving better calibration than baselines during extreme heat events.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DLNMs ignore demographic and geographic context despite its well-established relevance to heat vulnerability.

Method: Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs) — a hierarchical GNN encoder that uses granular census features to optimise DLNM coefficient vectors, preserving interpretable risk curve outputs.

Result: RGNN variants maintain lower point-errors and near-nominal uncertainty coverage during the 2022 heatwave where baselines collapse, evaluated across 10 regions of England and Wales on two unprecedented heat years.

Conclusion: RGNNs improve predictive calibration while preserving interpretable risk curve outputs from DLNMs.

Abstract: Estimating heat-related mortality risk is a core task in environmental epidemiology, typically addressed with Distributed Lag Non-linear Models (DLNMs); interpretable exposure-response surfaces fitted to temperature-mortality time series. DLNMs are effective but ignore demographic and geographic context, despite well-established relevance to heat vulnerability. We propose Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs), a hierarchical GNN encoder that uses granular census features to optimise DLNM coefficient vectors, preserving interpretable risk curve outputs while substantially improving predictive calibration. Evaluated across 10 regions of England and Wales on two unprecedented heat years, RGNN variants maintain both lower point-errors and near-nominal uncertainty coverage during the 2022 heatwave where baselines collapse.

</details>


### [312] [Agree on the Model, Verify the Inference: GKR Protocols for HND-Based Transformer Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21162)
*Xiaolong Liang,Juanjuan Li,Rui Qin,Yisheng Lv*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GKR-HND is a protocol that verifies Transformer inference by combining GKR-based polynomial verification with registered-model techniques, delegating expensive public computations to a worker while keeping a lightweight retained verifier that checks proofs and signed responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Outsourced Transformer inference faces security risks like model substitution and incomplete execution, while naive replay defeats the purpose of delegation by requiring full recomputation.

Method: The protocol uses GKR (Goldwasser-Kalai-Rothblum) transcripts for polynomial backbone verification, registered-weight openings, and delegates public evaluations to an assigned worker. The retained verifier checks the GKR proof path and verifies signed, request-bound responses from the worker under non-collusion assumptions.

Result: Experiments with pretrained HND (Homomorphic-Nonhomomorphic Decomposition) Transformers validate the proof path and delegated public computation without needing dense-matrix replay.

Conclusion: GKR-HND enables efficient and verifiable outsourced Transformer inference by avoiding full recomputation while maintaining integrity guarantees under honest-verifier and non-collusion assumptions.

Abstract: Outsourced Transformer inference exposes clients to model substitution and incomplete execution, while direct replay removes the computational benefit of delegation. We present GKR-HND, a registered-model protocol for verifying the polynomial backbone of Homomorphic--Nonhomomorphic Decomposition Transformers. The retained verifier checks the GKR transcript and registered-weight openings, but delegates expensive public evaluations to an assigned computation worker. Assuming an honest retained verifier and prover--worker non-collusion, the verifier accepts only when the worker's signed, request-bound response agrees with the proof claims. Experiments with pretrained HND models validate the proof path and the delegated public computation without dense-matrix replay.

</details>


### [313] [Automated Synthesis and Adversarial Validation of Executable Causal Research Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21173)
*Irena Girshovitz,Dan Zeltzer,Ran Gilad-Bachrach*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ARA (AI-based Epidemiology Research Assistant) is a framework that makes silent causal failures visible by integrating protocol construction, synthetic data generation via SCMs, and adversarial validation. While it didn't consistently improve numerical accuracy over standard LLM methods, it changed failure modes from silently returning incorrect causal estimates to surfacing protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, or downgraded interpretations—suggesting validity-first systems should be evaluated by their ability to flag unwarranted causal claims, not just answer accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated research systems silently fail when analysis code runs successfully but relies on invalid causal assumptions. The authors aim to make these failures visible by explicitly encoding causal design principles, assumptions, and constraints.

Method: ARA constructs structured causal protocols from natural language, generates synthetic data via Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with known ground-truth effects, and performs adversarial validation under controlled violations of identification assumptions.

Result: On the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark, ARA did not consistently improve numerical agreement compared to standard LLM-based generation. However, it changed the failure mode: instead of silently returning invalid causal estimates, it surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or downgraded non-causal interpretations.

Conclusion: Validity-first automated science systems should be evaluated not only by answer accuracy but also by whether they indicate when causal claims are unwarranted.

Abstract: While automated research systems promise to accelerate empirical analysis, they are prone to silent failures: instances in which analysis code executes successfully yet relies on invalid causal assumptions. We present the Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Epidemiology Research Assistant (ARA), a framework that makes these failures visible by explicitly encoding causal design principles, study-specific assumptions, and methodological constraints. ARA integrates protocol construction, synthetic data generation, and adversarial validation into a unified pipeline. The framework translates natural language research questions into structured causal protocols and executable analysis code by first constructing a protocol and then generating synthetic datasets using Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with known ground-truth effects. This synthetic-data step can also support pipeline development when access to confidential data, such as medical data, is restricted. The generated analysis is then evaluated under controlled violations of identification assumptions. We evaluate ARA on the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark, assessing recovery of identification strategies, causal quantities, treatment and outcome variables, and consistency between generated code and approved protocol. Protocol construction and adversarial validation did not consistently improve numerical agreement with benchmark estimates compared with standard LLM-based generation. However, they changed the failure mode: instead of silently returning causal estimates, ARA often surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or downgraded non-causal interpretations. These findings suggest that validity-first automated science systems should be evaluated not only by answer accuracy, but also by whether they indicate when causal claims are unwarranted.

</details>


### [314] [Filter Learning for Subgraphs: Algebras and Performance Risk Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21263)
*Purui Zhang,Feng Ji,Yanan Zhao,Bihan Wen,Wee Peng Tay*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a subgraph filter learning (SFL) framework using distance-aware Laplacian constructions to approximate spectral graph filters from partial observations, with theoretical risk bounds and empirical outperformance over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph signal processing tasks relying on spectral information require complete graph topology, which is often unavailable in practice.

Method: A systematic SFL framework with subgraph-supported operators, a subgraph filter algebra based on distance-aware Laplacian constructions, and least-squares risk bounds.

Result: The proposed algebraic models consistently outperform polynomial filters, distribution-agnostic operators, and direct numerical filter learning baselines on real-world datasets.

Conclusion: Structured subgraph filter algebra provides effective approximation of ambient graph filters under partial observations with theoretical guarantees.

Abstract: Graph signal processing tasks that leverage spectral information typically assume access to the complete graph topology, which is often unavailable in practice. We propose a systematic framework for subgraph filter learning (SFL), where subgraph-supported operators approximate ambient graph filters under partial observations. We formulate SFL as a statistical learning problem in which optimal subgraph operators are inherently data-dependent. To address the difficulty of directly estimating such operators, we develop a subgraph filter algebra based on distance-aware Laplacian constructions, defining a structured and controllable class of filters for effective approximation. We further establish performance risk bounds under the least squares loss, quantifying how well the learned operator approximates the restricted ambient mapping. Experiments real-world datasets show that, for SFL tasks, the proposed algebraic models consistently outperform polynomial filters, distribution-agnostic operators, and direct numerical filter learning baselines that attempt to recover the underlying structure from data.

</details>


### [315] [The Dark Room in the Reward Channel: Dense Prediction Rewards Collapse GRPO-Trained LLM Agents -- and What Actually Works](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21273)
*Yu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GRPO-based prediction rewards cause a "dark room" pathology in LLM agents, where the policy collapses by maximizing prediction accuracy at the cost of task success. The root cause is z-score normalization amplifying dense signals in all-fail groups, resulting in unbounded optimization pressure. The damage is specific to the reward channel, while auxiliary-loss channels remain beneficial.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense per-step supervision via prediction rewards is proposed as a remedy for sparse-reward, long-horizon LLM agent tasks, aiming to induce better memory and exploration.

Method: The authors apply potential-based prediction rewards under GRPO across Qwen3 models (1.7B/4B/8B) on ALFWorld. They conduct single-factor ablations (removing std normalization), propose a theoretical account based on z-scored advantage invariance in all-fail groups, perform preregistered predictions, and compare reward channel vs. auxiliary-loss channel delivery with a shuffled-gold placebo control.

Result: Prediction rewards under GRPO consistently collapse to a degenerate state (prediction accuracy → 1.0, task success → 0, episode length pinned at horizon). Removing std normalization recovers baseline performance. The reward channel is neutral while the auxiliary-loss channel gains ~20 points; shuffled-gold matches true-gold, indicating correct labels are unnecessary.

Conclusion: Z-scoring amplifies dense signals' within-group variance when all-fail groups dominate, causing collapse. Signals whose variance decays with mastery are structurally safe. The reward channel is not the right delivery mechanism for dense prediction signals; auxiliary losses are superior.

Abstract: Dense per-step supervision is an appealing remedy for sparse-reward, long-horizon LLM agents: reward the agent for predicting its next observation, and memory should follow. We show that under group-normalized RL (GRPO), this recipe does not merely fail -- it destroys the policy. Across Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B on ALFWorld, a potential-based prediction reward drives every run into a degenerate absorbing state (prediction accuracy -> 1.0, task success -> 0,episode length pinned at the horizon): the "dark room" pathology, built automatically by the optimizer. A single-factor ablation localizes the cause -- removing only GRPO's std normalization turns the same reward from catastrophic (0%) into baseline parity -- and a two-line proposition explains why: in all-fail groups the z-scored advantage is invariant to the shaping coefficient, so bounded rewards become unbounded pressure and annealing cannot help. Our central insight generalizes this: what z-scoring amplifies is a dense signal's within-group variance while all-fail groups dominate, so signals whose variance decays by mastery are structurally amplifier-safe.This variance-profile criterion retrodicts our collapses, carries preregistered predictions for arms that had not yet run, and is consistent with published reward-channel successes (a compatibility check, not an independent test). Finally, a controlled signal-delivery matrix (identical signal, varying only the consumption mechanism) shows the reward channel is at best neutral while the auxiliary-loss channel gains ~20 points -- and a shuffled-gold placebo matches the true-gold arm, so the gap survives without correct labels. Endpoints are single-seed; seed replication and group-size controls are preregistered and in progress.

</details>


### [316] [Multi-Task Learning for Heterogeneous Prediction from Video Game State with Transfer Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21290)
*Jonas Peché,Aliaksei Tsishurou,Alexander Zap,Günter Wallner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether multi-task learning (MTL) on video game telemetry data from team-based multiplayer games can improve generalization and reduce computational cost compared to single-task models. Using a multimodal architecture with rasterized vision, global context, and per-unit features, experiments on World of Tanks data evaluate MTL performance across loss weighting, gradient conflicts, pre-training/fine-tuning, and cross-map transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore whether multi-task learning can leverage multiple related supervision signals from game telemetry to improve generalization while reducing training and inference costs compared to specialized single-task models in team-based multiplayer games.

Method: A multimodal architecture adapting endpoint prediction to a general multi-task setting, combining rasterized vision inputs, global match context, and per-unit state information via an image encoder and attention-based interaction modeling. Experiments include comparing single-task vs. multi-task training, evaluating mixed loss weighting strategies and conflicting gradient handling, pre-training/fine-tuning under limited target data, and testing cross-map transfer under structured environment shift.

Result: Multi-task training improves generalization and reduces cost relative to single-task models; different loss weighting strategies and gradient conflict mitigation affect performance; pre-training/fine-tuning benefits limited-data regimes; and within-game transfer across maps shows structured environment shift impacts.

Conclusion: Multi-task learning is effective for video game prediction tasks, offering generalization improvements and efficiency gains. The study provides practical insights into handling multi-task optimization challenges and transfer scenarios in game analytics.

Abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) is a promising approach for prediction tasks derived from video game state data, as modern game telemetry provides multiple related supervision signals from the same structured observations. We study whether a shared model trained jointly across tasks in team-based multiplayer games can improve generalization while reducing training and inference cost compared to specialized single-task models. We adapt a multimodal architecture for endpoint prediction to a general multi-task setting that combines rasterized vision inputs, global match context, and per-unit state information through an image encoder and attention-based interaction modeling. Experiments on a large proprietary World of Tanks dataset compare single-task and multi-task training, evaluate weighting strategies for mixed losses and conflicting gradients, and test pre-training/fine-tuning under limited target-data regimes. We also examine within-game transfer across game maps under structured environment shift.

</details>


### [317] [AI Assistants Overassist](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21306)
*Verona Teo,Raghav Jain,Tobias Gerstenberg,Max Kleiman-Weiner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Int-Bench is a simulation-based benchmark evaluating how LLMs intervene as tutors during problem-solving. Compared to humans, LLMs intervene more frequently, earlier, and tend to provide full solutions rather than hints, prioritizing short-term task success over fostering deep learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how AI systems navigate intervention decisions during problem-solving, since the benefits of AI-assisted learning depend on when and how help is provided, yet this remains poorly understood.

Method: Int-Bench simulates a student solving problems while a teacher LLM monitors reasoning and decides whether, when, and how to intervene. Evaluated across code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers, comparing LLM teachers to human teachers on intervention frequency, timing, and impact on immediate success and generalization.

Result: LLMs intervene more frequently and earlier than humans, and tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints, unlike human teachers.

Conclusion: Current LLM assistants optimize for short-term success rather than supporting reasoning processes needed for deeper learning and long-term success.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as tutors and thought partners, helping users reason through problems. While guidance from AI assistants can scaffold thinking and foster learning, such benefits depend on how they help--for instance, intervening too early or too frequently may hinder true learning and cognitive engagement. Yet how AI systems navigate intervention decisions during problem-solving remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark for evaluating LLM interventions during learning. Int-Bench simulates a "student" solving a problem while a "teacher" monitors the student's reasoning and decides whether, when, and how to intervene. Across three domains--code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers--we evaluate LLM teachers on the frequency and timing of interventions, as well as their impact on both immediate task success and generalization to new problems. We also compare LLMs to humans, finding that LLMs intervene more frequently and earlier than humans. Moreover, in contrast to humans, they tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints. These findings suggest that current LLM assistants often optimize for short-term success rather than supporting the reasoning processes needed for deeper learning and long-term success.

</details>


### [318] [M$^3$-Gen: Interpretable Multimodal Generation of Gene Expression Profiles Using Clinical and Imaging Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21343)
*Francesca Pia Panaccione,Carlo Sgaravatti,Marco Venere*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: M$^3$-Gen is a GAN-based framework that generates gene expression profiles conditioned on histopathology images and clinical metadata, using contrastive learning and attention mechanisms to provide explainable multimodal integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gene expression data acquisition is limited by high costs and privacy concerns, hindering multimodal research and AI applications in biomedicine. The authors aim to generate realistic gene expression profiles from more readily available modalities (histopathology images and clinical metadata) to overcome these barriers.

Method: M$^3$-Gen uses a Generative Adversarial Network conditioned on histopathology images and clinical metadata. It learns a unified latent representation via contrastive learning, then uses attention-based mechanisms to guide generation of biologically coherent gene expression profiles while providing intrinsic explainability of which image regions influence specific gene expressions.

Result: Evaluations on TCGA dataset show M$^3$-Gen generates realistic and functionally meaningful gene expression data. The attention-based integration provides interpretability by identifying histopathology image regions that most strongly influence generated gene expression profiles.

Conclusion: M$^3$-Gen effectively addresses data scarcity in gene expression profiling by generating biologically coherent expression data from histopathology and clinical data, with built-in explainability that enhances model transparency for biomedical applications.

Abstract: Integrating heterogeneous biomedical data, including clinical metadata, histopathology images, and molecular profiles, is crucial for comprehensive disease understanding. However, gene expression data acquisition remains constrained by high costs and privacy concerns, limiting its use in multimodal research and AI-driven applications. We present MultiModal Molecular Generation (M$^3$-Gen), a novel framework for the generation of gene expression profiles by conditioning a Generative Adversarial Network on histopathology images and clinical metadata. M$^3$-Gen learns a unified latent representation from the clinical variables and the images, leveraging contrastive learning, and exploits the embeddings of the two modalities to guide a generative model in producing biologically coherent gene expression profiles. Evaluations on the TCGA dataset demonstrate that M$^3$-Gen generates realistic and functionally meaningful gene expression data. Importantly, by integrating multiple modalities in an attention-based mechanism, M$^3$-Gen provides intrinsic explainability: it allows the identification of which regions of the histopathology images most strongly influenced the generation of specific gene expression profiles, making the model's decisions interpretable by design.

</details>


### [319] [How Many Bits Can an Adapter Write? Measuring the Capacity and Memorization of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21351)
*Kaizhen Tan,Heqing Du,Yang Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LoRA adapters store fewer bits per parameter than full fine-tuning, with capacity depending more on where parameters are placed (MLP > attention) than their count, and this bit-based measure predicts privacy leakage better than parameter count, while also cleanly distinguishing supervised fine-tuning (which memorizes secrets) from reinforcement learning (which does not).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To challenge the common assumption that LoRA adapters are "skills" rather than compressed records of training data, and to quantify how much information they actually encode into a frozen base model.

Method: Extends compression-based memorization analysis to the frozen-base setting, directly measuring memorization in bits for low-rank adapters. Applies this to analyze parameter placement (attention vs. MLP), structural reliance (ablating frozen base structure), and practical fine-tuning scenarios (supervised vs. reinforcement learning on Qwen2.5).

Result: Adapters store a couple of bits per trainable parameter (well below full model budget). Capacity depends more on location than count: MLP parameters hold nearly twice as much as attention. Stripping frozen base structure eliminates capacity. Privacy leakage correlates with bits written, not parameter count. SFT memorizes secrets verbatim; RL with verifiable rewards does not.

Conclusion: Measuring what fine-tuning writes (in bits) turns the folklore of adapters as skills into a quantifiable, design-able property, enabling principled defenses against memorization and privacy leakage.

Abstract: A LoRA adapter is a few megabytes that almost everyone treats as a skill rather than a record of the data behind it. We put that assumption on a scale. Extending compression-based memorization analysis to the frozen-base setting, we measure directly, in bits, how much a low-rank adapter writes into a model it never changes. The answer is both smaller than full fine-tuning and less lawful than parameter counting would predict. Adapters store a couple of bits per trainable parameter, well short of a full model's budget, but that figure turns less on how many parameters an adapter carries than on where they sit. Move the same parameter budget from attention into the MLP and it holds nearly twice as much; strip the frozen base of its structure and the capacity all but disappears. Applied to realistic fine-tunes of Qwen2.5, the same instrument shows privacy leakage rising with the bits an adapter writes rather than the parameters it nominally has, and it draws a clean line between supervised and reinforcement learning: the secrets that supervised fine-tuning copies down verbatim, an adapter trained on verifiable rewards never records. Measuring what fine-tuning writes, rather than attacking it after the fact, turns a piece of folklore into a quantity one can design against.

</details>


### [320] [Gradient Concentration, Not Weight Saliency, Explains Representation-Level Class Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21353)
*Billel Habbati,Alessio Merlo,Luca Verderame,Meriem Guerar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Saliency-based weight masking in machine unlearning (SalUn) does not meaningfully contribute to representation-level forgetting; the observed effects are instead driven by gradient concentration in final layers and representation geometry, as saliency masks are statistically equivalent to random masks of equal sparsity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether saliency-based weight selection in machine unlearning methods like SalUn actually contributes to representation-level forgetting, as this assumption remains unvalidated despite widespread adoption.

Method: Controlled ablation of SalUn's saliency masking mechanism using matched-compute experimental design on CIFAR-10/100 with ResNet-18, comparing saliency-based masks, random masks of equal sparsity, and unconstrained updates under fixed objective, optimization, and budget. Evaluated via linear probing, prototype recovery, and layer-wise CKA.

Result: All three masking strategies show statistically equivalent representation-level recoverability. Forget gradients concentrate ~92% of squared gradient energy in final layers. Saliency masks exhibit low class specificity (specificity index 0.09-0.11) with highly overlapping parameter subsets across different forget classes.

Conclusion: Representation-level forgetting is governed by gradient concentration and representation geometry, not by the specific identity of saliency-selected weights. Effective unlearning likely requires objectives that directly act on latent representations rather than sophisticated weight-selection strategies.

Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data while preserving model utility. Many state-of-the-art approaches pursue this goal by restricting the forgetting update to a subset of parameters selected through gradient-based saliency. Although such methods are widely adopted, the actual contribution of saliency-based weight selection to representation-level forgetting remains unclear. In this work, we perform the first controlled ablation of the saliency masking mechanism used by SalUn. Using a matched-compute experimental design on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, we compare saliency-based masking against random masks of equal sparsity and unconstrained updates, while keeping the unlearning objective, optimization schedule, and computational budget fixed. Across multiple representation-level evaluations, including linear probing, prototype recovery, and layer-wise CKA, the three configurations exhibit statistically equivalent representation-level recoverability. We find that forget gradients are strongly concentrated in the final network layers (approximately 92% of the squared gradient energy on CIFAR-10) before any mask is applied, causing all masking strategies to operate within the same representational subspace. Furthermore, saliency masks show limited class specificity (specificity index 0.09-0.11), selecting highly overlapping parameter subsets across different forget classes. Our findings suggest that, in the studied setting, representation-level forgetting is primarily governed by gradient concentration and representation geometry rather than by the specific identity of saliency-selected weights. More broadly, the results support a growing body of evidence indicating that effective representation-level unlearning requires objectives that act directly on latent representations rather than on increasingly sophisticated weight-selection strategies.

</details>


### [321] [Emergent Misalignment Recruits a Pre-existing Persona Subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21356)
*Mohammed Suhail B Nadaf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Narrow fine-tuning causes broad emergent misalignment because it recruits a pre-existing low-rank persona subspace in the model; projecting out this subspace prevents misalignment, while injecting it induces misalignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why fine-tuning a language model on a narrow stream of bad advice generalizes to cause broad misalignment on unrelated questions (emergent misalignment).

Method: Extracted per-domain persona subspaces from a frozen instruction-tuned model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) via contrastive teacher forcing; analyzed subspace properties (low-rank core, overlap with style); tracked misalignment margin evolution during fine-tuning; performed intervention (projection/ injection) and weight editing experiments.

Result: Found a shared low-rank core across 4 unrelated domains (657x stronger than random-subspace null, 82% outside a style core). First optimizer step on insecure code climbs broad-misalignment margin more than educational framing. Projecting the subspace prevents misalignment (27.7%→0.0%); injecting it induces misalignment up to 45.4%. Weight-gradient projection is inert; post-hoc weight edits suppress but don't remove the disposition. Spreading bad data across 4 domains produces more misalignment than superposition+diversity account for.

Conclusion: Emergent misalignment arises from a pre-existing, multi-domain persona subspace that is recruited during narrow fine-tuning. The structure's provenance remains open as it is extracted from an aligned checkpoint.

Abstract: Fine-tuning an aligned language model on a narrow stream of bad advice can make it broadly misaligned on questions unrelated to the training data, a phenomenon called emergent misalignment. We ask why the narrow lesson generalizes at all, and we find that narrow fine-tuning recruits a persona structure that is present in the model before the fine-tune exists. From a frozen instruction-tuned model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) we extract per-domain persona subspaces by contrastive teacher forcing and find that 4 unrelated domains share one low-rank core at 657x a random-subspace null, with 82% of that core lying outside a style core built at matched diversity. The literal first optimizer step of fine-tuning on insecure code climbs a broad-misalignment margin harder than the same code framed as educational, and forecasts realized margin movement out to 375 steps. Projecting the subspace out of the residual stream throughout fine-tuning prevents broad misalignment (27.7% to 0.0% of judged generations) while a matched-rank random subspace changes nothing; injecting it into the never-fine-tuned model induces misalignment that grows with dose to 45.4%, past the fine-tuned model it is measured against. The same projection applied to the weight gradient is inert, and three post-hoc weight edits leave the disposition in place: the sharpest edit suppresses the behavior rather than removing it, and the ablated structure re-forms inside the subspace the edit cleared. Spreading a fixed budget of bad data across 4 domains produces more broad misalignment than mechanical weight superposition and matched diversity jointly account for. All measurements come from one model at 14B; the extraction is from an aligned instruction-tuned checkpoint, which leaves the structure's provenance open; and the intervention that prevents misalignment also abolishes the narrow trained behavior.

</details>


### [322] [Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366)
*Hossein Mobahi,Peter L. Bartlett*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HOPE is a mathematical framework that reframes neural network compression as low-rank projection in a Hilbert space of continuous functions, enabling data-free, hyperparameter-free pruning and neuron merging across heterogeneous layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep neural networks encode complex internal representations that are difficult to deconstruct. Network compression offers a promising lens to analyze these representations, but standard compression heuristics suffer from scale symmetries and architectural biases that obscure meaningful analysis.

Method: HOPE shifts compression from the discrete domain into a Hilbert space of continuous functions, modeling individual neurons as rank-1 Hilbert-Schmidt operators. This unifies pruning and neuron merging as low-rank subspace projection, and introduces macro block eviction to handle multi-layer structures like residual pathways under a single unified metric.

Result: HOPE enables unbiased architectural decisions across layers of different types and sizes, is data-free and hyperparameter-free, and demonstrates practical potential through proof-of-concept experiments in model compression and fine-tuning.

Conclusion: HOPE provides a principled, unified mathematical framework for deconstructing trained network weights, overcoming the biases of standard compression heuristics and enabling unbiased cross-layer architectural analysis.

Abstract: Deep neural networks encode complex representations, but deconstructing this internal knowledge remains a challenge. Given the link between learning and compression, network compression offers a promising lens to analyze this knowledge. However, standard compression heuristics often suffer from scale symmetries and architectural biases. To resolve these, we introduce Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE), a mathematical framework to gradually deconstruct the representations in trained network weights.
  HOPE shifts network compression from the discrete domain into a Hilbert space of continuous functions. By modeling individual neurons as rank-1 Hilbert-Schmidt operators, HOPE unifies pruning and neuron merging as low-rank subspace projection. Extending this formulation, HOPE introduces macro block eviction to encompass multi-layer structures like entire residual pathways under the same unified metric. This unified approach enables unbiased architectural decisions across layers with different types and sizes. HOPE is a data-free and hyperparameter-free framework. We present proof-of-concept experiments in model compression and fine-tuning to highlight the practical potential of our theory.

</details>


### [323] [Mean-to-Score Discrete Diffusion: Posterior-Mean Denoisers for Score Entropy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21372)
*Jingyuan Li,Xiaoyi Jiang,Yixuan Jiang,Wei Liu,Yi Zhu,Zuoqiang Shi,Pipi Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion (SEDD) has a realizability issue where score ratios may not correspond to any valid posterior, causing negative weights. Projecting scores onto the bridge polytope fixes this. The proposed M2S method predicts posterior means and converts to scores via a linear map, outperforming baselines on CIFAR-10 and OpenWebText.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SEDD's positivity constraint on score ratios ensures nonnegative jump rates but does not guarantee Bayes realizability—score ratios at a noisy state may not be jointly induced by any valid clean-token posterior. This causes violations (negative weights, incompatible scores) that degrade generative performance.

Method: Introduces M2S (mean-to-score): predict a clean-token posterior mean, then convert it to the score via an exact kernel-dependent linear map. For uniform corruption, this maps the simplex onto the bridge polytope; for absorbing-mask corruption, recovers MD4. Also applies projection of raw scores onto the bridge polytope to remove violations.

Result: Projection removes all negative weights and improves PPL from 203.6 to 175.1. In 28.4M CIFAR-10, M2S lowers BPD from 3.173 to 3.129 and FID-50k. 170M OpenWebText M2S reaches PPL 143.3 at 128 steps vs 183.6 for the best pure-uniform baseline.

Conclusion: Enforcing the bridge polytope constraint (via projection or M2S) is crucial for discrete diffusion performance. M2S provides a principled, general way to guarantee realizability for any CTMC with mild support conditions, yielding consistent improvements across architectures and datasets.

Abstract: Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion (SEDD) parameterizes discrete reverse processes with unconstrained positive score ratios. While positivity guarantees nonnegative reverse jump rates, it does not ensure Bayes realizability: ratios at a noisy state need not be jointly induced by any clean-token posterior under the forward kernel. The score-entropy loss has the correct population optimum but does not enforce this constraint away from it. In a trained pure-uniform SEDD checkpoint, roughly one quarter of complete score vectors violate the coordinate box, while more than half lie inside it yet remain materially incompatible with any valid posterior. Such violations can produce negative pre-normalization weights in finite-step sampling. Projecting raw scores onto the bridge polytope removes all observed negative weights and improves external generative PPL from $203.6$ to $175.1$ without changing the sampler. We introduce \emph{mean-to-score} (M2S), which predicts a clean-token posterior mean and converts it to the score through an exact kernel-dependent linear map. The construction applies to any known coordinate-wise continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) satisfying a mild support condition. For uniform corruption, it maps the probability simplex onto the bridge polytope; for absorbing-mask corruption, the resulting objective recovers MD4 exactly. In a controlled 28.4M-parameter CIFAR-10 comparison, M2S lowers test BPD from $3.173$ to $3.129$ and FID-50k from $\CifarSEDDFID$ to $\CifarMtwoSFID$. A 170M-parameter M2S model trained on about 262B OpenWebText token slots outperforms the evaluated pure-uniform SEDD, GIDD, and Neural CTMC checkpoints at every tested sampling budget, reaching generative PPL $143.3$ at 128 steps versus $183.6$ for the strongest pure-uniform baseline.

</details>


### [324] [A Diffusion-Model Subpopulation Digital Twin for Mobile Health Deployment: A Case Study on the HeartSteps Intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21403)
*Ziping Xu,Yuyi Chang,Chenshun Ni,Nithin Sugavanam,Asim H. Gazi,Pedja Klasnja,Emre Ertin,Susan A. Murphy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes "JITAI-Twins," digital twins of target subpopulations built using conditional time-series diffusion models, to simulate and compare candidate online algorithms before deploying just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs). The method involves three-stage updating (pre-training, fine-tuning, inference-time calibration) and is validated across HeartSteps v2-v4, showing better temporal and between-participant structure reproduction than simpler simulators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Poorly designed online learning algorithms in mobile-health interventions can burden and disengage participants. New algorithm design decisions need to be vetted against realistic simulated users before real-life deployment to avoid these negative outcomes.

Method: A conditional time-series diffusion model that is temporally consistent (future actions do not affect past). The model undergoes three-step updating: (1) pre-training on large observational data, (2) fine-tuning on small prior intervention deployments in related populations, and (3) inference-time calibration to the next target population using domain-scientist expertise.

Result: Validated on HeartSteps v2-v4 (physical-activity suggestion interventions), the proposed method reproduces the target subpopulation's temporal and between-participant structure better than simpler simulators.

Conclusion: The JITAI-Twins can simulate a target deployment before it runs, providing a prerequisite for testing and informing online algorithm design decisions in JITAIs.

Abstract: Mobile-health interventions increasingly use online learning and decision making algorithms to personalize when to nudge users toward healthier behavior, but a poorly designed algorithm can burden and disengage participants. New algorithm design decisions should therefore be vetted against realistic simulated users before each real-life deployment. We propose a method to develop ``JITAI-Twins'': digital twins of a target subpopulation for comparing candidate online algorithms before a just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI) deployment. The method builds on a conditional time-series diffusion model that is temporally consistent (future actions do not affect the generated past), and it supports repeated updating from three sources of information, in three steps: pre-training on a large observational dataset, fine-tuning on small prior intervention deployments in related populations, and inference-time calibration to the next target population from domain-scientist expertise. We validate the twin at each pre-deployment stage of the long-running HeartSteps series (v2 through v4) of physical-activity suggestion intervention deployments, treating each successive deployment as an upcoming study. The proposed method reproduces the target subpopulation's temporal and between-participant structure better than simpler simulators. These results suggest that our twin can be used to simulate a target deployment before it runs, the prerequisite for testing and informing online algorithm design decisions.

</details>


### [325] [Semantic-Aware Task Clustering for Constructive and Cooperative Multi-Tasking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21426)
*Ahmad Halimi Razlighi,Maximilian H. V. Tillmann,Edgar Beck,Bho Matthiesen,Armin Dekorsy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a semantic-aware task clustering method for cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) that groups semantically aligned tasks to avoid destructive cooperation and negative transfer, using hierarchical density-based spatial clustering followed by intra-cluster end-to-end training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cooperative multi-tasking in semantic communication can be either constructive or destructive depending on task semantic relationships. The authors aim to ensure constructive cooperation by grouping semantically aligned tasks together.

Method: A sequential two-stage optimization: (i) semantic clustering using hierarchical density-based spatial clustering after a short initial training phase, and (ii) intra-cluster end-to-end joint training within discovered groups.

Result: The proposed framework effectively mitigates destructive cooperation and negative transfer, achieving accuracy gains over unclustered multi-tasking and individual training baselines.

Conclusion: Semantic-aware task clustering is an effective approach to ensure constructive cooperation in CMT-SemCom systems by grouping semantically aligned tasks before joint training.

Abstract: Cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) improves task execution performance by leveraging shared representations. However, as we demonstrated in [1], cooperative multi-tasking can be either constructive or destructive, depending on the semantic relationships among tasks. To ensure constructive cooperation, we propose a semantic-aware task clustering method for CMT-SemCom. We have formulated a sequential multi-stage optimization problem in which semantically aligned tasks are clustered once after a short initial training phase, and then end-to-end (E2E) joint training is conducted exclusively within the discovered groups. Specifically, the problem decomposes into two stages: (i) a semantic clustering problem leveraging hierarchical density-based spatial clustering, and (ii) an intra-cluster E2E CMT-SemCom learning problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates destructive cooperation and negative transfer, yielding accuracy gains compared to unclustered multi-tasking and individual training baselines.

</details>


### [326] [KroQuant: Kronecker-Structured Block Transforms for Efficient Post-Training Quantization of Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21446)
*Yann Bouquet,Alireza Khodamoradi,Kristof Denolf,Mathieu Salzmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KroQuant introduces a Kronecker-structured invertible transform for post-training quantization of diffusion transformers to W4A4, achieving better quality and faster inference than prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard W4A4 PTQ of DiTs suffers from activation outliers that 4-bit formats cannot represent. Existing invertible transform solutions face a trade-off between quantization accuracy and online inference cost (per-channel scaling is cheap but less accurate; fixed Hadamard transforms require large costly block sizes; learned full-d transforms need expensive dense GEMMs).

Method: KroQuant applies a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element block of activations, storing fewer than half the parameters of per-channel scaling. It runs as small tensor-core GEMMs for efficiency. Offline LoRaQ weight calibration then absorbs residual per-weight quantization error.

Result: On MI350 GPU, the KroQuant quantizer kernel is up to 14% faster than SmoothQuant kernel. On PixArt-Σ, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant produces outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI, while preserving or improving image quality.

Conclusion: KroQuant demonstrates that a learned Kronecker-structured transform effectively bridges the accuracy-efficiency gap in DiT quantization, outperforming prior methods in both speed and output quality at W4A4.

Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) of diffusion transformers (DiTs) to W4A4 severely degrades output quality, because activations entering each linear layer contain outliers that 4-bit formats cannot represent. The standard fix applies an invertible linear transform to the activations and its inverse to the weights before quantizing both. Normalization layers between blocks force this transform to run online at every denoising step, making its inference computation cost the binding design constraint. Existing options trade quantization quality for inference cost: per-channel scaling (SmoothQuant) is computationally cheap but impacts the magnitude of the channels, which can harm quantization accuracy; fixed Hadamard transforms yield better quantization accuracy but require large block sizes that incur a high online cost; learned full-$d$ invertible transforms calibrate best but entail a prohibitive dense $d \times d$ matrix multiplication (GEMM) per layer per step.
  We propose KroQuant, a PTQ method that applies a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element block of the activation, storing less than half the parameters of per-channel scaling. The block-local structure runs as small tensor-core GEMMs, and on an MI350 GPU the KroQuant quantizer kernel is up to $14\%$ faster than the SmoothQuant kernel. Offline LoRaQ weight calibration then absorbs the residual per-weight quantization error. On PixArt-$Σ$, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant produces outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI, while preserving or improving image quality.

</details>


### [327] [Context-weighted Discrete Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21427)
*Daniil Cherniavskii,Daniel Severo,Karen Ullrich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes context-aware modifications to discrete flow matching—a context-weighted sampler and a scaled cross-entropy loss—that leverage local context information to improve generation quality and reduce perplexity by up to 63% on OpenWebText with minimal computational overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard factorized training objective in discrete flow matching exposes the model to targets of varying difficulty, mixing well-conditioned tokens with ambiguous, high-entropy ones. The authors empirically observe that token uncertainty correlates with available context density, motivating context-aware improvements.

Method: The authors propose (1) a context-weighted sampler that modifies the underlying continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) to incorporate local context information, and (2) a scaled cross-entropy loss function that reweights training signals from different tokens based on their context.

Result: The context-weighted sampler improves generation quality with negligible computational overhead. The scaled cross-entropy loss reduces generative perplexity by up to 63% on OpenWebText. The approach matches a strong semi-autoregressive block diffusion baseline while retaining arbitrary-order generation capability.

Conclusion: Local context is an important factor in discrete generative modeling, and simple context-aware modifications can significantly improve both sampling and training efficiency in discrete flow matching.

Abstract: Discrete flow matching provides a flexible framework for generative modeling on discrete structures. However, the standard factorized training objective exposes the model to targets of varying difficulty, mixing well-conditioned, predictable tokens with ambiguous, high-entropy ones. We empirically demonstrate that the uncertainty over the value of each token is closely related to the density of available context in its neighborhood. Motivated by this observation, we propose a simple modification to the underlying continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) that incorporates local context information. Our context-weighted sampler improves generation quality with negligible computational overhead, while our scaled cross-entropy loss function reweights the training signal from different tokens and reduces generative perplexity by up to 63% on OpenWebText. Moreover, our approach matches a strong semi-autoregressive block diffusion baseline in quality while retaining the ability to perform generation in any order. These results highlight the role of local context as an important factor in discrete generative modeling and show that simple context-aware modifications can significantly improve both sampling and training efficiency.

</details>


### [328] [Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21453)
*Rajiv Shailesh Chitale,Rahul Madhavan,Taneesh Gupta,Deepanway Ghosal,Aravindan Raghuveer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TTEL is an inference-time algorithm that performs token-level error localization using feedback to truncate erroneous trajectories and reuse valid prefixes, achieving strictly dominating Pareto frontiers and significant token savings (e.g., ~50% fewer tokens than independent sampling) across reasoning and programming benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard inference-time scaling methods (independent sampling, sequential refinement) lack token-level credit assignment, causing computational inefficiency as valid reasoning prefixes are frequently discarded.

Method: TTEL uses fixed or environment feedback to compare conditional probabilities under informed feedback against a null-context baseline, identifying the exact token-level step where an error occurs, then truncates the trajectory and branches a new generation to reuse the valid prefix.

Result: Establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning domains. On LiveCodeBench with Qwen3-8B, TTEL achieves pass@64 of 71.0% with ~360k tokens vs. ~735k tokens for independent sampling. Outperforms baselines on AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025 with both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.

Conclusion: Token-level error localization during inference enables more efficient test-time scaling by reusing valid prefixes, yielding better performance/compute trade-offs than standard methods.

Abstract: Scaling inference-time computation has emerged as a reliable method to improve the performance of large language models on complex reasoning and programming tasks. However, standard approaches such as independent sampling and sequential multi-turn refinement operate without token-level credit assignment, resulting in computational inefficiency, since valid reasoning prefixes are frequently discarded. In this work, we introduce Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization (TTEL), an inference-time algorithm that utilizes fixed or environment feedback to perform token-level error localization. By comparing conditional probabilities under informed feedback against a null-context baseline, TTEL isolates the step at which an error occurred. The algorithm then truncates the trajectory and branches a new generation, maximally reusing the valid prefix. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TTEL establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning domains, measured by pass-at-k vs. generated-token cost. With Qwen3-8B on LiveCodeBench, TTEL attains a pass@64 of 71.0% while generating approximately half as many tokens as independent sampling (360.4k vs. 735.0k). Generalizing to math benchmarks AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, TTEL cleanly outperforms competing test-time baselines across both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.

</details>


### [329] [Error Certificates for KV-Cache Eviction via Randomized Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21475)
*Peng Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Deterministic KV-cache eviction is provably incapable of monitoring its own errors; randomized eviction (Poisson-sampled tails with Hájek-corrected softmax) yields a per-step error certificate with 0.97 empirical coverage at no accuracy cost. On real workloads, the certificate enables attribution (AUC 0.73–0.75) to separate cache-induced from inherent failures, outperforming output confidence (0.47–0.54), but certificate-gated budget escalation shows no benefit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deterministic KV-cache eviction methods delete tokens based on importance scores but cannot detect or bound the attention-output error they introduce, making serving-time error estimation inconsistent. The paper seeks a principled way to make the eviction process self-diagnosing.

Method: Replace deterministic top-k eviction with randomized eviction using Poisson sampling on the tail tokens with known inclusion probabilities. Apply the Hájek (survey-sampling) correction — a single logit offset inside softmax — to debias attention. Use a survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set to produce a per-step error certificate. Evaluate on real workloads with pre-registered claims.

Result: Randomized eviction achieves 0.97 empirical coverage for the error certificate at no accuracy cost. The certificate cleanly separates cache-induced from inherent failures (AUC 0.73–0.75) versus output log-probability (AUC 0.47–0.54). However, certificate-gated budget escalation provides no benefit, and output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate. Three out of seven pre-registered claims were lost.

Conclusion: Randomization buys attribution, not prediction. The certificate is useful for diagnosing failure sources and scheduling recomputation, but not for predicting or dynamically controlling budgets.

Abstract: Deterministic KV-cache eviction keeps the top-$k$ tokens under an importance score and deletes the rest. We prove that this design cannot know what it destroyed: evicted values can be altered so that everything the serving system retains is unchanged while the true attention-output error grows arbitrarily, so no serving-time estimator of that error is consistent. Randomized eviction restores identifiability. With a Poisson-sampled tail at known inclusion probabilities, one logit offset performs the Hájek correction inside the softmax, and a survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set becomes a per-step error certificate with 0.97 empirical coverage at no accuracy cost. On real workloads we pre-registered seven claims and lost three: question-aware eviction at 25--50\% budgets is nearly free; output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate; certificate-gated budget escalation adds nothing. What survives is attribution: the certificate separates cache-induced from inherent failures (AUC 0.73--0.75, against 0.47--0.54 for output confidence) and schedules recomputation better than random or confidence gating. Randomization buys attribution, not prediction.

</details>


### [330] [Finite-Sample Coverage Audits for High-Recall Candidate Generation: Certification and Learning-Theoretic Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21480)
*Martin Anthony,Kaveh Salehzadeh Nobari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies the label complexity of certifying that the number of missed relevant items in a high-recall screening pipeline is small, proving that excluded-pool auditing is minimax optimal and providing a finite-sample toolkit for missed-mass certification, recall conversion, and stress-test certificates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In high-recall screening pipelines, the initial retrieval stage determines which items proceed to downstream tasks. Missed relevant items at this stage are irretrievably lost.
