The paper asks: how many audit labels are needed to certify, with finite-sample validity, that this missed relevant mass is small?

Method: The authors prove a lower bound showing that auditing only within the candidate (included) set cannot certify nontrivial missed-mass bounds, so the excluded pool must be sampled. They establish a matching minimax lower bound: to certify fewer than m missed relevant items with high probability when none exist, the audit must inspect O(N₀/m) excluded-pool labels. They develop finite-sample tools using binomial and hypergeometric inversion (not asymptotic approximations) for certification, recall conversion via two-pool design, family-wise certification of nested candidate generators, and stress-test certificates.

Result: Excluded-pool auditing is minimax rate-optimal for missed-mass certification in the zero-miss regime. The finite-sample toolkit provides exact guarantees without asymptotic approximations, and the certificates pair with observable review burden to select the least burdensome candidate generator meeting a missed-mass target.

Conclusion: All guarantees hold under a fixed pre-specified candidate generator (or family) and audit rule, prior to examining certification labels. The framework enables practical, statistically rigorous certification of recall in high-recall pipelines.

Abstract: An initial high-recall stage in an empirical pipeline decides which items pass to later review, labelling, or modelling, and relevant items it misses are lost to every subsequent stage. We study how many audit labels are needed to certify, with finite-sample validity, that this missed relevant mass is small, and our main results characterise the label complexity of this problem. We first show that no procedure using only labels from inside the candidate set can certify any non-trivial bound on the missed mass: the audit must sample the excluded pool, the only region where unrecovered relevant items can lie. We then prove a matching finite-corpus lower bound. Any valid audit that certifies fewer than $m$ missed relevant items with high probability when none are present, even if adaptive and permitted to label the entire included pool, must inspect on the order of $N_0/m$ excluded-pool labels. Excluded-pool auditing is therefore minimax rate-optimal, not merely convenient, for missed-mass certification in the zero-miss regime. Building on this characterisation, we develop an exact finite-sample toolkit, using binomial and hypergeometric inversion rather than asymptotic approximation, that certifies missed mass, converts it to recall through a two-pool design, certifies pre-specified families of nested candidate generators simultaneously, and produces stress-test certificates against declared perturbation mechanisms. These certificates can be paired with observable review burden to select the least burdensome pre-specified candidate generator meeting a missed-mass target. Every guarantee holds under one discipline: the candidate generator, or the pre-specified family from which it is selected, and the audit rule are fixed before the certification labels are examined.

</details>


### [331] [Compact Latent Coordination for Autonomous Vehicles at Unsignalized Intersections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21488)
*Gil Lifshits,Igal Bilik,Gilad Katz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MAPS is a hierarchical DRL architecture using a centralized Master agent to generate a proto-plan (compact embedding for global coordination) and decentralized Worker agents for vehicle-specific control, achieving collision-free navigation, reduced travel time across 72 intersection configurations, and strong zero-shot generalization from 3 to 5 agents (94% success rate).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unsignalized intersection coordination for autonomous vehicles is challenging for MARL due to combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, and rigid agent designs.

Method: A hierarchical DRL architecture (MAPS) with a centralized Master agent that produces a continuous proto-plan embedding encoding global strategy, and decentralized Worker agents that combine this embedding with local observations for vehicle-specific control, decoupling strategic intent from tactical execution.

Result: MAPS achieves collision-free navigation and significantly reduces average travel time across 72 intersection configurations, outperforming SOTA baselines. Zero-shot generalization from 3 to 5 agents yields 94% success rate.

Conclusion: Proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising framework for multi-vehicle coordination, enabling decoupled strategic and tactical optimization and robust generalization.

Abstract: Coordinating autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections remains a critical challenge for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems, which typically struggle with combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, or rigid agent designs. We propose Master-Agent Proto-plan System (MAPS), a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architecture in which a centralized Master agent generates a compact, continuous embedding, denoted as proto-plan, that encodes a global coordination strategy. Decentralized Worker agents integrate this embedding with local observations to execute vehicle-specific control, decoupling strategic intent from tactical execution and enabling independent optimization of each module.
  As a proof-of-concept evaluation of this coordination mechanism, we test MAPS across 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv. MAPS achieves collision-free navigation while significantly reducing average travel time, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. The learned proto-plans further exhibit robust generalization: a system trained with three agents achieves a 94% success rate when deployed zero-shot to five-agent scenarios, confirming that proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising framework for multi-vehicle coordination.

</details>


### [332] [Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21535)
*Alagappan Valliappan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Speculative decoding with native MTP draft heads becomes inefficient at long contexts because the draft's full attention over the KV cache grows linearly with context. The paper proposes Windowed-MTP, a training-free, drop-in modification that applies a sliding window plus attention sink to the draft only, bounding its KV working set to a constant (~99% KV reduction at 1M). Experiments on Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B show 28-44% per-decode-step cost reduction over native MTP at 1M context on a single GPU, with matched or improved acceptance and no distributional change.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speculative decoding with built-in MTP draft heads is standard in frontier models, but at million-token contexts the draft's full-attention KV read becomes the dominant cost, undermining the benefits of speculation. This problem worsens with deeper drafts and hybrid/linear-attention targets where verification is cheap, exposing the draft's attention overhead.

Method: Apply a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink to the draft's attention only (Windowed-MTP), leaving the target's full-attention verification unchanged. This is training-free, drop-in, and lossless since the target still decides every accepted token. A compact ring buffer reclaims unread draft KV entries.

Result: At 1M context on a single GPU, Windowed-MTP reduces per-decode-step cost by 28-44% across three model families while dropping ~99% of draft KV entries. End-to-end decode latency improves proportionally, and acceptance length is matched or improved. Reclaimed draft KV (7.7-11% of total) incurs no acceptance or quality cost.

Conclusion: Windowing the draft attention in speculative decoding is a simple, effective fix for long-context inefficiency of native MTP heads. It preserves the target's verified output distribution and yields consistent speedups, making speculation practical at million-token contexts.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by having a cheap draft propose tokens that a target verifies in parallel. Frontier models increasingly ship a built-in Multi-Token-Prediction (MTP/NEXTN) draft head under the assumption that the draft is negligibly cheap. At million-token context this breaks: an MTP draft head typically runs full attention over the entire KV cache at every draft step, so its read grows linearly with context and comes to dominate the draft cost -- precisely where speculation is most valuable. The effect compounds with draft length (a deep native draft can turn net-negative, slower than no speculation) and sharpens under hybrid/linear-attention targets, where cheaper verification leaves the draft's full-attention read exposed. We apply a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink to the draft's attention only (Windowed-MTP), leaving full-attention verification intact. It is training-free, drop-in, and lossless by construction: the full-attention target still decides every accepted token, so windowing changes only which tokens are proposed, never which are accepted. It bounds the draft's KV working set to a constant, dropping ~99% of KV entries at 1M. Across three architecture families (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and a Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, windowing cuts the per-decode-step cost over the shipping native MTP draft by +28% to +44%, an input-invariant margin that widens with context. Since per-token latency is this cost divided by acceptance length, at matched acceptance end-to-end decode latency improves by the same amount, and more where windowing also lifts acceptance, while preserving the target's verified output distribution. Finally, the unread draft KV -- 7.7-11% of total KV at 1M -- is reclaimed via a compact ring buffer at no acceptance or quality cost.

</details>


### [333] [Zero-Flow Two-Sample Tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21542)
*Yakun Wang,Leyang Wang,Song Liu,Taiji Suzuki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new two-sample test (ZF2ST) based on zero-flow discrepancy that uses neural networks to learn local misalignment patterns while maintaining valid statistical calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing two-sample tests struggle with structured distributional changes in high-dimensional spaces, and flexible methods like neural networks often compromise statistical calibration (type-I error control).

Method: Proposes zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD) based on the zero-flow criterion, separating witness learning (via regression-based or power-maximized approaches) from hypothesis evaluation to allow flexible neural networks while ensuring valid calibration.

Result: Demonstrates strong testing power on synthetic and image datasets, particularly for structured distributional changes, while maintaining well-calibrated type-I error.

Conclusion: ZF2ST effectively combines neural network flexibility with rigorous statistical testing, offering a practical solution for detecting structured distributional differences.

Abstract: We propose a new approach to two-sample testing for deciding whether two sets of samples are drawn from the same distribution. The test is built on a statistical discrepancy based on the zero-flow criterion, termed zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD). We prove the validity of ZFD and propose a practical testing procedure, termed the zero-flow two-sample test (ZF2ST). The key idea is to learn how samples from the two distributions are locally misaligned and use the resulting directional pattern as evidence of distributional difference. By separating witness learning from hypothesis evaluation, ZF2ST can use flexible neural networks while maintaining valid statistical calibration. We develop both regression-based and power-maximized approaches for learning the witness. Experiments on synthetic and image datasets demonstrate that ZF2ST can achieve strong testing power for structured distributional changes while maintaining well-calibrated type-I error.

</details>


### [334] [X$^3$-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21550)
*Dongjie Fu,Di Cao,Xize Cheng,Zihan Zhang,Wenxu Jia,Yifu Chen,Shengpeng Ji,Yu Zhang,Tao Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: X^3-OPD is a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning abilities from a text-based LLM to an audio-language model using a three-tier symmetric corpus, improving audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality on benchmarks like MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large audio-language models lack deep logical reasoning compared to text-based LLMs due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data.

Method: A cross-modal on-policy distillation framework (X^3-OPD) where the audio-language student generates reasoning trajectories based on its own acoustic perception, and a text teacher provides token-level guidance with matched textual inputs and verified answers. A three-tier symmetric corpus is constructed covering textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning, and spoken-dialogue reasoning with paralinguistic cues.

Result: X^3-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR benchmarks while largely preserving existing capabilities under domain shift.

Conclusion: Cross-modal on-policy distillation effectively bridges the reasoning gap between text and audio-language models, extending reasoning capabilities to non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context beyond textually recoverable content.

Abstract: While large audio-language models have achieved remarkable progress in auditory perception, they still lag behind text-based large language models in deep logical reasoning, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. To bridge this gap, we propose X$^3$-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning capabilities from a powerful text teacher to an audio-language student. During training, the student generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on its own acoustic perception, while the teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. We further construct a three-tier symmetric corpus covering textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning involving paralinguistic cues. This design extends cross-modal distillation beyond textually recoverable content to reasoning grounded in non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context. Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR demonstrate that X$^3$-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving the model's existing capabilities under domain shift.

</details>


### [335] [Graph Learning on Ensembles of Cyclic Peptides: An Investigation of Molecular Ensemble Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21561)
*Aaron Feller,Kris Deibler,Maxim Secor*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EnsembleEGNN is a molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes conformational ensembles of cyclic peptides using equivariant GNNs and set attention, pretrained on CREMP with self-supervised objectives. It outperforms sequence-only BERT baselines (R²=0.477 vs 0.439) and further improves when co-trained with BERT (R²=0.538).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Molecular property prediction typically uses a single representative conformation, ignoring that molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. The authors aim to incorporate ensemble information for better property prediction.

Method: EnsembleEGNN encodes each conformer via shared EGNN layers, then pools representations with a Set Attention Block. Pretrained on CREMP (cyclic peptide ensemble dataset) using masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction as multi-task self-supervised objectives.

Result: Training from scratch fails (R²=0.005). Pretrained model achieves R²=0.477, Pearson r=0.699, outperforming BERT baseline (R²=0.439, r=0.667). Co-training EnsembleEGNN with BERT yields R²=0.538, r=0.737.

Conclusion: Encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction.

Abstract: Molecular property prediction from structure often uses a single representative conformation, even though many molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. We introduce EnsembleEGNN, a molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes an ensemble by first encoding each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers, then pooling the resulting conformer representations with a Set Attention Block. We pretrain the model on CREMP, a cyclic peptide ensemble dataset, using a multi-task self-supervised objective combining masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. On the CREMP-CycPeptMPDB dataset, training EnsembleEGNN from scratch fails entirely ($R^2=0.005$). However, the pretrained model reaches $R^2=0.477$ and Pearson $r=0.699$, outperforming the sequence-only BERT baseline ($R^2=0.439$, Pearson $r=0.667$). When EnsembleEGNN is co-trained end-to-end with the BERT sequence encoder, the hybrid model improves further to $R^2=0.538$ and Pearson $r=0.737$. These results demonstrate that encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction.

</details>


### [336] [Beyond Sufficiency: Time Series Explanation with Counterfactual Necessity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21573)
*Hongnan Ma,Yiwei Shi,Mengyue Yang,Weiru Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TimePNS is a necessity-aware framework for time-series explanation that uses counterfactual interventions to identify subsequences that are both sufficient and necessary for a black-box model's predictions, outperforming sufficiency-only methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing sufficiency-oriented methods can assign high importance to spurious subsequences that support the prediction without being essential to the model's decision, lacking the ability to identify truly necessary temporal factors.

Method: TimePNS adopts a two-stage design: Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask; Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, which supervise a temporal gate that refines the initial explanation by suppressing non-essential components and emphasizing counterfactually necessary ones.

Result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.

Conclusion: TimePNS effectively bridges the gap between sufficiency and necessity in time-series explainability, providing more faithful and causally grounded explanations.

Abstract: Faithful explanations of time-series classifiers should identify subsequences that are not only sufficient to preserve a black-box model's prediction, but also necessary for maintaining it. However, existing sufficiency-oriented methods can assign high importance to spurious subsequences that support the prediction without being essential to the model's decision. We introduce \textbf{TimePNS}, a necessity-aware framework for time-series explanation. Inspired by Pearl's counterfactual notion of necessity, TimePNS assesses whether a temporal factor is necessary by intervening on it and measuring whether the original prediction is disrupted. The framework adopts a two-stage design. Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process together with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, which supervise a temporal gate that refines the initial explanation by suppressing non-essential components and emphasizing counterfactually necessary ones. Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show that TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.

</details>


### [337] [Expanding Flow Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21585)
*Sophia Tang,Pranam Chatterjee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EFlows and EFMs introduce a framework for flow-based generative models that handle variable-dimensional outputs by expanding state spaces through conditional noise augmentation, enabling efficient few-step generation across continuous and discrete modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing flow-based generative models are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths, limiting their applicability to settings where output size is a learnable degree of freedom.

Method: EFlows define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality via an expanding interpolant. EFMs distill this into few-step models using two learnable operations: an expand operator (augments state space conditioned on current state) and a transport map (pushes expanded state forward). Composition yields joint expansion and denoising.

Result: The framework recovers fixed-canvas flows as a special case, extends to discrete simplex for variable-size graph and variable-length sequence generation, and establishes principled handling of variable output dimensionality.

Conclusion: EFlows and EFMs provide a principled framework for flow-based generative modeling where output size is itself a learned, controllable degree of freedom across both continuous and discrete modalities.

Abstract: Flow-based generative models have enabled remarkable progress in fast and controllable generation across continuous and discrete state spaces, yet existing parameterizations are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths. Here, we introduce Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows), which define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality along an expanding interpolant that grows the state by augmenting it with conditional noise. Building on this construction, we propose Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs), a new class of flow maps that distill the expanding interpolant into efficient few-step generative models. Each EFM factors the map between any two timesteps into two learnable operations: an expand operator, which augments the state space with new coordinates or tokens conditioned on the current state, and a transport map, which pushes the expanded state forward along the interpolant. Composing these operators yields a single map that jointly expands and denoises the state, recovering existing fixed-canvas flows and flow maps as the special case in which the expand operator is the identity. We further extend the framework to the discrete simplex, enabling variable-size graph generation and variable-length sequence generation. Across both continuous and discrete modalities, we establish EFlows and EFMs as a principled framework for settings in which output size is itself a learned, controllable degree of freedom.

</details>

### [338] [Verifier-First Evaluation of Agentic LLMs for Infrastructure-as-Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20478)
*Mohamed Jouini*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Study evaluating 7 agentic strategies for Terraform/IaC generation from natural language, finding that iterative refinement with verifier feedback achieves best results (62.9% Qwen 7B, 84.4% GPT-4o pass@1), active retrieval boosts performance from 14% to 45.7%, and most OPA failures are resolvable with visible policy text.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IaC generation from natural language requires satisfying provider schemas, dependency planning, and organizational policy constraints beyond syntactic correctness, motivating systematic evaluation of agentic strategies.

Method: Evaluated 7 agentic strategies on IaC-Eval v2 benchmark (186 AWS/Terraform tasks with Rego v1 policies), using three verifier stages (terraform validate, terraform plan, opa eval) and McNemar's test with Wilson confidence intervals (n=186, alpha=0.05).

Result: (1) Active retrieval via ReAct agents raises pass@1 from 14.0% to 45.7%; (2) Iterative refinement achieves 62.9% (Qwen 7B) and 84.4% (GPT-4o) pass@1; (3) GEPA reflection optimization adds +7.5 pp; (4) SIMBA matches Active RAG without retrieval; (5) 79% of post-refinement OPA failures are information-gap issues.

Conclusion: Verifier feedback and iterative refinement are critical for IaC generation; policy visibility resolves most remaining OPA failures, motivating further exploration of policy-aware generation approaches.

Abstract: Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) generation from natural language requires satisfying provider schemas, dependency planning, and organizational policy constraints, not merely producing syntactically plausible configurations. We present a verifier-first empirical study of seven agentic strategies for Terraform generation evaluated on IaC-Eval v2, a modernized 186-task AWS/Terraform benchmark with Rego v1 intent policies. Our evaluation separates failures into three verifier stages (terraform validate, terraform plan, opa eval) and applies McNemar's test with Wilson confidence intervals on all pairwise comparisons (n=186, alpha=0.05).
  We report five principal findings. (1) Active retrieval via ReAct agents with MCP or ChromaDB-backed RAG raises Qwen2.5-Coder 7B from 14.0% to 45.7% pass@1 (p<0.0001), primarily by reducing VALIDATE_FAIL from 144 to 66 tasks. (2) Iterative refinement with verifier feedback achieves 62.9% (Qwen 7B) and 84.4% (GPT-4o) pass@1, exhibiting binary convergence -- tasks either resolve in one retry or exhaust the budget. (3) GEPA reflective instruction optimization raises the Active RAG baseline by +7.5 pp (p=0.026) using only 80 verifier-guided rollouts, providing evidence that prompt optimizers can improve verifiable IaC generation without weight updates. (4) SIMBA teacher-free demonstration injection achieves performance equivalent to Active RAG (p=1.0) without retrieval infrastructure, but fails to address the dominant SELF_DEFINED_PROPERTY error class (50% of failures). (5) A diagnostic Rego-injection experiment shows that 79% of post-refinement OPA failures are information-gap failures resolvable when policy text is visible (p=0.016), motivating policy

</details>


### [339] [Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation: to Enable More Secure Software Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20933)
*Jesse Phillips,Tracy Hall,Paul Rayson,Mo El-Haj*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a method combining task-specific Transformer models with LLMs via prompt engineering to improve source code summarization, observing gains of 7.8% in BLEU-4 and 5% in other metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Source code summaries are often missing, incomplete, or outdated in software systems, yet they are critical for maintenance and security in the SSDLC. Existing approaches (small Transformers or LLMs) each have drawbacks: Transformers score well on NLG metrics but reward lexical overlap over quality, while LLMs produce semantically rich but lexically divergent summaries that score poorly on standard metrics.

Method: The authors combine task-specific Transformer-generated summaries with LLM-based summarization through prompt engineering. They prompt four LLMs with four different prompt variants, using Transformer outputs as part of the prompts to guide the LLMs toward better summaries.

Result: The proposed "Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation" method yields a 7.8% improvement in BLEU-4 and a 5% improvement in another metric (cut off in abstract).

Conclusion: Combining Transformer-generated summaries in prompts can help LLMs produce better source code summaries, potentially improving software maintainability and security.

Abstract: Neural Source Code Summarisation (NSCS) aims to generate natural language summaries of source code to improve developers' and maintainers' understanding of code. Source code summaries are vital during the maintenance phase of the Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC), as they improve maintainers' understanding of code and help reduce the number of bugs and vulnerabilities in a software system. However, summaries are often missing, incomplete, or outdated in many software systems. Solutions to this problem use small, task-specific Transformer models or code-aware Large Language Models (LLMs). Task-specific Transformer-generated summaries often score well across many natural language generation (NLG) metrics, but these metrics reward lexical overlap rather than summary quality. Conversely, the ability of LLMs to capture semantics and produce high-quality summaries presents an exciting solution to this problem. This is especially relevant given the increased availability of LLMs and improvements in workstation hardware in recent years, which mean that some LLMs can now be run on developers' workstations. However, because of their abstractive nature, LLM-generated code summaries often differ greatly from developer-written summaries in the words and phrases they use, resulting in low scores across NLG metrics. We show how combining these two methods, by using Transformer-generated summaries in prompt engineering, may enable LLMs to create better source code summaries and help software practitioners maintain secure systems. We prompt four LLMs using four different prompts, with a task-specific Transformer used to assist the LLMs within the prompts. We present "Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation", a method through which we observe an improvement of 7.8% in BLEU-4 and 5%.

</details>


### [340] [Maintenance Signals in AI-Assisted GitHub Repositories: Evidence from GenAI Adopters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21079)
*Rikuto Tsuchida,Youmei Fan,Kazumasa Shimari,Raula Gaikovina Kula,Gema Rodríguez-Pérez,Kenichi Matsumoto*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: GenAI adoption in code generation shifts maintenance costs toward verification of generated content, management of external AI dependencies, and validation of AI-specific behavior, as observed through longer README files and issues concerning external dependencies in AI-assisted repositories on GitHub.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether GenAI adoption in code generation shifts effort from coding to documentation, validation, debugging, and maintenance, by studying observable maintenance-cost signals among GenAI adopters on GitHub.

Method: Analyzed 622 GitHub users signaling GenAI adoption, 179 repositories with visible AI-assistance configuration files, 179 matched traditional repositories, and 248 issues from AI-assisted repositories. Compared README structure, URLs, and issue content between AI-assisted and traditional repositories.

Result: AI-assisted repositories contain longer README files with more headers and code blocks but fewer external URLs; issues concerning GenAI technology often involve external dependencies like API rate limits and reliance on GenAI provider APIs.

Conclusion: AI assistance shifts maintenance costs toward verifying generated content, managing external AI dependencies, and validating AI-specific behavior.

Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can reduce code-generation effort, but it may shift work to documentation, validation, debugging, and maintenance. We study observable maintenance-cost signals among GenAI adopters on GitHub by analyzing 622 users who publicly signal adoption, 179 repositories with visible AI-assistance configuration files, 179 matched traditional repositories, and 248 issues created in AI-assisted repositories. AI-assisted repositories span diverse project types and contain longer README files with more headers and code blocks, while traditional repositories contain more external URLs. Issues concerning GenAI technology often involve external dependencies, such as API rate limits and reliance on GenAI provider APIs. These findings suggest that AI assistance shifts maintenance costs toward verifying generated content, managing external AI dependencies, and validating AI-specific behavior.

</details>


### [341] [Improving Communication of Changes in Model-Based Engineering with Model-Independent Change Descriptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21084)
*Philip Ochs,Lars Gesmann,Tobias Pett,Ina Schaefer*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes functions to map formal delta-model changes into model-independent language descriptions, bridging the gap between formal rigor and human interpretability for inter-disciplinary communication in model-based engineering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In model-based engineering, changes made by one discipline's engineer are difficult for engineers from other disciplines to understand. Existing approaches either use informal language (lacking objectivity/standardization) or formal change notions (lacking human interpretability), neither supporting effective inter-disciplinary communication.

Method: The authors propose functions to map formally specified changes (from delta modeling) to model-independent language descriptions. They conduct a mixed-methods evaluation involving: (1) quantitative assessment of technical feasibility via an implementation framework, (2) technical applicability via a case study, and (3) qualitative assessment of plausibility, practical applicability, and extensibility via a user study.

Result: The work demonstrates a promising starting point for automated, model-independent description of changes in model-based engineering projects. The mixed-methods evaluation shows feasibility, applicability, plausibility, and extensibility of the approach.

Conclusion: Mapping formal delta-model changes to model-independent language is a viable approach to bridge formal rigor and human interpretability, enabling better inter-disciplinary communication in model-based engineering.

Abstract: In model-based engineering, inter-disciplinary teams collaborate through models, which change over time for purposes of system development, what makes the proper description of such changes crucial for engineers. However, any change made by the engineer of one discipline will be difficult to understand by the engineers of other disciplines. To overcome this limitation, model-independent change descriptions can be derived instead, which preserve semantics of the changes and do not require model-specific knowledge. The two opposing approaches here are to describe changes using either informal language or formal notions of change. While informal language lacks objectivity and standardisation, formal notions of change lack human interpretability, and thus offering no support for inter-disciplinary communication. In this paper, we propose functions to map formally specified changes, represented in the approach of delta modelling, to change descriptions in model-independent language. In an exhaustive mixed-methods evaluation, we bridge the gap between the theoretical and the practical representation of changes. We quantitatively assess technical feasibility, with an implementation framework, and technical applicability, along a case study; and we qualitatively assess plausibility, practical applicability, and extensibility, in a user study. Our work shows a promising starting point for automated, model-independent description of changes in model-based engineering projects.

</details>


### [342] [Information is all you need: Requirements Engineering Quality Reframed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21319)
*Henning Femmer,Julian Frattini*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a holistic theory of requirements engineering (RE) quality based on information flow, modeling how knowledge particles transfer between roles and artifacts. It demonstrates via simulation why high-quality specifications get bypassed in agile contexts, offering actionable insights for calibrating RE processes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move beyond vague appeals to context in RE quality and provide a formal, coherent theoretical framework that unifies artifact- and process-based perspectives on RE quality through the lens of information transfer.

Method: The authors develop a holistic theory modeling information particles (discrete domain knowledge pieces) transferred between sources (stakeholders) and targets (developers, testers). They conduct an exemplary simulation to test the theory in an agile context.

Result: The simulation illustrates why a high-quality specification can be bypassed in agile contexts, showing that the theory can provide actionable insights for calibrating RE processes to optimize information flow.

Conclusion: The theory can serve as a coherent theoretical framework for understanding success or failure of RE processes and artifacts, with potential for organizational applications and process calibration.

Abstract: To move beyond this vague appeal to context, this vision proposes a novel holistic theory of requirements engineering (RE) quality. This theory models how information particles, i.e., discrete pieces of domain knowledge, are transferred between roles and artifacts. Since the RE process is ultimately an information transfer, holistic RE quality depends on the properties of information flow, i.e., how effectively and efficiently information is transferred from sources (like stakeholders) to targets (like developers and testers), uniting both artifact- and process-based perspectives on RE quality. In an exemplary simulation of the theory we illustrate why a high-quality specification gets bypassed in an agile context, thereby demonstrating that a simulation can provide actionable insights into calibrating the RE process to optimize the information flow. Beyond organizational applications, we envision that the theory can serve as a coherent theoretical framework for understanding the success or failure of RE processes and artifacts.

</details>


### [343] [Teaching Business Process Modeling to Leverage Soft Skills of Computing Students](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21344)
*Maria Istela Cagnin,Rick Kazman,Elisa Yumi Nakagawa*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Teaching business process modeling through an industry-driven, project-based approach helps computing students develop key soft skills (professionalism, initiative, motivation, communication, teamwork), better preparing them for AI-assisted software development.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Organizations rely on software systems for business processes and competitive advantage; computing professionals need to understand these processes to build effective systems. With AI increasing productivity but also job market competitiveness, soft skills are crucial for professionals to secure their positions.

Method: Industry-driven, project-based approach with 53 computing students who actively interacted with stakeholders and modeled organizational business processes; systematic collection of student feedback on soft skills practiced.

Result: Demonstrated that professionalism, initiative, motivation, communication, and teamwork can be leveraged through teaching business process modeling.

Conclusion: Teaching business process modeling is beneficial for future computing professionals as it contributes to preparing their soft skills for the era of AI-assisted software development.

Abstract: Background and Context: Organizations have highly depended on software systems to realize their business processes and achieve strategic business goals and competitive advantage; hence, computing professionals who can understand these processes could more effectively build such systems. At the same time, while Artificial Intelligence (AI) has increased the productivity in developing these and other systems, professionals should be better prepared due to the competitiveness of the job market; thus, soft skills could be an important factor to ensure their position in this market. Objective: This paper aims to analyze and present the impact of teaching business process modeling to leverage key soft skills of future computing professionals. Method and Findings: Our method involved an industry-driven, project-based approach with 53 computing students who actively interacted with stakeholders and modeled the organization's business process. We systematically collected the students' feedback, including the soft skills practiced and demonstrating that professionalism, initiative, motivation, communication, and teamwork can be leveraged. Implications: The main implication of this work for the Computer Science Education research community is to provide evidence that teaching business process modeling subjects is particularly beneficial for future professionals, as it could contribute to preparing them regarding their soft skills for the era of AI-assisted software development.

</details>


### [344] [Toward Federated Cognitive Digital Twins over the Edge-to-Cloud Continuum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21357)
*Alessandra Somma,Alessio Bucaioni*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Federated Cognitive Digital Twin (FCDT) architecture that combines federation (distributed twins) with cognition (semantic reasoning and AI) across the edge-to-cloud continuum to improve scalability, responsiveness, and decision-making in complex distributed Cyber-Physical Systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Digital Twin architectures suffer from centralized/monolithic designs causing scalability, latency, and resilience issues in distributed environments like smart cities, with limited semantic integration and high-level reasoning capabilities. While Federated Digital Twins (FDTs) and Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs) address some issues separately, they are not effectively combined.

Method: The paper proposes a Federated Cognitive Digital Twin (FCDT) architecture that distributes intelligence across the edge-to-cloud continuum using local twins (real-time monitoring, lightweight cognitive capabilities) and global twins (system-level reasoning, simulation, coordination), integrating distributed autonomy with cognitive reasoning.

Result: The proposed FCDT architecture improves scalability, responsiveness, and decision-making in complex distributed Cyber-Physical Systems compared to existing centralized or separately federated/cognitive approaches.

Conclusion: Combining federation and cognition within a unified edge-to-cloud architecture effectively addresses the limitations of current DT designs, offering a more scalable, responsive, and intelligent solution for distributed CPS environments.

Abstract: Digital Twins (DTs) are increasingly adopted to monitor, analyze, and optimize Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) through continuous interaction between physical assets and their digital counterparts. However, current DT architectures often rely on centralized and monolithic designs, leading to scalability, latency, and resilience issues in distributed environment such as smart cities. Moreover, they provide limited support for semantic integration and high-level reasoning, reducing the effectiveness of DT-based decision-making. Recent studies on Federated Digital Twins (FDTs) have addressed scalability by decomposing complex systems into interacting twins, but they still largely centralize intelligence in cloud components. In parallel, Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs) enhance DTs with semantic reasoning, explainability, and AI-driven decision support, yet they are typically difficult to integrate into distributed architectures. This paper proposes a Federated Cognitive Digital Twin (FCDT) architecture that combines federation and cognition within a unified approach. The architecture distributes intelligence across the edge-to-cloud continuum through local twins, which provide real-time monitoring and lightweight cognitive capabilities, and global twins, which perform system-level reasoning, simulation, and coordination. By integrating distributed autonomy with cognitive reasoning, the proposed approach improves scalability, responsiveness, and decision-making in complex distributed CPSs

</details>


### [345] [From Resource Flow to Executable Tests: Petri-Net-Guided LLM Test Generation for Concurrent Stateful Rust APIs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21530)
*Kaiwen Zhang,Guanjun Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a Petri-net-guided methodology for generating executable tests for concurrent stateful Rust APIs, bridging formal scenario design with LLM-based code synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can synthesize Rust tests but often violate API preconditions, remain shallow, or reduce concurrency to sequential traces. Model-based testing provides semantic control but requires substantial handwritten code to concretize abstract scenarios. The paper addresses the gap between formal scenario design and low-cost test concretization.

Method: The method uses colored Petri nets to represent API resources, lifecycle conditions, and causal dependencies. It derives legal deep-state, near-legal, and partial-order concurrent scenarios, using them as a constrained intermediate representation for LLM-based code synthesis. A local-faithfulness contract and structural repair loop preserve modeled intent, while Petri-guided schedule shaping prioritizes high-conflict concurrency skeletons. A layered semantic oracle distinguishes synthesis failures from expected API behavior violations.

Result: The approach enables systematic generation of executable tests for concurrent stateful Rust APIs, covering deep-state scenarios, near-legal boundary conditions, and partial-order concurrent interleavings, with automated concretization via LLMs.

Conclusion: The Petri-net-guided methodology effectively bridges formal scenario design and low-cost test concretization for concurrent stateful Rust APIs, combining the semantic rigor of model-based testing with the automation of LLM-based code synthesis.

Abstract: Concurrent stateful library APIs expose behavior through evolving resource ownership, lifecycle states, and competing interleavings. Large language models can synthesize executable Rust tests, but their outputs often violate API preconditions, remain shallow, or reduce concurrency to accidental sequential traces. Conversely, model-based and systematic testing techniques provide semantic control but commonly require substantial handwritten code to turn abstract scenarios into executable tests. This paper addresses the gap between formal scenario design and low-cost test concretization. We present a Petri-net-guided methodology for test generation over concurrent stateful Rust APIs. The method represents API resources, lifecycle conditions, and causal dependencies as colored tokens and transitions; derives legal deep-state, near-legal, and partial-order concurrent scenarios; and uses these scenarios as a constrained intermediate representation for LLM-based code synthesis. A local-faithfulness contract and structural repair loop preserve the modeled intent during concretization, while Petri-guided schedule shaping prioritizes high-conflict concurrency skeletons for systematic exploration. A layered semantic oracle then distinguishes synthesis failures from violations of the target API's expected behavior.

</details>
